<meta>This page continues the critique of Descartes's laws of motion, arguing that they violate the Law of Continuity by allowing for abrupt, non-geometrical changes in movement.</meta>

<page-num>35</page-num>

retrogression into absolute continuation, which is a great leap from one extreme to the other. In this case, body B ought to turn back a little less, and body C a little more than in the case of equality, from which this case can hardly be distinguished.

There are many other similar incongruities resulting from the Cartesian rules, which a reader applying our principle will easily notice; a similar case that I found in the rules of the *Search after Truth* came from the same source. Malebranche, in a way, admits that there are inconsistencies, but he does not stop believing that the laws of motion, which depend on the good pleasure of God, are regulated by His wisdom. Mathematicians would be almost as surprised to see these kinds of irregularities in nature as they would be to see a parabola to which the properties of an ellipse with an infinitely distant focus might be applied. I believe such inconsistencies will never be encountered in nature. The better nature is known, the more it is found to be geometrical. It is easy to judge from this that these inconsistencies do not actually arise from what Malebranche asserts—namely, the false hypothesis of the perfect hardness of bodies, which I admit is not found in nature. Even if we were to suppose this hardness, regarding it as infinitely fast elasticity, nothing would result from it that could not be perfectly adjusted to the true laws of nature regarding elastic bodies in general; we would never encounter rules as disconnected as those I have criticized. It is true that in composite things, a small change can sometimes produce a massive effect; for example, a spark falling into a large mass of gunpowder is capable of destroying an entire city. But this is not contrary to our principle, and these cases can be explained by general principles. However, regarding elements or simple things, nothing similar could happen; otherwise, nature would not be the result of infinite wisdom.

Thus it is seen (more clearly than what is commonly said) how true physics must actually be derived from the source of divine perfection. It is God who is the ultimate reason for things, and the knowledge of God is no less the principle of the sciences than His essence and His will are the principles of beings. Most reasonable philosophers agree with this, but very few of them can use it to discover important truths.

<meta>This page transitions from the critique of specific laws of motion to a broader philosophical argument for reconciling mechanical physics with the concept of divine purpose (final causes), referencing Socrates’ critique of materialist thinkers.</meta>

<page-num>36</page-num>

Perhaps these modest attempts will inspire others to go much further. It is a way of sanctifying philosophy to make its streams flow from the fountain of God's attributes. Far from excluding *final causes* and the consideration of a being acting with wisdom, it is from there that everything in physics must be derived. This is what Socrates, in Plato's *Phaedo*, has already admirably noted when reasoning against Anaxagoras and other materialist philosophers. These thinkers, after initially recognizing an intelligent principle above matter, do not use it at all when they begin to philosophize about the universe; instead of showing that this intelligence does everything for the best—and that this is the reason for the things it saw fit to produce in accordance with its goals—they try to explain everything by the mere collision of mindless particles, confusing the conditions and instruments with the true cause. It is (as Socrates said) as if, in order to explain why I am sitting in prison awaiting the fatal blow instead of being on my way to the Boeotians or other peoples where it is known I could have escaped, someone were to say it is because I have bones, tendons, and muscles that can be bent as needed for sitting. "Upon my word," he says, "these bones and muscles would not be here, and you would not see me in this position, if my mind had not judged it more honorable for Socrates to suffer what the laws of the country ordain." This passage in Plato deserves to be read in its entirety, for these are very beautiful and sound reflections. Nevertheless, I admit that specific effects in nature can and should be explained mechanically, without forgetting, however, the admirable designs and uses that Providence has seen fit to provide. But the general principles of physics, and even of mechanics itself, depend on the direction of a sovereign intelligence and cannot be explained without taking it into account. In this way, piety must be reconciled with reason, so that good people may be reassured if they fear the results of mechanical or corpuscular philosophy—as if it would lead us away from God and immaterial substances—whereas, with the necessary corrections and a proper understanding, it should actually lead us to Him.

# V.

## LETTER FROM LEIBNITZ TO ARNAULD IN WHICH HE STATES HIS PERSONAL VIEWS ON METAPHYSICS AND PHYSICS. 1690.

->[From the French.]<-

SIR—I am now on the point of returning home after a long journey, undertaken at the command of my prince for the purpose of historical research. In this work, I found certificates, titles, and undeniable proofs sufficient to justify the common origin of the illustrious houses of Brunswick and Este, which Messrs. Justel, du Cange, and others had good reasons to question, because there were contradictions and falsehoods among the historians of Este in this respect, along with a complete confusion of dates and persons. At present, I am thinking of returning and resuming my former way of life. Having written to you two years ago shortly before my departure, I take the same liberty today to inquire about your health and to let you know how the thought of your eminent merit is always present in my mind. 

When I was in Rome, I saw the denunciation of a new heresy attributed to you or your friends. Afterward, I saw a letter from the Reverend Father Mabillon to one of my friends, which stated that Reverend Father Le Tellier's defense of the missionaries against the practical morals of the Jesuits had given many people favorable impressions of those Fathers; however, he had heard that you had replied to it and that it was said you had overthrown that Father’s arguments by geometrical reasoning. All of this leads me to think that you are still in a condition to serve the public, and I pray to God that it may be so for a long time to come. It is true that this is in my own interest, but it is a praiseworthy interest which may give me the means to learn—whether it be in common with all others who shall read your works, or personally, when your judgments shall instruct me—if the limited leisure you have may permit me to hope for that advantage again.

Body is an aggregate of substances, and not, properly speaking, a single substance. Consequently, it must be that everywhere in the body there are found indivisible substances—incapable of being generated and incorruptible—which possess something corresponding to souls. That each substance expresses the entire universe, but one more distinctly than another, especially each regarding certain things and according to its own point of view. That the union of the soul with the body, and also the operation of one substance on another, consists merely in that perfect mutual agreement, expressly established by the order of the first creation, by virtue of which each substance, following its own laws, agrees with what the others require; and the operations of one thus follow or accompany the operation or change of the other. That intelligences or souls capable of reflection and of the knowledge of eternal truths and of God have many privileges that exempt them from the changes of bodies. order of the past, because it conforms to the absolute will of God which is known by the event; but that we must try to render the future—as far as it depends on us—conformable to the presumptive will of God or to his commandments; to "beautify our Sparta" and to labor to do good, without being depressed, however, when success fails, and this in the firm belief that God can find the times most suited for changes for the better. Those who are not satisfied with the order of things cannot boast of loving God as he should be loved. Justice is but the love of the wise person. Love is a universal benevolence which the wise person fulfills according to the measure of reason, for the purpose of obtaining lasting contentment, which consists in a continual advancement toward greater perfection, or at least in the variation of a similar degree of perfection.

As regards physics, it is necessary to understand the nature of force, a thing entirely different from motion, which is something more relative. This force is to be measured by the quantity of effect. There is an absolute force, a directive force, and a respective force. Each of these forces continues in the same degree in the universe, or in each machine not in communication with others, and the two latter forces, taken together, compose the first or absolute force. However, the same quantity of movement is not preserved, since I show that otherwise perpetual motion would be easily discovered, and the effect would be more powerful than its cause.

It was some time ago that I published in the *Leipsic Acta* an essay on physics to find the physical cause of the movements of the stars. I establish as a basis that all movement of a solid in a liquid—taking place in a curved line or where the velocity is continually changing—comes from the movement of the liquid itself; from this, I draw the inference that the stars have conforming but fluid orbits. I have demonstrated an important general proposition, namely: that every body that moves with a circulation which is harmonious (that is, such that while the distances from the center are in arithmetical progression, the velocities are in harmonious progression, or reciprocal to the distances), and which furthermore has a paracentric movement—that is, of gravity or of levity regarding the same center (following a certain law which this attraction or repulsion maintains)—the said body necessarily has areas proportional to the times, just as Kepler observed among the planets. And I will not speak, either, of an entirely new analysis which belongs to geometry and is entirely different from algebra; and still less of some other things for which I have not yet had time to prepare essays. All of this I should like to be able to explain to you in a few words, in order to have your opinion on them—which would be of the greatest use to me—if you had as much leisure as I have deference for your judgment. But your time is too precious, and my letter is already sufficiently long. Therefore I close here, and am, sir,

# VI.

## LETTER ON THE QUESTION OF WHETHER THE ESSENCE OF BODY CONSISTS IN EXTENSION. 1691.

->[From the French.]<-

You ask, sir, for the reasons I have for believing that the idea of body or of matter is different from that of extension. It is true, as you say, that many capable men are today of the opinion that the essence of body consists in length, breadth, and depth. Nevertheless, there are still others—who cannot be accused of too much attachment to scholasticism—who are not satisfied with this opinion.

M. Nicole, in a certain passage in his *Essais*, states that he is one of them, and it seems to him that there is more bias than insight in those who do not appear repelled by the difficulties encountered there.

It would require a very extensive discourse to explain clearly what I think on the subject. However, here are some considerations that I submit to your judgment, and I ask you to make yours known to me.

If the essence of body consisted in extension, this extension alone should be sufficient to account for all the properties of body. But this is not so. We notice in matter a quality, called by some *natural inertia*, by which a body resists movement in a certain way; so that it is necessary to employ some force to set it in motion (even when setting aside the consideration of weight), and a large body is moved with more difficulty than a small body. For example:

<image-desc>A geometric diagram labeled FIG. I. consisting of a circle marked A and a square marked B.</image-desc>

->FIG. I.<-

If body A, in motion, encounters body B, at rest, it is evident that if body B were indifferent to motion or to rest, it would allow itself to be pushed by body A without resisting it, and without decreasing the velocity or changing the direction of body A; and after their meeting, A would continue its path and B would go along with it, preceding it. But it is not like this in nature. The

<summary>Leibniz argues that the essence of matter is not merely extension (spatial dimensions) because bodies possess "natural inertia," a quality that causes them to resist motion. He illustrates this with a thought experiment where a moving body's velocity is decreased when it strikes a resting body.</summary>
<keywords>essence of body, extension, natural inertia, matter, motion, M. Nicole, physics, Leibniz</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Leibniz's argument from the previous page, where he suggests that if matter were only extension, a moving body would not lose speed upon impact with a stationary body.</meta>

the larger body B is, the more it will decrease the velocity with which body A moves, even to the point of forcing it to move backward if B is much larger than A. Now *if there were nothing in bodies but extension, or position*—that is, what geometricians recognize in them, joined to the single notion of change—this extension would be entirely indifferent to this change. The results of the collision of bodies would be explained by the mere geometric composition of movements; that is to say, after the collision, the body would move forward with a motion composed of the impetus it had before the impact and the motion it received from the other body so as not to hinder it. That is, in this case of collision, it would proceed with the difference between the two velocities and in that same direction.

Just as the velocity of 2A 3A, or 2B 3B, in Figure II, is the difference between 1A 2A and 1B 2B; and in the *case of contact*, Figure III, when the

In particular, as I said at the beginning, the body in motion would carry forward the one at rest without suffering any reduction of its speed, regardless of whether the size, equality, or inequality of the two bodies changed in any respect—a thing utterly irreconcilable with experience. And even if we were to suppose that size should cause a change in the motion, we would have no principle for determining the means of estimating it in detail, or for knowing the

<summary>Leibniz argues that the observable laws of motion and inertia cannot be explained if matter is defined solely by geometric extension. He demonstrates that a purely geometric model would wrongly predict that a moving body loses no velocity when colliding with a stationary one.</summary>

--- Page 57 ---
<meta>This page continues Leibniz’s critique of the purely geometric view of matter, arguing that the principles of motion and the nature of "substance" require metaphysical concepts like force and action.</meta>

resulting direction and velocity. In any case, we should lean toward the opinion of the conservation of motion; however, I believe that I have proved that the same force is preserved, and that its quantity is different from the quantity of motion.

All this shows that there is in matter something other than what is purely geometrical—that is, other than extension and its change, pure and simple. And when we consider it well, we perceive that there must be joined to it some higher or metaphysical notion, namely: that of substance, action, and force. These notions show that everything that is acted upon must act in return, and everything that acts must experience some reaction. Consequently, a body at rest cannot be carried along by another in motion without changing something of the direction and the velocity of the acting body.

I agree that naturally every body is extended, and that there is no extension without body. Nevertheless, the notions of place, of space, and of pure extension must not be confused with the notion of substance, which, besides extension, includes resistance—that is, action and passion.

This consideration seems to me important, not only to understand the nature of extended substance, but also to avoid neglecting higher and immaterial principles in physics, which would be to the detriment of piety. For although I am persuaded that everything takes place mechanically in physical nature, I also continue to believe that even the principles of mechanics—that is, the first laws of motion—have a more exalted origin than what pure mathematics can provide. I imagine that if this were better known or more considered, many pious persons would not have such a poor opinion of corpuscular philosophy, and modern philosophers would better combine the knowledge of nature with the knowledge of its Author.

I will not elaborate on other reasons concerning the nature of body, for that would lead me too far afield.

*To prove that the nature of the body does not consist in extension, I made use of an argument explained in the* Journal des Savans *of June 18, 1691, the gist of which is that we cannot explain by mere extension the* natural inertia *of bodies; that is, that which*

<summary>Leibniz argues that matter consists of more than just geometric extension, requiring metaphysical concepts like force and substance to explain the laws of motion. He suggests that recognizing these immaterial principles can reconcile mechanical philosophy with religious piety.</summary>
<keywords>Leibniz, conservation of force, metaphysical substance, action and passion, corpuscular philosophy, natural inertia, mechanics vs mathematics</keywords>

--- Page 58 ---
<meta>This page continues Leibniz's argument that matter cannot be defined by extension alone, as the laws of physics require the metaphysical concepts of force and substance to explain resistance and motion.</meta>

causes matter to resist movement—or, in other words, that which ensures a body already in motion cannot carry along another at rest without being slowed down by it. Because extension itself is indifferent to movement or rest, nothing should prevent the two bodies from moving together at the full velocity of the first, which it attempts to impart to the second. To this, an answer was made in the *Journal* of July 16th of that same year (which I learned about only recently): that *a body should indeed be indifferent to movement or rest, assuming its essence consists only of being extended*; however, a body pushing another must still be slowed down by it (not due to extension, but due to force), because the same force previously applied to one body is now applied to both.

Now, the force that moves one of the bodies at a certain velocity must move the two together at a lower velocity. It is as if it were said in other words that if a body consisted only of extension, it should be indifferent to motion; but since in reality it is not indifferent—as it resists what should give it motion—it is necessary to use the concept of *force* in addition to that of *extension*. Thus, this reply concedes exactly what I intend. And in truth, those who favor the system of *Occasional Causes* have already clearly seen that force and the laws of motion depending on it cannot be derived from extension alone. Since they assumed that matter consists only of extension, they were forced to deny it force and action, instead having recourse to the general cause: the pure will and action of God. Regarding this, it can be said that they reasoned very well *ex hypothesi* <note>according to the hypothesis</note>. But the hypothesis has not yet been proven; and since the conclusion does not seem to align with physics, it is more probable that the hypothesis is mistaken (which also involves many other difficulties). We must recognize something in matter beyond mere extension; for extension, like space, is incapable of action or resistance, which belong only to substances.

Those who claim that extension itself is a substance reverse the order of words as well as of thought. Beyond extension, there must be a subject that is extended—that is, a substance that is repeated or continued. For *extension* signifies only a repetition or continued multiplication of what is extended;

### VII.

## OBSERVATIONS ON DESCARTES' *Principles of Philosophy*. 1692.

->[From the Latin.]<-

ON ARTICLE 1. Regarding Descartes' statement that we must doubt everything in which there is the smallest uncertainty, it would be better to express it through this superior and more descriptive rule: We ought to consider what degree of acceptance or dissent everything deserves; or more simply, We ought to investigate the reasons for any dogma. In this way, the Cartesian disputes regarding doubt would end. But perhaps the author preferred <term>παραδοξολογεῖν</term> <note>to speak paradoxically</note> in order to wake the indifferent reader with something new. Yet I wish he himself had remembered his own rule, or rather, that he had understood its true power. We can best explain this and its application by using the example of mathematicians. They agree that there are axioms or postulates upon which all other things rest. We admit these because they immediately satisfy the mind and because they are confirmed by countless examples; nevertheless, it would be important for the perfection of science to demonstrate them. This is what Apollonius and Proclus attempted in ancient times, and recently Roberval <note>Gilles de Roberval (1602–1675), a French mathematician</note>, among others, has attempted. And certainly, just as Euclid wished to prove that two sides of a triangle, when added together, are greater than the third (as a certain ancient writer jestingly said, even donkeys know enough to head toward their food in a straight line rather than a detour), because he truly wished that geometrical truths should rest on logical reasons rather than sensory images; so he also could have demonstrated that two straight lines (which do not meet if extended) can have only one common point, if he had possessed a good definition of straightness. I know that the demonstration of axioms is of great use to a true analysis or art of discovery. Thus, if Descartes had wished to follow what is best in his own rule, he ought to have worked toward demonstrating the principles of the sciences, and to have done in philosophy what Proclus wished to do in geometry, where it is actually less necessary. But it seemed better to our author to seek applause rather than certainty. Nor would I blame him for being content with

<summary>Leibniz critiques Descartes' method of universal doubt, suggesting instead that we should evaluate the degree of evidence for our beliefs. He argues that philosophical principles should be demonstrated with the same rigor that mathematicians like Euclid used for geometric axioms to truly advance the art of discovery.</summary>
<keywords>Descartes, Principles of Philosophy, doubt, axioms, geometry, Euclid, Apollonius, Proclus, Roberval, demonstration, analysis</keywords>

--- Page 61 ---
<meta>This page continues Leibniz's critique of Descartes' *Principles of Philosophy*, specifically contrasting Descartes' method of doubt with the practical use of axioms in geometry.</meta>

probability, if he had not aroused our minds by such a great profession of strictness. But I blame Euclid much less when he makes assumptions without proof, for he maintained that we know that if a few hypotheses are admitted, all else is sure and thus equal to them in trustworthiness. If Descartes or other philosophers had done something similar to this, we would not be troubled. And the skeptics also, who condemn the sciences on the pretext that they use principles not immediately demonstrated, ought to regard this as said to them. I, on the contrary, hold that the geometers ought rather to be praised because they prop up the sciences by these, as it were, pegs, and devise an art of proceeding and of deducing many things from few; for if they had wished to defer the invention of theorems or problems until all axioms or postulates had been demonstrated, we should perhaps today have no geometry.

On Article 2. For the rest, I do not see what use there is in considering doubtful things as false. This would not be to cast aside prejudices, but to change them. But if fiction is understood in this way, it must not be abused—as, for example, when later on in Article 8 a <term>paralogism</term> <note>a piece of illogical or fallacious reasoning</note> will seem to arise when the distinction of the mind from the body is discussed.

On Article 4. Moreover, we can neither know nor should we desire anything from sensory things other than that they harmonize as well among themselves as with indubitable reasons, and in such a way that future things may, to a certain degree, be foreseen from past things. Any other truth or reality will be sought in them in vain than that which this consistency vouches for; nor should skeptics ask for anything else, nor the dogmatists promise it.

On Article 5. We cannot otherwise doubt mathematical demonstrations except as error may be feared in the calculations of arithmeticians. This cannot be remedied except by examining the calculations often, or by different calculations, with confirming proofs being added. This weakness of the human mind, arising from a lack of attention and of memory, cannot be perfectly removed, and what is adduced by Descartes as a remedy is useless. The same thing suffices as a guarantee in other departments which suffices in mathematics; indeed, all reasoning, even the Cartesian, however proved or accurate, will yet be subject to this doubt, whatever may finally be thought of any powerful deceptive genius or of the difference between sleep and wakefulness.

<summary>Leibniz critiques Descartes' method of treating doubtful things as false, arguing instead for the practical necessity of unproven axioms as seen in Euclidean geometry. He also asserts that mathematical and sensory certainty relies on internal consistency and repeated verification rather than Descartes' philosophical remedies for human fallibility.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the author's critical commentary on Descartes' *Principles of Philosophy*, moving from a discussion of doubt and sensory consistency to the nature of free will, primary truths, and the distinction between mind and body.</meta>

# ON ARTICLE 6. 
We have free will not in our thinking, but in our acting. It is not within my will whether honey shall seem sweet or bitter; neither is it in the power of my will whether a theorem proposed to me shall seem true or false. Rather, it is a matter of consciousness alone to perceive what seems to be the case. Whoever has affirmed anything is conscious of either a present feeling or reason, or at least of a present memory renewing a past feeling or a perception of a past reason; although we are often deceived in this by a failure of memory or a lack of attention. But consciousness of anything, whether present or past, assuredly does not belong to our will. We know that this one thing is in the power of our faculty of will: namely, that it may command attention and diligence. Thus, although it may not directly create an opinion in us, it can nevertheless indirectly contribute to it. So it happens that men often finally believe that what they wish for is true, after they have accustomed the mind to attending most of all to those things which favor it. In this way, they bring it about that the belief satisfies not only the will but also consciousness. Cf. Art. 31.

# ON ARTICLE 7. 
*I think, therefore I am* is well remarked by Descartes to be among the first truths. But it was only fair that he should not neglect others equal to this. In general, therefore, it may be said: Truths are either of fact or of reason. The first of the truths of reason is, as Aristotle rightly observed, the principle of contradiction or, what amounts to the same thing, the principle of identity. First truths of fact are as numerous as immediate perceptions, or those of consciousness, so to speak. Moreover, I am not only conscious of my thinking but also of my thoughts. It is no more certain that I think than that this or that is thought by me. Thus, first truths of fact may be conveniently referred to these two: *I think*, and *Various things are thought by me*. From this, it follows not only that I am, but also that I am affected in various ways.

# ON ARTICLE 8. 
This is not valid: “I am able to assume or imagine that no corporeal things exist, but I am not able to imagine that I do not exist or that I do not think; therefore I am not corporeal, nor is thought a mode of body.” And I marvel that such an able man could attribute so much weight to such a flimsy <term>sophism</term>; certainly he adds nothing more in this article. What he brings forward in his *Meditations* will be examined in its proper place. He who thinks that the mind is corporeal will not admit that you can affirm

...that no corporeal things exist; but he will admit this: that you can doubt (as long as you are ignorant of the nature of the mind) whether corporeal things exist or do not exist. Since, nevertheless, you see clearly that your mind does exist, he will concede that only this one thing follows: namely, that you can doubt whether the mind is corporeal. Nor will anything further be extracted from this argument by any amount of twisting. But this provided an opening for the paralogism (fallacious reasoning) in Article 2 above, where the liberty was assumed of rejecting what is doubted as if it were false—as if it were permissible to assume that there are no corporeal things simply because it can be doubted whether they exist, which ought not to be conceded. It would be otherwise if we knew the nature of the mind as perfectly as we know its existence; for then, whatever did not appear in it, it would be agreed was not in it.

# ON ARTICLE 13. 
I have already remarked, regarding Article 5, that the errors which may arise from a lack of memory or attention—and which occur also in arithmetical calculations (even after a perfect method has been found, as with numbers)—are recounted here to no purpose. No art can be devised in which such errors are not to be feared, especially when the reasoning must be long and drawn out; therefore, we must have recourse to re-examinations. As for the rest, God seems to be summoned here for a sort of show or pomp. Not to mention that the strange fiction or doubt—whether we are not made to err even in the most evident matters—ought to move no one, since the nature of evidence is against it and the experiences and successes of all life are contrary to it. 

And if ever this doubt could justly be raised, it would be absolutely insuperable; it would confront even Descartes himself and everyone else, even when presenting the most evident things. I say this, not to mention that it must be recognized that this doubt is not established by denying God, nor removed by introducing him. For even if there were no God, provided it were possible for us to continue to exist, there would be no reason for our being less capable of truth; and although it is conceded that there is a God, it does not therefore follow that a creature who is exceedingly fallible and imperfect does not exist—especially since it may be that its imperfection is not native, but perhaps brought on by a great sin, as Christian theologians teach concerning original sin, yet in such a way that this sin cannot be imputed to God. Moreover, although God does not seem to be here aptly in-

...introduced, I think, nevertheless, but in a different way, that true knowledge of God is the principle of higher wisdom; for God is no less the first cause than the ultimate reason of things; nor are things known better than by their causes and reasons.

# ON ARTICLE 14. 
The argument for the existence of God drawn from the very notion of Him was first discovered and stated—so far as is known—by Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, in his surviving work *Liber contra Insipientem*. It was examined here and there by the writers of scholastic theology and by Aquinas himself, from whom Descartes (not without studying it) seems to have borrowed it. This reasoning possesses some beauty but is nevertheless imperfect. 

The argument amounts to this: whatever may be demonstrated from the notion of a thing can be attributed to that thing. Now, from the notion of the most perfect or greatest being, existence can be demonstrated. Therefore, existence can be attributed to the most perfect being (God); or, God exists. The assumption is proved thus: the most perfect or greatest being includes all perfections; therefore, it also includes existence, which undoubtedly is among the perfections, since to exist is more or greater than not to exist. This is the extent of the argument. 

But if "perfection" or "magnitude" had been omitted, the argument might have been constructed even more strictly and concisely in this way: A "necessary being" exists (or a being whose essence includes existence, or a being who exists by its own nature), as is evident from the terms. Now, God is such a being (from the definition of God); therefore, God exists. 

These arguments are valid, provided it is admitted that a most perfect or necessary being is possible and does not imply a contradiction—or, what is the same thing, that the essence from which existence follows is possible. But as long as this has not been demonstrated, it certainly should not be thought that the existence of God has been perfectly demonstrated by such an argument. And generally, it should be known (as I have previously urged) that nothing can be safely inferred from a definition concerning the thing defined as long as it is not established that the definition expresses something possible. For if, by chance, it implies some hidden contradiction, it might happen that something absurd would be deduced from it. Meanwhile, from this argument, we become acquainted with this wonderful privilege of the divine nature: that, provided it is possible, it exists by itself—a condition which is not sufficient for proving the existence of other things.

<summary>The author critiques the Ontological Argument for God's existence, originally proposed by Anselm and adopted by Descartes, arguing it is logically incomplete unless the possibility of a "most perfect being" is first proven. He concludes that while the argument shows God must exist if He is possible, a definition alone cannot prove existence without establishing that the definition is not self-contradictory.</summary>

Meanwhile, the existence of that which lacks only the proof of possibility is accepted with great faith. As for the rest, the fact that some necessary thing exists is evident from the fact that contingent things exist.

**ON ARTICLE 18.** We have an idea of a most perfect being, and therefore the cause of this idea (that is, the most perfect being) exists. This, which is Descartes’ second argument, is even more doubtful than the possibility of God. It is also denied by many of those who zealously acknowledge that God is not only possible but that he actually exists. Nor is it true—as I remember Descartes saying somewhere—that whenever we speak of something and understand what we say, we possess an idea of that thing. For it often happens that we combine incompatible concepts, as when we think of *quickest motion*. This is admitted to be impossible and therefore lacks an idea; nevertheless, we admit that we speak of this with understanding. Indeed, I have explained elsewhere that we often think only confusedly about what we are speaking of, and we are not conscious of an idea existing in our mind unless we understand the thing and analyze it sufficiently.

**ON ARTICLE 20.** The third argument is burdened with this same flaw, as well as others, since it assumes that the idea of God's highest perfection is within us, and from this, it concludes that God exists because we, who possess this idea, exist.

**ON ARTICLE 21.** From the fact that we exist now, it follows that we shall continue to exist hereafter, unless a reason for change exists. Thus, unless it were established elsewhere that we could not even exist except by the favor of God, nothing would be proved for the existence of God from our duration—as if, indeed, one part of this duration could be entirely independent of the other, which is not to be admitted.

**ON ARTICLE 26.** Although we are finite, we may nevertheless know many things concerning the infinite—such as asymptotic lines, or those lines which, when produced *ad infinitum*, always approach but never meet; or concerning infinite spaces whose area is no greater than a finite measure; or concerning the final members of infinite series. Otherwise, we would know nothing certain concerning God either. Moreover, it is one thing to know something of a

**ON ARTICLE 28.** Regarding what pertains to the ends which God set for himself, I clearly think both that those goals of God are to be known and investigated with great benefit, and that contempt for this inquiry is not free from danger or suspicion. **ON ARTICLES 31, 35.** I do not admit that errors depend more upon the will than upon the intellect. To believe that what is false is true, or what is true is false, when this could be known by investigating, is to err. Similarly, through consciousness or memory, certain perceptions or reasons arise, and therefore they do not depend on the will—except insofar as it may happen in some indirect way (and sometimes unknown to us) that we seem to ourselves to see the things we want to see. (Cf. Article 6). We judge, therefore, not because we will it, but because it appears so to us. As for the saying that the will is broader than the intellect, this is more impressive-sounding than it is true; in a word, I might say it is but window-dressing for the public. We will nothing unless it appears so to the intellect. The origin of all errors is the same as the cause observed for calculation errors among mathematicians. For it often happens, due to a lack of attention or memory, that we do what we should not do, or leave undone what we should do, or think that we have done what we have not, or think that we have not done what we have. Thus it happens that in calculations (to which reasoning in the mind corresponds) the correct figures are not recorded, wrong ones are put down, something is overlooked among the things that ought to be taken into account, and the method is disrupted. ...distracted, it does not, for its present operations, sufficiently attend to the matter; or, by an error of memory, it assumes something was previously proved which only stays with us deeply because it has been frequently repeated, steadily observed, or eagerly desired. The remedy for our errors is the same as the remedy for errors in calculation: namely, that we attend to both the matter and the form, that we proceed slowly, that we repeat and vary the process, that we establish examinations or proofs, that we divide longer reasonings into parts (allowing the mind a chance to breathe), and that we confirm each part, as far as possible, with specific proofs. 

And since we must sometimes act in a hurry, the most important thing is to have acquired presence of mind through habit—just as those who, in the midst of chaos and even without writing or calculations, are still able to compute large numbers. In this way, the mind is not easily distracted by the external senses or by its own imaginations or emotions, but instead always rises above what it is doing and retains the power of observation, or, as we commonly say, of turning itself back upon itself. Thus, in the moment, it may say to itself, acting as its own advisor: "See what you are doing; tell yourself why you are here; the hour is passing." 

The Germans admirably call this *sich begreiffen*; the French, no less fortunately, call it *s'aviser*, as if one were to warn oneself or suggest things to oneself—just as the <term>nomenclators</term> suggested to Roman candidates the names and merits of citizens worthy of selection, or as a prompter suggests the opening words of a scene to an actor, or as a certain youth reminded Philip, king of Macedon: "Remember you are mortal." 

But this turning of the mind, *s'aviser*, is not within our power or the choice of our will; on the contrary, it must first occur to the intellect, and it depends on our current degree of perfection. It is the role of the will to strive beforehand with zeal to ensure the mind is well-prepared. This is effectively done both by considering the experiences, losses, or dangers of others, and by using our own—though the latter (while permissible) comes at the risk of losing time or suffering at least a slight or trivial injury. At the same time, we must accustom the mind to a certain order and method of thinking so that, later, it may occur to us when needed as if it were voluntary. Nevertheless, there are errors that escape us or are not avoided through no fault of our own, where we are in trouble not because of a failure of judgment, but because of a lack of memory...

<summary>The author argues that human error arises from a lack of attention or memory and can be corrected by slow, methodical reasoning and the cultivation of presence of mind. This self-reflective awareness (s'aviser) must be developed through habit and the will's preparation of the intellect.</summary>

### ON ARTICLE 37.
The highest perfection of man is not so much that he acts freely as it is that he acts with reason; or rather, both are the same, since the freer one is, the less the use of reason is disturbed by the violence of the emotions.

### ON ARTICLE 39.
To ask whether there is liberty in our will is the same as to ask whether choice is in our will. Free and voluntary mean the same thing. For "free" is the same as "spontaneous with reason"; and "to will" is to be moved to action by a reason perceived by the intellect. Moreover, the more unconditional the reason is, and the less the impulse contains of bare and confused perception mixed within it, the freer the action is. To abstain from judgments does not belong to our will but to the intellect, which suggests some attention to itself, as has been already said regarding Article 35.

### ON ARTICLE 40.
If anyone, thinking that God has preordained all things and yet that he himself is free, and finding that his arguments exhibit conflict among themselves, makes only this one reply (as Descartes instructs)—namely, that his mind is finite and cannot comprehend such things—he seems to me to reply to the conclusion, not to the argument, and to cut the knot rather than untie it. The question is not whether you comprehend the thing itself, but rather whether you fail to comprehend your own absurdity when I point it out. There must certainly be no contradiction in the mysteries of faith, any more than in the mysteries of nature. Therefore, if you wish to excel as a philosopher, it is necessary that you take up the argument which one of your opponents infers with some appearance of truth from your assertions, and point out the defect in it; this can assuredly always be done, unless you have erred.

The rules of Aristotle and the geometers are better, namely: that we should admit nothing—with the exception, of course, of principles (that is, first truths and hypotheses)—unless it is proved by a legitimate argument. By "legitimate," I mean an argument burdened neither with a defect of form nor of matter. It is a defect of matter if anything is assumed except for principles or, again, things already proved from principles by legitimate argument. However, I understand the "right form" to be not only the common syllogistic form, but also any other previously demonstrated form that concludes by the force of its own structure. This includes the forms of the operations used by arithmeticians and algebraists, the forms used by bookkeepers, and indeed, to some degree, the forms of judicial processes; for occasionally we are content to proceed with a certain degree of resemblance. ### ON ARTICLES 47, 48.

Furthermore, the majority of those he does name are not actually simple. This is an investigation of greater importance than is generally thought.

We must take special care to demonstrate truths that are entirely simple—but which are nevertheless not accepted because of people's preconceived opinions—by using even simpler truths.

### On Article 52.
I admit that there is one principle of substance and one attribute of it that expresses its essence; however, I do not know whether it can be explained in just a few words, such that once you understand <term>individual substance</term>, other kinds of substances can be explained through definitions. But I see it asserted with great confidence by many—though it is never proved—that extension constitutes the common nature of <term>corporeal substance</term>. Certainly, neither motion, nor action, nor resistance, nor passivity is derived from it; nor do the laws of nature observed in the motion and interaction of bodies come from the mere notion of extension, as I have shown elsewhere. Indeed, the notion of extension is not primitive but can be analyzed further. For extension requires that there be a whole *continuum* in which many things exist simultaneously. Furthermore, extension—the notion of which is relative—requires something that is extended or continued. For example, in milk, that thing is whiteness; in a body, it is the very thing that constitutes its essence. Extension is the repetition of this underlying quality (whatever it may be). And I certainly agree with Huygens (whose opinion in natural philosophy and mathematics carries great weight with me) that the concept of an empty space and of mere extension is the same. In my opinion, neither mobility itself nor ἀντιτυπία <note>antitypia: resistance to penetration or impenetrability</note> can be understood from mere extension, but rather from the subject of extension, which not only establishes a place but also fills it.

### On Article 54.
I do not recall it having been perfectly demonstrated yet—either by our author or by his followers—that <term>thinking substance</term> lacks extension, or that extended substance lacks thought; thus, it is not evident that one attribute is not required for the other in the same subject, nor indeed that they can coexist. Nor is this surprising; for the author of the book *The Search After Truth* (which contains some excellent points) correctly remarks that the Cartesians offer no distinct notion of thought. Thus, it is not strange if they are unclear about what is involved in it.

### On Article 63.

### On Articles 65 to 68.
Descartes performed a useful service, following the ancients, in eradicating the prejudice by which we regard heat, color, and other phenomena as something existing outside of us. It is evident that what seemed very hot is soon felt by the same hand to be lukewarm; and he who observes a green color in a powdered mixture, when his eye is presently aided <note>likely by a magnifying lens or microscope</note>, no longer perceives a green color but a mixture of yellow and blue. With better equipment, other experiences, or further reasoning, the causes of these two might also be perceived. From this, it appears that no such thing exists outside of us, the <term>phantasm</term> <note>a mental image or illusion</note> of which hovers before our imagination. We are usually like boys who are convinced that a pot of gold is to be found at the very end of the rainbow where it touches the earth, which they try in vain to find by running.

### On Articles 71 to 74.

For the prejudices of infancy involve unproven assertions. Furthermore, fatigue lessens attention; and the ambiguity of words belongs to the abuse of signs and creates an error in form. Thus, it is as if (as the German proverb says) "X" were put in place of "V" in a calculation, or as if a quack doctor, in a prescribed formula, should select <term>sandarach</term> <note>a resin from the sandarac tree</note> instead of <term>dragon’s blood</term> <note>a bright red resin used as a pigment or medicine</note>.

## ON PART II.

**ON ARTICLE 1.** The argument by which Descartes seeks to demonstrate that material things exist is weak; it would therefore be better not to try. The essence of the argument is this: The reason why we believe in material things is external to us, and hence comes either from God, or from another source, or from the things themselves. It is not from God, for if no things existed, He would be a deceiver; it is not from another source (this he has forgotten to prove); therefore, it is from the things themselves, and thus they themselves exist. It might be replied that a sensation may come from something other than God, who—just as He permits all other evils for certain significant reasons—might also permit this deception of us without having the character of a deceiver, especially since it is accompanied by no harm, for it would actually be unpleasant for us not to be deceived. Besides, the deception within this argument, which the argument conceals, is that it may be that the perceptions are from God or from another source, but the judgment (concerning the cause of the sensation, whether it is from a real object outside of us)—and therefore the deception—comes from ourselves. This is just what happens when colors and other things of this sort are considered to be real objects. Moreover, souls might have deserved, through previous sins, to lead this life full of deception where they grasp at shadows instead of things; the Platonists do not seem to be opposed to this view, to whom this life seemed as

**ON ARTICLE 4.** That body consists in extension alone is something Descartes tries to demonstrate by listing the other attributes which he removes, but it ought to have been shown that the list is sufficient. Furthermore, not all attributes are properly removed; certainly those who admit atoms—that is, bodies of the greatest hardness—denied that hardness consists in this: namely, that the body does not yield to the motion of the hands, but rather in this: that it preserves its form. And those who place the essence of body in <note>ἀντιτυπία (*antitypia*): resistance to touch, or impenetrability</note>, or impenetrability, do not derive its notion from our hands or senses, but from the fact that it does not give place to another homogeneous body unless it itself can go elsewhere. Just as if we imagine that against a cube there run six other cubes precisely similar to and resembling the first, so that each one of them with one of its sides accurately coincides with one side of the intercepting cube; on this supposition, it would be impossible for either the intercepting cube itself or a part of it to be moved, whether it be understood as flexible or as rigid. But if that middle cube be held to be penetrable extension or empty space, then the six meeting cubes will oppose their angles to each other mutually; if, however, they are flexible, nothing will prevent the middle parts of these from breaking into the intercepting cubical space. From this we also understand what the difference is between hardness, which belongs to certain bodies, and impenetrability, which belongs to all; Descartes ought to have remembered this latter quality no less than hardness.

**ON ARTICLES 5, 6, 7.** Descartes has excellently explained that rarefaction and condensation—such as we perceive by the senses—may take place although neither an interspersed vacuum nor a change of dimensions of the same part of matter be admitted.

**ON ARTICLES 8 TO 19.** Quite a few of those who defend a vacuum consider space as a substance, nor can they be refuted by the Cartesian arguments; other principles are needed to end this dispute. They will admit that quantity and number do not exist outside of the things to which they are attributed, but they will deny that space or place is the quantity of a body; they will rather believe that space has quantity or capacity, and that a body is equal to it in content. Descartes had to show that internal space or place does not differ from the substance of a body. Those who disagree will

Hence, if motion consists of nothing but this relative change, it follows that nature provides no reason why motion must be attributed to one thing rather than to others. The consequence of this would be that there is no real motion. Therefore, for an object to be said to move, we require not only that it change its position relative to others, but also that the cause of the change—the force or action—resides within the object itself.

**ON ARTICLE 45.** Before I begin to examine the specific laws of motion set down by our author, I will provide a general criterion—a touchstone, as it were—by which they may be judged; I am accustomed to calling this the *law of continuity*. I recently explained it elsewhere, but it must be repeated and expanded upon here. Certainly, when two hypotheses or two different sets of data continuously approach each other until one eventually merges into the other, it must also be that the *quæsita aut eventa* <note>the outcomes sought or results</note> of both also continuously approach one another, and finally, one vanishes into the other, and vice versa. This occurs with ellipses: if one focus remains stationary while the other focus moves further and further away, the resulting new ellipses will continuously approach a parabola and finally merge completely into it, since the distance of the receding focus will have become immeasurable. Consequently, the properties of these ellipses will more and more closely resemble the properties of a parabola until they finally merge with them. A parabola can thus be considered an ellipse with one infinitely distant focus; therefore, all the properties of ellipses can also be verified for a parabola, as if it were such an ellipse. Indeed, geometry is full of such examples; but nature—whose most wise Author employs the most perfect geometry—observes this same principle, otherwise no ordered progress would be maintained within it. Thus, as motion gradually decreases, it finally vanishes into rest, and as inequality is continuously diminished, it ends in true equality, so that rest

### ON ARTICLE 64.

The author closes the Second and General Part concerning the principles of material things with a certain admonition which seems to me to need restriction. He says truly that in order to explain the phenomena of nature there is no need of other principles than those found in abstract mathematics or in the theory of magnitude, figure, and motion. Nor does he recognize any other matter than that which is the subject of geometry. I indeed fully assent that all the special phenomena of nature can be explained mechanically if they are sufficiently examined by us, nor can the causes of material things be understood in any other way. But I think also that this ought to be repeatedly considered: that the very mechanical principles, and hence the general laws of nature, are derived from higher principles; they cannot be explained by the mere consideration of quantity and of that which is geometrical. Rather, there is in them something metaphysical, independent of the notions which the imagination presents, and which must be referred to a substance devoid of extension. For in addition to extension and its variations, there is in matter force itself, or the power of acting, which forms a transition from metaphysics to nature, and from material things to the immaterial. This force has its own laws derived from principles—not of mere absolute and, so to speak, brute necessity as in mathematics, but of perfect reason. But once these are joined together in a general discussion, and when a reason is afterward given for the phenomena of nature, all can be explained mechanically. Just as it is futile to use fundamental perceptions and desires (*archæi* <note>ancient or governing principles thought by some to direct natural processes</note>), operating ideas, forms of substances, and souls, it would be equally futile to call upon the universal cause of all—like a *Deus ex machina*—to explain each natural thing by His simple will. I remember the author of *Philosophia Mosaica* <note>A work by Robert Fludd</note> does this, the words of Sacred Scripture being poorly understood. He who will consider this properly will hold a

...middle position in philosophy and will satisfy theology no less than physics. He will understand that it was not so much a mistake of the schoolmen to hold the doctrine of *intelligible forms* as it was to apply it in the way they did, at a time when the inquiry was really about the modifications and instruments of substance and its manner of acting—that is, its mechanism. Nature has, as it were, an empire within an empire, and so to speak, a double kingdom: one of reason and one of necessity, or of forms and of particles of matter. For just as all things are full of spirits, they are also full of organized bodies. These realms, without being confused with one another, are each governed by their own laws; the reason for perception and desire is not found in the modifications of extension, any more than the reason for nutrition and other organic functions is to be found in forms or spirits. 

But this highest substance, which is the universal cause of all things, brings it about through His infinite wisdom and power that these two very different series are referred to the same corporeal substance and harmonize perfectly with each other, just as if one were controlled by the influence of the other. If you observe the necessity of matter and the order of efficient causes, you see that nothing happens without a cause that satisfies the imagination and follows the mathematical laws of mechanism. Conversely, if you regard the circle of ends as a golden chain and the world of forms as an intelligible world—where the heights of ethics and metaphysics are joined into one because of the perfection of the supreme author—you notice that nothing can be done without the highest reason. 

For GOD, the eminent form, and the first efficient cause are the same, and He is the end or final reason of all things. Moreover, it is our duty to revere His footprints in things—not only to admire His instruments in operation and the mechanical causes of material things, but also the higher uses of His wonderful ingenuity. Just as we recognize God as the architect of bodies, we must also recognize Him especially as the king of minds, whose intelligence rules all things for the best. This constitutes the most perfect Republic of the Universe under the most powerful and wisest of Monarchs. Thus, in the specific phenomena of nature and in every consideration, we shall consult equally the utility of life and the perfection of the mind, and wisdom no less than piety.

# VIII.

## LEIBNITZ'S REPLY TO THE EXTRACT FROM THE LETTER OF M. FOUCHER, CANON OF DIJON, PUBLISHED IN THE "JOURNAL" OF MARCH 16, 1693.

->[From the French.]<-

One ought to be very glad, sir, that you give a reasonable meaning to the doubt of the Academicians. It is the best apology that you could make for them. I will be delighted to see their views organized and clarified by your efforts at some time. But you will be obliged to lend them a ray of your light from time to time, as you have begun to do.

It is true that I wrote two short discourses twenty years ago: one on the theory of abstract motion, in which I considered it outside of the system as if it were a purely mathematical thing; the other on the hypothesis of concrete and systematic motion, such as is actually encountered in nature. There may be some good in them since you and others judge them so. However, there are many points on which I believe I am better informed at present; among others, I explain *indivisibles* today in an entirely different way. That was the attempt of a young man who had not yet fathomed mathematics. The laws of abstract motion that I provided at that time would truly hold good if there were nothing else in a body but what is conceived according to Descartes and even according to Gassendi. But as I have found that nature treats bodies quite differently regarding motion, it is one of my arguments against the received notion of the nature of body, as I have indicated in the *Journal des Savans* of June 2, 1692.

As regards indivisibles, when by that word one understands simple extremities of time or of a line, no new extremities could be conceived within them, nor any actual or pretended parts. Thus, points are neither large nor small, and no leap is required to pass them. However, although there are such *indivisibles* everywhere, continuity is not composed of them, as the objections of the skeptics appear to suppose. In my opinion, these objections have nothing insurmountable about them, as will be found by reducing them to form. Gregory of St. Vincent has well shown by calculations

He argues that while indivisible points exist as extremities, they do not constitute the substance of continuity itself.</summary>

I am so much in favor of the actual infinite that instead of admitting that nature abhors it, as is commonly said, I hold that nature employs it everywhere in order better to mark the perfections of its author. So I believe that there is no part of matter which is not—I do not say divisible, but actually divided—and consequently the smallest particle must be regarded as a world full of an infinity of different creatures.

<header>IX.</header>

### EXTRACT FROM A LETTER TO THE ABBÉ NICAISE ON THE PHILOSOPHY OF DESCARTES. 1793.

->[From the French.]<-

I hold the Bishop d’Avranches in very high regard, and I ask you, sir, to give him my respects when the opportunity arises. One of my friends in Bremen sent me a book by Herr Swelling, a professor there, written against the censure of that illustrious prelate, to get my opinion of it. I replied that the best answer the Cartesians could give would be to benefit from the advice of d’Avranches: to free themselves from the sectarian spirit, which is always contrary to the advancement of science; to combine the reading of Descartes’ excellent works with those of other great men, both ancient and modern; not to despise antiquity, from which Descartes took many of his best ideas; to devote themselves to experiments and demonstrations instead of those general reasonings that only serve to support laziness and hide ignorance; to try to make some progress and not be content with being simple paraphrasers of their master; and not to neglect or despise anatomy, history, languages, or criticism just because they do not know their importance and value. They should not imagine that we already know everything that is necessary or all we may hope to know. Finally, they should be modest and studious, so as not to bring upon themselves that fitting saying: *Ignorantia inflat* <note>Latin: "Ignorance puffs up [with pride]"</note>. 

I will add that I do not know how or by what star—the influence of which is the enemy of every kind of secret—it has happened that the Cartesians have accomplished almost nothing new, and that almost all discoveries have been made by people who are not part of that sect. I only know of the little pipes of M. Rohault, which do not deserve to be called a Cartesian discovery. It seems that those who tie themselves to a single master lower themselves through this kind of slavery and conceive of almost nothing except in imitation of him. I am certain that if Descartes had lived longer, he would have given us many important things. This shows us either that his success was due more to his personal genius than to his method, or else that he did not publish his method. In fact, I remember reading in one of his letters that he intended only to write a discourse on his method, and to

Nevertheless, I imagine that this method was not as perfect as we are led to believe. I think so based on his geometry. # ON THE REFORM OF METAPHYSICS AND OF THE NOTION OF SUBSTANCE. 1694.

->[From the Latin.]<-

I see that most of those who enjoy devoting themselves to the study of mathematics have a dislike for metaphysics, because in the former they find clarity and in the latter obscurity. I think the principal reason for this is that general concepts, which are believed to be perfectly known by everyone, have become ambiguous and obscure through human negligence and the inconsistency of people's thoughts. Furthermore, what are ordinarily provided as definitions are not even nominal definitions, because they explain absolutely nothing. It is not surprising that this evil has spread into the other sciences, which are subordinate to this first and architectonic <note>Meaning a foundational or master science that organizes others</note> science. Thus, we have subtle distinctions in place of clear definitions, and in place of truly universal axioms, we have general rules that are more often broken by exceptions than supported by examples. And yet, by a kind of necessity, men frequently make use of metaphysical terms and flatter themselves that they understand what they have learned to say. It is manifest that the true and fruitful meanings not only of *substance* but also of *cause*, of *action*, of *relation*, of *similarity*, and of *most other general terms* lie for the most part hidden. Therefore, it is not surprising that this queen of the sciences, which is called *first philosophy* and which Aristotle defined as the science desired or to be sought for (*ζητουμένη*), remains today among those sciences still being sought. Plato, it is true, often inquires into the value of concepts in his Dialogues; Aristotle does the same in his books entitled *Metaphysics*; nevertheless, they do so without much apparent profit. The later Platonists fall into monstrosities of language, and the disciples of Aristotle, especially the *Scholastics*, were more eager to raise questions than to answer them. In our day, some distinguished men have also devoted themselves to the *first philosophy*, but up to the present time, they have not had much success. It cannot be denied that Descartes brought many excellent things to it, and that he has, above all, the merit of having renewed *Platonic*

<summary>Leibniz argues that metaphysics remains obscure and neglected because fundamental terms like "substance" and "cause" lack clear definitions, unlike the clarity found in mathematics. He critiques the historical failures of the Scholastics and contemporary philosophers, including Descartes, to successfully establish metaphysics as a foundational science.</summary>
<keywords>metaphysics, substance, Aristotle, Plato, Descartes, Scholastics, first philosophy, definitions, clarity, architectonic science</keywords>

--- Page 83 ---
<meta>This page continues the author's critique of Descartes' metaphysical failings, specifically regarding the definition of substance, and introduces the author's own concept of active force as central to a reformed metaphysics.</meta>

study by turning the mind away from sensory things and having afterward usefully employed academic skepticism; but soon, through a kind of inconsistency or an impatience to affirm, he was led astray. He no longer distinguished the certain from the uncertain, and thus incorrectly claimed that the nature of corporeal substance consists in extension, while holding a false conception of the union of the soul and the body. The cause of this was that the nature of substance in general was not understood. For he had jumped, as it were, to the solution of the most serious questions without having explained the notions they implied. Hence, nothing shows more clearly how far his metaphysical meditations are removed from certainty than the writing in which, at the request of Mersenne and others, he vainly tried to clothe them in a mathematical garb. I also see that other men gifted with rare insight have approached metaphysics and treated parts of it with depth, but they have shrouded them in so much obscurity that they seem to guess rather than to prove. But it seems to me that metaphysics needs clarity and certainty even more than mathematics does, because the latter carries its own proofs and corroborations, which is the main cause of its success; whereas in metaphysics we are deprived of this advantage. Therefore, a specific plan is necessary for its explanation which, like a thread in the Labyrinth, serves us—no less than the method of Euclid—for resolving our problems in the manner of a calculus, while nevertheless always preserving the clarity that should not be sacrificed even in common conversation.

How important these things are is apparent, especially from the notion of substance which I provide, because it is so fruitful that from it first truths follow—even those concerning God, souls, and the nature of bodies. These are truths that are partly known but not sufficiently proved, and partly unknown until now, but which would be of the greatest use in the other sciences. To give a foretaste of them, it is enough for me to say that the idea of *energy* or virtue—called *kraft* by the Germans and *la force* by the French, and for the explanation of which I have designed a special science of dynamics—adds much to the understanding of the notion of substance. <meta>This page continues the author's exploration of substance, specifically transitioning from the critique of Descartes to the introduction of "active force" as an inherent property of all substances, both corporeal and spiritual.</meta>

nevertheless has need, in order to pass into action, of an external excitation and, as it were, of a stimulus. But active force includes a sort of act or <term>ἐντελέχειαν</term>, which is midway between the faculty of acting and the action itself, and involves an effort, and thus of itself passes into operation; nor does it need aid other than the removal of impediments. This may be illustrated by the example of a heavy hanging body straining the rope which sustains it, or a tense bow. For although gravity or elastic force may and must be explained mechanically from the motion of the ether, nevertheless the final reason for motion in matter is the force impressed upon it at creation—a force inherent in every body, but which is variously limited and confined in nature by the very meeting of bodies. I say, then, that this property of acting resides in every substance, and that some sort of action is always born of it; and that, consequently, corporeal substance, no less than spiritual substance, never ceases to act. This is a truth which those who place its essence in mere extension or even in impenetrability, and who have imagined that they conceived of a body at absolute rest, seem not to have sufficiently understood. It will appear also from our meditations that a created substance receives from another created substance, not the force of acting itself, but only the limits and determination of an already pre-existing tendency or virtue of acting. I omit here other considerations useful for the solution of the difficult problem concerning the mutual operation of substances.

<summary>The author defines active force as an inherent "entelechy" in all substances that naturally tends toward action unless impeded, contrasting this with passive extension. XI.

## A NEW SYSTEM OF NATURE, AND OF THE INTERACTION OF SUBSTANCES, AS WELL AS OF THE UNION WHICH EXISTS BETWEEN THE SOUL AND THE BODY. 1695.

->[From the French.]<-

1. I developed this system many years ago and shared it with several learned men, and in particular with one of the greatest theologians and philosophers of our time, who, after being informed of some of my opinions by a very distinguished person, had found them highly paradoxical. However, once he received my explanations, he withdrew his condemnation in a most generous and edifying manner. Having approved of some of my propositions, he stopped criticizing the others with which he did not yet agree. Since then, I have continued my meditations as far as opportunity has allowed, so that I might offer the public only thoroughly examined views. I have also tried to answer the objections raised against my essays on <term>dynamics</term>, which are related to these thoughts. Finally, because many people have wanted to see my opinions more clearly explained, I have ventured to publish these meditations, even though they are not at all for a general audience nor suited to be enjoyed by every type of mind. I have done this primarily so that I might benefit from the judgment of those who are experts in these matters. It would be too difficult to seek out and challenge individually everyone who might be inclined to offer the instruction which I will always be happy to receive—provided it stems from a love of truth rather than a passion for preconceived opinions.

2. Although I am someone who has worked very hard at mathematics, I have never stopped meditating on philosophy since my youth; it always seemed to me that there was a way to establish something stable within it through clear demonstrations. I had delved deeply into the territory of the <term>scholastics</term> when mathematics and modern authors prompted me, while still young, to withdraw from it. Their elegant ways of explaining nature mechanically charmed me; and, with good reason, I looked down on the methods of those who use only "forms" or "faculties," from which nothing is learned. But

He describes his intellectual journey from scholastic philosophy to the mechanical explanations favored by modern mathematicians and authors.</summary>

<keywords>Leibniz, New System, substance, soul and body, dynamics, scholastics, mechanical philosophy, meditations, interaction of substances</keywords>

--- Page 86 ---
<meta>This page continues Leibniz's explanation of his philosophical development, transitioning from his early interest in mechanical materialism to his discovery of the necessity of force and "substantial forms" to explain the nature of substance.</meta>

Afterwards, when I tried to investigate the principles of mechanics to find proof for the laws of nature which experience had made known, I perceived that the mere consideration of an extended mass was not sufficient, and that it was necessary to employ in addition the notion of *force*, which is very easily understood, although it belongs to the realm of metaphysics. It also seemed to me that the opinion of those who transform or degrade animals into simple machines—notwithstanding its apparent possibility—is contrary to appearances and even opposed to the order of things.

3. In the beginning, when I had freed myself from the grip of Aristotle, I occupied myself with the consideration of the void and atoms, for this is what best occupies the imagination. But after many reflections, I perceived that it is impossible to find the principles of *true unity* in mere matter, or in that which is only passive, because there everything is but a collection or mass of parts to infinity. Now, multiplicity cannot have its reality except from real unities, which originate otherwise and are entirely different things from the points out of which it is certain the *continuum* could not be composed. Therefore, in order to find these real unities, I was compelled to resort to a formal atom, since a material being could not be at the same time material and perfectly indivisible—or, in other words, endowed with true unity. It became necessary, therefore, to recall and, as it were, reinstate the *substantial forms* so criticized nowadays, but in a way that makes them understandable and distinguishes their proper use from the misuse that had befallen them. I found then that their nature is force, and that from this, something similar to sensation and desire results; therefore, it was necessary to conceive of them similarly to the idea we have of souls. But just as the soul ought not to be used to explain the details of the inner workings of the animal body, I likewise judged that it was not necessary to use these forms to explain particular problems in nature, although they are necessary in order to establish true general principles. Aristotle calls them the *first entelechies*. I call them, perhaps more clearly, primitive forces, which contain in themselves not only the *act* or fulfillment of possibility, but also an original activity.

4. I saw that these forms and these souls ought to be indivisible, just as much as our mind, as indeed I remembered was the...

7. But the most important question of all still remained: What becomes of these souls or these forms after the death of the animal or after the destruction of the individual organized substance? This is a most difficult question, especially since it seems unreasonable that souls should remain uselessly in a chaos of confused matter. This finally led me to believe that there was only one reasonable opinion to hold: namely, that not only the soul but also the animal itself and its <term>organic machine</term> are preserved, although the destruction of its physical parts has rendered it so small that it escapes our senses now just as much as it did before it was born. Furthermore, no one can accurately determine the true time of death, which for a long time can be considered merely as a suspension of visible actions; indeed, in simple animals, it is never anything else. This is seen in the <term>resuscitation</term> of drowned flies after being buried under powdered chalk, and other similar examples, which make it clear enough that there would be many more resuscitations—and far more complex ones—if humans were in a position to set the machine in motion again. And apparently it was something of this sort that the great Democritus, atomist as he was, spoke of, although Pliny mocks the idea. It is, then, natural that the animal—having always been living and organized, as people of great insight are beginning to recognize—should always remain so. And since, therefore, there is no first birth nor entirely new generation of the animal, it follows that there will be no final extinction nor complete death when taken in its <term>metaphysical rigor</term>. Consequently, instead of the *<term>transmigration</term>* of souls, there is only a *<term>transformation</term>* of one and the same animal, as its organs are folded differently and are more or less developed.

8. Nevertheless, <term>rational souls</term> follow much higher laws and are exempt from everything that could make them lose their status as citizens in the <term>society of spirits</term>. God has planned for them so well that no changes in matter can make them lose the moral qualities of their personality.
