9. Regarding the ordinary bodies of animals and other corporeal substances—whose complete extinction has been believed in until now, and whose changes depend more on mechanical rules than on moral laws—I noted with pleasure that the author of the book *On Diet*, which is attributed to Hippocrates, had foreseen something of the truth when he said in express terms that animals are not born and do not die, and that the things which are supposed to begin and to perish only appear and disappear. This was also the opinion of Parmenides and of Melissus, according to Aristotle, for these ancients were more profound than is commonly thought.

10. I am as well-disposed as anyone to do justice to the moderns; nevertheless, I think they have carried reform too far—for instance, in confusing natural things with artificial ones, for the reason that they have not had sufficiently high ideas of the majesty of nature. They conceive that the difference between its machines and ours is only that of the large to the small. This caused a very capable man, the author of *Conversations on the Plurality of Worlds*, to say recently that in regarding nature close at hand, it is found to be less admirable than had been believed, being only like the workshop of an artisan. I believe that this does not give a worthy idea of nature and that only our system can finally make men realize the true and immense distance that exists between the most trifling productions and mechanisms of the divine wisdom and the greatest masterpieces of the art of a finite mind; this difference consists not merely in degree, but also in kind. It must then be known that the machines of nature have a truly infinite number of organs and that they are so well protected and so resilient against all accidents that it is not possible to destroy them. A natural machine remains a machine even to its smallest parts and, what is more, it remains always the same machine it has been, being only transformed by the different folds it receives—sometimes expanded, sometimes compressed and, as it were, concentrated when believed to be lost.

<meta>This page continues Leibniz's philosophical inquiry, moving from the distinction between natural and artificial machines to the necessity of indivisible "metaphysical points" (souls) as the only true unities in nature, and beginning his investigation into the problem of soul-body interaction.</meta>

...take place neither in the machines of art nor in the simple mass of matter, however well organized it might be, which can only be considered as an army, or as a herd of cattle, or as a pond full of fish, or as a watch composed of springs and wheels. Nevertheless, if there were no real substantial unities, there would be nothing substantial or real in the mass. It was this which forced Cordemoi to abandon Descartes and to embrace Democritus' doctrine of the atoms in order to find a true unity. But atoms of matter are contrary to reason, setting aside the proof that they are made up of parts, for the invincible attachment of one part to another (if such a thing could be conceived or reasonably supposed) would not at all destroy their diversity. Only atoms of substance—that is, unities which are real and absolutely devoid of parts—are the sources of actions and the absolute first principles of the composition of things, being, as it were, the final elements in the analysis of substances. They might be called *metaphysical points*; they possess a certain *vitality* and a kind of *perception*, and *mathematical points* are their *points of view* for expressing the universe. But when corporeal substances are compressed, all their organs together form only a *physical point* to our sight. Thus, physical points are only indivisible in appearance; mathematical points are so in reality, but they are merely modalities; only metaphysical points or those of substance (constituted by forms or souls) are exact and real, and without them there would be nothing real, for without true unities there could be no multiplicity.

12. After having established these propositions, I thought I was entering port, but when I came to meditate on the union of the soul with the body, I was as if cast back into the open sea. For I found no way of explaining how the body can cause anything to pass into the soul, or *vice versa*; nor how one substance can communicate with another created substance. Descartes gave up the attempt on that point, as far as can be learned from his writings, but his disciples, seeing that the common view was inconceivable, were of the opinion that we perceive the qualities of bodies because God causes thoughts to arise in the soul upon the occasion of the movements of matter; and when the soul wished to move the body in its turn, they judged that it was God who moved it for the soul. And as the communication of motions again seemed inconceivable to them, they believed that God gave motion to a body on the

<summary>Leibniz argues that true reality requires indivisible "metaphysical points" or souls, as material atoms are logically impossible, and introduces the problem of how these substances interact with the body.</summary>

...occasion for the motion of another body. This is what they call the system of *Occasional Causes*, which has been very popular on account of the beautiful remarks of the author of the *Search after Truth* <note>Nicolas Malebranche</note>.

13. It must be admitted that the difficulty has been well understood when its impossibility is stated, but it does not appear that the problem is solved by explaining what actually takes place. It is indeed true that there is no real influence of one created substance upon another, speaking in metaphysical strictness, and that all things with all their realities are continually produced by the power of God; but in resolving problems, it is not enough to employ a general cause and to call in what is called the *Deus ex Machina*. For when this is done and there is no other explanation which can be drawn from secondary causes, it is, properly speaking, having recourse to a miracle. In philosophy, it is necessary to try to give reasons by making known the way in which things are done by divine wisdom, in conformity with the idea of the subject concerned.

14. Being then obliged to admit that it is not possible for the soul or any true substance to receive any influence from without, unless it be by divine omnipotence, I was led gradually to an opinion which surprised me, but which appears inevitable and which has, in truth, great advantages and many beauties. It is this: it must then be said that God created the soul, or every other real unity, in the first place in such a way that everything within it arises from its own substance through perfect *spontaneity* regarding itself and in *perfect harmony* with objects outside itself. Thus, our internal feelings (that is, those within the soul itself and not in the brain or more refined parts of the body) being only phenomena resulting from external objects or true appearances, and like well-ordered dreams, it is necessary that these internal perceptions within the soul itself come to it by its own proper original constitution—that is, by the representative nature (capable of expressing beings outside itself by relation to its organs) which has been given to it at its creation and which constitutes its individual character. This results in each of these substances, in its own way and according to a certain point of view, representing exactly the entire universe; and perceptions or impressions of external things reach the soul at the proper point in virtue of its own *laws*, as if it were in a world apart, and as if there existed nothing

but God and itself (to use the manner of speaking of a certain person of great elevation of mind, whose piety is well known); there is also perfect harmony among all these substances, producing the same effects as if they communicated with each other by a transmission of kinds or of qualities, as philosophers generally suppose.

Furthermore, the organized mass, within which is the point of view of the soul, being expressed more closely by it, finds itself reciprocally ready to act *of itself*, following the laws of corporeal machines, at the moment when the soul *wills* it, without either one disturbing the laws of the other. The nerves and the blood have just at that time received the impulse which is necessary in order to make them respond to the passions and perceptions of the soul; it is this mutual relationship, regulated beforehand in every substance of the universe, which produces what we call their *inter-communication* and alone constitutes the *union between the soul and body*. And we may understand from this how the soul has its seat in the body by an immediate presence which could not be greater, for it is there as the unit is in the complex of units, which is the multitude.

15. This hypothesis is very possible. For why could God not give to a substance in the beginning a nature or internal force which could produce within it in sequence (as in a *spiritual or formal automaton*, but free here since it has reason as its share), everything that should happen to it? That is to say, all the appearances or expressions it should have, and that without the aid of any created being? All the more so as the nature of the substance necessarily demands and essentially includes a progression or change, without which it would not have the power to act. And this nature of the soul, being representative of the universe in a very exact (although more or less distinct) manner, the series of representations which the soul will produce for itself will naturally correspond to the series of changes in the universe itself; just as, in turn, the body has also been accommodated to the soul for those instances where it is conceived as acting from without. This is all the more reasonable as bodies are only made for those spirits which are capable of entering into communion with God and of celebrating His glory. Thus, from the moment the possibility of this *hypothesis of harmonies* is perceived, we perceive also that it is the most reasonable and that it gives a marvelous idea of the harmony of the universe and of the perfection of the works of God.

16. This great advantage is also found in it: instead of saying that we are FREE only in appearance and in a way that is practically sufficient (as many capable people have believed), it should instead be said that we are only enchained in appearance. According to the strictness of metaphysical expressions, we are in a state of perfect independence regarding the influence of all other creatures. This again sheds a marvelous light upon the *immortality* of the soul and the consistently uniform preservation of our individuality, which is regulated perfectly by its own nature beyond the risk of all external accidents, regardless of any appearance to the contrary. Never has a system so clearly proved our high standing. Every spirit, being like a separate world sufficient unto itself, independent of every other creature, encompassing the infinite, and expressing the universe, is as durable, as stable, and as absolute as the universe of creatures itself. Therefore, we ought always to appear in it in the way best suited to contribute to the perfection of the society of all spirits, which constitutes their moral union in the city of God. Here is also found a new *proof of the existence of God*, which is surprisingly clear. For this perfect harmony among so many substances that have no communication with one another can only originate from a common cause.

17. Besides all these advantages which make this system commendable, it can also be said that this is more than a hypothesis, since it seems nearly impossible to explain the facts in any other intelligible way, and since several great difficulties that have troubled the mind until now seem to disappear on their own as soon as this system is well understood. Customary ways of speaking can still be retained. For we can say that the substance—the disposition of which explains the changes in others in an intelligible manner (in the sense that it may be supposed the others were adapted to it from the beginning, according to the order of the decrees of God)—is the one which must be conceived of as acting upon the others. Furthermore, the action of one substance upon another is not the emission or transfer of an entity, as is commonly believed, and cannot be reasonably understood except in the way I have just mentioned. It is true that we can easily conceive of both the emission and reception of parts within matter, by which we are right to explain all physical phenomena mechanically; but as the material mass is not

18. These considerations, however metaphysical they may appear, still have a marvelous use in physics for establishing the laws of motion, as our *Dynamics* can clarify. For it can be said that in the collision of bodies, each one suffers only because of its own elasticity, due to the motion that is already within it. And as for absolute motion, it can in no way be determined mathematically, since everything ends in relations; therefore, there is always a perfect equality of hypotheses, as in astronomy. Consequently, no matter how many bodies are considered, it is arbitrary to assign rest or a certain degree of velocity to any one that may be chosen, without being contradicted by the phenomena of straight, circular, and composite motion. Nevertheless, it is reasonable to attribute real movements to bodies according to the hypothesis which explains phenomena in the most intelligible manner, since this description conforms to the idea of action which I have just established.

# XII.

## THE REPLY OF M. FOUCHER TO LEIBNITZ CONCERNING HIS NEW SYSTEM OF THE INTERACTION OF SUBSTANCES. 1695.

->[From the French.]<-

ALTHOUGH your system is not new to me, Sir, and although I made known my opinion to you in part when replying to a letter you wrote me on this subject more than ten years ago, I will still not fail to tell you again what I think of it, since you ask me once more.

The first part aims only to make known the unities in all substances that constitute their reality, distinguish them from others, and form—to speak in the manner of the schools—their *individuation*; this is what you remark *first* on the subject of matter or extension. I agree with you that it is right to inquire after the unities that form the composition and the reality of extension; for without this, as you very justly remark, an infinitely divisible extension is only a chimerical compound, the principles of which do not exist, since without unities no true multitude is possible. Nevertheless, I am surprised that people are indifferent to this subject, for the essential principles of extension cannot exist in reality. In truth, points without parts cannot exist in the universe, and two points joined together form no extension; it is impossible for any length to subsist without breadth, or any surface without depth. And it is of no use to propose physical points, for these points are extended and involve all the difficulties we wish to avoid. But I will no longer delay on this subject, on which you and I have already had a discussion in the *Journal* of March 16, 1693, and of August 3 of the same year.

You introduce, on the other hand, another kind of unities which, strictly speaking, are unities of composition or of relation, and which concern the perfection or completion of a whole which, being organic, is intended for certain functions; for example, a clock is one unit, an animal is one unit; and you believe that you can give the name of substantial forms to the natural unities of animals and plants, so that these unities shall form their individuation in distinguish-

<keywords>Simon Foucher, Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, interaction of substances, individuation, extension, unities, physical points, substantial forms, organicism, divisibility</keywords>

In reality, this principle must be internal, as much on the part of their soul as of their body. But whatever arrangement there may be in the animal's organs, that does not suffice to make it sentient. For ultimately, all of this concerns merely the organic and mechanical composition, and I do not see how you are thereby justified in establishing a *sensitive principle in brutes that differs substantially from that of men.* And after all, it is not without reason that the Cartesians acknowledge that if we admit a sensitive principle capable of distinguishing good from evil, it is therefore also necessary to admit in them reason, discernment, and judgment. It would even reach such an extent that although no movement should take place in the body, the soul would never cease to think that there was one; just as those who are asleep think that they are moving their limbs and are walking, when nevertheless those limbs are at rest and do not move at all. Thus, during the waking state, souls would remain always convinced that their bodies would move according to their desires, even though these empty and useless masses would be inactive and would remain in a continuous lethargy. 

Truly, sir, do we not see that these opinions are constructed specifically, and that these *ex post facto* systems have been invented only to rescue certain principles which have been adopted? In fact, the Cartesians, assuming that there is nothing in common between spiritual and physical substances, cannot explain how one acts on the other; and consequently, they are compelled to say what they do. But you, sir, who could free yourself by other ways, I am surprised that you trouble yourself with their difficulties. For who does not see that when a scale is in equilibrium and inactive, if a new weight is added to one of the sides, movement immediately appears and one of the counter-weights makes the other rise in spite of the effort which the latter makes to descend. You conceive that *material beings are capable of efforts and of movement*; and it follows very naturally that the strongest effort must surpass the weakest. On the other hand, you recognize also that *spiritual beings may make efforts*; and as there is no effort which does not imply some resistance, it is necessary either that this resistance be stronger or weaker; if stronger, it overcomes; if weaker, it yields. Now it is not impossible that the mind, making an effort to move the body, finds it endowed with a contrary effort which resists—sometimes more, sometimes less—and this suffices to cause it to suffer thereby. It is in this way that St. Augustine, in his books on music, intentionally explains the action of spirits on bodies.

I know that there are many other questions to be raised before resolving from first principles all those which might be debated;

This order requires that philosophers begin by agreeing as to the infallible mark of truth, and confine themselves to demonstrating from first principles; and by waiting, one can always separate that which is conceived clearly and sufficiently from other points or subjects which contain some obscurity.

This, sir, is what I can say at present regarding your system, without speaking of the other fine subjects which you treat there incidentally, and which would merit particular discussion.

XIII.

### EXPLANATION OF THE NEW SYSTEM CONCERNING THE COMMUNICATION BETWEEN SUBSTANCES, TO SERVE AS A REPLY TO THE MEMOIR OF M. FOUCHER INSERTED IN THE "Journal des Savans" OF SEPTEMBER 12, 1695. 1696.

->[From the French.]<-

I remember, sir, that I believed I was fulfilling your wishes by communicating my philosophical hypothesis to you many years ago, although I assured you at the same time that I had not yet made up my mind to declare it publicly. I asked for your opinion of it in exchange, but I do not remember receiving any objections from you; otherwise, as willing to learn as I am, I should not have given you occasion to make the same objections to me twice. However, after the publication, they are still timely. For I am not one of those in whom a prejudice takes the place of reason, as you will find when you are able to bring forward some precise and weighty arguments against my opinions—something which apparently has not been your intention on this occasion. You have wished to speak as a skillful academician and thus provide an opportunity for a thorough examination of these subjects.

I did not wish to explain here the principles of extension, but rather those of *effective* extension or of corporeal mass; and these principles, in my opinion, are *real unities*; that is, substances endowed with true unity. The unity of a clock, which you mention, is to me entirely different from that of an animal, as the latter is capable of being a substance endowed with a true unity, like what we call the *ego* within us; whereas a clock is nothing but a collection. It is not in the arrangement of the organs that I place the sensitive principle of animals, and I admit that it concerns only the corporeal mass. So it seems that you do not consider me to be wrong when I require true unities and when, for this reason, I restore <term>substantial forms</term>. But when you seem to say that the soul of animals must possess reason if feeling is attributed to it, you make use of a conclusion whose logic I do not see.

You admit, with praiseworthy sincerity, that my hypothesis of harmony or of concomitance is possible. But you do not conceal a

You ask then, sir, what purpose all this contrivance that I attribute to the <term>Author of Nature</term> might serve? As if one could attribute too much of it to Him, and as if this exact correspondence that <term>substances</term> have among themselves—through laws of their own which each one received in the beginning—was not something admirably beautiful in itself and worthy of its Author. You also ask what advantage I find in this. I reply, second, that this correspondence serves to explain the <term>communication of substances</term> and the <term>union of the soul and body</term> through <term>laws of nature</term> established beforehand, without having to resort either to a <term>transmission of species</term>, which is inconceivable, or to new assistance from God, which appears very unsuitable. For it must be understood that just as there are laws of nature in matter, so there are similar laws in souls or forms, and these laws bring about what I have just stated.

I will be asked further: how does it happen that God does not content Himself with producing all the thoughts and modifications of the soul without these *useless* bodies which, it is said, the soul can neither *move* nor *know*? The reply is easy: it is because God willed that there should be more substances rather than fewer, and He thought it good that these modifications of the soul should correspond to something external. There is no useless substance; they all cooperate in God's design. I am also unwilling to admit that the soul *does not know* the body at all, even though this knowledge is gained without the influence of one upon the other. I would even have no difficulty saying that the soul *moves* the body. Just as a <term>Copernican</term> speaks truly of the "rising of the sun," a <term>Platonist</term> of the reality of matter, or a <term>Cartesian</term> of the reality of sensible qualities—provided they are rightly understood—so I believe it is quite true to say that substances act upon one another, provided it is understood that one is the cause of changes in the other as a consequence of the <term>laws of harmony</term>. You know that <term>Descartes</term> believed that the same <term>quantity of motion</term> is preserved in bodies. It has been shown that he was mistaken on that point, but I have made it apparent that it is always true that the same <term>moving force</term>—for which he had substituted the <term>quantity of motion</term>—is preserved. However, the changes which take place in bodies as a consequence of the modifications of the soul embarrassed him, because they seemed to violate this law. He believed that he had found a solution, which in truth is ingenious, by saying that we must distinguish between <term>movement</term> and direction, and that the soul cannot increase or diminish the <term>moving force</term>, but that it changes the direction or determination of the course of the <term>animal spirits</term>, and that it is in this way that voluntary movements take place. It is true that he was unwilling to explain how the soul acts to change the course of bodies, which is just as inconceivable as saying that it gives them movement, unless one has recourse, as I do, to <term>pre-established harmony</term>. But it should be known that there is another law of nature, which I have discovered and demonstrated, and which <term>Descartes</term> did not know. It is that not only is the same quantity of <term>moving force</term> preserved, but also the *same quantity of direction toward whichever side of the world is chosen.* That is to say, by drawing any straight line you please and taking as many bodies as you please, you will find—when considering all these bodies together, without omitting any of

XIV.

## SECOND EXPLANATION OF THE SYSTEM OF THE COMMUNICATION BETWEEN SUBSTANCES. 1696.

->[From the French.]<-

By your reflections, sir, I see clearly that the idea which one of my friends has published in the *Journal de Paris* needs explanation.

You do not understand, you say, how I could prove what I put forward concerning the communication or harmony of two substances as different as the soul and the body. It is true that I believe I have found the means of doing so, and this is how I propose to satisfy you. Imagine two clocks or watches which are perfectly synchronized. Now, this may take place in three ways. The *first* consists of a mutual influence; the *second* is to have a skilled craftsman assigned to them who regulates them and keeps them always in agreement; the *third* is to construct these two clocks with so much skill and accuracy as to ensure their future harmony. Now, put the soul and the body in place of these two clocks; their agreement may be brought about by one of these three ways. The way of influence is that of common philosophy; but as we cannot conceive of material particles which may pass from one of these substances into the other, this view must be abandoned. The way of the continual assistance of the Creator is that of the system of <term>occasional causes</term>; but I hold that this is to make a *Deus ex Machina* intervene in a natural and ordinary matter, in which, according to reason, He ought not to cooperate except in the way in which He does in all other natural things. Thus, there remains only my hypothesis; that is, the way of harmony. From the beginning, God has made each of these two substances of such a nature that, merely by following its own unique laws received with its being, it nevertheless agrees with the other, just as if there were a mutual influence or as if God always put His hand to it in addition to His general cooperation. After this, I have no need to prove anything, unless you wish to require me to prove that God is sufficiently skilled to make use of this pre-arranged design, examples of which we see even among men. Now,

<summary>Leibniz uses the analogy of two synchronized clocks to explain the relationship between the soul and the body, arguing that they do not influence each other but were designed by God to act in harmony. He rejects the theories of physical influence and occasional causes, favoring his own hypothesis of pre-established harmony.</summary>
<keywords>Leibniz, pre-established harmony, soul and body, clock analogy, occasional causes, Deus ex Machina, substances, philosophy of mind</keywords>

--- Page 105 ---
<meta>This page continues Leibniz's defense of his hypothesis of pre-established harmony, following his analogy of the two synchronized clocks representing the soul and the body. He argues that his system is the most worthy of God and best preserves the independence of mental and physical substances.</meta>

taking for granted that He can do it, you can easily see that this is the way that is most beautiful and most worthy of Him. You suspected that my explanation would be opposed to the very idea we have of the mind and of the body; but you will soon clearly see that no one has better established their independence. For while it has been necessary to explain their communication by a kind of miracle, this has always given many people cause to fear that the distinction between the body and the soul was not as real as was believed, since it was necessary to go to such lengths to maintain it. I shall not be at all sorry to consult enlightened persons concerning the thoughts which I have just explained to you.

XV.

# THIRD EXPLANATION. EXTRACT FROM A LETTER OF LEIBNIZ ON HIS PHILOSOPHICAL HYPOTHESIS AND THE CURIOUS PROBLEM PROPOSED BY HIS FRIENDS TO THE MATHEMATICIANS. 1696.

->[From the French.]<-

Some wise and insightful friends, having considered my new hypothesis concerning the great question of the union of soul and body, and having found it important, have asked me to provide some explanations for the difficulties that have been raised, which arise from the fact that it has not been well understood.

I thought that the matter might be made intelligible to every kind of mind by the following comparison:

Imagine two clocks or two watches that agree perfectly. Now this may happen in *three ways*. The first consists of the mutual influence of one clock on the other; the second, in the care of a man who attends to them; the third, in their own accuracy.

The *first way*, which is that of influence, was experimented on by the late Mr. Huygens, to his great astonishment. He had two large pendulums attached to the same piece of wood; the continual vibrations of these pendulums communicated similar vibrations to the particles of wood; but since these different vibrations could not coexist very well in their order and without hindering each other unless the pendulums agreed, it happened by a kind of miracle that even when their beats had been purposely disturbed, they soon began to beat together again, almost like two chords that are in unison.

The *second way* of making two clocks, even if they are poor ones, always agree, would be to have a skilled workman who would see to it that they are kept in constant agreement. This is what I call the *way of assistance*.

Finally, the *third way* would be to construct these two clocks from the start with such skill and accuracy that we might be certain of their future agreement. This is the way of the *pre-established agreement*.

Now, put the soul and the body in the place of these two clocks. Their harmony or sympathy will take place by one of these three

<summary>Leibniz introduces his famous clock analogy to explain how the soul and body interact, proposing three possible methods for their synchronization: mutual influence, external assistance, or pre-established harmony.</summary>
<keywords>Leibniz, soul and body, clock analogy, Christiaan Huygens, pre-established harmony, way of assistance, mind-body problem, synchronization</keywords>

--- Page 107 ---
<meta>This page continues Leibniz's explanation of the three possible methods for explaining the union of soul and body, following his clock analogy where two clocks can only stay in sync via mutual influence, a constant external adjuster, or perfect internal construction.</meta>

methods. The way of *influence* is that of traditional philosophy; but as we cannot conceive of material particles or properties, or immaterial qualities, which can pass from one of these substances into the other, we are forced to abandon this view. The way of *assistance* is that of the system of occasional causes; but I maintain that this is making a *Deus ex Machina* intervene in a natural and ordinary matter, when, according to reason, he should not intervene except in the manner in which he cooperates in all the other affairs of nature.

Thus, there remains only my hypothesis; that is, the way of a *harmony pre-established* by a *pre-arranged divine contrivance*, which from the beginning has formed each of these substances in a way so perfect and regulated with so much accuracy that merely by following its own laws, received with its existence, it nevertheless agrees with the other, just as if there were mutual influence, or as if God, in addition to his general cooperation, constantly applied his hand to it.

After this, I do not think I need to prove anything, unless it is that you wish me to prove that God has everything necessary to make use of this pre-arranged contrivance, examples of which we see even among men, according to their skill. And assuming that he can do it, you clearly see that this is the most admirable way and the one most worthy of him.

It is true that I have other proofs yet, but they are more profound, and it is not necessary to state them here.

<header>XVI.</header>

# REFLECTIONS ON LOCKE’S *Essay on Human Understanding*. 1696.
->[From the French.]<-

I find so many signs of unusual insight in what Mr. Locke has given us regarding *Human Understanding* and *Education*, and I consider the subject so important, that I have thought that the time I give to such profitable reading would be well spent—all the more so as I have myself meditated deeply on the foundations of our knowledge. For this reason, I have noted down on this sheet some of the reflections that occurred to me while reading his *Essay* on the Understanding. Of all investigations, there is none more important, because it is the key to all others.

The first book mainly considers the principles said to be innate. Mr. Locke does not accept them any more than he does *innate ideas*. He undoubtedly had good reasons for opposing common prejudices on this point, for the names of "ideas" and "principles" are greatly abused. Ordinary philosophers create principles according to their whims; and the Cartesians, who claim more accuracy, do not fail to entrench themselves behind so-called ideas of extension, matter, and the soul, wishing in this way to exempt themselves from the necessity of proving what they propose, on the excuse that those who meditate on these ideas will find the same thing they do. That is to say, those who accustom themselves to their way of thinking will have the same preconceptions, which is very true.

My opinion, then, is that nothing should be taken as fundamental principles except experiences and the axiom of identity (or, what is the same thing, the law of contradiction). This is fundamental, since otherwise there would be no difference between truth and falsehood, and all research would stop at the beginning if saying "yes" or "no" were a matter of indifference. We cannot, therefore, help but assume this principle as soon as we wish to reason. All other truths are capable of proof, and I greatly respect Euclid's method which, without stopping at what would be thought to be suffi-

Yet Euclid was right in taking some axioms for granted, not as if they were truly primitive and undemonstrable, but because he would have come to a standstill if he had wished to draw conclusions only after an accurate discussion of principles. Thus, he judged it proper to content himself with having pushed the proofs up to this small number of propositions, so that it can be said that if they are true, all that he says is also true. He has left to others the trouble of demonstrating these principles themselves which, besides, are already justified by experience; but in these matters, this does not satisfy us. This is why Appolonius, Proclus, and others have taken the trouble to demonstrate some of Euclid’s axioms. This manner of proceeding ought to be imitated by philosophers in order to finally arrive at some established positions, even if they are but provisional, in the way of which I have just spoken.

As for ideas, I have given some explanation of them in a short essay entitled *Meditationes de Cognitione, Veritate et Ideis*, and I wish that Mr. Locke had seen and examined it; for I am one of the most docile of men, and nothing is more fitted to advance our thoughts than the considerations and remarks of persons of merit, when they are made with care and sincerity. Here I shall only say that true or real ideas are those of whose possible fulfillment we are assured; the others are doubtful, or (in case of proof of impossibility), chimerical. Now the possibility of ideas is proved as much *a priori* by demonstrations—by making use of the possibility of other simpler ideas—as *a posteriori* by experience; for what exists cannot fail to be possible. But primitive ideas are those whose possibility is undemonstrable, and which indeed are nothing else than the attributes of God.

As regards the question of whether there are ideas and truths created *with us*, I do not consider it absolutely necessary for the beginning or for the practice of the art of thinking to decide it; whether they all come to us from without, or whether they come from within us, we will reason correctly if we observe what I have just said on this subject and if we proceed with order and without prejudice. For I have found that these things had not been well understood. I am in no way in favor of the *Tabula rasa* of *Aristotle*; and there is something sound in what *Plato* called *reminiscence*. It is true that this happens confusedly and without distinguishing them, much like how when I hear the sound of the ocean, I hear the sound of every particular wave that makes up the total sound, even though I cannot discern one wave from another. In the *second book*, which goes into the details of ideas, I confess that *Mr. Locke’s* reasons for proving that the soul is sometimes without thought do not seem convincing to me, unless he defines "thoughts" only as those perceptions clear enough to be distinguished and remembered. I maintain that the soul, and even the body, is never without action, and that the soul is never without some perception. Even in dreamless sleep, we have some confused and dim awareness of where we are and of other things. But even if experience did not confirm this, I believe it could be demonstrated. It is much like how we cannot prove absolutely by experience whether there is a *vacuum* in space, or whether matter is ever truly at rest. And yet, these kinds of questions seem to me, as they do to Mr. Locke, to be decided through demonstration.

I agree with the distinction he rightly makes between matter and space. But regarding the *vacuum*, many learned people have believed in it; *Mr. Locke* is among that number. can bear witness. The proof of a vacuum based on motion, which Mr. Locke uses, assumes that bodies are inherently *hard* and composed of a certain number of inflexible parts. In that case, it would be true that regardless of how many finite atoms were taken, motion could not occur without a vacuum; however, all parts of matter are divisible and flexible.

There are some other things in this second book that catch my attention; for example, when it is stated in chapter XVII that infinity should be assigned only to *space*, *time*, and *number*. I agree with Mr. Locke that, strictly speaking, it can be said that there is no space, no time, and no number that is infinite. Rather, it is only true that no matter how large a space, a time, or a number may be, there is always another larger than it, *to infinity* <note>*ad infinitum*</note>. Thus, the true infinite is not found in a whole made up of parts. Nonetheless, it is found elsewhere: namely, in the absolute, which is without parts and which influences compound things because they result from the limitation of the absolute. Therefore, since the *positive infinite* is nothing other than the absolute, it can be said that in this sense there is a positive idea of the infinite, and that it precedes the idea of the finite. For the rest, by rejecting a composite infinite, we do not deny what the mathematicians—and especially the excellent Mr. Newton—prove regarding *infinite series* <note>*de Seriebus infinitis*</note>.

Regarding what is said in chapter XXX about *adequate ideas* <note>*de ideis adaequatis*</note>, it is permissible to give terms the meaning one finds appropriate. Nevertheless, without finding fault with Locke’s meaning, I categorize ideas by degrees; I call those "adequate" when there is nothing more left to explain, much like in numbers. Now, since all ideas of sensory qualities—such as light, color, and heat—are not of this nature, I do not count them among the *adequate* ideas. Furthermore, it is not through the ideas themselves nor *from the outset* <note>*a priori*</note>, but through experience that we know their reality or possibility.

There are also many good things in the *third book*, where he treats *words* or *terms*. It is very true that *everything* cannot be defined, and that sensory qualities have no *nominal definition* and may be called "primitive" in this sense; but they can nonetheless receive a *real definition*. I have shown the difference between these two kinds of definition in the meditation quoted above. To make fitting remarks upon them would be to write a book as large as the work itself. It seems to me that the axioms in it are considered a little less than they deserve to be. I do not despise identical propositions, and I have found that they are of great service even in analysis. It is very true that we know our own existence by an immediate intuition, and that of God by demonstration; and that a mass of matter, the parts of which are without perception, cannot form a whole that thinks. I do not despise the argument, invented some centuries ago by Anselm, which proves that the perfect being must exist; although I find something lacking in this argument because it takes for granted that the perfect being is possible. For if this one point were proved in addition, the whole demonstration would be complete.

As for the knowledge of other things, it is very well said that experience alone does not suffice to advance sufficiently in physics. A penetrating mind will draw more conclusions from some very ordinary experiences than another could draw from the most choice; besides, there is an art of experimenting and of interrogating nature, so to speak. Yet it is always true that progress cannot be made in the details of physics except in proportion to the experience one has.

XVII.

## On the Ultimate Origin of Things. 1697.
### [From the Latin.]

In addition to the world, or the aggregate of finite things, there is a unique Being who governs—not only like the soul in me, or rather like the Ego itself in my body, but in a much higher relation. For one Being dominating the universe not only rules the world but also creates and fashions it; He is superior to the world and, so to speak, <term>extramundane</term> <note>existing outside the physical world</note>, and by this very fact is the ultimate reason of things. For the <term>sufficient reason</term> for existence can be found neither in any particular thing nor in the whole aggregate or series of things. 

Suppose a book on the elements of geometry had been eternal, and that others had been successively copied from it; it is evident that, although we might account for the present book by the book which served as its model, we could nevertheless never reach a complete reason for them, no matter how many books we assumed. We might always wonder why such books have existed from all time; that is, why books exist and why they are written as they are. What is true of books is also true of the different states of the world; for despite certain laws of transformation, a succeeding state is, in a certain way, only a copy of the preceding one. To whatever earlier state you may go back, you will never find there a complete reason why, indeed, there is any world at all, or why such a world as this exists. 

For even if you imagine the world to be eternal, since you propose nothing but a succession of states and find a sufficient reason for them in none of them individually—and as any number of them together does not help you in providing a reason for them—it is evident that the reason must be sought elsewhere. For in eternal things, it must be understood that even where there is no cause, there is a reason. In <term>perduring</term> <note>enduring or continuing</note> things, this reason is necessity itself or essence; but in the series of changing things, if it were supposed that they succeed each other eternally, this reason would be (as will soon be seen) the prevalence of inclinations where the reasons are not necessitating (by an absolute or metaphysical necessity, the opposite of which would imply a contra-

<summary>Leibniz argues that the existence of the world requires a "sufficient reason" found in an extramundane Being, as an eternal succession of physical states cannot explain its own existence. He distinguishes between the absolute necessity of eternal essences and the "inclinations" that govern the changing world.</summary>
<keywords>Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, sufficient reason, extramundane, metaphysical necessity, cosmology, ultimate origin, geometry analogy</keywords>

--- Page 115 ---
<meta>This page continues Leibniz’s argument regarding the ultimate origin of things, moving from the analogy of the eternal book to the philosophical distinction between physical and metaphysical necessity.</meta>

diction), but inclining. From this it follows that by supposing the eternity of the world, an ultimate <term>extramundane</term> <note>existing outside the physical world</note> reason of things, or God, cannot be escaped.

The reasons of the world, therefore, lie hidden in something <term>extramundane</term> different from the chain of states or series of things, the aggregate of which constitutes the world. We must therefore pass from <term>physical</term> or <term>hypothetical necessity</term>, which determines the later states of the world by the earlier ones, to something which is <term>absolute</term> or <term>metaphysical necessity</term>, the reason for which cannot be given. For the present world is necessary, physically or hypothetically, but not absolutely or metaphysically. It being granted, indeed, that the world is as it is, it follows that things may hereafter be as they are. But as the ultimate origin must be in something which is <term>metaphysically necessary</term>, and as the reason for that which exists can only come from that which exists, there must exist some one being who is <term>metaphysically necessary</term>, or whose <term>essence</term> is <term>existence</term>; and thus there exists something which differs from the plurality of beings or from the world, which, as we have recognized and shown, is not <term>metaphysically necessary</term>.

But in order to explain a little more clearly how temporary, contingent, or physical truths arise from eternal, essential, or metaphysical truths, we ought first to recognize this: from the very fact that something exists rather than nothing, there is in possible things—that is, in the very possibility or <term>essence</term>—a certain need for existence, and, so to speak, some claim to existence; in a word, that <term>essence</term> itself tends toward <term>existence</term>. From this it further follows that all possible things, whether expressing essence or possible reality, tend by equal right toward existence, according to their quantity of essence or reality, or according to the degree of <term>perfection</term> <note>defined here as the quantity of essence</note> which they contain; for <term>perfection</term> is nothing else than the quantity of <term>essence</term>.

Hence it is most clearly understood that among the infinite combinations of possibles and possible series, that one exists through which the most <term>essence</term> or possibility is brought into existence. And indeed there is always in things a <term>principle of determination</term> which is to be taken from the greatest and the smallest, or in such a way that the greatest effect is obtained with the least expenditure, so to speak. And here the time, place, or as many say, the receptivity or capacity of the world may be considered as the

<summary>Leibniz argues that the world requires a metaphysically necessary creator because its physical states are only hypothetically necessary. He proposes that all possible things have a drive toward existence, and the existing world is the one that maximizes essence and perfection.</summary>

But, you might say, however ingenious this comparison between a certain determining metaphysical mechanism and the physical mechanism of heavy bodies may appear, it nonetheless fails in this: heavy bodies truly exist, whereas possibilities and essences—prior to or outside of existence—are only fancies or fictions in which the reason for existence cannot be found. Thus, the world is not only the most admirable machine, but insofar as it is composed of souls, it is also the best republic, through which as much happiness or joy is brought to souls as is possible, in which their physical perfection consists.

<meta>This page continues Leibniz's argument regarding the perfection of the universe, moving from the metaphysical necessity of a most perfect world to addressing the human perception of its apparent flaws and imperfections.</meta>

closely, it clearly appears from what has been argued that the contrary should be affirmed; that is, that all things and, consequently, souls attain the highest degree of perfection possible. And in truth, it is not proper to judge before having examined the whole law, as the <term>jurisconsults</term> say. We know only a very small part of the eternity that extends into immensity; for the memory of the few thousand years that history passes down to us is indeed a very small thing. And yet, from such a short experience, we dare to judge the immense and the eternal—like men who, born and raised in a prison or, if you prefer, in the subterranean salt mines of the <term>Sarmatae</term>, think there is no other light in the world than the lamp whose feeble gleam is barely enough to guide their steps. Let us look at a very beautiful picture and cover it in such a way that we see only a very small part of it; what else will appear in it, no matter how closely we examine it or how near we approach it, except a confused mass of colors without selection or art? And yet, when we remove the covering and view it from the proper perspective, we will see that what appeared to be thrown onto the canvas haphazardly was executed with the greatest skill by the author of the work. 

What the eyes discover in a picture, the ears discover in music. The most illustrious composers often introduce discords into their harmonies to excite and pique, so to speak, the listener, who—anxious about the outcome—is all the more pleased when everything is soon restored to order. Just as we rejoice to have passed through slight dangers and experienced small ills—whether because of a feeling of self-satisfaction, or because we find pleasure in the frightening images presented by tight-rope dancing or leaping between swords (*sauts perilleux*); so we playfully release laughing children, pretending to throw them far away from us, like the ape which, having taken Christian, King of the Danes, while he was still an infant wrapped in swaddling clothes, carried him to the top of the roof, and when everyone was frightened, brought him back laughing, safe and sound to his cradle. According to the same principle, it is dull to eat nothing but sweets; we must mix them with sharp, acidic, and even bitter things that excite the palate. He who has not tasted bitter things has not earned sweet things and will not even appreciate them. It is the law of joy itself that pleasure should not be uniform, for uniformity produces disgust and makes us dull rather than joyful.

<meta>This page continues Leibniz's argument regarding the perfection of the universe, moving from the metaphysical necessity of a most perfect world to addressing the human perception of its apparent flaws and imperfections.</meta>

Regarding what we said—that a part may be disturbed without harming the general harmony—this must not be understood as meaning that no account is made of the parts, or that it is enough for the entire world to be perfect in its proportions even if the human race were unhappy. It is not as if there were no regard for justice in the universe or no concern for our fate, as some think who do not judge the whole of things correctly enough. For it must be known that just as in a well-constituted republic as much care as possible is taken for the good of the individual, so too the universe cannot be perfect if individual interests are not protected as far as the universal harmony will permit. 

And in this regard, no better law could be established than the law of justice itself, which wills that everyone participate in the perfection of the universe and in a happiness of their own, proportioned to their own virtue and to the goodwill they hold toward the common good. By this, what we call the charity and love of God is fulfilled, in which alone—according to the judgment of the wisest theologians—the force and power of the Christian religion itself consist. And it should not appear astonishing that such a large role should be given to souls in the universe, since they reflect the most faithful image of the supreme Author and relate to him not only as a machine relates to its builder, but also as a citizen relates to a prince. Furthermore, they are to continue as long as the universe itself, and in a way, they express and concentrate the whole within themselves, so that it can be said that souls are whole parts.

As regards the afflictions of good people specifically, we must hold it as certain that a greater good results for them; this is true not only theologically but also physically. Just as grain cast into the ground "suffers" before producing its fruit, we may affirm generally that afflictions, though temporary evils, are in effect good, since they are shortcuts to greater perfections. Similarly in physics, liquids that ferment slowly also take more time to improve, whereas those with greater agitation reject certain parts with more force and are improved more quickly.

And we might say of this that it is a matter of drawing back in order to leap forward better (*qu’on recède, pour mieux sauter*).

We should therefore regard these considerations not merely as agreeable and consoling, but also as most true. And, in general, I feel that there is nothing truer than happiness, and nothing happier or sweeter than truth.

XVIII.

## REPLY TO REFLECTIONS, FOUND IN THE "*Journal des Savants*" OF THIS YEAR, RELATING TO THE CONSEQUENCES OF CERTAIN PASSAGES OF THE PHILOSOPHY OF DESCARTES. 1697.

->[From the French.]<-

I am accused of *wishing to build my reputation on the ruins of Descartes'. I have a right to complain about this. Far from wishing to ruin the reputation of this great man, I find that his true merit is not sufficiently known, because his most excellent qualities are not adequately considered or imitated.* People focus on his weakest passages because these are most easily understood by those who are unwilling to give themselves the trouble of thinking deeply, yet who would still like to understand the foundation of things. This is why, to my great regret, his followers add almost nothing to his discoveries; this is the usual result of a sectarian spirit in philosophy. Since all my views are focused only on the public good, I have occasionally said things to provoke them, knowing well that their insight would lead them very far if they did not believe that their master had already done enough. I have always declared that I *highly esteem Descartes; there are few who approach him in genius.* I know only Archimedes, Copernicus, Galileo, Kepler, Jung, Huygens, Newton, and a few others of such power; to these, Pythagoras, Democritus, Plato, Aristotle, Suisset, Cardan, Gilbert, Verulam, Campanella, Harvey, Pascal, and some others might be added. It is nevertheless true that *Descartes used deception in order to profit from the discoveries of others without wishing to appear indebted to them.* He treated some excellent men in an unjust and unworthy way when they offended him, and he had an unbridled ambition to establish himself as the leader of a faction. But this does not diminish the beauty of his thoughts. Rather than approving of those who despise him and who repay merit with ingratitude, it is this very behavior that I primarily blame in Descartes, and even more so in several of his followers, whose misguided attachment to a single author fosters prejudice and prevents them from benefiting from the light

<meta>This page continues the author's defense of his philosophical and mathematical reputation, specifically addressing his relationship to Cartesianism and the critique of Descartes' rejection of final causes.</meta>

of so many others. I am accustomed to say that the *Cartesian philosophy is, as it were, the antechamber of the truth, and that it is difficult to penetrate far beyond without having passed through this; but one deprives themselves of the true knowledge of the heart of things if they stop there.*

As for the small reputation that I am honored to have been granted, I have not acquired it by refuting Descartes; I have no need of that method; law, history, and literature contributed to it before I had even thought of mathematics. And if our new analysis—the calculus of which I have proposed—surpasses that of Descartes as much as, or more than, his surpassed preceding methods, his work remains nonetheless very worthy of esteem. It has been necessary for the progress of science to correct those who think his method suffices for everything. This cannot be done better than by proposing problems to them that are beautiful and attractive, and even simple for those who know our method, but which not one of the Cartesian analysts has been able to solve.

---

Let us come now to the heart of our dispute. I am not the first who has blamed Descartes for having rejected the search for final causes. Besides the Reverend Father Malebranche, the late Mr. Boyle did so with much zeal and reliability, not to speak of numerous other serious, moderate, and well-disposed authors—men who otherwise think highly of Descartes. The reply is made here that he banished final causes from physics and that he was right in doing so, but that he would have been wrong if he had banished them from ethics: *For the entire good and the entire evil of our free actions depends upon their end.* This reply is surprising. The question is not concerning our free actions, but concerning God and His wisdom, which appears among the things that Descartes ought not to have neglected. And the reply, far from excusing him, would imply—if it were true—that according to him, final causes belong only to our free actions. But I suppose that this is not the view of the author of the *Reflections*, nor that of Descartes. Nevertheless, his silence might be harmful to his intention. He did not wish to use this means to prove the existence of God; he may be excused on this point, although many have blamed him for it; but he has not done well in other—

<meta>This page continues the author's critique of Descartes, specifically arguing that Descartes neglected the role of divine wisdom in the physical structure of the universe, and it transitionally connects to the previous page's discussion of God.</meta>

wise everywhere, passing by so important a point, which ought to have been employed in some passages of his *Principles of Philosophy*. If God is the author of things and if he is supremely wise, one could not very well reason about the structure of the universe without allowing considerations of his wisdom to enter into it, just as one could not well reason concerning a building without entering into the designs of the architect. I have cited elsewhere an excellent passage from the *Phaedo* of Plato (which is the dialogue on the death of Socrates), where the philosopher Anaximander, who had posited two principles—an intelligent mind and matter—is blamed for not having employed this intelligence or this wisdom in the progress of his work, having contented himself with the shapes and motions of matter; and this is exactly the case with our too materialistic modern philosophers.

But, it is said, in physics we do not ask *why* things are but *how* they are. I reply that both questions are asked there. Often we can better judge the means by the end. Besides, to explain a machine, we could do no better than to state its design and to show how all its parts contribute to it. This may even be useful in finding the origin of the intention. I wish that this method were employed also in medicine. The animal body is a machine, at once hydraulic, pneumatic, and pyrobolic, the design of which is to maintain a certain motion; and by showing what contributes to this design and what is injurious to it, physiology as well as therapeutics would be understood. Thus it is seen that final causes are of service in physics, not only to make us admire the wisdom of God, which is the principal reason, but also for knowing things and for managing them. I have elsewhere shown that while we may still dispute the efficient cause of light—which, as the most intelligent people now acknowledge, Descartes has not explained sufficiently well—yet the final cause suffices for discovering the laws which it follows. For provided we imagine that nature had as its design the conducting of rays from a given point to another given point by the easiest path, we find all these laws perfectly, by simply employing, as I have done in the *Acta Eruditorum* of Leipsic, some lines of analysis. . . . Molineux thanked me for this in his *Dioptrics*, and he highly approved of the remark which I made on that occasion regarding the important use of final causes, which lead us to the consideration of Sovereign Wisdom by showing us at the same time the laws of nature which are its consequence.

<meta>This page continues the author's critique of Descartes' philosophical system, specifically addressing the claim in Article 47 of the third part of his *Principles of Philosophy* regarding the succession of forms in matter and its implications for necessity and providence.</meta>

The author of the *Reflections* asks me to provide the passage where Descartes says that matter successively receives all the forms of which it is capable. He searched Articles 203 and 204 of the fourth part of his *Principles* for it, but it is found in Article 47 of the third part. I shall quote it in the original Latin. The author remarks in the summary that any falsehood in his suppositions regarding the origin of the world would not be harmful, and to prove this further he adds: “Atque omnino parum refert quid hoc pacto supponatur, quia postea juxta leges naturae est mutandum. Et vix aliquid supponi potest, ex quo non idem effectus (quanquam fortasse operosius), per easdem naturae leges deduci possit. Cum earum ope materia formas omnes, quarum est capax, successive assumat, si formas istas ordine consideremus, tandem ad illam quae est hujusmodi poterimus devenire.” From this, it may be judged whether I have misrepresented this author, and whether he does not positively state—not only that matter can take, but also that it effectively as well as successively *does* take—all the forms of which it is susceptible, and that it is thus of little importance what suppositions are made. There is much to be said against this reasoning.

In order to support it, it would be necessary to suppose that the same state of the universe always returns exactly after a certain period; otherwise, if a state of the world were taken that actually follows another, this latter state could never be deduced from the former, even if matter should receive all the forms of which it is capable.

But these periods involve other difficulties, so much so that all the infinite possibilities would have to occur within this finite, periodic interval, and all eternity could produce nothing new.

To say also, with Descartes, that he is at liberty to suppose almost anything he wishes, it would not be enough for each supposition or hypothesis to finally lead to our world; for the distance might be so great and the passage from one to the other might be so long and difficult that it would be impossible for the human mind to follow and comprehend it.

But the only proposition in question here is the one I have cited, and the strange consequences of which I have noted: for if everything possible and everything imaginable, however unworthy it may be, comes to pass one day; if every fable or fiction has been or will become true history, there is nothing but necessity, and no choice, no providence. And it is this consequence that the author

Nevertheless, I am unwilling to attack the religion and piety of Descartes, as has been unjustly attributed to me. I protested the contrary in express terms, for a doctrine may be dangerous without the person circulating it, or the person following it, noticing the fact or approving of its consequences. Nevertheless, it is good to make them known so that we may be on our guard against them, since it clearly appears that Spinoza and some others have drawn these conclusions. For there are minds disposed to seize upon the worst passages and who are clever at deducing the most dangerous conclusions. I would not have spoken of Spinoza if I had thought that what I wrote would be published, for fear that it would be believed that I wished to bring hatred upon the Cartesians, knowing well that they have sometimes been wronged by mistaken zeal. As one of the best uses of true philosophy, and particularly of physics, is to nourish piety and to lead us to God, I am not displeased with those who have given me this opportunity to explain myself in a way that may make a good impression on someone; although I wish it had been done without attributing to me a passion and partiality from which, perhaps, few people are further removed than I. To express in a few words the feeling I have toward an author whose reputation I am wrongly accused of wishing to ruin (an undertaking that would be as unjust as it is impossible), I will say that he who does not acknowledge the eminent merit of Descartes is not very perceptive; but he who acknowledges and esteems none but him and those who follow him will never amount to much.

XIX.

## ON NATURE IN ITSELF; OR, ON THE FORCE RESIDING IN CREATED THINGS, AND THEIR ACTIONS. 1698.

->[From the Latin.]<-

(1). I have recently received from the very illustrious John Christopher Sturm—a man especially distinguished for his work in mathematics and physics—the Apology which he published at Altorf in defense of his Dissertation, *De Idolo Naturae*. This dissertation had been attacked by Gunther Christopher Schelhammer, the eminent and respected physician of Kiel, in his own book on nature. As I have previously examined the same question, and as I have had some discussions on this subject through letters with the eminent author of the Dissertation—mention of which he made in a way very gratifying to me by publicly recalling some details of our correspondence in the first volume of his *Select Physics* (Vol. I, Sec. 1, Chap. 3, epilog. § v, pp. 119, 120)—I have therefore been even more inclined to give serious attention to such an important subject. I judge it necessary that my view and the entire question should be set forth a little more distinctly, based on those principles which I have already often indicated. This apologetic dissertation seemed to offer a favorable opportunity for my purpose, because it was easy to see that the author had treated the essential points of the question in a few words. For the rest, I do not take sides between these illustrious men.

(2). Universal nature is, so to speak, the *handiwork of God*, and it is so great that every natural machine (and this is the true but little observed difference between nature and art) is composed of truly infinite organs; consequently, it requires infinite wisdom and power in its author and director. This is why I consider the "omniscient heat" of Hippocrates, the "soul-giving Colcho-goddess" of Avicenna, the "very wise plastic virtue" of Scaliger and others, and the "hylarchic principle" of Henry More to be partly impossible and partly superfluous. It is enough for me that the mechanism of things is constructed with so much wisdom that all these marvels come to pass through its very development; organized beings are evolved, I think, according to a preconceived plan. I am therefore of the same opinion as the illustrious author when he rejects the fiction of a certain created "nature" whose wisdom forms and governs the mechanisms of bodies; but it does not follow from this, I believe—and reason does not allow—that every created, indwelling, active force must be rejected.

(3.) We have just spoken of what it is not; let us now examine more closely what this nature is, which Aristotle was not wrong in calling the *principle of motion and of rest*, although this philosopher seems to me to take the word in too broad a meaning. He understands by it not only local motion or rest in a place, but in general *change* and στάσις <gloss>stasis</gloss> or persistence. From this also, as I may say in passing, the definition which he gives of motion is truly obscure; it is, however, not as absurd as it seems to those who suppose that he meant to define only local motion. 

But let us return to the matter at hand. Robert Boyle, a man eminent and skilled in the accurate observation of nature, wrote a small book on nature in itself. The thought of that book, if I remember correctly, is summed up in this: that we ought to regard nature as being the very mechanism of bodies. (5.) But we must now examine what he says about the notion of nature in his apologetic dissertation, and what seems to us insufficient in it. He grants, in Chapter IV, §§ 2, 3, and often elsewhere, that the movements which take place now are the result of the *eternal law* once decreed by God, which law he calls soon after *volition and command*; and that there is no need for a new command from God, for a new volition, and still less for a new effort or a kind of laborious operation (§ 3). He repels as an unfair imputation on the part of his opponent the thought that God moves things as a woodcutter does his two-edged axe, or as a miller governs his mill by holding back the waters or by turning them loose on the wheel. But in truth, as indeed it seems to me, this explanation is not sufficient. For I ask whether this volition or this command—or, if you prefer, this divine law decreed originally—attributed to things only an *extrinsic denomination*; or whether, in forming them, it created in them some permanent impression, or as Schelhammer (notable as much for his judgment as for his experience) rightly calls it, an *indwelling law* (although it is most often unknown to the creatures in whom it resides), from which proceed all actions and all passions. The first appears to be the doctrine of the authors of the system of Occasional Causes, and especially of the very ingenious Malebranche; the latter is accepted (and as I believe, rightly) as the most true.

(6.) And in truth, since this past order does not exist at present, it can produce nothing now unless it then left behind some enduring effect, which still continues and operates. And he who thinks otherwise renounces, if I judge rightly, all distinct explanation of things; and it can be said that anything is, with equal justification, the result of anything else, if that which is absent in space and time can operate here and now without an intermediary. Thus it is not sufficient to say that in creating things in the beginning God willed that they should observe a certain law in their progress, if his will is conceived to have been so ineffective that things were not affected by it and no lasting effect was produced in them. And assuredly it is contrary to the notion of the divine power and will, which is pure and absolute, that God should will and nevertheless in willing produce or change nothing; that he is always

This amounts to the same thing as saying that nature itself, or the substance of all things, would be God—a dangerous doctrine recently introduced into the world or renewed by a subtle but profane author. In truth, if physical things contained nothing but matter, it would be quite true to say that they are in a state of flux and have nothing substantial, as the Platonists long ago recognized very well.

(13). The second argument, which the distinguished Sturm derives from the nature of motion, does not seem to me to be necessarily conclusive. He says that motion is only the successive existence of a thing in different places. Let us allow this for now, even though we are not at all satisfied with it, and even though it expresses the result of motion rather than its so-called formal cause; nevertheless, the force of motion is not thereby excluded. For a body is not only in its assigned place at the actual moment of its motion, but it also has a tendency or exertion to change its place, so that the succeeding state follows naturally from the present by the force of nature. Otherwise, at the actual moment—and therefore at any moment—body A, which is moved by body B, would in no way differ from a body at rest. Based on the opinion of that distinguished man, if it were contrary to ours on this point, it would follow that there would be no difference whatever in bodies, because in the fullness of a mass that is inherently uniform, no other difference can be assumed than that which relates to motion. Finally, it would further follow that there would be absolutely no change in bodies, and that they would always remain in the same state. For if any portion of matter does not differ from another that is equal and similar to it (which the distinguished Sturm must admit, since he eliminates active forces, impulses, and all other qualities and modifications except for existence in a certain place, which would be successively one after another); if, moreover, the state at one instant does not differ from the state at another instant except by the rearrangement of parts of matter that are equal, similar, and at every point fitting to each other, it evidently follows that—due to the perpetual replacement of indiscernible things—it will be absolutely impossible to distinguish the different states in the world of bodies at different moments. In truth, it would only be an external designation by which one part of matter would be distinguished from another; that is, by the future—namely, that it would later be in another and still another place. But for the present state, there is no difference; and not even from the future could a well-founded difference be drawn, because we could never arrive at any true present difference, even later on.

<meta>This page continues the argument that without active force and inherent internal differences, matter would be indistinguishable and motion would be imperceptible, leading to a refutation of perfectly uniform substance.</meta>

ence, since by no mark can one place be distinguished from another place, nor (on the hypothesis of the perfect uniformity of matter itself) matter from other matter in the same place. In vain also would we resort to *figure* after motion. In a mass that is perfectly similar, indistinguishable, and full, there arises no figure, nor any limit or distinction of various parts, except from the motion itself. If, then, motion does not contain any mark of distinction, it will impart none to figure; and as everything substituted for what was there before is perfectly equivalent, no one, even if they were omniscient, could grasp the least indication of change. Consequently, everything will be just as if no change and no distinction occurred in bodies, and we could never in this way account for the diverse appearances that we perceive. 

And it would be as if we were to imagine two perfect concentric spheres, perfectly similar in themselves and in all their parts, one of which should be enclosed in the other so that not the least opening should be left; then, if we suppose that the inner sphere is either in motion or at rest, not even an angel, to say nothing more, would be able to perceive any difference between the states at different times, and would have no sign by which to distinguish whether the inner sphere is at rest or in motion, or according to what law the motion proceeds. Moreover, not even the boundary of the spheres can be defined, because of the lack of both an opening and a difference; just as in this case, motion cannot be noticed because of that same lack of difference. 

Therefore, it must be considered certain (although those who have not sufficiently investigated these things have noticed it little) that such things are foreign to the nature and order of things, and that (which is among the number of my new and greater axioms) there is *nowhere any perfect similarity*. From this it follows also that we find in nature neither corpuscles of extreme hardness, nor a fluid of extreme thinness, nor subtle matter universally diffused, nor ultimate elements, called by some by the name of primary or secondary. It is, I believe, because he understood something of this that Aristotle—more profound in my opinion than many think—judged that in addition to local change, there was a need for alteration, even if matter were to remain invariable.
