But for a long time now, I have understood (by laying aside the prejudices of youth) that atoms together with a vacuum must be rejected. The celebrated author adds that the existence of matter through diverse moments is to be attributed to the divine will; why not then, he says, attribute to the same its existence here and now? I reply that this, like all other things insofar as they involve some perfection, must undoubtedly be attributed to God. But just as this universal first cause, which preserves all things, does not destroy but rather produces the natural permanence—or once granted, perseverance in existence—of the thing which begins to exist, so it will not destroy but rather strengthen the natural efficacy—or perseverance in action once communicated—of the thing set in motion.

(14). Many other things are encountered in this apologetic dissertation which present difficulties, such as what is said in Chapter IV, § 11, concerning motion transmitted from one ball to another through several intermediaries: that the last ball is moved by the *same* force by which the first is moved, whereas, it seems to me, it is moved by an equivalent but not the same force. For (what may appear surprising), each ball, repelled by the next one hitting it, is set in motion by its *own* force, namely, its elasticity. (I do not here discuss at all the cause of this elasticity, nor do I deny that it ought to be explained mechanically by the movement of an indwelling and unstable fluid). So also, it will rightly seem surprising when he says, in § 12, that a thing which cannot set itself in motion cannot by itself continue that motion. For it is instead evident that, just as there is a need for force to communicate motion, so once the impulse is given, far from there being a need for a new force to continue it, there is rather a need for a new force to stop it. For the question here is not about that preservation of motion by means of a universal cause necessary to things, which, as we have remarked, could not destroy the efficiency of things without taking away their existence.

# XX.

## ETHICAL DEFINITIONS. 1697–1698.

->[From the French.]<-

Regarding charity or disinterested love, about which I see that troublesome disputes have arisen, I think that one could not better resolve the issue than by providing a true definition of love. I believe that in the preface to the work [*Codex Diplomaticus Juris Gentium*], which is known to you, sir, I previously did this by identifying the source of justice. For JUSTICE is fundamentally nothing other than charity in accordance with wisdom. CHARITY is universal benevolence. BENEVOLENCE is a disposition or inclination to love, and it has the same relationship to love that habit has to action. And LOVE is this act or active state of the soul that makes us find our pleasure in the happiness or satisfaction of others. This definition, as I have since noted, is capable of solving the enigma of disinterested love and of distinguishing it from the bonds of self-interest or debauchery. I remember a conversation I had several years ago with the Count ————— and other friends, in which only human love was discussed; this problem was debated, and my solution was found satisfactory. When one loves a person sincerely, one does not seek one's own advantage or a pleasure separate from that of the beloved person, but instead seeks pleasure in the contentment and happiness of that person. And if this happiness did not please us for its own sake, but merely because of some advantage resulting from it for us, this would no longer be pure and sincere love. It must be, then, that pleasure is found immediately in this happiness, and that grief is found in the unhappiness of the beloved person. For whatever produces pleasure directly through itself is also desired for its own sake, as constituting (at least in part) the goal of our wishes, and as something that enters into our own happiness and gives us satisfaction.

This serves to reconcile two truths that appear incompatible: for we do everything for our own good, and it is impossible for us to feel otherwise, no matter what we may say. Nevertheless, we do not yet love completely purely when we seek the good of the beloved object not for its own sake and because it pleases us in itself, but because of an

<summary>Leibniz provides a series of ethical definitions, defining justice as charity guided by wisdom and love as finding one's own pleasure in the happiness of another. He argues that this definition reconciles the inherent human drive for self-interest with the possibility of pure, disinterested love.</summary>

<keywords>ethics, charity, justice, benevolence, love, disinterested love, Leibniz, Codex Diplomaticus Juris Gentium, felicity, self-interest</keywords>

--- Page 142 ---
<meta>This page continues Leibniz's philosophical letter to Nicaise from 1697, further refining the definition of disinterested love and its relationship to divine perfection and human happiness.</meta>

advantage we foresee from it. But it is apparent from the notion of love which we have just given that we seek, at the same time, our own good for ourselves and the good of the beloved object for its own sake, when the good of this object is immediately, ultimately (*ultimato*) and in itself our end, our pleasure, and our good; as happens in regard to all the things desired because they are pleasing in themselves, and are consequently good of themselves, even if one should have no regard for the consequences; these are ends and not means.

Now divine love is infinitely above the love of creatures, for other objects worthy of being loved constitute, in fact, part of our contentment or our happiness, insofar as their perfection touches us; while, on the other hand, the happiness of God does not compose a part of our happiness, but the whole. He is its source and not its accessory, and since the pleasures of lovable earthly objects can cause harm by their consequences, only the pleasure taken in the enjoyment of the divine perfections is surely and absolutely good, without the possibility of danger or excess.

These considerations show what the true disinterestedness of pure love consists of, which cannot be separated from our own contentment and happiness, as M. de la Trappe has aptly remarked. This is because our true happiness essentially embraces the knowledge of the happiness of God and of the divine perfections—that is to say, the love of God. And consequently, it is impossible to prefer one to the other by a thought founded on distinct notions. And to wish to separate oneself from oneself and from one's own good is to play with words; or, if you wish to look at the effects, it is to fall into an excessive quietism. It is to desire a mindless, or rather an affected and simulated inaction in which, under the pretext of resignation and the annihilation of the soul as it is swallowed up in God, one may move toward practical libertinism, or at least toward a hidden theoretical atheism, such as that of Averroës and others more ancient who taught that our soul finally lost itself in the universal spirit, and that this is perfect union with God.—*Extract from a letter to Nicaise, 1697.*

The error concerning pure love appears to be a misunderstanding, which, as I have already said to you, sir, comes perhaps from not paying sufficient attention to forming definitions of terms.

To LOVE truly and disinterestedly is nothing other than being led to find pleasure in the perfections or the happiness of the object, and consequently to experience grief in whatever may be contrary to these perfections. This love properly has as its object substances capable of happiness; however, some resemblance of this is found regarding objects that have perfections without being aware of them—as, for example, a beautiful picture. Someone who finds pleasure in contemplating it and would feel pain in seeing it ruined, even if it belonged to another, would love it, so to speak, with a disinterested love. This could not be said of someone who only had in view the profit from selling it or the winning of applause by displaying it, without otherwise caring whether or not it was ruined once it no longer belonged to him. This shows that pleasure and action cannot be removed from love without destroying it, and that *M. des Preaux* <note>Nicolas Boileau-Despréaux, a French poet and critic.</note> in the beautiful verses you sent me, was right both in recommending the importance of divine love and in opposing a love that is imaginary and ineffective. I explained my definition in the preface of my *Codex Diplomaticus Juris Gentium* (published before these new disputes arose), because I needed it to provide the definition of JUSTICE, which in my opinion is nothing but charity regulated according to wisdom. Since CHARITY is a universal benevolence, and BENEVOLENCE is a habit of loving, it was necessary to define what it means to love. And since to LOVE is to have a feeling that makes us find pleasure in what leads to the happiness of the beloved object, and since WISDOM (which forms the rule of justice) is nothing but the science of happiness, I showed through this analysis that happiness is the basis of justice. I also showed that those who would provide the true elements of jurisprudence—which I do not find laid down as they should be—ought to begin by establishing the science of happiness. This science does not yet appear well determined, although books on Ethics are full of discourses on blessedness or the supreme good.

As PLEASURE, which is nothing but the feeling of exceptional perfection, is one of the principal points of HAPPINESS—which in turn consists in a lasting state of possessing what is necessary to taste pleasure—it would be desirable if the science of pleasures, which the late *M. Lautin* <note>Jean-Baptiste Lantin, a French magistrate and scholar.</note> contemplated, had been completed.—->*Extract from a letter to Nicaise, 1698.*<-

[The following Ethical Definitions, translated from the Latin, are undated.]

Justice is the charity of the wise.
Charity is general benevolence.
Benevolence is the habit of love.
To love anyone is to delight in their happiness.
Wisdom is the science of happiness.
Happiness is lasting joy.
Joy is a state of pleasure.
Pleasure or delight is a sense of perfection; that is, a sense of something which helps or which sustains any power.
One is perfected whose power is increased or helped.
Demonstrate this hypothesis elsewhere:
The world is governed by the wisest and most powerful of monarchs, whom we call God.

### Propositions.

The end or aim of God is his own joy or love of himself.
God created creatures, and especially those endowed with mind, for his own glory or out of love for himself.
God created all things in accordance with the greatest harmony or beauty possible.
God loves all.
God bestows on all as much as is possible.
Neither hatred, nor wrath, nor sadness, nor envy belong to God.
God loves to be loved, and loves those who love him.
God loves souls in proportion to the perfection which he has given to each of them.
The perfection of the universe, or the harmony of things, does not allow all minds to be equally perfect.
The question of why God has given more perfection to one mind than to another is among senseless questions, as if you should ask whether the foot is too large or the shoe pinching the foot is too small. And this is a mystery, the ignorance of which has obscured the whole doctrine of the predestination and justice of God.
He who does not obey God is not the friend of God.
He who obeys God from fear is not yet the friend of God.
He who loves God above all things is at last the friend of God.
He who does not seek the common good does not obey God.
He who does not seek the glory of God does not obey God.

# XXI.

## ON THE CARTESIAN DEMONSTRATION OF THE EXISTENCE OF GOD.

->1700-1.<-

->[From the French.]<-

In truth, metaphysics is natural theology, and the same God who is the source of all good is also the principle of all knowledge. This is because the idea of God embraces that of absolute being—that is to say, what is simple in our thoughts, from which everything we think takes its origin. Descartes had not considered the matter from this side; he gives two ways of proving the existence of God: the *first is* that there is an idea of God within us, since we undoubtedly think of God and since we cannot think of anything without having an idea of it. Now, if we have an idea of God and if it is a true one—that is, if it is of an infinite being and if it represents Him faithfully—it cannot be caused by anything less, and consequently, God Himself must be its cause. He must therefore exist. The *other argument* is even shorter. It is that God is a being who possesses all perfections and, consequently, possesses existence, which is among the perfections; hence He exists. It must be confessed that these arguments are a little suspicious because they move too quickly and force a conclusion on us without enlightening us, whereas true demonstrations usually provide the mind with some solid nourishment. However, it is difficult to find the heart of the matter, and I see that a number of capable men who have raised objections to Descartes have overlooked this.

Some have believed that there is no idea of God because He is not subject to the imagination, assuming that an idea and an image are the same thing. I do not share their opinion, and I know well that there is an idea of thought, of existence, and of similar things for which there is no image. For when we think of something and notice what allowed us to recognize it, this, as it exists in our soul, is the idea of the thing. This is why there is also an idea of what is not material or imaginable.

Others admit that there is an idea of God, and that this idea embraces all perfections, but they cannot understand how existence follows from it—whether it be because they do not admit that existence is

<keywords>Descartes, ontological argument, existence of God, metaphysics, natural theology, ideas vs. images, perfections, absolute being</keywords>

<meta>This text continues Leibniz's philosophical reflections on the existence of God, specifically critiquing the Cartesian argument that existence follows from the idea of a perfect being. among the number of perfections, or because they do not see how a simple idea or thought can imply existence outside of us. For myself, I firmly believe that he who has acknowledged this idea of God and who fully sees that existence is a perfection, ought to admit that this perfection belongs to God. In fact, I do not doubt the idea of God any more than His existence; on the contrary, I claim that I have a demonstration of it. However, I would not want us to flatter ourselves and persuade ourselves that we could succeed in so great a matter at so little cost. Paralogisms are dangerous in this matter; when they are not successful, they backfire upon us and strengthen the opposing side. I say, then, that we must prove with all imaginable precision that there is an idea of an all-perfect being—that is to say, of God. It is true that the objections of those who think they can prove the contrary because there is no image of God are, as I have just shown, worthless; but it must also be admitted that the proof which Descartes offers for establishing the idea of God is imperfect. How, he will say, can we speak of God without thinking of Him? And could we think of God without having the idea of Him? Yes, undoubtedly; we sometimes think of impossible things, and this has even been demonstrated. For example, Descartes held that the quadrature of the circle is impossible, and yet we do not stop thinking of it and drawing conclusions as to what would happen if it were possible. *Motion of ultimate swiftness* is impossible in any body whatsoever, for if it were supposed in a circle, for example, another concentric circle, surrounding the first and attached firmly to it, would be moved with a velocity still greater than the first, which consequently is not of the ultimate degree, contrary to what we have supposed. Despite all this to the contrary, we think of this ultimate swiftness, which has no true idea since it is impossible. So *the greatest of all circles* is an impossible thing, and *a number made up of all possible units* is no less so: there is proof of it. And nevertheless, we think of all this. This is why there is certainly room to doubt whether the idea of *the greatest of all stars* is to be trusted and whether it does not involve some contradiction; for I well understand, for example, the nature of motion and of swiftness, and what "greatest" is. But for all that, I do not understand whether all this is compatible and whether there is a way of joining all this and making from it an idea of the greatest swiftness of which

<meta>This text continues Leibniz's critique of the Cartesian ontological argument. motion is capable. So although I know what a star is, and what "largest" and "most perfect" are, nevertheless, I do not yet know whether there is a hidden contradiction in joining all these together, as there is, in fact, in the other examples mentioned. That is to say, in a word, I do not know for all this whether such a star is possible; for if it were not, there would be no idea of it. However, I admit that God, in this respect, has a great advantage over all other things. For it is sufficient to prove that he is *possible* to prove that he exists—a thing not encountered anywhere else that I know of. Furthermore, I infer from this that there is a presumption that God exists, for there is always a presumption on the side of possibility; that is to say, everything is held to be possible until its impossibility is proven. There is, therefore, also a presumption that God is possible—that is, that he exists—since in him, existence is a consequence of the possibility. This may suffice for practical life, but it is not sufficient for a formal demonstration. I have debated much on this point with several Cartesians, but finally, I have gotten some of the more capable ones to frankly admit, after having understood the force of my arguments, that this possibility still remains to be demonstrated. There are even some who, after being challenged by me, have undertaken to demonstrate this, but they have not yet completed it.—*Extract from an undated letter to (probably) the Grand Duchess Sophia.*

---

I have not yet seen the work published at Basle in the year 1699, entitled *Judicium de argumento Cartesii pro existentia Dei petito ab ejus idea*; but having formerly casually examined the same argument in an essay *On Knowledge, Truth and Ideas*, inserted in the *Acta* of Leipzig in the year 1684, I am curious to read what a capable man says in the *Histoire des Ouvrages des Savans*, May 1700, in favor of the arguments of Descartes and against the Latin work published at Basle. And I will say to you, sir, that I hold a position midway between the work and the reply. The author of the work believes that the argument is a sophism, the author of the reply considers it a demonstration, and I myself believe that it is an imperfect argument which silently takes for granted a proposition the proof of which, if added, would complete the demonstration. Thus, the argument is not to be despised; it is at least a good beginning. *Est aliquid prodire tenus, si non datur ultra.*

<summary>Leibniz argues that the Cartesian proof for God's existence is incomplete because it assumes the logical possibility of a "most perfect being" without proving it. While he grants a presumption of God's existence for practical purposes, he insists that a rigorous demonstration requires proving that the idea of God contains no hidden contradictions.</summary>
<keywords>God, existence of God, possibility, demonstration, Cartesians, Descartes, Grand Duchess Sophia, Basle, Leipzig, 1684, 1699, 1700, ontological argument, perfection, logic, contradiction</keywords>

--- Page 149 ---
<meta>This text continues Leibniz’s critique of the ontological argument, specifically the transition from the "idea" of a perfect being to the "existence" of that being, emphasizing that one must first prove that such a being is logically possible.</meta>

Geometricians, who are the true masters of the art of reasoning, have seen that for demonstrations drawn from definitions to be valid, it is necessary to prove—or at least postulate—that the concept contained in the definition is possible. This is why Euclid placed among his *postulates* that the circle is something possible, by requesting that a circle be described when its center and radius are given. The same precaution applies to every kind of reasoning, and particularly to the argument of Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury (in *Liber contra insipientem* <note>Book Against the Fool</note>), cited and examined by St. Thomas and other Scholastics, and revived by Descartes, which proves that God, being the greatest or most perfect being, includes that perfection called *existence*, and that consequently He exists. To this, it may be said that the reasoning is sound, assuming that the supremely perfect being, or one that encompasses all perfections, is possible; and that it is the privilege of the divine nature (*ens a se* <note>a being through itself</note>) that its essence includes existence—that is, that it exists provided that it is possible. And even omitting all mention of perfection, it may be said that *if a necessary being is possible, it exists*. This is undoubtedly the most beautiful and the most important of modal propositions, because it provides a transition from potentiality to actuality, and it is only here that *posse ad esse valet consequentia* <note>the inference from possibility to existence is valid</note>. Also, the principle of existences is found here.

The author of the work presents a counter-example to Descartes, reasoning as he does but reaching a false conclusion; for he says that existence is contained in the idea of a very perfect body (or one which encompasses all perfection), and therefore such a body exists. In my opinion, the reply to this must be that the idea of a "very perfect body" in this sense is impossible, for a body, being limited by its essence, cannot include all perfections. The work and the reply rely a bit too much on the terms and distinctions of "real" (or "formal") and "objective," and "essence" and "existence," where I do not think it is necessary to follow them. It is enough to remark that the author of the work, having considered the reasoning of those who say that *God must necessarily exist because it is not impossible for God to be*, has touched upon the essential point and has replied reasonably well that it does not follow that a thing is possible simply because we do not see its impossibility, our knowledge being limited. But this might have led him to think that the argument is not a sophism and that those who have proposed it

<summary>Leibniz argues that for God's existence to be proven from His definition, one must first prove that the concept of a supremely perfect being is logically possible. He asserts that while "possibility implies existence" is unique to God, we cannot assume possibility simply because we do not perceive a contradiction.</summary>

The author of the reply, as far as I can understand him, does not investigate this sufficiently; he has good reason (p. 211) for rejecting this restriction: *that a wholly perfect being includes existence if it be supposed that there is a wholly perfect being*, that is to say, an actual one. But if we understand it this way: *if it be supposed that a wholly perfect being is possible, or exists among essences*, then the restriction is valid. He is right in saying that it is not permissible to doubt things which are known to us under the pretext that our knowledge is limited. But this does not appear to be the meaning of the author of the work. I have already remarked in my previously mentioned essay that the true sign of perfectly distinct knowledge is that the possibility of the concept in question can be proved *a priori* <note>reasoning from causes to effects, or from first principles</note>. Thus, he is fundamentally wrong here in attributing to himself a clear and distinct concept when he cannot verify it by the sign which is essential to it. The example of the proposition that *two and two are four* is not applicable here because it can be demonstrated by definitions whose possibility is already recognized.

I have already elsewhere given my opinion concerning St. Anselm's demonstration of the existence of God, revived by Descartes; the substance of which is that that which embraces in its idea all perfections, or the greatest of all possible beings, also includes existence in its essence, since existence is among the perfections, and otherwise something could be added to that which is perfect. I take a middle position between those who take this reasoning for a sophism <note>a clever but false argument</note> and the opinion of Reverend Father Lami, explained here, who considers it a complete demonstration. I admit, then, that it is a demonstration, but an imperfect one, which demands or supposes a truth which deserves to be further demonstrated. For it is tacitly supposed that GOD, or the PERFECT BEING, is possible. If this point were again demonstrated, as it should be, it could be said that the existence of God was demonstrated geometrically *a priori*. And this shows what I have

<meta>This text continues the critique of the ontological argument, transitioning from the requirement of proving an idea's possibility to a simpler demonstration of God's existence based on the definition of a necessary being.</meta>

...already said, we cannot reason perfectly about ideas except by knowing their possibility. Geometricians have paid attention to this, but the Cartesians have not done so sufficiently. However, it can be said that this demonstration is nonetheless important and, so to speak, presumptive. For every being must be considered possible until its impossibility is proven. I doubt, however, whether Reverend Father Lami was right in saying that it was adopted by the School <note>The Scholastic philosophers of the medieval universities</note>. For the author of the marginal note remarks here, quite justly, that St. Thomas had rejected it.

However this may be, an even simpler demonstration might be formed, not mentioning perfections at all, so as not to be stopped by those who might venture to deny that all perfections are compatible, and consequently that the idea in question is possible. For by simply saying that God is a being of itself or primitive, <term>*ens a se*</term>, that is, one which exists by its essence, it is easy to conclude from this definition that such a being exists if it is possible. Or rather, this conclusion is a corollary which is derived immediately from the definition and hardly differs from it. For the essence of a thing being only that which constitutes its particular possibility, it is very clear that to exist by its essence is to exist by its possibility. And if the *being of itself* were defined in even closer terms, by saying that it is the *being which must exist because it is possible*, it is manifest that all that could be said against the existence of such a being would be to deny its possibility.

On this subject, we might again form a modal proposition, which would be one of the best fruits of all logic: namely, that *if a necessary being is possible, it exists*. For *necessary being* and *being by its essence* are one and the same thing. Thus, the reasoning taken from this angle appears to have solidity; and those who insist that actual existence can never be inferred from mere notions, ideas, definitions, or possible essences, in truth fall into what I have just said—namely, they deny the possibility of *being of itself*. But it is well to notice that this angle itself serves to show that they are wrong, and finally fills the gap in the demonstration. For if *being of itself* is impossible, all beings through *others* are also impossible, since they exist ultimately only through a being of itself; thus, nothing could exist. This reasoning leads us to another important modal proposition, equal to the preceding one, and which, joined with it, completes the demonstration. It might be

# XXII.
# CONSIDERATIONS ON THE DOCTRINE OF A UNIVERSAL SPIRIT. 1702.

Many ingenious people have believed, and believe now, that there is but one spirit, which is universal and which animates the entire universe and all its parts, each one according to its structure and organs, just as the same breath of wind makes the various pipes of an organ produce different sounds. They believe that when an animal has its organs well-placed, it produces the effect of an individual soul, but when the organs are spoiled, this individual soul again becomes nothingness, or returns, so to speak, into the ocean of the universal spirit.

Aristotle has seemed to many to hold a similar opinion, which Averroes, a celebrated Arabian philosopher, has renewed. He believed that there was in us an *intellectus agens* or active understanding, and also an *intellectus patiens* or passive understanding: that the former, coming from without, was eternal and universal for all, but that the passive understanding was unique to each person and departed at the death of man. In the last two or three centuries, this has been the doctrine of some Peripatetics, such as Pomponatius, Contarenus, and others; and traces of it are to be recognized in the late M. Naudé, as his letters and the *Naudæana*, which have been lately published, show. They taught this in secret to their most intimate and best-qualified disciples, while in public they had the cleverness to say that this doctrine was in reality true according to philosophy—by which they understood that of Aristotle *par excellence*—but that it was false according to faith. From this, finally, have arisen the disputes over the "double truth" which the last Lateran Council condemned.

I have been told that Queen Christina had a decided leaning toward this opinion, and as M. Naudé, who was her librarian, was imbued with it, he probably communicated to her what he knew of the secret views of the celebrated philosophers with whom he had had intercourse in Italy. Spinoza, who admits only one substance, is not far removed from the doctrine of a single, universal spirit, and even the New Cartesians, who claim that God alone acts, establish it likewise without noticing it. Apparently Molinos and several

Other New Quietists—among them a certain Joannes Angelus Silesius, who wrote before Molinos and whose works have recently been reprinted, and even Weigelius before them—embraced this opinion of the sabbath or rest of souls in God. This is why they believed that the cessation of specific functions was the highest state of perfection.

It is true that the Peripatetic philosophers did not make this spirit entirely universal; for besides the intelligences which, according to them, animated the stars, they posited an intelligence for this world here below, and this intelligence performed the role of the active understanding in the souls of men. They were led to this doctrine of an immortal soul common to all men by false reasoning. For they took for granted that an actual infinite multiplicity is impossible and that it was therefore not possible for there to be an infinite number of souls—though there *must* be, nevertheless, if individual souls existed. Since the world and the human race were, according to them, eternal, and new souls were always being born, if these all continued to exist, there would now be an actual infinity. This reasoning was considered proof among them, but it was full of false suppositions. For neither the impossibility of actual infinity, nor the idea that the human race has existed eternally, nor the generation of new souls would be admitted [as certain], since the Platonists teach the preexistence of souls and the Pythagoreans teach metempsychosis, claiming that a certain fixed number of souls remains forever and undergoes changes.

The doctrine of a universal spirit is good in itself, for all those who teach it effectively admit the existence of divinity—whether they believe that this universal spirit is supreme (in which case they hold that it is God himself) or whether they believe, with the Cabalists, that God created it. This latter view was also the opinion of Henry More, an Englishman, and of certain other modern philosophers, and especially of certain chemists who believed in a universal Archæus or world-spirit; some have even maintained that it was this spirit of the Lord which, as the beginning of Genesis says, “moved upon the waters.”

But when they go so far as to say that this universal spirit is the only spirit and that there are no souls or individual spirits, or at least that these individual souls cease to exist, I believe that they exceed the limits of reason and propose, without grounds, a doctrine

I have shown above that the alleged demonstration of the <term>Peripatetics</term>, who maintained that there was but one spirit common to all men, has no force and rests only on false suppositions. <term>Spinoza</term> has claimed to prove that there is only one substance in the world, but these proofs are contemptible or unintelligible. One of the most obvious reasons urged against individual souls is the difficulty regarding their origin. The <term>scholastic philosophers</term> have disputed greatly over the origin of <term>forms</term>, among which they include souls. Opinions differed greatly as to whether there was an <term>eduction</term> of power from matter, just as a statue is extracted from marble; or whether there was a <term>traduction</term> of souls, so that a new soul should be born of a preceding soul just as one fire is lit from another; or whether souls already existed and only made themselves known after the <term>generation</term> of the animal; or finally, whether souls were created by God every time there was a new generation.

Those who denied individual souls believed that they were thereby freeing themselves from all difficulties, but this is cutting the knot instead of untying it. There is no force in an argument that would run like this: *the explanations of a doctrine have been varied; therefore, the whole doctrine is false.* This is the way skeptics reason, and if it were accepted, there would be nothing that could not be rejected. The experiments of our time lead us to believe that souls, and even animals, have always existed—although in a small volume—and that <term>generation</term> is only a kind of growth. In my opinion, what has greatly contributed to inclining brilliant individuals toward the doctrine of a single <term>universal spirit</term> is the fact that ordinary philosophers popularized a theory concerning <term>separate souls</term> and the functions of the soul as being independent of the body and of the organs, which they could not sufficiently justify. They had good reason for wishing to maintain the <term>immortality of the soul</term> as being in accordance with divine perfections and true morality; but seeing that, at death, the organs visible in animals became disordered and finally decayed, they believed themselves obliged to resort to the idea of "separate souls"—that is to say, to believe that the soul existed without any body and did not even then cease to have its thoughts and activities. And in order to better prove this, they tried to show that the soul, even in this life, has abstract thoughts independent of material ideas. Now, those who rejected this separate state and this independence as being contrary to experience and reason were all the more compelled to believe in the extinction of the individual soul and the preservation of only the single, universal spirit.

I have examined this matter carefully, and I have proved that there are indeed in the soul some materials of thought or objects of the understanding which the external senses do not provide—namely, the soul itself and its activities (*nihil est in intellectu quod non fuerit in sensu, nisi ipse intellectus* <note>"Nothing is in the intellect which was not first in the senses, except the intellect itself."</note>); and those who believe in a universal spirit will readily grant this, since they distinguish it from matter. I find, nevertheless, that there is never an abstract thought which is not accompanied by some images or physical traces, and I have established a perfect <term>parallelism</term> between what takes place in the soul and what takes place in matter. I have shown that the soul, with its activities, is something distinct from matter, but that it is nevertheless always accompanied by organs which must correspond to it; and that this relationship is reciprocal and always will be.

Nature has given us an example in sleep and fainting, which ought to make us believe that death is not a cessation of all functions, but only a suspension of certain more noticeable functions. And I have explained elsewhere an important point which, not having been sufficiently considered, has the more easily inclined men toward the opinion of the mortality of souls: namely, that a large number of minute perceptions—equal and balanced, having no background and no distinguishing marks—are not noticed and cannot be remembered. But to wish to conclude from this that the soul is then altogether without functions is the same thing as when ordinary people believe that there is a vacuum or nothing where there is no visible matter, and that the earth is without motion because its motion is not noticeable, being uniform and without jolts. 

We have innumerable minute perceptions which we cannot distinguish; a great deafening noise—as, for example, the murmur of a whole assembled crowd—is composed of all the little murmurs of individual persons which we would not notice separately, but of which we nevertheless have a sensation; otherwise, we would not be aware of the whole. So when an animal is deprived of the organs capable of giving it sufficiently distinct perceptions, it does not follow at all that there do not remain to it smaller and more uniform perceptions, nor that it is deprived of all organs and all perceptions. The organs are only folded up and reduced to a small volume, but the order of nature demands that everything redevelop and, some day, return to a visible state, and that there be in these changes a certain well-regulated progress which serves to make things ripen and become perfect. It appears that Democritus himself saw this resuscitation of animals, for Plotinus says that he taught a resurrection.

Here are some of them: you see, in the first place, that the comparison to the wind, which makes various pipes sound differently, appeals to the imagination but explains nothing—or rather, it implies exactly the opposite. For this universal breath in the pipes is only a collection of many separate breaths; furthermore, each pipe is filled with its own air which can even pass from one pipe to another. Thus, this comparison would actually establish the existence of individual souls and would even support the transmigration of souls from one body to another, as air can change pipes.

And if we imagine that the universal spirit is like an ocean, composed of countless drops which are detached from it when they animate some particular organic body, but reunite with the ocean after the destruction of the organs, you are again forming a physical and crude concept that does not fit the subject and gets caught in the same difficulties as the "breath" analogy. For just as the ocean is a collection of drops, God would likewise be an assembly of all souls, much like a swarm of bees is an assembly of those small creatures. But since this swarm is not a real substance in itself, it is clear that in this view, the universal spirit would not be a true being. Instead of saying that it is the only spirit, we would have to say that it is nothing at all in itself, and that nature contains only individual souls, of which the spirit would merely be the mass. Moreover, these drops, once reunited with the ocean of the universal spirit after the destruction of the organs, would actually be souls existing separately from matter. We would then fall back into the very position we wished to avoid, especially if these drops retain something of their previous state or still have some functions—and might even acquire more sublime ones—within the ocean of divinity or the universal spirit. For if you claim that these souls, once reunited with God, lack any function of their own, you fall into an opinion contrary to reason and all sound philosophy; it is as if any existing being could ever reach a state where it would be without any function or impression. Simply because one thing is joined to another, it does not cease to have its own particular functions, which, when joined with those of the other, produce the functions of the whole. There are a number of individual active beings, since there are a number of particular and opposite actions and passions <note>In this philosophical context, "passions" refers to being acted upon or passive states, the opposite of "actions."</note>, which could not be attributed to the same subject; and these active beings are the individual souls.

We know also that there are degrees in all things. There is an infinity of degrees between any movement and perfect repose, between hardness and a perfect fluidity which is without any resistance, and between God and nothingness. There is likewise an infinity of degrees between any active being whatsoever and a purely passive being. Consequently, it is not reasonable to admit only one active being—namely the universal spirit—with a single passive being—namely matter.

It must also be considered that matter is not a thing opposed to God, but that it is rather opposed to the limited active being; that is, to the soul or to form. For God, from whom matter as well as form comes, is the supreme being opposed to nothingness; and the purely passive is something more than nothingness, being capable of something, while nothing can be attributed to nothingness. Thus, with each particular portion of matter must be connected the particular forms—that is, souls and spirits—which belong to it.

I do not wish here to refer back to a demonstrative argument which I have employed elsewhere, and which is drawn from the unities or simple things, among which individual souls are included. For this unavoidably obliges us not only to admit individual souls, but also to avow that they are immortal by their nature, and as indestructible as the universe; and, what is more, that each soul is in its way a mirror of the universe, without any interruption, and that it contains in its depths an order corresponding to that of the universe itself. The souls diversify and represent the universe in an infinity of ways—all different and all true—and multiply it, so to speak, as many times as is possible, so that in this way they approach divinity as much as is possible, according to their different degrees, and give to the universe all the perfection of which it is capable.

After this, I do not see on what reason or probability the doctrine of individual souls can be challenged. Those who do so admit that what is in us is an effect of the universal spirit. But the effects of God are self-sustaining, not to say that even the modifications and effects of creatures are in a way durable, and that their impressions only unite without being destroyed. Therefore, if in accordance with

<summary>The author argues for the existence of individual souls as distinct active beings, asserting that they are immortal, indestructible unities that mirror the universe's complexity and approach divinity through their various degrees of perfection.</summary>

Reason and experience, as we have shown, demonstrate that the animal—with its more or less distinct perceptions and with certain organs—always subsists. If, consequently, this effect of God always subsists in these organs, why would it not be permissible to call it the soul, and to say that this effect of God is a soul, immaterial and immortal, which in a way imitates the universal spirit? Moreover, this doctrine resolves all difficulties, as is apparent from what I have just stated here and in other writings which I have produced on these subjects.

## XXIII.

# ON THE SUPERSENSIBLE ELEMENT IN KNOWLEDGE, AND ON THE IMMATERIAL IN NATURE: A Letter to Queen Charlotte of Prussia, 1702.

->[From the French.]<-

Madame:

The letter written not long ago from Paris to Osnabruck, which I recently read by your order at Hanover, seemed truly ingenious and beautiful to me. And as it deals with two important questions—*whether there is something in our thoughts that does not come from the senses*, and *whether there is something in nature that is not material*—concerning which I acknowledge that I do not entirely share the opinion of the letter's author, I should like to be able to explain myself with the same grace as he, in order to obey your commands and satisfy Your Majesty's curiosity.

We use the external senses as a blind man uses a stick—to use the comparison of one of the ancients—and they let us know their specific objects, which are colors, sounds, odors, flavors, and tactile qualities, but they do not let us know what these sensible qualities are, nor in what they consist. For example, whether red is the rotation of certain small globules claimed to cause light; whether heat is the whirling of a very fine dust; whether sound is made in the air like circles in the water when a stone is thrown into it, as certain philosophers claim—this is what we do not see. And we could not even understand how this rotation, these whirlings, and these circles, if they were real, should cause exactly these perceptions of red, heat, and noise that we have. Thus, it may be said that sensible qualities are in fact occult qualities, and that there must be others more manifest which can make the former more explicable. And far from understanding only sensible things, it is exactly these that we understand the least. And although they are familiar to us, we do not understand them any better because of it; just as a pilot understands the nature of the magnetic needle that turns toward the north no better than any other person, although he always has it before his

<summary>The author begins a letter to Queen Charlotte of Prussia to discuss whether all knowledge originates in the senses and whether nature contains immaterial elements. He argues that sensory perceptions like color and heat are "occult qualities" because the senses reveal their presence but not their true underlying nature.</summary>
<keywords>epistemology, sensory perception, immateriality, Queen Charlotte of Prussia, occult qualities, external senses, philosophy of mind</keywords>

--- Page 164 ---
<meta>This page continues the 1702 letter to Queen Charlotte of Prussia regarding the nature of knowledge and the distinction between sensory perception and the understanding.</meta>

eyes in the compass, and although he does not admire it any the more for that reason.

I do not deny that many discoveries have been made concerning the nature of these occult qualities; for example, we know by what kind of refraction blue and yellow are formed, and that these two colors mixed form green. But for all this, we cannot yet understand how the perception we have of these three colors results from these causes. Also, we do not even have nominal definitions of such qualities by which to explain terms. The purpose of nominal definitions is to give sufficient marks by which a thing may be recognized; for example, assayers have marks by which they distinguish gold from every other metal, and even if a man had never seen gold, these signs might be taught to him so that he would infallibly recognize it if he should some day meet with it. But it is not the same with these sensible qualities, and marks to recognize blue, for example, could not be given if we had never seen it. So it is that blue is its own mark, and in order for a man to know what blue is, it must necessarily be shown to him.

It is for this reason that we are accustomed to say that the notions of these qualities are *clear*, for they serve to recognize them; but these same notions are not *distinct*, because we cannot distinguish or develop that which they include. It is an *I know not what* of which we are conscious, but for which we cannot account. Whereas we can make another understand what a thing is of which we have some description or nominal definition, even though we should not have the thing itself at hand to show him. However, we must do the senses the justice of saying that, in addition to these occult qualities, they make us know other qualities which are more manifest and which furnish more distinct notions. And these are those which we ascribe to *common sense*, because there is no external sense to which they are particularly attached and belong. And here, definitions of the terms or words employed may be given. Such is the idea of numbers, which is found equally in sounds, colors, and touch. It is thus that we perceive also *figures*, which are common to colors and to touch, but which we do not notice in sounds. Although it is true that in order to conceive distinctly numbers and even figures, and to form sciences of them, we must come to something which the senses cannot furnish, and which the understanding adds to the senses.

<meta>This page continues a philosophical discussion on the distinction between sensory perception, the imagination, and the pure understanding, specifically addressing how mathematical and metaphysical ideas are formed.</meta>

Just as our soul compares, for example, the numbers and shapes found in colors with the numbers and shapes found by touch, there must be an *internal sense* in which the perceptions of these different external senses are found united. This is what is called the *imagination*, which simultaneously includes the notions of the *particular*, which are *clear but confused*, and the notions of the *common sense*, which are *clear and distinct*. These clear and distinct ideas, which are subject to the imagination, are the objects of the mathematical sciences—namely, arithmetic and geometry (which are *pure mathematical sciences*) and the application of these sciences to nature (forming *mixed mathematics*). It is also evident that particular sensory qualities are capable of being explained and reasoned about only insofar as they involve what is common to the objects of several external senses and belong to the internal sense. For those who try to explain sensory qualities clearly always turn to the ideas of mathematics, and these ideas involve *size or a multitude of parts*. It is true that the mathematical sciences would not be demonstrative—and would consist of a simple induction or observation, which would never guarantee the perfect universality of the truths found there—if something higher, which *intelligence alone* can provide, did not come to the aid of the imagination and the senses.

There are, therefore, objects of an even different nature which are not included at all in what is observed in the objects of the senses, whether specifically or in common, and which consequently are not objects of the imagination either. Thus, besides the *sensible and imageable*, there is that which is *purely intelligible*, being the object of the *understanding alone*; such is the object of my thought when I think of myself.

This thought of the *Ego*, which perceives sensory objects, and of my own action resulting from it, adds something to the objects of the senses. To think of a color and to observe that one is thinking of it are two very different thoughts—as different as the color is from the Ego that thinks of it. And as I conceive that other beings may also have the right to say *I*, or that it could be said for them, it is through this that I conceive what is called *substance in general*. It is also the consideration of the Ego itself which provides other metaphysical notions, such as cause, effect, action, similarity, etc., and even those of *logic* and of *ethics*. Thus, it can be said that

He distinguishes between sensory qualities and the intelligible reflection of the self, which forms the basis for logic and ethics.</summary>

<keywords>internal sense, imagination, mathematical sciences, arithmetic, geometry, mixed mathematics, intelligence, sensible, imageable, intelligible, understanding, Ego, substance in general, logic, ethics</keywords>

...there is nothing in the understanding which does not come from the senses, except the understanding itself, or that which understands.

There are, then, three levels of ideas: the *purely sensory*, which are the objects appropriate to each specific sense; the sensory and, at the same time, *intellectual*, which pertain to the common sense; and the *purely intellectual*, which belong to the understanding. The first and the second can both be imagined, but the third are beyond the imagination. The second and third are intellectual and distinct, but the first are confused, even if they are clear or recognizable.

*Being* itself and *truth* are not known entirely through the senses, for it would not be impossible for a creature to have long and orderly dreams, resembling our *life*, of such a kind that everything it thought it perceived through the senses was nothing but a mere *appearance*. There must, therefore, be something beyond the senses that distinguishes the true from the apparent. However, the truth of the demonstrative sciences is free from these doubts, and must even serve as a standard for judging the truth of sensory things. For as capable philosophers, both ancient and modern, have already well-noted: even if everything I think I see were only a dream, it would still be true that I, who think while dreaming, would be something, and would actually think in many ways, for which there must always be some reason.

Thus, what the ancient Platonists observed is very true and very worthy of consideration: that the existence of <note>Based on the context and the contrast later in the sentence, the original text likely meant to say "intellectual things" here rather than "sensible things."</note> sensory things, and particularly of the *Ego* that thinks and is called the spirit or soul, is incomparably more certain than the existence of sensory things. Thus, speaking with metaphysical rigor, it would not be impossible for there to be, at heart, only these intellectual substances, and that sensory things are merely appearances. On the other hand, our lack of attention makes us mistake sensory things for the only real things. It is also worth observing that if I were to discover any demonstrative truth—mathematical or otherwise—while dreaming (as might actually happen), it would be just as certain as if I had been awake. This shows us how intellectual truth is independent of the truth or the external existence of sensory and material things.

This concept of *being* and of *truth* is therefore found in the

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of the understanding and the "natural light" of reason, completing the thought from the previous page that certain truths are fundamentally internal to the self.</meta>

incontestable in the Ego and in the understanding, rather than in the external senses and in the perception of external objects.

There we also find what it is to affirm, to deny, to doubt, to will, and to act. But above all, we find there the force of the consequences of reasoning, which are a part of what is called the natural light. For example, from this premise, that *no wise man is wicked*, we may, by reversing the terms, draw this conclusion: that *no wicked man is wise*. Whereas from this sentence, that *every wise man is praiseworthy*, we cannot conclude by reversing it that *everyone praiseworthy is wise*, but only that *some praiseworthy ones are wise*. Although we may always reverse particular affirmative propositions—for example, if *some wise man is rich*, it must also be that *some rich men are wise*—this cannot be done in particular negatives. For example, we may say that *there are charitable persons who are not just*, which happens when charity is not sufficiently regulated; but we cannot infer from this that *there are just persons who are not charitable*; for in justice are included at the same time charity and the rule of reason.

It is also by this natural light that the axioms of mathematics are recognized; for example, that *if from two equal things the same quantity be taken away, the things which remain are equal*; likewise that *if in a balance everything is equal on the one side and on the other, neither will incline*—a thing which we foresee without ever having experienced it. It is upon such foundations that we establish arithmetic, geometry, mechanics, and the other demonstrative sciences, in which, in truth, the senses are very necessary in order to have certain ideas of sensible things, and experiences are necessary to establish certain facts, and even useful to verify reasonings as by a kind of proof. But the force of the demonstrations depends upon intelligible notions and truths, which alone are capable of making us discern what is necessary, and which, in the conjectural sciences, are even capable of determining demonstratively the degree of probability concerning certain given suppositions, in order that we may choose rationally among opposite appearances the one which is greatest. Nevertheless, this part of the art of reasoning has not yet been cultivated as much as it ought to be.

But to return to necessary truths, it is universally true that we know them only by this natural light, and not at all by the experi-

For example, although we may have experienced countless times that every massive body tends toward the center of the earth and is not sustained in the air, we are not sure that this is necessary as long as we do not understand the reason for it. Thus, we could not be sure that the same thing would occur in the air at a higher altitude, at a hundred or more leagues above us; and there are philosophers who imagine that the earth is a magnet, and as the ordinary magnet does not attract a needle when it is moved a little distance from it, they think that the attractive force of the earth does not extend very far either. I do not say that they are right, but I do say that one cannot go very certainly beyond the experiences he has had if he is not aided by reason.

This is why geometricians have always considered that what is only proved by *induction* or by examples in geometry or in arithmetic is never perfectly proved. For

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the distinction between empirical observations and universal truths, arguing that while the senses provide the material for thought, the "natural light" of reason within us is necessary to understand universal and absolute principles.</meta>

In truth, there are *experiments* that succeed countless times and under normal circumstances, yet it is found in some extraordinary cases that there are *instances* where the experiment does not succeed. For example, if we have found a thousand times that iron placed by itself on the surface of water sinks to the bottom, we are not certain that this must always happen. And without turning to the miracle of the prophet Elisha, who made the iron float, we know that an iron pot may be made so hollow that it floats, and that it can even carry a considerable weight besides, just as boats made of copper or tin do. Even abstract sciences like geometry furnish cases in which what normally occurs no longer does. For example, we normally find that two lines which continually approach each other eventually meet, and many people would almost swear that this could never be otherwise. Nevertheless, geometry provides us with extraordinary lines, which for this reason are called *asymptotes*, which when extended *ad infinitum* continually approach each other and yet never meet.

This consideration also shows that there is a *light born within us*. For since the senses and induction could never teach us truths that are thoroughly universal, nor those that are absolutely necessary, but only what currently is and what is found in particular examples; and since we nevertheless know the necessary and universal truths of the sciences—a privilege we have over the beasts—it follows that we have derived these truths in part from what is within us. Thus, we may lead a child to these truths through simple questions, in the manner of Socrates, without telling him anything and without making him experiment at all on the truth of what he is asked. This could very easily be practiced with numbers and other similar matters.

I agree, nevertheless, that in our present state, the external senses are necessary for us to think, and that if we had none, we could not think. But that which is necessary for something does not, for that reason, constitute its essence. Air is necessary for life, but life is something other than air. The senses provide us with the material for reasoning, and we never have thoughts so abstract that something from the senses is not mingled with them; but reasoning requires something else in addition to what comes from the senses.

As to the second question—whether there are *immaterial substances*—in order to solve it, it is first necessary to explain oneself. Until now, matter has been understood as that which includes only purely passive and indifferent concepts: namely, extension and impenetrability, which must be determined by something else to take any form or action. Thus, when it is said that there are immaterial substances, it means that there are substances which include other concepts—namely, perception and the principle of action or of change—which could not be explained by either extension or impenetrability. These beings, when they have feeling, are called *souls*, and when they are capable of reason, they are called *spirits*. Thus, if one says that force and perception are essential to matter, they are treating matter as a corporeal substance that is complete, which includes both form and matter, or the soul along with the organs. It is as if it were said that there were souls everywhere. This might be true, and it would not be contrary to the doctrine of immaterial substances. For it is not intended that these souls be outside of matter, but simply that they are something more than matter, and are neither produced nor destroyed by the changes which matter undergoes, nor subject to dissolution, since they are not composed of parts.

Nevertheless, it must also be admitted that there is *substance separated from matter*. To see this, one has only to consider *that there are numberless forms which matter might have received in place of the series of variations which it has actually received.* For it is clear, for example, that the stars could move quite otherwise, as space and matter are indifferent to every kind of motion and figure.

Hence, the reason or universal determining cause by which things exist, and exist as they are rather than otherwise, must be outside of matter. And even the existence of matter depends on this, since we do not find in its concept that it carries within itself the reason for its own existence.

Now this ultimate reason of things—which is common to them all and universal because of the connection existing between all parts of nature—is what we call *God*, who must necessarily be an infinite and absolutely perfect substance. I am inclined to think that all immaterial finite substances (even the genii or angels according to the opinion of the ancient Church Fathers) are united

Perception also could not be explained by any mechanism whatsoever. It is in this also that our virtue and perfection consist, just as our happiness consists in the pleasure which we take in it.

And since every time we penetrate into the depths of things, we find there the most beautiful order we could wish for, even surpassing what we have imagined there, as all those who have fathomed the sciences know; we may conclude that it is the same in all the rest. Not only do immaterial substances always exist, but their lives, progress, and changes are also regulated to advance toward a certain end, or rather to approach it more and more, as do the *asymptotes*. And although we sometimes recoil, like lines which move backward, advancement nonetheless finally prevails and wins.

The natural light of reason does not suffice for knowing the details of this, and our experiences are still too limited to catch a glimpse of the laws of this order. The revealed light guides us meanwhile through faith, but there is reason to believe that in the course of time we shall know them even more by experience, and that there are spirits which know them already more than we do.

<header>XXIV.</header>

# AN EXPLANATION OF CERTAIN POINTS IN HIS PHILOSOPHY: An Extract from a letter to Lady Masham. 1704.

->[From the French.]<-

Since I am entirely in favor of the principle of uniformity—which I believe nature observes in the heart of things even while it varies in its methods, degrees, and perfections—my entire hypothesis consists of recognizing in substances that are hidden from our view and observation something parallel to what appears in those within our reach. Thus, assuming for now that there is within us a simple being endowed with action and perception, I think that nature would be poorly connected if the particle of matter forming human bodies were the only thing endowed with that which would make it infinitely different from everything else (even in terms of physics) and completely different in kind from all other known bodies. This leads me to believe that such active beings are present everywhere in matter, and that there is no difference between them except in their manner of perception. And since our own perceptions are sometimes accompanied by reflection and sometimes not—and because reflection leads to abstractions and universal, necessary truths, no traces of which are to be seen in animals and even less in the other bodies surrounding us—there is reason to believe that this simple being within us, which is called the soul, is distinguished by this from the souls of other known bodies.

Whether these principles of action and perception are called *Forms*, *Entelechies*, *Souls*, or *Spirits*, or whether these terms are distinguished according to the concepts one wishes to attribute to these things, the things themselves will not be changed by it. You will ask what becomes of these simple beings or souls that I place in animals and in other creatures, insofar as they are organic; I reply that they must be no less inextinguishable than our own souls, and that they cannot be produced or destroyed by the forces of nature.

Furthermore, to maintain the analogy of the *future* or *past*, as well as of *other* bodies, with what we experience at *present* in our own bodies, I maintain that not only do these souls or entelechies all have a

He concludes that these "simple beings" in animals and organic matter are just as indestructible by natural means as the human soul.</summary>
<keywords>Leibniz, Lady Masham, principle of uniformity, substance, perception, reflection, soul, entelechy, organic creatures, immortality</keywords>

...sort of organic body with them, proportioned to their perceptions, but also that they will always have one, and have always had one, as long as they have existed; so that not only the soul but also the animal itself (or that which is analogous to soul and animal, not to dispute over names) remains. *This very maxim—not to suppose unnecessarily anything in creatures except what corresponds to our experiences—has led me to my System of the Pre-established Harmony.* For we experience that bodies act among themselves according to mechanical laws, and that souls produce within themselves some internal actions. And we see no way of conceiving the action of the soul upon matter, or of matter upon the soul, or anything corresponding to it; for it cannot be explained by any machine how material variations—that is to say, mechanical laws—cause perception to arise; nor how perception can produce a change of velocity or of direction in animal spirits and other bodies, however subtle or coarse they may be. Thus, the inconceivability of any other hypothesis, as much as the good order of nature which is always uniform (not to mention other considerations), has made me believe that the soul and the body follow their laws perfectly, each one its own separately,

without the laws of the body being troubled by the actions of the soul, and without bodies finding windows through which to influence souls. It will then be asked where this agreement of the soul with the body comes from. The defenders of *occasional causes* teach that God accommodates the soul to the body and the body to the soul at every moment. But since it is impossible for this to be anything other than miraculous, it is unsuited to a philosophy that must explain the ordinary course of nature; for it would be necessary for God to continually disturb the natural laws of bodies. This is why I believed it was infinitely more worthy of God’s economy and of the uniformity and harmony of his work to conclude that he created souls and bodies at the beginning in such a way that each, while following its own laws, agrees with the other. It cannot be denied that this is possible for him whose wisdom and power are infinite. In this, I still only attribute to souls and bodies, for all time and everywhere, what we experience in them whenever that experience is distinct—that is to say, mechanical laws in bodies and internal actions in the soul. The whole consists only in the present state joined with the tendency toward changes, which take place in the body according to moving forces and in the soul according to the perceptions of good and evil.

The only surprising thing that follows from this is that the works of God are infinitely more beautiful and more harmonious than previously believed. And it may be said that the subterfuge of the Epicureans against the argument drawn from the beauty of visible things—when they say that among the countless productions of chance it is not surprising if some world like our own has passably succeeded—is destroyed; for the perpetual correspondence of beings that have no influence upon one another can only come from a common cause of this harmony. Mr. Bayle (who is profound), having meditated on the consequences of this hypothesis, acknowledges that one never more highly exalted what we call divine perfections, and that the infinite wisdom of God, great as it is, is not too great to produce such a pre-established harmony, the possibility of which he seemed to doubt. But I had him consider that even men produce *automata* that act as if they were rational, and that God (who is an infinitely greater artist, or rather, with whom everything is art to the greatest extent possible) has traced out the path for matter in order to make it act as minds require. XXV.

## CONSIDERATIONS ON THE PRINCIPLES OF LIFE AND ON PLASTIC NATURES; by the Author of the System of Pre-established Harmony. 1705.

->[From the French.]<-

As the dispute that has arisen over *plastic natures* and the *principles of life* has given the celebrated persons interested in it the occasion to speak of my system, for which some explanation seems to be required (see *Biblioth. Chois.*, vol. 5, art. 5, p. 301, and also *l’ Histoire des Ouvrages des Savans*, of 1704, art. 7, p. 393), I have thought it would be appropriate to add something to what I have already published on the subject in various passages of the *Journals* quoted by Bayle in his Dictionary, article *Rorarius*. I indeed admit principles of life diffused throughout all nature, and which are immortal since they are indivisible substances or **UNITS**, just as bodies are multitudes liable to perish through the dissolution of their parts. These principles of life, or these souls, have perception or desire. When I am asked if there are substantial forms, I reply by making a distinction. For if this term is taken as Descartes takes it when he maintains against Regis that the rational soul is the substantial form of man, I will answer, Yes. But I answer, No, if the term is taken as those take it who imagine that there is a substantial form of a piece of stone, or of any other non-organic body; for the principles of life belong only to organic bodies. It is true (according to my system) that there is no portion of matter in which there are not numberless organic and animated bodies; among which I include not only animals and plants, but perhaps also other kinds that are entirely unknown to us. But for all this, it must not be said that each portion of matter is animated, just as we do not say that a pond full of fish is an animated body, although a fish is.

However, my opinion on the *principles of life* is in certain points different from that hitherto taught. One of these points is that everyone has believed that these principles of life change the course of the motion of bodies, or at least give God the occasion to change it, whereas, according to my system, this course is not changed at all in the order of nature, God having pre-established it as it

<summary>The author clarifies his views on the principles of life and substantial forms, arguing that while life is pervasive through organic bodies, inorganic matter itself is not animated. He asserts that these principles of life do not alter the physical motion of bodies, which is instead pre-established by God.</summary>
<keywords>plastic natures, principles of life, Pre-established Harmony, Leibniz, substantial forms, organic bodies, indivisible substances, Descartes, Regis, Rorarius, animation of matter</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Leibniz's "Considerations on the Principles of Life and on Plastic Natures" (1705), further explaining how his system of Pre-established Harmony resolves the philosophical difficulties regarding the interaction between the soul and the body.</meta>

ought to be. The Peripatetics believed that souls had an influence on bodies and that, according to their will or desire, they gave some impression to bodies. And the celebrated authors who have caused the present dispute—by their principles of life and their plastic natures—have held the same view, although they are not Peripatetics. We cannot say the same of those who have employed <term>ἀρχαί</term>, or hylarchic principles, or other immaterial principles under different names. Descartes, having correctly recognized that there is a law of nature according to which the same quantity of force is preserved (although he was mistaken in its application by confusing quantity of force with quantity of motion), believed that we should not attribute to the soul the power of increasing or diminishing the force of bodies, but simply that of changing their direction by altering the course of the animal spirits. And those Cartesians who introduced the doctrine of Occasional Causes believed that since the soul was unable to exert any influence on the body, it was necessary for God to change the course or direction of the animal spirits according to the volitions of the soul. 

But if the new law of nature that I have demonstrated had been known in Descartes' time—which affirms that not only the same quantity of total force of bodies in communication is preserved, but also their total direction—he would probably have discovered my system of Pre-established Harmony. For he would have recognized that it is as reasonable to say that the soul does not change the quantity of the direction of bodies as it is reasonable to deny the soul the power of changing the quantity of their force; both are equally contrary to the order of things and to the laws of nature, just as both are equally inexplicable. Thus, according to my system, souls or the principles of life do not change anything in the ordinary course of bodies, and do not even give God an occasion to do so. Souls follow their own laws, which consist of a certain development of perceptions according to goods and evils; and bodies also follow their own laws, which consist of the laws of motion. Nevertheless, these two beings of an entirely different kind are in perfect accord, and correspond like two clocks perfectly regulated on the same basis, although perhaps of an entirely different construction. This is what I call Pre-established Harmony, which removes every notion of a miracle from purely natural actions and makes things run their course

<summary>Leibniz argues that his system of Pre-established Harmony explains the soul-body relationship better than the Peripatetic or Cartesian models by demonstrating that both force and direction are conserved in nature. He uses the famous analogy of two perfectly synchronized clocks to illustrate how souls and bodies follow their own independent laws while remaining in perfect agreement.</summary>
