regulated in an intelligible manner; whereas the common system relies on absolutely inexplicable influences. In the system of Occasional Causes, God—by a kind of general law and as if by agreement—is obliged to change the natural course of the soul’s thoughts at every moment to accommodate them to the impressions of the body, and to disrupt the natural course of the motions of bodies according to the desires of the soul. This can only be explained as a perpetual miracle, while I explain it quite clearly through the natures that God has established in things.

My system of Pre-established Harmony provides a new proof, previously unknown, of the existence of God. It is quite obvious that the agreement of so many substances—where none has any influence upon the others—could only come from a universal cause upon which they all depend. This cause must have infinite power and wisdom to pre-establish all these harmonies. Mr. Bayle himself thought that there has never been a hypothesis that so clearly highlights the knowledge we have of divine wisdom.

The system moreover has the advantage of maintaining, in all its rigor and universality, the great principle of physics: that a body's motion never changes except when another body in motion strikes it. *Corpus non moveri nisi impulsum a corpore contiguo et moto.* <note>A body does not move unless pushed by a contiguous and moving body.</note> This law has been violated until now by all those who have accepted souls or other immaterial principles, including all Cartesians. The followers of Democritus, Hobbes, and some other radical materialists—who have rejected all immaterial substance—were the only ones to have preserved this law until now. They believed they had found a reason to insult other philosophers, as if the others held a very irrational opinion. 

But the basis of their triumph was merely apparent and *ad hominem* <note>An argument directed against the person's specific circumstances rather than the universal truth of the matter.</note>; far from helping them, it serves to confound them. Now that their illusion has been exposed and their advantage turned against them, it seems it can be said that this is the first time the best philosophy has also proven to be the most consistent with reason in every respect, with nothing remaining that can oppose it. This general principle, although it excludes specific "first movers" by making us deny this quality to the soul or to created immaterial principles, leads us all the more surely and clearly to the universal First Mover, from whom the succession and harmony of perceptions equally originate. But one does not suffice without the other regarding the general nature of their origin, for they emanate from a source in which the power that constitutes efficient causes and the wisdom that regulates final causes are found united. This maxim also—that there is no motion which does not have its origin in another motion, according to the laws of mechanics—leads us again to the first mover. Because matter is indifferent in itself to all motion or rest, and yet nevertheless always possesses motion with all its force and direction, this motion could not have been placed in it except by the author of matter himself.

There is still another difference between my opinion and the opinions of other authors who favor the principles of life. It is that I believe both that these principles of life are immortal and that they are everywhere; whereas according to the common opinion, the souls of brutes perish, and according to the Cartesians, only man truly has a soul and even perception and desire. This is an opinion which will never be approved, and which has only been embraced because it was seen that it was necessary either to grant immortal souls to brutes or to admit that the soul of man might be mortal. But it should rather have been said that since every simple substance is imperishable and every soul is consequently immortal, that which could not be reasonably denied to brutes cannot fail also to always exist—though in a way very different from our own, since brutes, as far as can be judged, lack that reflection which makes us think of ourselves. 

And we do not see why men have been so reluctant to grant immaterial, imperishable substances to the bodies of other organic creatures, since the defenders of atoms have introduced material substances which do not perish, and since the soul of a brute has no more reflection than an atom. For there is a wide difference between feeling, which is common to these souls, and the reflection which accompanies reason, since we have a thousand feelings without reflecting upon them; and I do not think that the Cartesians have ever proved, or can prove, that every perception is accompanied by consciousness. It is also reasonable that there may be substances capable of perception below us, just as there are above us; and that our soul, far from being the last of all, is in a middle position from which one may descend and ascend. Otherwise, there would be a defect of order which certain philosophers...

This view leads us to another where I am again obliged to diverge from the accepted opinion. It will be asked of those who share my opinion what the souls of <term>brutes</term> will do after the death of the animal, and they will attribute to us the dogma of <term>Pythagoras</term>, who believed in the <term>transmigration of souls</term>—which not only the late M. But it must be known that I am far from this opinion, because I believe that not only the soul but also the same animal subsists. People who are very accurate in experiments have already in our day perceived that it may be doubted whether an entirely new animal is ever produced, and whether animals fully alive, as well as plants, are not already in miniature in <term>germs</term> before conception. This doctrine being granted, it will be reasonable to think that what does not begin to live also does not cease to live, and that death, like generation, is only the transformation of the same animal, which is sometimes enlarged and sometimes diminished. This again reveals to us hitherto unthought-of marvels of divine contrivance. This is that the <term>machines of nature</term>, being machines even to their smallest parts, are indestructible by reason of the envelopment of one little machine in a greater *ad infinitum*. Thus, one finds oneself obliged at the same time to maintain the <term>pre-existence</term> of the soul as well as of the animal, and the substance of the animal as well as of the soul.

I have gradually been led to explain my view of the formation of plants and animals, since it appears from what I have just said that they are never formed altogether anew. Thus, there is a machine within the parts of the natural machine *ad infinitum*, and so many envelopes and organic bodies enfolded one within another that an organic body could never be produced entirely anew and without any preformation; nor could an already existing animal be entirely destroyed. I may say of it *non mi bisogna, e non mi basta* <note>it is not necessary for me, and it is not enough for me</note>, for the very reason of the preformation and organism *ad infinitum* which provides me the material plastic natures suited to the requirements of the case; whereas the immaterial plastic principles are as little necessary as they are incapable of satisfying the case. For since animals are never formed naturally from a non-organic mass, the mechanism—which is incapable of producing these infinitely varied organs *de novo* <note>anew</note>—can very well derive them through the development and transformation of a pre-existing organic body. Meanwhile, those who employ plastic natures, whether material or immaterial, in no way weaken the proof of God’s existence drawn from the marvels of nature, which appear particularly in the structure of animals—provided that these defenders of immaterial plastic natures add a particular direction from God, and provided that those who, like me, make use of a material cause by assenting to plastic mechanism, maintain not only a continual preformation, but also an original divine pre-establishment. Thus, whichever way we take, we cannot overlook the divine existence when wishing to explain these marvels, which have always been admired but which have never been more apparent than in my system.

We see by this that not only the soul but also the animal must always subsist in the ordinary course of things. But the laws of nature are made and applied with so much order and so much wisdom that they serve more than one end; and God, who occupies the position of inventor and architect regarding the mechanism of nature, occupies the position of king and father to substances possessing intelligence, and of these the soul is a spirit formed after His image. Before ending, it will perhaps be well to note, among the other advantages of my system, that of the universality of the laws which I employ, which are always without exception in my general philosophy: and it is just the opposite in other systems. For example, I have already said that the laws of mechanics are never violated in natural motions, that the same force is always preserved, as also the same direction, and that everything takes place in souls as if there were no body, and that everything takes place in bodies as if there were no souls; that there is no part of space which is not full; that there is no particle of matter which is not actually divided, and which does not contain organic bodies; that there are also souls everywhere, as there are bodies everywhere; that souls and the same animals always subsist; that organic bodies are never without souls, and that souls are never separated from all organic body; although it is nevertheless true that there is no portion of matter of which it can be said that it is always affected by the same soul. I do not admit, then, that there are naturally souls entirely separated, nor that there are created spirits entirely detached from all body, in which I am of the opinion of several ancient Church Fathers. God only is above all matter, since he is its author; but creatures, free or freed from matter, would be at the same time detached from the universal concatenation, and like deserters from the general order. This universality of laws is confirmed by its great facility of explanation, since the uniformity, which I think is observed in all nature, brings about that everywhere else, in all time and in every place, it can be said that *all is as it is here*, to the degrees of greatness and of near perfection; and that thus those things which are farthest removed and most concealed are perfectly explained by the analogy of what is visible and near to us.

<meta>This page begins a new section containing a letter from Leibniz to Pierre Coste, following a discussion on the intersection of natural laws and divine grace.</meta>

XXVI.

# LETTER TO M. COSTE ON NECESSITY AND CONTINGENCY. 1707.

->[From the French]<-

Hanover, Dec. 19, 1707.

To M. COSTE, London:

I thank you very much for sharing with me the latest additions and corrections by Locke, and I am also pleased to learn what you tell me regarding his last dispute with Limborch. The liberty of indifference, around which the dispute turns and about which you, sir, ask my opinion, consists of a certain subtlety that few people trouble themselves to understand, yet many people nevertheless reason about. This leads us back to the consideration of necessity and contingency.

A truth is *necessary* when its opposite involves a contradiction, and when it is not necessary, it is called *contingent*. It is a necessary truth that God exists, that all right angles are equal, etc.; but that I myself exist, and that there are bodies in nature that exhibit an angle that is actually right, are contingent truths. For the entire universe could have been otherwise; time, space, and matter are absolutely indifferent to motions and forms. And God has chosen from among an infinite number of possibilities what he judged most fit. But since he has chosen, it must be affirmed that everything is included in his choice and that nothing could be changed, since he has once and for all foreseen and regulated everything—he who could not regulate things piecemeal or by fits and starts. Therefore, the sins and evils which he has judged proper to permit for the sake of greater goods are included in his choice. This is the necessity that can now be ascribed to things in the future, which is called *hypothetical* or *consequent* necessity (that is to say, founded upon the consequence of the hypothesis of the choice made). This does not destroy the contingency of things, and does not produce that absolute necessity which contingency does not allow. And nearly all theologians and philosophers (for we must except the Socinians <note>A sect that, among other things, denied God's certain foreknowledge of contingent future events.</note>) acknowledge the hypothetical necessity that I have just explained, which cannot be challenged without overthrowing the attributes of God and even the nature of things.

<summary>Leibniz defines the difference between absolute necessity and contingency, explaining that while the universe is contingent, it follows a "hypothetical necessity" based on God's deliberate and perfect choice.</summary>
<keywords>necessity, contingency, liberty of indifference, Pierre Coste, John Locke, God's choice, hypothetical necessity, Socinians, divine providence</keywords>

--- Page 185 ---
<meta>This page continues the letter from Leibniz to Pierre Coste regarding the nature of liberty, necessity, and contingency, specifically addressing the concept of "liberty of indifference."</meta>

Nevertheless, although all the facts of the universe are now certain in relation to God, or (what amounts to the same thing) are determined in themselves and even linked among themselves, it does not follow that their connection is always truly necessary; that is to say, that the truth, which declares that one fact follows another, is necessary. And this must be applied particularly to *voluntary actions*. When a choice is proposed—for example, to go out or not to go out—it is a question whether, with all the circumstances, internal and external, motives, perceptions, dispositions, impressions, passions, and inclinations taken together, I am still in a contingent state, or whether I am compelled to make a choice, for example, to go out. That is to say, whether this proposition, which is true and determined in fact—*In all these circumstances taken together I shall choose to go out*—is contingent or necessary. To this I reply that it is contingent, because neither I nor any other mind more enlightened than I could demonstrate that the opposite of this truth implies a contradiction. And supposing that by *liberty of indifference* is understood a liberty opposed to necessity (as I have just explained it), I acknowledge this liberty; for I am really of the opinion that our liberty, as well as that of God and of the blessed spirits, is exempt not only from compulsion but furthermore from absolute necessity, although it cannot be exempt from determination and from certainty.

But I find that there is need of great precaution here in order not to fall into a chimera which shocks the principles of good sense, and which would be what I call an *absolute indifference* or an *indifference of equilibrium*, which some conceive in liberty, and which I believe is chimerical. It must be observed, then, that the connection of which I just spoke is not necessary, speaking absolutely, but that it is nonetheless certainly true; and that in general, every time that all the circumstances taken together cause the balance of deliberation to be heavier on one side than on the other, it is certain and infallible that that side will carry the day. God or the perfect sage would always choose the best that is known, and if one thing was no better than another, they would choose neither. In other intelligent substances, passions often take the place of reason, and it can always be said in regard to the will in general that the *choice follows the greatest inclination*, by which I understand passions as well as reasons, whether true or apparent.

Nevertheless, I see that there are people who imagine that we are sometimes determined toward the side which is less weighted; that God sometimes chooses the least good, all things considered; and that man sometimes chooses without an object and against all his reasons, dispositions, and passions—finally, that one sometimes chooses without any reason that determines the choice. But I hold this to be false and absurd, since it is one of the greatest principles of good sense that nothing ever occurs without a cause or a determining reason. Thus, when God chooses, it is by reason of the Best; when man chooses, it will be the side that has struck him most. Moreover, if he chooses that which he sees to be less useful and less agreeable, it will perhaps have become the most agreeable to him through caprice, through a spirit of contradiction, or through similar reasons of a depraved taste, which would nonetheless be determining reasons, even if they were not conclusive reasons. And no example to the contrary can ever be found.

Thus, although we have a <term>liberty of indifference</term> which saves us from necessity, we never have an <term>indifference of equilibrium</term> which exempts us from determining reasons; there is always something which inclines us and makes us choose, but without being able to necessitate us. And just as God is always infallibly led to the best, although he is not led necessarily (other than by a <term>moral necessity</term>), so we are always infallibly led to that which strikes us most, but not necessarily. Since the contrary implies no contradiction, it was not necessary or essential that God should create, nor that he should create this world in particular, although his wisdom and goodness have led him to it.

It is this that Mr. Bayle, as subtle as he was, did not sufficiently consider when he thought that a case similar to the <term>ass of Buridan</term> was possible, and that a man placed in circumstances of perfect equilibrium could nonetheless choose. For it must be said that the case of a perfect equilibrium is chimerical and never occurs, as the universe is not able to be divided or cut into parts that are equal and identical. The universe is not like an ellipse or any other such oval, which a straight line drawn through its center can cut into two congruent parts. The universe has no center and its parts are infinitely varied; thus, the case will never occur where all will be perfectly equal and will strike equally from one side and from the other, and although we are not always capable of perceiving all the

I would not even oppose one who maintains that there are globes in the universe where prophecies are more common than on our own, just as there will perhaps be a world in which dogs have noses good enough to scent their game at a thousand leagues; perhaps also there are globes in which <term>genii</term> <note>spiritual beings or minor deities</note> have more freedom than here below to involve themselves in the actions of rational animals. But when the question is to reason on what is actually practiced here, our presumptive judgment must be founded on the custom of our globe, where prophetic visions of this sort are very rare. XXVII.

## REFUTATION OF SPINOZA. c. 1708.

->[From the Latin.]<-

The author <note>Wachter</note> passes on (ch. 4) to Spinoza, whom he compares with the Cabalists. Spinoza (Ethics, pt. 2, prop. 10, scholium) says: “Everyone must admit that nothing exists or can be conceived without God. For it is acknowledged by everyone that God is the sole cause of all things—of their essence as well as of their existence; that is, God is the cause of things, not only in respect to their being made (*secundum fieri*), but also in respect to their being (*secundum esse*).” The author <note>Wachter</note> appears to approve of this statement from Spinoza. And it is true that we must speak of created things only as permitted by the nature of God. But I do not think that Spinoza has succeeded in this. Essences can, in a certain way, be conceived of without God, but existences involve God. And the very reality of essences, by which they exert an influence upon existences, comes from God. The essences of things are co-eternal with God. And the very essence of God embraces all other essences to such a degree that God cannot be perfectly conceived without them. But existence cannot be conceived without God, who is the final reason of things.

This axiom—“To the essence of a thing belongs that without which it can neither be nor be conceived”—is to be applied to necessary things or to species, but not to individuals or contingent things. For individuals cannot be distinctly conceived. Hence they have no necessary connection with God, but are produced freely. God has been inclined toward these by a determining reason, but he has not been necessitated.

Spinoza (On the Improvement of the Understanding, p. 374) places among fictions the dictum: “Something can be produced from nothing.” But, in truth, modes which are produced, are produced from nothing. Since there is no matter for modes, assuredly neither the mode, nor a part of it, has pre-existed; instead, only another mode existed which has disappeared and to which this present one has succeeded.

The Cabalists seem to say that matter, on account of the lowliness of its essence, can neither be created nor can it exist; hence,

<meta>This page continues the critique of Spinoza’s philosophy, shifting focus from the nature of God and essence to the nature of matter, extension, and substance, contrasting Spinoza's monism with the author's theory of monads.</meta>

<page-num>176</page-num>

...that there is absolutely no matter, or that spirit and matter, as Henry More maintains in his Cabalistic theses, are one and the same thing. Spinoza, likewise, denies that God could have created any corporeal and material mass to be the subject of this world, "because," he says, "those who differ do not know by what divine power it could have been created." There is some truth in these words, but I think it is not sufficiently understood. Matter does, in reality, exist, but it is not a substance, since it is an aggregate or resultant of substances: I speak of matter as far as it is secondary or an extended mass, which is not at all a homogeneous body. But that which we conceive of as homogeneous and call primary matter is something incomplete, since it is merely potential. Substance, on the contrary, is something full and active.

Spinoza believed that matter, as commonly understood, did not exist. Hence, he often warns us that matter is poorly defined by Descartes as extension (*Ep.* 73), and extension is poorly explained as a very lowly thing which must be divisible in place, "since (*de Emend. Intel.*, p. 385) matter ought to be explained as an attribute expressing an eternal and infinite essence." I reply that extension, or if you prefer, primary matter, is nothing but a certain indefinite repetition of things as far as they are similar to each other or indiscernible. But just as number supposes things that are numbered, so extension supposes things which are repeated, and which have, in addition to common characteristics, others peculiar to themselves. These accidents, peculiar to each one, render the limits of size and shape—which were before only possible—actual. Merely passive matter is something very lowly, that is, lacking in all power; but such a thing consists only in the incomplete or in abstraction.

Spinoza (*Eth.*, pt. 1, prop. 13, corol. and prop. 15, schol.) says: "No substance, not even corporeal substance, is divisible." This statement is not surprising according to his system, since he admits but one substance; but it is equally true in mine, although I admit innumerable substances, for, in my system, all are indivisible or *monads*.

He says (*Eth.*, pt. 3, prop. 2, schol.) that "the mind and the body are the same thing, only expressed in two ways," and (*Eth.*, pt. 2, prop. 7, schol.) that "thinking substance and extended substance are one and the same, known now under the attribute of thought, now under that of extension." He says in the same scho—

<meta>This page continues the critique of Spinoza’s philosophy, focusing on the distinction between God, the mind, and the objects of thought, while rejecting Spinoza’s monism and his view of God as a necessary cause of all things.</meta>

<language>English</language>

...lium, "This, certain Hebrews seem to have seen as if through a cloud, who indeed maintain that God, the intellect of God, and the things known by it, are one and the same." This is not my opinion. Mind and body are no more the same than are the principle of action and the principle of passion. Corporeal substance has a soul and an organic body—that is, a mass made up of other substances. It is true that the same substance thinks and has an extended mass joined to it, but it does not consist of this mass, since all of this can be taken away from it without altering the substance; moreover, every substance perceives, but not every substance thinks. Thought indeed belongs to the monads—especially all perception—but extension belongs to compounds. It can no more be said that God and the things known by God are one and the same thing than that the mind and the things perceived by the mind are the same. The author [Wachter] believes that Spinoza posited a common nature in which the attributes of thought and extension reside, and that this nature is spiritual; but there is no extension belonging to spirits unless the word is taken in a broader sense for a certain subtle animal, such as angels were regarded by the ancients. The author [Wachter] adds that mind and body are the modes of these attributes. But how, I ask, can the mind be the mode of thought, when it is the principle of thought? Thus the mind should rather be the attribute and thought the modification of this attribute. It is astonishing also that Spinoza, as was seen above (*de Emend. Intel.*, p. 385), seems to deny that extension is divisible into and composed of parts; which has no meaning, unless, perhaps, like space, it is not a divisible thing. But space and time are orders of things and not things.

The author [Wachter] rightly says that God found in himself the origins of all things, as I remember Julius Scaliger once said that "things are not produced by the passive power of matter but by the active power of God." And I assert this of forms or of activities or entelechies.

What Spinoza (*Eth.*, pt. 1, prop. 34) says—that "God is, by the same necessity, the cause of himself and the cause of all things," and (*Polit. Tract.*, p. 270, c. 2, no. 2) that "the power of things is the power of God"—I do not admit. God exists necessarily, but he produces things freely, and the power of things is produced by God but is different from the divine power, and things themselves operate, although they have received their power to act.

Spinoza (Letter 21) says: 

> “That everything is in God and moves in God, I assert with Paul and perhaps with all other philosophers, although in a different manner. I would even dare to say that this was the opinion of all the ancient Hebrews, so far as it can be conjectured from certain traditions, although these are in many ways corrupted.” 

I believe that everything is in God, not as a part in a whole, nor as an accident in a subject, but in the way that a place—specifically a spiritual and enduring place, not one measured or divided—contains that which is placed within it. That is, just as God is immense or omnipresent, the world is present to Him. And it is in this way that all things are in Him; for He is where they are and where they are not, and He remains when they pass away, and He was already there before they arrived.

The author <note>Wachter</note> says that it is the consistent opinion of the cabalists that God produced certain things indirectly and others directly. From this, he next speaks of a certain created first principle which God caused to proceed directly from Himself, and through the mediation of which all other things have been produced in series and in order; this they are accustomed to address by various names: Adam Cadmon, Messiah, the Christ, λόγος, the Word, the first-born, the first man, the celestial man, the guide, the shepherd, the mediator, etc. Elsewhere he gives a reason for this assertion. The fact itself is recognized by Spinoza, so that nothing is missing except the name. 

> “It follows,” he says (*Ethics, part 1, proposition 28, scholium*), “in the second place, that God cannot properly be called the remote cause of individual things, except to distinguish these from those which God produces directly, or rather which follow from His absolute nature.” 

Moreover, he explained (proposition 21) what those things are that are said to follow from the absolute nature of God: 

> “All things which follow from the absolute nature of any attribute of God must exist always and be infinite, or are eternal and infinite through the same attribute.” 

— These propositions of Spinoza, which the author cites, are entirely without foundation. God produces no infinite creature, nor could it be shown or demonstrated by any argument in what respect such a creature would differ from God.

The theory of Spinoza—namely, that from each attribute there springs a particular infinite thing; from extension a certain something infinite in extension; from thought a certain infinite under-

standing, arises from his varied imagination of certain heterogeneous divine attributes, like thought and extension, and perhaps innumerable others. For in reality, extension is not an attribute in itself since it is only the repetition of perceptions. An infinitely extended thing is only imaginary: an infinite thinking being is God himself. The things which are necessary and which proceed from the infinite nature of God are the eternal truths. A particular creature is produced by another, and this again by another. Thus, therefore, by no conception could we reach God even if we should suppose a progress *ad infinitum* <note>to infinity</note>, and, notwithstanding, the last no less than the one which precedes is dependent upon God.

Tatian says, in his *Oration to the Greeks*, that there is a spirit dwelling in the stars, the angels, the plants, the waters, and men, and that this spirit, although one and the same, contains differences in itself. But I do not approve of this doctrine. It is the error of the world-soul universally diffused, which, like the air in pneumatic organs, makes different sounds in different organs. Thus, when a pipe is broken, the soul will desert it and will return into the world-soul. But we must know that there are as many incorporeal substances, or if you will, souls, as there are natural, organic machines.

But what Spinoza (*Ethics*, *part* 2, *proposition* 13, *scholium*) says—"All things, although in different degrees, are animated"—rests upon another strange doctrine; "for," he says, "of everything there is necessarily in God an idea, of which God is the cause, in the same way as there is an idea of the human body." But there is plainly no reason for saying that the soul is an idea. Ideas are something purely abstract, like numbers and figures, and cannot act. Ideas are abstract and numerical: the idea of each animal is a possibility, and it is an illusion to call souls immortal because ideas are eternal, as if the soul of a globe should be called eternal because the idea of a spherical body is eternal. The soul is not an idea, but the source of innumerable ideas, for it has, besides the present idea, something active, or the production of new ideas. But according to Spinoza, at any moment the soul will be different because the body being changed the idea of the body is different. Hence it is not strange if he considers creatures as transitory modifications. The soul, therefore, is something vital or something containing active force.

Spinoza begins where Descartes ended: in *Naturalism*. He is also wrong to say (Letter 58) that “the world is the result of the divine nature,” although he adds that it was not made by chance. There is a middle ground between what is necessary and what is accidental: specifically, what is free. The world is a voluntary effect of God, based on inclining or prevailing reasons. And even if the world were supposed to be eternal, it would still not be necessary. God could have either not created it or created it differently, but he was not to do so. Spinoza thinks (Letter 49) that “God produces the world by the same necessity by which he knows himself.” But it must be replied that things are possible in many different ways, whereas it was entirely impossible for God not to know himself.—Spinoza says (*Ethics*, part 1, proposition 17, scholium):

> “I know there are many who believe they can prove that supreme intelligence and free will belong to the nature of God; for they say they know nothing more perfect to attribute to God than that which is the highest perfection in us. . . . Therefore, they prefer to assert that God is indifferent to all things, and that he creates nothing except what he has decided to create by some absolute will. But I think I have shown (Proposition 16) clearly enough that all things follow from the supreme power of God by the same necessity, in the same way that it follows from the nature of a triangle that its three angles are equal to two right angles.”

—From these first words, it is evident that Spinoza does not attribute intellect and will to God. He is right to deny that God is indifferent and that he decrees anything by absolute will; rather, he decrees by a will which is based on reasons. That things proceed from God as the properties of a triangle proceed from its nature is proven by no argument; furthermore, there is no analogy between essences and existing things.

In the scholium of Proposition 17, Spinoza says that “the intellect and the will of God agree with ours only in name, because ours come after things and God’s come before things;” but it does not follow from this that they agree only in name. “The human mind,” says Spinoza (*Ethics*, part 5, proposition 23, proof), “cannot be entirely destroyed with the body, but there remains something of it which is eternal. But this has no relation to time, for we attribute duration to the mind only during the duration of the body.” In the scholium following, he adds, “This idea which expresses the essence of the body under the form of eternity [*sub specie æternitatis*] is a certain mode of thought which belongs to the essence of the mind and which is necessarily eternal, etc.” This is illusory. This idea is like the figure of the sphere, the eternity of which does not prove its existence, since it is but the possibility of an ideal sphere. Thus it is saying nothing to say that “our mind is eternal in so far as it expresses the body under the form of eternity,” and it would be likewise eternal because it understands eternal truths such as those regarding the triangle. “Our soul has no duration nor does time relate to anything beyond the actual existence of the body.” Thus Spinoza, in the place cited, thinks that the mind perishes with the body because he believes that only a single body remains always, although this can be transformed.

The author [Wachter] adds: “I do not see that Spinoza has anywhere said positively that minds migrate from one body into another, and into different dwellings and various regions of eternity. Nevertheless it might be inferred from his thought.” But he errs. The same soul, according to Spinoza, cannot be the idea of another body, just as the figure of a sphere is not the figure of a cylinder. The soul, for Spinoza, is so fugitive, that it does not exist even in the present moment, and the body too only exists in idea. Spinoza says (*Ethics*, part 5, proposition 2) that “memory and imagination disappear with the body.” But I for my part think that some imagination and some memory always remain, and that, without them, there would be no soul. It must not be believed that the mind exists without feeling or without a soul. A reason without imagination and memory is a conclusion without premises. Aristotle, also, thought that <term>νοῦς</term>, mind, or the acting intellect remains, and not the soul. But the soul itself acts and the mind is passive.

<meta>This page continues the critique of Spinoza’s philosophy regarding the nature of the soul and mind, specifically addressing the concept of the soul as a "spiritual automaton" and the nature of the will.</meta>

certain laws and like a spiritual *automa*" (he meant to say *automaton*). The author <note>Wachter</note> interprets this passage as referring to the soul alone and not to the mind, and says that the soul acts according to the laws of motion and according to external causes. Both are mistaken. I say that the soul acts spontaneously and yet like a spiritual automaton; and that this is true also of the mind. The soul is no less exempt than the mind from impulses from external things, and the soul no more than the mind acts determinately; just as in bodies everything is done by motions according to the laws of force, so in the soul everything is done through effort or desire, according to the laws of the Good. The two realms are in harmony. It is true, nevertheless, that there are certain things in the soul which cannot be explained in an adequate manner except by external things, and to that extent the soul is subject to the external; but this is not by a physical influx, but by a moral one, so to speak—insofar as God, in creating the mind, had more regard for other things than for the mind itself. For in the creation and preservation of each thing, he has regard for all other things.

Spinoza is wrong in calling <note>Ethics, part 3, 9, scholium</note> the will the effort of each thing to persist in its being; for the will tends toward more particular ends and a more perfect mode of existence. He is also wrong in saying <note>part 3, proposition 7</note> that the effort is identical with the essence, whereas the essence is always the same and efforts vary. I do not admit that affirmation is the effort of the mind to persist in its being—that is, to preserve its ideas. We have this effort even when we affirm nothing. Moreover, according to Spinoza, the mind is an idea; it does not have ideas. He is also wrong in thinking that affirmation or negation is volition, since volition involves, in addition, the reasoning of the Good.

Spinoza <note>Epistle 2, to Oldenburg</note> says that "the will differs from this or that volition, just as whiteness differs from this or that white color: consequently, the will is not the cause of volition, just as humanity is not the cause of Peter and of Paul. Particular volitions therefore have need of another cause. The will is only an entity of reason." So says Spinoza. But we take the will to be the power of choosing, the exercise of which is the volition. Therefore, it is indeed by the will that we will; but it is true that there is a need for other special causes to determine the will—namely, in order for it to produce a certain volition. It must be modified in a certain manner. The

The will does not, therefore, relate to volitions as a species, or the abstract idea of a species, relates to individuals. Mistakes are neither free nor acts of the will, although we often participate in our errors through free actions.

Furthermore, Spinoza says (*Tractatus Politicus*, chapter 2, number 6), “Men conceive of themselves in nature as an empire within an empire (*Malcuth in Malcuth*, the author adds). For they think that the human mind is not the product of natural causes, but that it is immediately created by God, so independent of other things that it has absolute power to determine itself and to use its reason correctly. But experience proves to us all too clearly that it is no more in our power to have a sound mind than to have a sound body.” So says Spinoza. In my opinion, every substance is an empire within an empire; but while harmonizing exactly with all the rest, it receives no influence from any being except for God. Nevertheless, through God, its author, it depends upon all the others. It comes immediately from God, and yet it is created to conform to other things. For the rest, not all things are equally within our power. For we are more inclined toward one thing or another. *Malcuth*, or the realm of God, does not suppress either divine or human liberty, but only the “indifference of equilibrium,” as those say who think there are no reasons for the actions they do not understand.

Spinoza thinks that the mind is greatly strengthened if it knows that what happens, happens by necessity; but by this compulsion, he does not make the heart of the sufferer content, nor cause him to feel his malady any less. He is, on the contrary, happy if he understands that good results from evil and that the things that happen are best for us if we are wise.

From what precedes, it is clear that what Spinoza says regarding the intellectual love of God (*Ethics*, part 4, proposition 28) is only an outward show for the common people, since there is nothing lovable in a God who produces without choice and by necessity, without any distinction between good and evil. The true love of God is founded not on necessity but on goodness. Spinoza (*On the Improvement of the Understanding*, page 388) says that “there is no science, but that we have only experience of particular things—that is, of things whose existence has no connection with their essence, and which, consequently, are not eternal truths.” This contradicts what he said elsewhere—namely, that all things are necessary, and that all things proceed necessarily from the divine essence. Likewise, he combats (Eth., pt. 2, prop. 10, schol.) those who claim that the nature of God belongs to the essence of created things; and yet he had established before <note>Eth., pt. 1, prop. 15</note> that things do not exist and cannot be conceived without God, and that they necessarily arise from him. For this reason, he maintains (Eth., pt. 1, prop. 21) that finite and temporal things cannot be produced immediately by an infinite cause, but that (Prop. 28) they are produced by other causes that are individual and finite. But how, then, will they finally spring from God? For in this case, they cannot come from him mediately, since we could never reach anything in this way that is not similarly produced by another finite thing. It cannot, therefore, be said that God acts by mediating through secondary causes, unless he produces those secondary causes. Therefore, it should rather be said that God produces substances and not their actions, in which he only concurs.

# XXVIII.

## REMARKS ON THE OPINION OF MALEBRANCHE THAT *We See All Things in God*, WITH REFERENCE TO LOCKE'S EXAMINATION OF IT. 1708.

->[From the French.]<-

There is, in the posthumous works of Locke published in London in 1706, 8vo., an examination of the opinion of Malebranche that we see all things in God. It is acknowledged at the start that there are many fine thoughts and judicious reflections in the book on *The Search after Truth*, and that this made him hope to find therein something satisfactory on the nature of our ideas. But he has remarked at the beginning (§ 2) that this Father <note>Malebranche</note> makes use of what Locke calls the <term>argumentum ad ignorantiam</term>, in claiming to prove his opinion, because there is no other means of explaining the thing: but according to Mr. Locke, this argument loses its force when the feebleness of our understanding is considered. I am nevertheless of the opinion that this argument is good if one can perfectly enumerate the means and exclude all but one. Even in Analysis, M. Frenicle employed this method of exclusion, as he called it. Nevertheless, Locke is right in saying that it is of no use to say that this hypothesis is better than the other, if it is found not to explain what one would like to understand and even to involve things which cannot harmonize.

After having considered what is said in the first chapter of the second part of book third, where Malebranche claims that what the soul can perceive must be in immediate contact with it, Mr. Locke asks (§ 3, 4.) what it is to be in immediate contact, this not appearing to him intelligible except in bodies. Perhaps it might be replied that one acts immediately on the other. And as Malebranche, admitting that our bodies are united to our souls, adds that it is not in such a way that the soul perceives it, he is asked (§ 5.) to explain that act of union or at least in what it differs from that which he does not admit. Father Malebranche will perhaps say that he does not know the union of the soul with the body except by faith, and that the nature of body consisting in extension alone, nothing can be deduced therefrom toward explaining the

<meta>This page continues the critique of Nicolas Malebranche’s philosophy, specifically focusing on the interaction between the soul and the body, and comparing Malebranche’s views with those of John Locke and the author’s own system of Pre-established Harmony.</meta>

soul's action on the body. He grants an inexplicable union, but he demands one that will serve to explain the interaction of the soul and body. He also claims to explain why material beings could not be united with the soul as is required; this is because these beings have extension while the soul does not, and therefore there is no relation between them. But at this point Locke asks very appropriately (§ 7) if there is any more of a relation between God and the soul. It seems indeed that the Reverend Father Malebranche should have emphasized not the lack of relation, but the lack of connection that appears between the soul and the body, whereas between God and His creatures there is such a connection that they could not exist without Him.

When the Father says (§ 6) that there is no purely intelligible substance except God, I declare that I do not understand him well enough. There is something in the soul that we do not understand clearly; and there are many things in God that we do not understand at all.

Mr. Locke (§ 8) makes a remark at the end of the Father's chapter that is equivalent to my views; for in order to show that the Father has not excluded every way of explaining the matter, he adds: 

> "If I were to say that it is possible that God has made our souls in such a way, and has so united them to bodies, that during certain motions of the body the soul would have specific perceptions—but in a manner inconceivable to us—I would have said something as clear and as instructive as what he says." 

In saying this, Mr. Locke seems to have had in mind my system of *Pre-established Harmony*, or something similar.

Mr. Locke objects (§ 20) that the sun is useless if we see it in God. Since this argument also applies to my system, which claims that we see the sun within ourselves, I answer that the sun was not made solely for us, and that God wishes to show us the truth regarding what is outside of us.

He also objects (§ 22) that he cannot conceive how we could see something confusedly in God, where no confusion exists. One might answer that we see things confusedly when we see too many of them at once.

After Father Malebranche said that God is the place of spirits just as space is the place of bodies, Mr. Locke says (§ 25) that he does not understand a word of this. But he understands at least what

space, place, and body are. He also understands that the Father draws an analogy between *space, place, and body*, and between *God, place, and spirit*. Thus, a good part of what he says here is intelligible. One might merely object that this analogy is not proven, although some relations are easily perceived that might provide an occasion for the comparison. I often observe that certain people seek, through this affectation of ignorance, to evade what is said to them as if they understood nothing; they do this not to reproach themselves, but either to reproach those speaking—as if their jargon were unintelligible—or to exalt themselves above the matter and those who discuss it, as if it were not worthy of their attention.

Nevertheless, Mr. Locke is right in saying that Father Malebranche’s opinion is unintelligible in connection with his other opinions, since for him, space and body are the same thing. The truth has escaped him here, and he has conceived of something common and immutable to which bodies have an essential relation, and which indeed produces their relation to one another. This order provides an occasion for creating a fiction and for conceiving of space as an immutable substance; but what is real in this notion relates to simple substances (including spirits) and is found in God, who unites them.

Since the Father says that ideas are representative beings, Mr. Locke asks (§ 26) whether these beings are substances, modes, or relations. I believe it may be said that they are nothing but relations resulting from the attributes of God.

When Mr. Locke declares (§ 31) that he does not understand how the variety of ideas is compatible with the simplicity of God, it seems to me that he should not raise an objection on this point against Father Malebranche, for there is no system that can make such a thing comprehensible. We cannot comprehend the <term>incommensurable</term> and a thousand other things, the truth of which we nevertheless know, and which we are right to use to explain others that depend on them. There is something similar to this in all simple substances, where there is a variety of affections within the unity of substance.

The Father maintains that the idea of the *infinite* is prior to that of the finite. Mr. Locke objects (§ 34) that a child has the idea of a number or of a square before that of the infinite. He is right if he takes ideas to be images; but in taking them as the

foundations of notions, he will find that in the *continuum* the notion of an extended thing, taken absolutely, is prior to the notion of an extended thing where a modification is added. This must be further applied to what is said in §§ 42 and 46.

The argument of the Father <note>Father Nicolas Malebranche</note> which Mr. Locke examines (§ 40)—that God alone, being the end of spirits, is also their sole object—is not to be despised. It is true that it needs something more in order to be called a demonstration. There is a more conclusive reason which shows that God is the sole immediate external object of spirits, and that is that there is nothing but Him who can act upon them.

It is objected (§ 41) that the Apostle begins with the knowledge of creatures in order to lead to God, and that the Father does the opposite. I believe that these methods harmonize. The one proceeds *a priori*, the other *a posteriori*; and the latter is the more common. It is true that the best way to know things is through their causes, but this is not the easiest. It requires too much attention to sensible things.

In replying to § 34, I have noted the difference between an image and an idea. It seems that this difference is challenged (§ 38) by finding difficulty in the distinction between an image <gloss>sensation</gloss> and an idea. But I think that the Father understands by "image" <gloss>sensation</gloss> a perception of the imagination, whereas there may be ideas of things which are neither sensible nor imaginable. I affirm that we have as clear an idea of the color of a violet as of its shape (as is objected here), but not one as distinct or as intelligible.

Mr. Locke asks if an indivisible and unextended substance can have, at the same time, different modifications relating to inconsistent objects. I reply: Yes. That which is inconsistent in the same object is not inconsistent in the representation of different objects conceived at the same time. Therefore, it is not necessary for there to be different parts in the soul, just as it is not necessary for there to be different parts in a point, even though different angles meet there.

It is asked with good reason (§ 43) how we know of created beings if we do not see anything immediately but God? It is because the objects—the representations of which God causes us to have—possess something that resembles the idea we have of substance, and it is this which leads us to judge that there are other substances.

It is supposed (§ 46) that God has the idea of an angle which is the closest to a right angle, but that He does not show it to anyone, no matter how much one may desire to see it. I reply that such an angle is a fiction, like the fraction closest to one, or the number closest to zero, or the smallest of all numbers. The nature of continuity does not permit any such thing.

The Father <note>Nicolas Malebranche</note> had said that we know our soul by an inner feeling of consciousness, and that for this reason our knowledge of the soul is more imperfect than our knowledge of things, which we see in God. Mr. Locke then remarks very *apropos* (§ 47) that since the idea of our soul is in God as much as the ideas of other things, we should see it in God as well. The truth is that we see all things in ourselves and in our souls, and the knowledge we have of the soul is very true and accurate, provided we pay attention to it. It is by the knowledge we have of the soul that we understand being, substance, and God Himself; and it is by reflecting on our thoughts that we know extension and physical bodies. Nevertheless, it is true that God provides everything positive in this, and all the perfection involved in it, through an immediate and continual emanation. This is by virtue of the dependence all creatures have on Him, and it is in this way that a good meaning may be given to the phrase that God is the object of our souls and that we see all things in Him.

Perhaps the Father's intention in the saying being examined (§ 53)—that we see the essences of things in the perfections of God and that it is the universal reason which enlightens us—is to show that the attributes of God are the foundations of the simple notions we have of things. Being, power, knowledge, diffusion, and duration, when taken absolutely, exist in Him, and they do not exist in creatures except in a limited way.

<header>XXIX.</header>

# LETTER TO WAGNER ON THE ACTIVE FORCE OF THE BODY, ON THE SOUL, AND ON THE SOUL OF ANIMALS. 1710.

->[From the Latin.]<-

1. I am happy to reply to the questions you asked about the nature of the soul, for I see from the doubts you raised that my view is not sufficiently clear to you. This seems to be due to a preconception drawn from my essay published in the <term>*Acta Eruditorum*</term>, where I challenged the famous Sturm regarding the active force of the body. You say that I did not sufficiently justify active force for matter there, and while I attribute resistance to matter, I also attribute reaction to it, and consequently action. You suggest that since there is an active principle everywhere in matter, this principle should be enough to account for the actions of animals, and therefore they do not need an incorruptible soul.

2. I reply, first, that I do not attribute the active principle to bare or primary matter, which is merely passive and consists only of <term>*antitypia*</term> and extension. Instead, I attribute it to the body, or to "clothed" or secondary matter, which additionally contains an original <term>entelechy</term> or active principle. Second, I reply that the resistance of bare matter is not action, but mere passion, since it possesses <term>*antitypia*</term> or impenetrability. Through this, it indeed resists whatever would penetrate it, but it does not react unless an elastic force is added. This elastic force must be derived from motion, and therefore the active force of matter must be added to it. Third, I reply that this active principle—this first <term>entelechy</term>—is, in fact, a vital principle, also gifted with the faculty of perception and incorruptible, for the reasons I recently stated. This is exactly what I consider to be the soul in animals. Therefore, while I admit that active principles are added everywhere in matter, I also propose that vital or perceiving principles are spread throughout it. These are <term>monads</term> and, so to speak, metaphysical atoms that lack parts and cannot be produced or destroyed naturally.

3. Next, you ask for my definition of the soul. I reply that "soul" may be used in both a broad and a strict sense. Broadly speaking, the soul

<summary>Leibniz clarifies his theory of active force, distinguishing between passive "bare matter" and the "clothed matter" of bodies which contain vital, perceiving principles called monads. He argues that these monads act as the souls of animals and are indestructible, metaphysical atoms.</summary>

<keywords>Leibniz, Wagner, soul of animals, active force, primary matter, antitypia, entelechy, monads, perception, metaphysical atoms</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the Letter to Wagner (1710), further defining the hierarchy of living principles—life, soul, and mind—and explaining the relationship between the eternal soul and the ever-changing organic body.</meta>

will be the same as life or the vital principle; that is, the principle of internal action existing in the simple thing or <term>monad</term>, to which external action corresponds. And this correspondence of internal and external, or representation of the external in the internal, of the composite in the simple, of multiplicity in unity, constitutes, in reality, <term>perception</term>. However, in this sense, <term>soul</term> is attributed not only to animals but also to all other perceiving beings. In the strict sense, <term>soul</term> is used to refer to a more noble species of life, or <term>sentient life</term>, where there is not only the faculty of perceiving, but also that of feeling, specifically because attention and memory are joined to perception. Just as, in turn, <term>mind</term> is a more noble species of soul—that is, <term>mind</term> is a <term>rational soul</term>, where reason or reasoning from universal truths is added to feeling. Therefore, just as the mind is the rational soul, so the soul is sentient life, and life is the perceptive principle. I have shown, moreover, through examples and arguments, that not all perception is feeling, but that there is also <term>insensible perception</term>. For example, I could not perceive green unless I perceived the blue and yellow from which it results. At the same time, I do not feel the blue and yellow unless, perhaps, a microscope is used.

4. You will remember, moreover, that in my opinion, not only are all lives, all souls, all minds, and all <term>primitive entelechies</term> everlasting, but also that a certain natural machine—which we call an <term>organic body</term>—is perpetually united to each primitive entelechy or vital principle. This machine, moreover, even though it generally preserves its form, remains in a state of flux and is, like the <term>ship of Theseus</term>, perpetually repaired. Therefore, we cannot be certain that even the smallest particle of matter we received at birth remains in our body, even though the same machine is gradually and completely transformed, increased, diminished, enfolded, or unfolded. Hence, not only is the soul everlasting, but some animal always remains, although no specific animal should be called everlasting because the animal form does not persist; just as the caterpillar and the butterfly are not the same animal, even though the same soul is in both. Every natural machine, therefore, has this quality: it is never completely destructible, since, however thick a covering may be dissolved, there always remains a little machine not yet destroyed, like the costume of <term>Harlequin</term> in the comedy, for whom, after the removal of many tunics, there always remained a fresh one. And we

we should be the less astonished at this for this reason: that nature is everywhere organic and ordered by a most wise author for certain ends, and that nothing in nature ought to be criticized as unrefined, although it may sometimes appear to our senses as merely a crude mass. Thus, we escape all the difficulties which arise from the nature of a soul absolutely separated from all matter; so that, in truth, a soul or an animal before birth or after death does not differ from a soul or an animal living the present life except in the condition of things and degrees of perfection, but not by its entire genus of being. And likewise, I think that Genii are minds endowed with bodies that are very penetrating and suitable for action, which perhaps they are able to change at will, which is why they do not deserve to be called even animals. Thus, all things in nature are analogous, and the subtle may be understood from the coarse, since both are structured in the same way. God alone is a substance really separated from matter, since he is *actus purus* <note>pure act or actualization</note>, endowed with no passive power—which, wherever it exists, constitutes matter. And, indeed, all created substances have <term>antitypia</term> <note>resistance or impenetrability</note>, by which it happens naturally that one is outside the other, and so penetration is excluded.

5. But although my principles are very general and hold no less in man than in brutes, yet man stands out marvelously above brutes and approaches the Genii, because from the use of reason he is capable of society with God, and thus of reward and of punishment in the divine government. And therefore he preserves not only life and soul like the brutes, but also self-consciousness and memory of a former state, and, in a word, personality. He is immortal, not only physically but also morally, which is why, in the strict sense, immortality is attributed only to the human soul. For if a man did not know that in the other life rewards or punishments would be awarded to him for this life, there would really be no punishment and no reward, and as regards morals, it would be just as if I were extinguished and another, happier or unhappier, should succeed me. And thus I hold that souls, latent doubtless in seminal <term>animalcules</term> <note>microscopic organisms or seeds of life</note> from the beginning of things, are not rational until, by conception, they are destined for human life; but when they are once made rational and rendered capable of consciousness and of society with God, I think that they never lay aside the character of citizens in the Republic of God; and since it is most

<summary>Leibniz explains that nature is entirely organic and that souls are always embodied, with the exception of God, who is pure act. He distinguishes human souls from those of animals by their capacity for reason, memory, and moral responsibility within the "Republic of God."</summary>
<keywords>nature, soul, matter, Genii, actus purus, antitypia, brutes, reason, personality, immortality, seminal animalcules, Republic of God</keywords>

--- Page 207 ---
<meta>This page continues the Letter to Wagner (1710), concluding the argument that human souls, unlike those of lower animals, maintain the memory and self-consciousness necessary for divine reward and punishment within a perfectly ordered universe.</meta>

justly and beautifully governed, it follows that by the very laws of nature—on account of the parallelism between the kingdom of grace and the kingdom of nature—souls are made more fit for rewards and punishments by the force of their own actions. In this sense, it may be said that virtue brings its own reward and sin its own punishment. This occurs because, by a certain natural consequence before the final state of the soul (depending on whether it departs atoned for or unatoned for), a certain natural divergence arises. This divergence is preordained by God in nature, consistent with divine promises and threats, and aligned with grace and justice. Added to this is the intervention of Genii <note>intermediate spirits or higher intelligences</note>—good or bad, according to those we have associated with—whose operations are certainly natural, although their nature is more sublime than ours. We see, indeed, that a person waking from a deep sleep, or even recovering from a stroke <note>apoplexy</note>, usually recovers the memory of their former state. The same must be said of death, which can make our perceptions murky and confused but cannot entirely erase them from memory; when that use of memory returns, rewards and punishments take place. Thus, the Savior compared death to sleep. Moreover, the preservation of personality and of moral immortality cannot be attributed to animals <note>brutes</note> who are incapable of divine society and law.

6. Therefore, no one needs to fear dangerous consequences from this doctrine, since a true natural theology—one that is not only consistent with revealed truth but even wonderfully supportive of it—can be demonstrated by beautiful reasoning from my principles. Indeed, those who deny souls to animals <note>brutes</note> and deny all perception and organization to other parts of matter do not sufficiently recognize the Divine Majesty. They introduce something unworthy of God: something unpolished—that is, a void of perfections or forms—which you may call a metaphysical void. This is to be rejected no less than a material or physical void. But those who grant true souls and perception to animals <note>brutes</note> and yet claim that their souls can perish naturally, take away the demonstration showing that our own minds cannot perish naturally. They fall into the dogma of the Socinians <note>a sect that believed the soul is not naturally immortal but is preserved only by God's grace</note>, who think that souls are preserved only miraculously or by grace, but believe that by nature they ought to perish; this robs natural theology of its largest part. Besides, the opposite can be completely demonstrated, since a substance lacking parts cannot be destroyed naturally.

Wolfenbüttel, June 4, 1710.

# THE THEODICY.

## ABRIDGMENT OF THE ARGUMENT REDUCED TO SYLLOGISTIC FORM.
## 1710.

->[From the French.]<-

Some intelligent persons have desired that this supplement should be added <note>to the *Theodicy*</note>, and I have all the more readily yielded to their wishes as, in this way, I have an opportunity to remove certain difficulties once more and to make some observations which were not sufficiently emphasized in the work itself.

I. *Objection.* Whoever does not choose the best is lacking in power, or in knowledge, or in goodness.
God did not choose the best in creating this world.
Therefore, God has been lacking in power, or in knowledge, or in goodness.

*Answer.* I deny the minor premise—that is, the second premise of this syllogism—and our opponent proves it with this:

*Prosyllogism.* Whoever makes things in which there is evil, which could have been made without any evil, or the making of which could have been omitted, does not choose the best.
God has made a world in which there is evil; a world, I say, which could have been made without any evil, or the making of which could have been omitted altogether.
Therefore, God has not chosen the best.

*Answer.* I grant the minor premise of this prosyllogism; for it must be admitted that there is evil in the world which God has made, and that it was possible to make a world without evil, or even not to create a world at all, for its creation depended on the free will of God. However, I deny the major premise—that is, the first of the two premises of the prosyllogism—and I might content myself with simply demanding its proof. But in order to make the matter clearer, I wish to justify this denial by showing that the best plan is not always the one that seeks to avoid evil, since it may happen that the evil is accompanied by a greater good. For example, a general of an army will prefer a great victory with a slight wound to a con-

In this, I have followed the opinion of St. Augustine, who has said a hundred times that God permitted evil in order to bring about good—that is, a greater good; and that of Thomas Aquinas <note>in Book II of the *Sentences*, distinction 32, question 1, article 1</note>, that the permitting of evil tends toward the good of the universe. I have shown that the ancients called Adam's fall *felix culpa*, a happy sin, because it was redeemed with immense advantage through the incarnation of the Son of God, who has given to the universe something nobler than anything that would have ever existed among creatures without this. And for a clearer understanding, I have added—following many respected authors—that it was in accordance with order and the general good for God to give certain creatures the opportunity to exercise their liberty, even when He foresaw that they would turn toward evil, which He could so well rectify. This is because it was not right that, in order to prevent sin, God should always act in an extraordinary manner.

To overcome this objection, therefore, it is sufficient to show that a world with evil might be better than a world without evil; but I have gone even further in the work, and have even proved that this universe must be, in reality, better than every other possible universe.

As for the minor premise, that is no longer to be admitted; that is, it is not at all to be admitted that there is more evil than good in intelligent creatures. There is no need even to grant that there is more evil than good in the human race, because it is possible, and in fact very probable, that the glory and the perfection of the blessed are incomparably greater than the misery and the imperfection of the damned. Thus, the excellence of the total good in the smaller number exceeds the total evil in the larger number. The blessed approach the Divinity, by means of the <term>Divine Mediator</term>, as closely as may suit such creatures, and they make such progress in good as is impossible for the damned to make in evil, even as the damned approach as nearly as they can to the nature of demons. God is infinite, and the devil is limited; good may and does advance *ad infinitum* [to infinity], while evil has its limits. It is therefore possible, and even credible, that in comparing the blessed and the damned, the opposite of what I said might happen in the comparison of intelligent and non-intelligent creatures takes place. Namely, it is possible that in the comparison of the happy and the unhappy, the proportion of degree exceeds that of number, and that in the comparison of intelligent and non-intelligent creatures, the proportion of number is greater than that of value. I have the right to suppose that a thing is possible so long as its impossibility is not proven; and indeed, what I have presented here is more than just a supposition.

But in the second place, if I should admit that there is more evil than good in the human race, I still have good grounds for not admitting that there is more evil than good in all intelligent creatures. *III. Objection.* If it is always impossible not to sin, it is always unjust to punish.
Now, it is always impossible not to sin; or, in other words, every sin is necessary.
Therefore, it is always unjust to punish.
The minor premise of this is proved as follows:
1. *Prosyllogism.* All that is predetermined is necessary. Every event (and consequently sin as well) is necessary.
Again, this second minor premise is proved thus:
2. *Prosyllogism.* That which is future, that which is foreseen, and that which is involved in its causes, is predetermined.

*Answer.* I admit, in a certain sense, the conclusion of the second prosyllogism, which is the minor premise of the first; but I shall deny the major premise of the first prosyllogism—namely, that everything predetermined is necessary. I say this while understanding the *necessity* of sinning, for example, or the impossibility of not sinning or of not performing any action, as the necessity with which we are here concerned: that is, that which is *essential and absolute*, and which destroys the morality of an action and the justice of punishment. For if anyone understood another kind of necessity or impossibility—namely, a necessity that was only *moral*, or which was only *hypothetical* (as will be explained shortly)—it is clear that I should deny the major premise of the objection itself. I might content myself with this answer and demand proof of the denied proposition; but I have again desired to explain my procedure in this work, in order to better clarify the matter and to throw more light on the whole subject, by explaining the *necessity* which ought to be rejected and the *determination* which must take place. That necessity which is contrary to morality and which ought to be rejected, and which would render punishment unjust, is an insurmountable necessity that would make all opposition useless, even if we should wish with all our heart to avoid the necessary action and should make all possible efforts to that end. Also, their prevision and predetermination is not absolute, but it presupposes the will: if it is certain that we shall perform them, it is no less certain that we shall choose to perform them. These voluntary actions and their consequences will not take place regardless of what we do or whether we wish for them or not; instead, they happen through what we shall do and through what we shall wish to do, which leads to them. And this is involved in prevision and in predetermination, and even constitutes their ground. And the necessity of such an event is called conditional or hypothetical necessity, or the necessity of consequence, because it presupposes the will and other requirements; whereas the necessity which destroys morality and renders punishment unjust and reward useless exists in things which will happen whatever we may do or whatever we may wish to do—in a word, it is in that which is essential; and this is what is called an absolute necessity. 

Thus, it is to no purpose, regarding what is absolutely necessary, to make prohibitions or commands, to propose penalties or prizes, or to praise or to blame; it will happen regardless. On the other hand, in voluntary actions and in that which depends upon them, precepts armed with the power to punish and to reward are very often of use and are included in the order of causes which make an action exist. And it is for this reason that not only effort and labor but also prayers are useful; God having had these prayers in view before He regulated things and having had that consideration for them which was proper. This is why the precept which says *ora et labora* (pray and work) holds altogether good; and not only those who (under the empty excuse of the necessity of events) pretend that the care which business demands may be neglected, but also those who reason against prayer, fall into what the ancients even then called the *lazy sophism*. 

Thus, the predetermination of events by causes is exactly what contributes to morality instead of destroying it, and causes incline the will without compelling it. *Answer.* I deny the major premise of this syllogism. Examples have been given and the application to God himself has been made. We do not desire these evils; but we are willing to permit them for the sake of a greater good which we cannot reasonably help preferring to other considerations, and it is a consequent will, which results from antecedent wills, by which we will the good. I know that some persons, in speaking of the antecedent and consequent will of God, have understood by the "antecedent" that which wills that all men should be saved; and by the "consequent," that which wills, in consequence of persistent sin, that they should be damned. V. *Objection*. Whatever produces everything that is real in a thing is its cause.

*Answer*. I might content myself with denying the major or the minor premise, since the term *real* admits of interpretations which would render these premises false. But in order to explain more clearly, I will make a distinction. *Real* signifies either that which is positive only, or it also includes privative beings <note>Entities or qualities defined by the absence or lack of something</note>: in the first case, I deny the major premise and admit the minor; in the second case, I do the contrary. I might have limited myself to this, but I have chosen to proceed still further and give the reason for this distinction. I have been very glad, therefore, to draw attention to the fact that every reality that is purely positive or absolute is a perfection; and that imperfection comes from limitation—that is, from the privative—for to limit is to refuse progress, or the greatest possible progress. Now, God is the cause of all perfections and, consequently, of all realities considered as purely positive. But limitations or privations result from the imperfection of creatures, limiting their receptivity. *Answer.* I deny the <term>major premise</term> of this. It is true that God could overcome the greatest resistance of the human heart, and he does so sometimes—whether by internal grace or by external circumstances that have a great effect on souls—but he does not always do this. Why is there this distinction, it may be asked, and why does his goodness seem limited? It is because, as I have already said in answering the first objection, it would not have been orderly to always act in an extraordinary manner and to overturn the connection of things. The reasons for this connection—by which one person is placed in more favorable circumstances than another—are hidden in the depths of God's wisdom; they depend upon the universal harmony. The best plan of the universe, which God could not fail to choose, made it so. We judge from the event itself, since God has made it, that it was not possible to do better. Far from it being true that this conduct is contrary to goodness, it is supreme goodness that led him to it. This objection with its solution might have been drawn from what was said regarding the first objection, but it seemed useful to address it separately.

VIII. *Objection.* He who cannot fail to choose the best is not free.
God cannot fail to choose the best.

*Answer.* I deny the <term>major premise</term> of this argument; rather, it is true and most perfect liberty to be able to use one's free will for the best, and to always exercise this power without ever being turned from it either by external force or by internal passions. The first of these causes slavery of the body, and the second, slavery of the soul. There is nothing less servile than to be always led toward the good, and always by one's own inclination, without any constraint and without any dissatisfaction. Seneca said somewhere that God commanded but once, but that he obeys always, because he obeys laws which he willed to prescribe to himself; *semel jussit, semper paret*.
