Otherwise, the necessity of the good would be geometrical (so to speak), or metaphysical and altogether absolute; the contingency of things would be destroyed, and there would be no choice. 

But this sort of necessity, which does not destroy the possibility of the opposite, has this name only by analogy; it becomes effective not by the pure essence of things, but by what is outside of them and above them—namely, by the will of God. This necessity is called moral because, to the wise, necessity and *what ought to be* are equivalent things; and when it always has its effect—as it truly does in the perfect sage, that is, in God—it may be said that it is a happy necessity. The closer creatures approach to it, the closer they approach to perfect happiness. Also, this kind of necessity is not what we try to avoid and which destroys morality, rewards, and praise. For what it brings about does not happen regardless of what we may do or will, but because we will it well. And a will for which it is natural to choose well merits praise all the more; it also carries its reward with it, which is supreme happiness. And as this constitution of the divine nature gives entire satisfaction to him who possesses it, it is also the best and the most desirable for the creatures who are all dependent on God. If the will of God did not have the principle of the best as its rule, it would either tend toward evil, which would be the worst, or it would be in some way indifferent to good and evil and would be guided by chance. <page-num>XXXI.</page-num>

## ON WISDOM—THE ART OF REASONING WELL, THE ART OF DISCOVERY, THE ART OF REMEMBERING.

->[From the French.]<-

Wisdom is a perfect knowledge of the principles of all the sciences and of the art of applying them. I call *principles* all the fundamental truths which are sufficient for drawing all conclusions from them when necessary, after some practice and with a little application. In short, it is that which serves to guide the mind in regulating one's conduct, in living honorably and anywhere—even if one were among barbarians—in preserving health, in perfecting oneself in every kind of thing one may need, and finally, in providing the comforts of life. The art of applying these principles to practical needs encompasses the art of judging well or reasoning, the art of discovering unknown truths, and finally, of remembering what one knows at the right moment and when one has need of it.

THE ART OF REASONING WELL consists of the following maxims:

1. Nothing is ever to be recognized as true unless it is so manifest that no ground for doubt can be found. This is why it is useful, when beginning one’s investigations, to imagine oneself interested in defending the opposite view, in order to see if this motivation could not prompt one to find that the matter has something solid to be said in its favor. For prejudices must be avoided, and nothing should be attributed to things except what they actually contain. But one must also never be stubborn.

2. When there appears to be no way to achieve this certainty, we must, while waiting for greater insight, content ourselves with probability. But we must distinguish the degrees of probability, and we must remember that everything we infer from a principle which is only probable must bear the marks of the imperfection of its source, especially when several probabilities must be assumed in order to reach this conclusion, for it then becomes even less certain than each probability which serves as its basis.

3. To infer one truth from another, a certain connection, which shall be without interruption, must be observed. For as one may

feel sure that a chain will hold when he is assured that each separate link is of good material and that it connects the two neighboring links—namely, the one preceding and the one following it—so we may be sure of the accuracy of the reasoning when the subject matter is solid, that is to say, when nothing doubtful enters into it, and the form consists in a perpetual concatenation of truths which allows for no gap. For example: A is B, B is C, and C is D; therefore, A is D. This concatenation will always teach us never to put in the conclusion more than what was in the premises.

**The Art of Discovery** consists of the following maxims:

1. In order to know a thing, we must consider all the requirements of that thing—that is to say, everything which suffices to distinguish it from every other thing. This is what is called definition, nature, or reciprocal property.

2. Having once found a means of distinguishing it from every other thing, this same first rule must be applied to the consideration of each condition or requirement which enters into this means, and all the requirements of each requirement must be considered. And this is what I call true *analysis*, or the breaking down of a difficulty into several parts.

3. When we have pushed the analysis to the end—that is to say, when we have considered the requirements which enter into the consideration of the thing proposed, and even the requirements of the requirements, and when we have finally come to the consideration of certain natures which are understood only through themselves, which are without requirements and which need nothing outside of themselves in order to be conceived—we have reached a perfect knowledge of the thing proposed.

4. When the thing deserves it, we must try to have this perfect knowledge present in the mind all at once; and this is done by repeating the analysis several times until it seems to us that we see the whole of it at a single glance of the mind. And for this result, a certain progression in repetition must be observed.

5. The mark of perfect knowledge is when nothing presents itself in the thing in question for which we cannot account, and when there is no circumstance the outcome of which we cannot predict beforehand. It is very difficult to carry through an analysis of things, but it is not so difficult to complete the analysis of truths of which we have need. Because the analysis of a truth

Most often the beginning of the analysis of a thing suffices for the analysis or perfect knowledge of the truth which we know of the thing.

6. We must always begin our investigations with the easiest thing, such as the most general and the simplest; likewise those things on which it is easy to make experiments and to find their reasoning, such as numbers, lines, and motions.

7. We must proceed in order, from easy things to those which are difficult, and we must try to discover some progression in the order of our meditations, so that we may have nature itself as our guide and voucher.

8. We must try to omit nothing in all our distributions or enumerations. For this, dichotomies by opposite members are very useful.

9. The first of several analyses of different particular matters will be the catalog of simple thoughts, or those which are not far removed from being simple.

10. Having the catalog of simple thoughts, we shall be in a position to recommence *a priori* and to explain the origin of things, beginning at their source, in a perfect order and in a combination or synthesis absolutely complete. And this is all that our mind can do in its current state.

->**THE ART OF REMEMBERING**<-
in the nick of time, and when one needs what they know, consists of the following observations:

1. We must accustom ourselves to be present-minded—that is to say, to be able to meditate just as well in a tumult, on occasion, and in danger, as in our private study. This is why we must test ourselves on various occasions and even seek them out; with this precaution, however, that we do not expose ourselves without good reason to irreparable evil. In the meantime, it is good to exercise ourselves on occasions when the danger is imaginary or small, as in our sports, conversations, discussions, exercises, and plays.

2. We must accustom ourselves to enumerations. This is why it is well to exercise ourselves in collecting all possible cases of the matter in question, all the species of a genus, all the advantages or disadvantages of a means, and all possible ways of aiming at some end.

3. We must accustom ourselves to distinctions; specifically, when two or more very similar things are presented, we must be able to find all their differences on the spot.

4. We must accustom ourselves to analogies; specifically, when two or more very different things are presented, we must be able to find their resemblances.

5. We must be able to cite on the spot things that closely resemble the given thing or that are very different from it. For example, when someone denies some general maxim, it is helpful if I can provide some examples immediately. And when another quotes a maxim against me, it is useful if I can instantly counter him with an instance. When someone tells me a story, it is beneficial if I can provide a similar one then and there.

6. When there are truths or pieces of knowledge in which the natural connection between the subject and its predicate is unknown to us—as happens in matters of fact and in truths of experience—we must make use of certain devices to remember them. Examples include the specific properties of simple, natural, civil, and ecclesiastical history, geography, customs, laws, canons, and languages. I see nothing so well-suited to help us retain these things as humorous verses and sometimes certain diagrams; also, hypotheses invented to explain them by imitating natural things (such as an appropriate etymology, whether true or false, for languages—*Regula mundi*, by imagining certain orders of providence for history).

7. Finally, it is beneficial to make a written *inventory* of the most useful knowledge, along with a *register or alphabetical table*. Finally, a *portable manual* should be drawn from this, containing what is most necessary and most common.

# XXXII.

## THE PRINCIPLES OF NATURE AND OF GRACE. 1714.

->[From the French.]<-

1. Substance is a being capable of action. It is either simple or compound. *Simple substance* is that which has no parts. *Compound substance* is a collection of simple substances or *monads*. *Monas* is a Greek word that signifies unity, or that which is one.

Compounds, or bodies, are multitudes; and simple substances—lives, souls, and spirits—are unities. And there must be simple substances everywhere, because without simple substances there would be no compounds; and consequently, all of nature is full of life.

2. Monads, having no parts, cannot be formed or decomposed. They cannot begin or end naturally; and consequently, they last as long as the universe, which will indeed be changed but will not be destroyed. They cannot have shapes; otherwise, they would have parts. And consequently, a monad, in itself and at any given moment, could not be distinguished from another except by its internal qualities and actions, which can be nothing else than its perceptions (that is, representations of the compound, or of what is external, within the simple), and its *appetitions* (that is, its tendencies to move from one perception to another), which are the principles of change. For the simplicity of substance does not prevent a multiplicity of modifications, which must be found together in this same simple substance, and must consist in the variety of its relations to things which are external. Just as in a center or point, as simple as it is, there is found an infinity of angles formed by the lines which meet there.

3. Everything in nature is full. There are everywhere simple substances, separated in reality from each other by activities of their own which continually change their relations; and each simple substance, or monad, which forms the center of a compound substance (as, for example, of an animal) and the principle of its unity, is surrounded by a mass composed of an infinity of other monads, which constitute the body proper of this central monad; and in accordance with the states of this body, it represents, as a center, the things which are outside of itself. And this body is or-

--- Page 224 ---
<meta>This page continues the text of Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz's "The Principles of Nature and of Grace" (1714), following the definition of monads and their internal perceptions and appetitions.</meta>

ganic, when it forms a sort of automaton or natural machine; which is a machine not only in its entirety, but also in its smallest perceptible parts. And since, because of the fullness of the world, everything is connected and each body acts upon every other body, more or less according to the distance, and is itself affected by it in reaction, it follows that each monad is a living mirror—or one endowed with internal activity—representing the universe from its own point of view, and is as orderly as the universe itself. And perceptions in the monad arise from one another by the law of appetites, or by the *final causes* of good and evil, which consist in perceptible, orderly, or disorderly perceptions; just as the changes of bodies and external phenomena arise from one another by the laws of *efficient causes*, that is, of motions. Thus there is perfect *harmony* between the perceptions of the monad and the movements of bodies, established from the beginning between the system of efficient causes and that of final causes. And in this lies the agreement and physical union of the soul and the body, although neither one can change the laws of the other.

4. Each monad, with a specific body, constitutes a living substance. Thus there is not only life everywhere, provided with limbs or organs, but there is also an infinity of degrees among monads, some dominating more or less over others. But when the monad has organs so adjusted that through them there is clarity and distinctness in the impressions it receives—and consequently in the perceptions that represent them (as, for example, when the shape of the humors of the eyes causes light rays to be concentrated and act with more force)—this can even extend to *feeling* <note>sentiment</note>, that is, to a perception accompanied by memory, or one of which a certain echo remains for a long time to be heard when the occasion arises. Such a living being is called an animal, just as its monad is called a soul. And when this soul is elevated to *reason*, it is something more sublime and is counted among spirits, as will soon be explained.

It is true that animals are sometimes in the condition of simple living beings, and their souls in the condition of simple monads; namely, when their perceptions are not distinct enough to be remembered, as happens in a deep, dreamless sleep or in a faint. But perceptions which have become entirely confused must be developed again in animals, for reasons which I shall shortly (§ 12)

<meta>This page continues Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz's "The Principles of Nature and of Grace" (1714). The word "enumerate" at the start of this page appears to be an OCR error for "accompanied by memory," which completes the definition of "feeling" from the previous page's final sentence.</meta>

accompanied by memory. Therefore, it is well to make a distinction between perception—which is the internal state of the monad representing external things—and apperception, which is consciousness or the reflective knowledge of this internal state. This consciousness is not given to all souls, nor at all times to the same soul. It is for lack of this distinction that the Cartesians have failed, by taking no account of the perceptions of which we are not conscious, just as people take no account of imperceptible bodies. This is also what led the same Cartesians to believe that only spirits are monads, that there are no souls in brutes, and still less other *principles of life*.

And just as they offended the common opinion of men too much by denying feeling to brutes, they have, on the other hand, conformed too much to the prejudices of the masses by confusing a *long swoon*—caused by a great confusion of perceptions—with death in the strict sense, where all perception would cease. This confirmed the ill-founded belief in the destruction of some souls and the poor opinion of some so-called "strong minds" who have argued against the immortality of our soul.

5. There is a continuity in the perceptions of animals which bears some resemblance to reason; but it is founded only on the memory of *facts*, and not at all on the knowledge of *causes*. Thus, a dog avoids the stick with which it has been beaten because memory represents to it the pain which the stick caused. And men, insofar as they are empiricists—that is to say, in three-fourths of their actions—act simply as brutes. For example, we expect that there will be daylight tomorrow because we have always had that experience; only an astronomer foresees it by reason, and even this prediction will finally fail when the cause of day, which is not eternal, shall cease. But true reasoning depends upon necessary or eternal truths, such as those of logic, numbers, and geometry, which establish an indubitable connection of ideas and unfailing consequences. The animals in which these consequences are not observed are called *brutes*; but those which know these necessary truths are properly those called rational animals, and their souls are called spirits. These souls are capable of performing acts of reflection and of considering that which is called the *ego*, substance, monad, soul, spirit—in a word, immaterial things and truths. It is this which makes us capable of the sciences and of demonstrative knowledge.

6. Modern research has taught us, and reason confirms it, that living beings whose organs are known to us—that is to say, plants and animals—do not arise from putrefaction or from chaos, as the ancients believed, but from *pre-formed* seeds, and consequently through the transformation of pre-existing living beings. There are animalcules in the seeds of large animals which, by means of conception, take on a new appearance that they make their own, and through which they can nourish themselves and increase their size in order to pass to a larger stage and to achieve the propagation of the large animal. It is true that the souls of human spermatic animals are not rational and do not become so until conception determines these animals for human nature. And as animals generally are not born entirely during conception or generation, neither do they perish entirely in what we call *death*; for it is reasonable that what does not begin naturally should not end in the natural order either. Therefore, leaving behind their mask or their rags, they merely return to a more subtle stage where they can, nevertheless, be just as perceptive and just as well-ordered as in the larger one. And what we have just said of large animals also takes place in the generation and death of smaller spermatic animals, in comparison with which the former may be considered large; for everything extends *ad infinitum* <note>to infinity</note> in nature.

Thus, not only souls, but also animals, are incapable of being generated and are imperishable: they are only developed, unfolded, reclothed, unclothed, and transformed. Souls never leave their entire body and do not pass from one body into another that is entirely new to them.

There is therefore no *metempsychosis* <note>the transmigration of souls from one body to another</note>; but there is *metamorphosis*. Animals change, taking and leaving only parts: the same thing happens gradually and through small invisible particles, yet continuously in nutrition; and it happens suddenly and visibly, though rarely, in conception or death, which cause a gain or loss of everything at once.

7. Up to this point, we have spoken as simple *physicists*; now we must proceed to *metaphysics* by making use of the great principle, little employed in general, which teaches that *nothing happens without a sufficient reason*; that is to say, that nothing happens without it being possible for one who understands things well enough to give a reason sufficient to determine why it is so and not otherwise. This principle being established, the first question

which should rightly be asked, would be, *Why is there something rather than nothing?* For nothing is simpler and easier than something. Further, suppose that things must exist, we must be able to give a reason why they must exist so and not otherwise.

8. Now this <term>sufficient reason</term> for the existence of the universe could not be found in the series of contingent things, that is, of bodies and of their representations in souls; for matter being indifferent in itself to motion and to rest and to this or another motion, we could not find the reason of motion in it, and still less of a certain motion. And although the present motion which is in matter comes from the preceding motion, and that from still another preceding, yet in this way we should never make any progress, go as far as we might; for the same question would always remain.

Therefore it must be that the sufficient reason which has no need of another reason, be outside this series of contingent things and be found in a substance which is its cause, or which is a necessary being, carrying the reason of its existence within itself; otherwise we should still not have a sufficient reason in which we could rest. And this final reason of things is called *God*.

9. This simple primitive substance must contain in itself eminently the perfections contained in the derivative substances which are its effects; thus it will have perfect power, knowledge and will: that is, it will have omnipotence and sovereign goodness. And as justice, taken generally, is only goodness conformed to wisdom, there must too be sovereign justice in God. The reason which has caused things to exist by him, makes them still dependent upon him in existing and in working: and they are continually receiving from him that which gives them some perfection; but the imperfection which remains in them, comes from the essential and original limitation of the creature.

10. It follows from the supreme perfection of God, that in creating the universe he has chosen the best possible plan, in which there is the greatest variety together with the greatest order; the best arranged ground, place, time; the most results produced in the most simple ways; the most of power, knowledge, happiness and goodness in the creatures that the universe could permit. For since all the possibles in the understanding of God laid claim to existence in proportion to their perfections, the actual world, as the

11. The <term>supreme wisdom</term> of God compelled him to choose the *laws of movement* best adjusted and most suited to abstract or metaphysical reasons. He preserves there the same quantity of total and absolute force, or actions; the same quantity of respective force or reaction; and lastly the same quantity of directive force. Furthermore, action is always equal to reaction, and the total effect is always equivalent to the full cause. And it is not surprising that we could not, by the mere consideration of *efficient causes* or of matter, account for those <term>laws of movement</term> which have been discovered in our time, some of which I discovered myself. For I have found that it was necessary to have recourse to *final causes*, and that these laws do not depend upon the *principle of necessity*, like logical, arithmetical, and geometrical truths, but upon the *principle of fitness*, that is, upon the choice of wisdom. And this is one of the most effective and evident proofs of the existence of God for those who can examine these matters thoroughly.

12. It follows, furthermore, from the perfection of the supreme author, that not only is the order of the entire universe the most perfect possible, but also that each living mirror representing the universe in accordance with its point of view—that is to say, each <term>monad</term> or *substantial centre*—must have its perceptions and its desires as well-regulated as is compatible with all the rest. From this it follows further that souls—that is, the most dominant monads, or rather, animals—cannot fail to awaken from the state of stupor in which death or some other accident may place them.

13. For everything in existence is regulated once and for all with as much order and harmony as is possible, since supreme wisdom and goodness cannot act except with perfect harmony. The present is pregnant with the future, the future could be read in the past, and the distant is expressed in the near. One could become acquainted with the beauty of the universe in each soul if one could unfold all its folds, which only develop visibly over time. Each soul knows the infinite and knows all, but only confusedly. Just as when walking on the seashore and hearing the great noise it makes, I hear the individual sounds of each wave of which the total sound is composed, but without distinguishing them; so our confused perceptions are the result of the impressions which the whole universe makes upon us. It is the same with each monad. God alone has a distinct consciousness of everything, for he is the source of all. It has been well said that he is like a center that is everywhere, but his circumference is nowhere, since everything is immediately present to him without any withdrawal from this center.

14. As regards the rational soul, or *spirit*, there is something in it more than in the monads, or even in simple souls. It is not only a mirror of the universe of creatures, but also an image of the Divinity. The *spirit* has not only a perception of the works of God, but it is even capable of producing something which resembles them, although in miniature. For, to say nothing of the wonders of dreams where we effortlessly and even involuntarily invent things that we would have to think about for a long time while awake in order to discover, our soul is architectonic in its voluntary actions also. By discovering the sciences according to which God has regulated things (*pondere, mensura, numero* <note>by weight, measure, and number</note>, etc.), it imitates—within its own department and in the little world where it is permitted to exercise itself—what God does in the large world.

15. This is why all spirits, whether of men or of <term>genii</term>, entering by virtue of reason and of the eternal truths into a sort of society with God, are members of the City of God. This is to say, they are members of the most perfect state, formed and governed by the greatest and best of monarchs; where there is no crime without punishment and no good action without a proportionate reward; and finally, as much virtue and happiness as is possible. This occurs not by a disruption of nature—as if what God prepares for souls disturbed the laws of bodies—but by the very order of natural things, in virtue of the harmony pre-established for all time between the realms of *nature* and of *grace*, between God as Architect and God as Monarch. Thus, nature leads to grace, and grace, while making use of nature, perfects it.

Since God is the most perfect and most happy, and consequently the most lovable of substances, and since *truly pure love* consists in the state which finds pleasure in the perfections and happiness of the loved object, this love should give us the greatest pleasure of which we are capable when God is its object.

17. And it is easy to love him as we should, if we know him as I have just described. We see how much pleasure honors give to men, although they do not consist of sensory qualities at all.

Martyrs and fanatics (though the affection of the latter is poorly regulated) show what the pleasure of the spirit can accomplish; and what is more, even sensory pleasures are essentially intellectual pleasures that are only confusedly known.

Music charms us, even though its beauty consists only in the harmony of numbers and in the calculation of the beats or vibrations of sounding bodies which meet at certain intervals—of which we are not conscious, but which the soul continues to perform. The pleasures that sight finds in proportions are of the same nature; and those caused by the other senses amount to almost the same thing, although we cannot explain it so clearly.

18. It may be said that even from the present time onward, the *love of God* allows us to enjoy a foretaste of future happiness. This is not like the Stoics, who force themselves to be patient, but is instead a present contentment that assures us of future happiness. And besides this present pleasure, nothing can be more useful for the future; for the love of God also fulfills our hopes and leads us on the road to supreme happiness. # THE MONADOLOGY. 1714.
## [From the French.]

<margin>✓</margin>
1. THE *monad* of which we shall speak here is simply a simple substance that enters into compounds; *simple* means that it is without parts.*

2. And there must be simple substances, since there are compound substances; for the compound is only a collection or *aggregate* of simple substances.

<margin>✓</margin>
3. Now, where there are no parts, neither extension, shape, nor divisibility is possible. And these monads are the true atoms of nature—in a word, the elements of things.

4. Dissolution is also not to be feared at all, and there is no conceivable way in which a simple substance can perish naturally.†

5. For the same reason, there is no way in which a simple substance can begin naturally, since it cannot be formed by composition.

6. Thus, it may be said that monads can only begin or end *all at once*; that is to say, they can only begin by creation and end by annihilation, whereas that which is compound begins or ends by its parts.

<margin>✓</margin>
7. There is also no way of explaining how a monad can be altered or changed internally by any other created thing, for nothing can be rearranged within it, nor can any internal movement be conceived that can be excited, directed, increased, or diminished within it, as can be done in compounds where there is change among the parts. Monads have no windows through which anything can enter or depart. *Accidents* cannot detach themselves or go out from substances, as the *sensible species* of the Scholastics formerly did. Likewise, neither substance nor accident can enter a monad from the outside.

8. Nevertheless, monads must have some qualities, otherwise they would not even be entities. And if simple substances did not differ at all in their qualities, there would be no way of perceiving any changes in things, since what is in the compound can only

---

<note>* Theodicy, § 10.</note> <note>† § 89.</note>

...come from the simple ingredients, and if the monads were without qualities they could not be distinguished from one another, since they also do not differ in quantity. Consequently, assuming a plenum, each place in any movement could receive only the equivalent of what it had before, and one state of things would not be distinguishable from another.

9. Moreover, it is necessary that each monad should differ from every other. For there are never two beings in nature exactly alike, where it is not possible to find an internal difference or one founded upon an intrinsic characteristic.

10. I also take it for granted that every created being, and consequently the created monad also, is subject to change, and even that this change is continuous in each.

11. It follows from what has just been said, that the natural changes of the monads proceed from an internal principle, since an external cause could not influence their interior.*

12. But besides the principle of change, there must be a *detail of that which changes*, which forms, so to speak, the specification and variety of the simple substances.

13. This detail must involve a multitude within the unity or within the simple substance. For since every natural change happens by degrees, something changes and something remains; consequently, there must be a plurality of affections and of relations in the simple substance, although not of parts.

14. The transient state, which involves and represents multitude in unity or in the simple substance, is only what we call *perception*, which must be distinguished from apperception or from consciousness, as will appear in what follows. Here is where the Cartesians especially failed, having taken no account of the perceptions of which we are not conscious. It is this also which made them suppose that only spirits are monads and that there are no souls in animals or other entelechies. They, along with the common people, have also confused a long state of unconsciousness [*étourdissement*] with death strictly speaking, and have therefore agreed with the old Scholastic prejudice of entirely separate souls, and have even confirmed weaker minds in their belief in the mortality of the soul.

15. The action of the internal principle which causes the change or the passage from one perception to another, may be called *appetition*—

16. We experience in ourselves a multitude within a simple substance when we find that even the slightest thought of which we are conscious involves variety in its object. Thus, all those who admit that the soul is a simple substance must also admit this multitude within the monad, and Mr. Bayle should not find in it the difficulties which he mentions in his *Dictionary*, in the article *Rorarius*.

17. We must also confess that *perception*, and what depends on it, is *inexplicable by mechanical causes*—that is, by figures and motions. And, assuming there were a machine so constructed as to cause thought, feeling, and perception, we could imagine it enlarged while preserving the same proportions, so that we might enter it like a mill. And this granted, we would only find, upon visiting it, pieces that push against one another, but never anything by which to explain a perception. It must be sought, therefore, in the simple substance and not in the compound or machine. Nothing but this, also, can be found in the simple substance; and it is in this alone that all the *internal actions* of simple substances consist.

18. The name *entelechies* might be given to all simple substances or created monads, for they have within themselves a certain perfection (ἔχουσι τὸ ἐντελές); there is a certain self-sufficiency (αὐτάρκεια) which makes them the sources of their internal actions and, so to speak, incorporeal automata.

19. If we choose to give the name *soul* to everything that has *perceptions* and *desires* in the general sense which I have just explained, all simple substances or created monads may be called souls. But as feeling is something more than a simple perception, I agree that the general name of monads or entelechies shall suffice for those simple substances which have only perception, and that only those substances shall be called *souls* whose perception is more distinct and is accompanied by memory.

20. For we experience in ourselves a state in which we remember nothing and have no distinguishable perceptions, as, for instance, when we fall into unconsciousness or when we are overpowered by a profound and dreamless sleep. In this state the soul does not differ

21. And it does not follow at all that the simple substance is therefore without any perception. This is indeed impossible for the reasons mentioned above; for it cannot perish, nor can it exist without some state, which is nothing other than perception. But when there is a great number of minute perceptions where nothing is distinct, we are stunned—as when we turn continually in the same direction many times in succession, which causes a dizziness that may make us lose consciousness and does not allow us to see anything distinctly. Thus, death may produce this condition in animals for a time.

22. And as every present state of a simple substance is naturally the consequence of its preceding state, so its present is big with its future.†

23. Therefore, since we are aware of our perceptions upon being awakened from a stupor, we must have had them immediately before, although we were entirely unconscious of them; for one perception can only come naturally from another perception, just as one motion can only come naturally from another motion.‡

24. From this we see that if there were nothing distinct—nothing, so to speak, in relief and of a higher flavor—in our perceptions, we would always be in a dazed state. This is the condition of the naked monad.

25. So also we see that nature has given higher perceptions to animals by the effort she has taken to provide them with organs which collect many rays of light or many waves of air, in order to make them more effective through their union. There is something of the same kind in smell, in taste, in touch, and perhaps in a multitude of other senses which are unknown to us. I shall presently explain how that which takes place in the soul represents that which occurs in the organs.

26. Memory provides souls with a kind of sequence which imitates reason, but which ought to be distinguished from it. 30. These reflective acts provide the principal objects of our reasonings.†

31. Our reasonings are founded on *two great principles*: that of *contradiction*, by virtue of which we judge that to be *false* which involves a contradiction, and that *true* which is opposed or contradictory to the false.‡

32. And that of *sufficient reason*, by virtue of which we consider that no fact can be real or existent, and no statement true, unless there is a sufficient reason why it is so and not otherwise, although most often these reasons cannot be known to us.||

<meta>This page continues the philosophical argument concerning the nature of knowledge and the existence of God, following the previous discussion of human reason and reflection as the distinguishing features of the rational soul.</meta>

33. There are also two kinds of *truths*: those of *reasoning* and those of *fact*. Truths of reasoning are necessary, and their opposite is impossible; truths of fact are contingent, and their opposite is possible. When a truth is necessary, its reason can be found by analysis, resolving it into simpler ideas and truths until we reach those which are primitive.*

34. This is how mathematicians, through analysis, reduce speculative theorems and practical canons to *definitions, axioms*, and *postulates*.

35. Finally, there are simple ideas that cannot be defined; there are also axioms and postulates—in a word, primary principles—which cannot be proved and indeed need no proof. These are *identical propositions*, the opposite of which contains an explicit contradiction.

36. But there must also be a *sufficient reason* for *contingent truths*, or those *of fact*—that is, for the series of things spread throughout the universe of created objects. In these cases, the resolution into particular reasons could involve endless detail because of the immense variety of objects and the division of bodies *to infinity*. There is an infinity of shapes and movements, both present and past, which serve as the efficient cause of my current writing; and there is an infinity of minor inclinations and dispositions of my soul, past and present, which serve as the final cause.†

37. And as all this *detail* only involves other contingencies, either earlier or more detailed, each of which requires a similar analysis for its explanation, we make no progress. Therefore, the sufficient or final reason must be outside the sequence or *series* of this detail of contingencies, however infinite it may be.

38. And thus, the final reason of things must be found in a necessary substance, in which the detail of changes exists only eminently, as in their source; and this is what we call GOD.‡

39. Since this substance is the sufficient reason for all this detail, which is also linked together throughout, *there is but one God, and this God suffices*.

40. We may also judge that this supreme substance, which is unique, universal, and necessary, has nothing outside of itself which is independent of it, and being the simple series of possible

41. From this it follows that God is absolutely perfect—*perfection* being nothing other than the magnitude of positive reality taken in its strictest sense, setting aside the limits or boundaries in that which is limited. And where there are no limits—that is, in God—perfection is absolutely infinite.*

42. It also follows that created beings derive their perfections from God's influence, but that their imperfections arise from their own nature, which is incapable of existing without limits. For it is by this that they are distinguished from God.†

43. It is also true that in God is the source of not only existences but also essences, insofar as they are real, or of that which is real in what is possible. This is because God's understanding is the realm of eternal truths, or of the ideas on which they depend; without Him, there would be nothing real in possibilities—not only would nothing exist, but nothing would even be possible.‡

44. Nevertheless, if there is a reality in essences or possibilities, or in the eternal truths, this reality must be founded upon something existing and actual; consequently, it must be founded in the existence of the necessary Being, in whom essence involves existence—or for whom being possible is sufficient for being actual.||

45. Hence, God (or the necessary Being) alone has this privilege: that He must exist if He is possible. And since nothing can hinder the possibility of that which possesses no limits, no negation, and consequently no contradiction, this alone is sufficient to establish the existence of God *a priori*. We have also proved it by the reality of the eternal truths. But we have just proved it *a posteriori* as well, since contingent beings exist that can only find their final or sufficient reason in a necessary Being who contains the reason for His existence within Himself.

47. Thus, God alone is the original unity or the primary simple substance, of which all created or derived monads are the products. They are born, so to speak, from moment to moment by continual fulgurations of the Divinity, limited by the receptivity of the creature, for whom such limitation is essential.†

48. In God there is *Power*, which is the source of all; then *Knowledge*, which contains the details of ideas; and finally *Will*, which brings about changes or products according to the principle of the best. This corresponds to what, in created monads, forms the subject or basis, the perceptive faculty, and the appetitive faculty. But in God these attributes are absolutely infinite or perfect, while in created monads or in the entelechies (or *perfectihabies*, as Harmolaus Barbarus translated the word), they are only imitations in proportion to their perfection.‡

49. The creature is said to *act* externally insofar as it is perfect, and to *be acted upon* by another insofar as it is imperfect. Thus, *action* is attributed to the monad insofar as it has distinct perceptions, and *passion* (being acted upon) insofar as it has confused perceptions.||

50. And one creature is more perfect than another when there is found within it that which serves to explain *a priori* what takes place in another; it is in this way that it is said to act upon the other.

51. But in simple substances, the influence of one monad upon another is purely *ideal*, since it can take effect only through the intervention of God. This occurs because, within the ideas of God, one monad may reasonably demand that God—in regulating the others from the beginning of things—should take it into account. For since a created monad can have no physical influence on the interior of another, it is only in this way that one can be dependent upon another.¶

52. And it is for this reason that the actions and passions of creatures are mutual. For God, in comparing two simple substances, finds in each one reasons that compel him to adjust the other to it. Consequently, that which in certain respects is active is, from another point of view, passive; *active* insofar as what is...

60. Besides, we can see in what I have just said *a priori* reasons why things could not be otherwise, because God, in regulating everything, has regard for each part, and particularly for each monad. Since its nature is representative, nothing can limit it to representing only a part of things; although it may be true that this representation is only confused regarding the details of the whole universe, and can be distinct only in the case of a small part of things—that is, in the case of those which are nearest or largest in relation to each of the monads—otherwise each monad would be a divinity. It is not in the object, but only in the modification of the knowledge of the object, that monads are limited. They all tend confusedly toward the infinite, toward the whole, but they are limited and distinguished by their degrees of distinct perceptions.

61. And in this respect, compound substances correspond with simple substances. For since the world is a *plenum*, making all matter connected, and since in a *plenum* every movement has some effect on distant bodies in proportion to their distance, so that each body is affected not only by those which touch it and feels in some way all that happens to them, but also by their means is affected by those which touch the first with which it is in immediate contact, it follows that this communication extends to any distance whatever. Consequently, each body feels all that passes in the universe, so that he who sees all could read in each that which happens everywhere else, and even that which has been or shall be, perceiving in the present that which is removed in time as well as in space; σύμπνοια πάντα <note>All things breathe together.</note>, said Hippocrates. But a soul can read in itself only that which is distinctly represented in it. It cannot develop its laws all at once, for they reach into the infinite.

62. Thus, although each created monad represents the entire universe, it represents most distinctly the body which is particularly assigned to it and of which it forms the entelechy; and as this body represents the whole universe by the connection of all matter in a plenum, the soul also represents the whole universe by representing that body which especially belongs to it.*

63. The body belonging to a monad, which is its entelechy or soul, constitutes, with the entelechy, what may be called a *living*

Now, this body of a living being or of an animal is always organic; for since every monad is, in its own way, a mirror of the universe, and since the universe is arranged in perfect order, there must also be order in the representative—that is, in the perceptions of the soul—and consequently in the body, according to which the universe is represented in it.*

64. Thus, each organic body of a living being is a kind of divine machine or natural automaton, which infinitely surpasses all artificial automata. This is because a machine made by human art is not a machine in every one of its parts; for example, the tooth of a brass wheel has parts or fragments which to us are no longer artificial and have nothing in themselves to show the use for which the wheel was intended in the machine. But nature's machines—that is, living bodies—are machines even in their smallest parts *ad infinitum*. This is the difference between nature and art—that is, between the divine art and ours.

<margin>† Prelim., § 70 ; Theod., § 195.</margin>
65. And the Author of nature has been able to devise these divine and infinitely marvelous works of art because each portion of matter is not only divisible *ad infinitum*, as the ancients perceived, but also each part is actually subdivided without end into parts, each of which has its own motion; otherwise, it would be impossible for each portion of matter to express the entire universe.†

66. Hence, we see that there is a world of creatures, of living beings, of animals, of <term>entelechies</term>, and of souls in the smallest particle of matter.

67. Each portion of matter may be conceived as a garden full of plants and as a pond full of fish. But each branch of a plant, each limb of an animal, and each drop of its fluids is also such a garden or such a pond.

68. And although the earth or air contained between the plants of the garden, or the water between the fish of the pond, is neither plant nor fish, they still contain more of them—though for the most part, these are so tiny that they are imperceptible to us.

<margin>‡ Preface, pp. 40, 41.</margin>
69. Therefore, there is nothing uncultivated, nothing sterile, and nothing dead in the universe; there is no chaos and no confusion, except in appearance. It is just as a pond seen from a distance might appear to have a confused movement and swarming, so to speak, of fish, without the individual fish themselves being perceived.‡

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the relationship between souls and bodies, specifically exploring how souls are always joined to matter and the true nature of birth and death as transformations rather than beginnings or endings.</meta>

70. We see, therefore, that every living body has a ruling <term>entelechy</term>, which is the soul in an animal; but the parts of this living body are filled with other living beings—plants and animals—each of which also has its own entelechy or governing soul.

71. However, it should not be imagined—as some who misunderstood my thinking have done—that each soul has a mass or portion of matter assigned or united to it forever, or that it possesses other inferior living beings destined to serve it forever. For all bodies, like rivers, are in a state of perpetual flux, with parts constantly entering and leaving them.

72. Thus, the soul changes its body only gradually and by degrees, so that it is never stripped of all its organs at once. Animals often undergo a metamorphosis, but never <term>metempsychosis</term> or the transmigration of souls. There are also no entirely separate souls, nor *genii* without bodies. God alone is entirely without a body.<note>Théodicy, § 90, 124.</note>

73. For this reason, there is strictly speaking neither a complete birth nor an absolute death where the soul is separated from the body. What we call birth is a development or increase, just as what we call *death* is an envelopment and a decrease.

74. Philosophers have been greatly puzzled by the origin of forms, <term>entelechies</term>, or souls. However, today—since we know through precise investigations of plants, insects, and animals that organic bodies in nature are never produced from chaos or decay, but always from seeds containing some *pre-formation*—it is believed that not only was the organic body already there before conception, but the soul was in that body too; in short, the animal itself existed. Through conception, this animal has merely been prepared for a greater transformation into an animal of another kind. We see something similar outside of birth, such as when worms become flies or caterpillars become butterflies.<note>§§ 86, 89, 90, 187, 188, 403, 397; Preface, p. 40, etc.</note>

75. Those animals, some of which are raised by conception to the level of larger animals, may be called <term>spermatics</term>; but those among them that remain in their own class—which is the majority—are

Thus, not only will there be no generation, but also no total destruction or death in the strict sense. These reasonings, made <term>a posteriori</term> and drawn from experience, harmonize perfectly with principles deduced <term>a priori</term>, as mentioned above.*

77. Thus it may be said that not only the soul (a mirror of an indestructible universe) is indestructible, but also the animal itself, although its physical machine often partially perishes and acquires or sheds organic remains.

78. These principles have given me the means of explaining naturally the union, or rather the agreement, of the soul and the organic body. The soul follows its own specific laws, and the body also follows its own laws; they meet by virtue of the <term>pre-established harmony</term> between all substances, since they are all representations of one and the same universe.†

79. Souls act according to the laws of <term>final causes</term>, through desires, ends, and means. Bodies act in accordance with the laws of <term>efficient causes</term> or of motion. These two realms, that of efficient causes and that of final causes, are in harmony with each other.

80. Descartes recognized that souls cannot give any force to bodies, because there is always the same amount of force in matter; nevertheless, he believed that the soul could change the direction of bodies. But this was because, in his day, the law of nature which enforces the <term>conservation of total direction</term> in matter was not known. If he had known this, he would have discovered my system of the pre-established harmony.‡

81. Through this system, it happens that bodies act as if (though it is impossible) there were no souls, and souls act as if there were no bodies, and both act as if each influenced the other.

90. Finally, under this perfect government, there will be no good action without reward and no bad action without punishment, and everything must result in the well-being of the good. This is what causes wise and virtuous persons to work toward everything that seems to conform to the divine will (whether presumptive or antecedent), and yet to content themselves with what God actually sends through his secret, consequent, and decisive will. They recognize that if we could sufficiently comprehend the order of the universe, we would find that it surpasses all the wishes of the wisest, and that it is impossible to make it better than it is—not only for everyone in general, but also for ourselves in particular, provided we are attached, as we should be, to the author of all. He is not only the architect and efficient cause of our being, but also our master and final cause, who ought to be the sole aim of our will and who alone can secure our happiness.†

### XXXIV.

### ON THE DOCTRINE OF MALEBRANCHE. A Letter to M. Remond de Montmort, containing Remarks on the Book of Father Tertre against Father Malebranche. 1715.

->[From the French.]<-

SIR, I have just received your package, and I thank you for the interesting articles which you have sent me. I will say nothing regarding the continuation of Homer; but as he is the most ancient of all the authors whose works remain to us (after the sacred books), I wish that someone would undertake to clarify the historical and geographical difficulties that remote antiquity has created in these works. This is especially true for the *Odyssey*, regarding ancient geography; for, however mythical the travels of Ulysses may be, it is nonetheless certain that Homer brought him to countries spoken of at that time, but which are now difficult to recognize.

I turn now to the philosophical articles concerning the Reverend Father Malebranche (whose passing I deeply regret), which aim to clarify the natural theology of the Chinese. The *Refutation* of this Father's system, divided into three small volumes, is undoubtedly the work of a man of ability, for it is clear and ingenious. I even approve of some of it, but other parts are too extreme. There is too much divergence shown here from the views of Descartes and Father Malebranche, even when they are interpreted favorably. It is time to abandon these enmities, which the Cartesians have perhaps brought upon themselves by showing too much contempt for the ancients and for the schoolmen, in whose work there is nevertheless a solidity that deserves our attention. Thus, justice should be shown to both sides, and we should benefit from the discoveries of both, just as it is right to reject what each proposes without foundation.

1. It is right to refute the Cartesians when they claim that the soul is nothing but thought, as well as when they say that matter is nothing but extension. For the soul is a subject or <term>concretum</term> that thinks, and matter is an extended subject, or a subject endowed with extension. This is why I maintain that space must not be con-

<summary>In this letter to Remond de Montmort, Leibniz discusses the importance of ancient geography in Homer's works and begins a critique of Father Tertre's refutation of Malebranche. He argues for a balanced approach that respects both modern Cartesian insights and the solid foundations of ancient and scholastic philosophy.</summary>
<keywords>Nicolas Malebranche, Remond de Montmort, Father Tertre, Homer, Odyssey, Descartes, Cartesians, schoolmen, natural theology, China, soul, matter, extension, concretum</keywords>

--- Page 248 ---
<meta>This page continues the author's critique of Father Malebranche’s philosophy, specifically addressing the nature of matter, the activity of the soul, and the relationship between substances.</meta>

founded with matter, although I agree that naturally there is no void space; the scholastics are right to distinguish between the concrete and the abstract when it comes to exactness.

2. I concede to the Cartesians that the soul actually always thinks, but I do not grant that it is conscious of all these thoughts. For our great perceptions and our great appetites, of which we are conscious, are composed of innumerable tiny perceptions and small inclinations of which we cannot be conscious. And it is in these insensible perceptions that the reason is found for what happens within us; just as the reason for what takes place in sensible bodies consists of insensible movements.

3. There is also good reason for refuting Reverend Father Malebranche, especially when he maintains that the soul is purely passive. I think I have demonstrated that every substance is active, and especially the soul. This is also the idea which the ancients and the moderns have had of it; and the entelechy of Aristotle, which has caused such a stir, is nothing other than force or activity; that is, a state from which action naturally flows if nothing hinders it. But matter, primary and pure, taken without the souls or lives which are united to it, is purely passive; properly speaking, it is also not a substance, but something incomplete. And secondary matter—for example, a body—is not a substance, but for another reason: because it is a collection of several substances, like a pond full of fish or a flock of sheep; and consequently, it is what is called *unum per accidens*, in a word, a phenomenon. A true substance, such as an animal, is composed of an immaterial soul and an organized body; and it is the compound of these two which is called *unum per se*.

4. As to the *efficiency* of secondary causes, it is again right to maintain it against the opinion of this Father. I have demonstrated that each simple substance, or monad (such as souls), follows its own laws in producing its actions, without being capable of being disturbed in them by the influence of another created simple substance; thus, bodies do not change the ethico-logical laws of souls, any more than souls change the physico-mechanical laws of bodies. This is why secondary causes really act, but without any influence of one created simple substance upon another; and souls harmonize with bodies and among themselves by virtue of the pre-established harmony, and not at all by a mutual physical influ-

<meta>This page continues the author's critique of the "Refutation" of Father Malebranche, focusing on the nature of the union between soul and body, the definition of extension as an attribute rather than a substance, and the human understanding of the infinite.</meta>

influence; except in the case of the metaphysical union of the soul and its body which makes them compose a *unum per se* [a unity in itself], an animal, a living being. It has been right, therefore, to refute the opinion of those who deny the action of secondary causes; but it must be done without reintroducing false influences, such as the *species* of the schools.

5. Father Malebranche made use of this argument: that extension, not being a mode of being of matter, must be its substance. The author of the *Refutation* (Vol. I, p. 91) distinguishes between the positive modes of being; and he claims that extension is one of the modes of being of the second sort, which he thinks can be conceived on their own. But these are not positive modes of being; they all consist of various limitations, and none can be conceived except through the being of which they are the modes and ways. And as to extension, it may be said that it is not a mode of being of matter, and yet it is not a substance either. What is it, then? you will ask, sir. I reply that it is an attribute of substances, and there is a clear difference between attributes and modes of being.

6. It appears to me, also, that the author of the *Refutation* does not effectively challenge the opinion of the Cartesians regarding the infinite, which they rightly consider to be prior to the finite, and of which the finite is but a limitation. He says (Vol. I, p. 303) that if the mind had a clear and direct view of the infinite, Father Malebranche would not have needed so much reasoning to make us think of it. But by the same argument, he would reject the very simple and very natural knowledge we have of the Divine. These kinds of objections amount to nothing, for there is a need for labor and application in order to give people the attention necessary for even the simplest notions, and this end will only be reached by calling them back from their distractions to themselves. It is also for this reason that the theologians who have composed works on eternity have much need of discussion, comparisons, and examples to make it well understood, even though there is nothing simpler than the notion of eternity. But it is because, in such matters, everything depends on attention. The author adds (Vol. I, p. 307) that in this alleged knowledge of the infinite, the mind merely sees that lengths may be put end to end and repeated as many times as is wished. Very good; but this author should consider that knowing that this repetition can always be made is already knowing the infinite.

<meta>This page continues the author's critique of the "Refutation" of Father Malebranche, transitioning from a discussion on the nature of the infinite and divine knowledge to an analysis of Malebranche's natural theology and his theory of ideas.</meta>

7. The same author examines in his second volume the natural theology of Father Malebranche; but his work seems to me overdone, although he declares that he merely presents the doubts of others. Because the Father says that God is being in general, this is interpreted as a vague and conceptual being, such as a genus in logic; and it takes very little more to accuse Malebranche of atheism. But I think that the Father did not mean a vague and indeterminate being, but rather absolute being, which differs from particular, limited beings as absolute and boundless space differs from a circle or a square.

8. There is more reason to challenge the opinion of Malebranche regarding ideas. For there is (seemingly) no necessity to consider them as something external to us. It is sufficient to regard ideas as notions—that is to say, as modifications of our soul. This is how the schoolmen, Descartes, and Arnauld regard them. But since God is the source of possibilities and consequently of ideas, the Father may be excused and even praised for having changed the terms and given a more exalted meaning to ideas, by distinguishing them from notions and by treating them as perfections in God in which we participate through our knowledge. This mystical language of the Father was not strictly necessary; but I find it useful, for it more clearly illustrates our dependence on God. It even seems that Plato, when speaking of ideas, and St. Augustine, when speaking of truth, had similar thoughts, which I find very remarkable; and this is the part of Malebranche’s system which I should like to see retained, along with the phrases and formulas that depend on it, as I am very glad that the most substantial part of mystical theology is preserved. And far from saying, with the author of the *Refutation* (*Vol. 2, p. 304*), that the system of St. Augustine is slightly infected with the language and opinions of the Platonists, I would say that it is thereby enriched and highlighted.

9. I say almost the same regarding the opinion of Father Malebranche when he affirms that *we see all things in God*. I say that it is an expression which may be excused and even praised, provided it is correctly understood; for it is easier to fall into error in this than in the previous point regarding ideas. It is, therefore, worth noting that not only in Malebranche’s system but also in mine, God alone is the immediate external object of souls, exercising a real influence upon them. And although the current school seems to admit other

10. The third volume refutes the system of revealed theology of Father Malebranche, especially in reference to <term>grace</term> and <term>predestination</term>. But as I have not sufficiently studied the author's particular theological opinions, and as I think I have sufficiently clarified the matter in my essay *The Theodicy* (*La Théodicée*), I excuse myself from entering into it at present.

But this requires a separate letter; this one which I have just written is already sufficiently long. Referring to my preceding letter for the rest, I am zealously, sir, your very humble and very obedient servant,

LEIBNITZ.

Hanover, Nov. 4, 1715.

<page-num>XXXV.</page-num>
<header>LETTERS TO SAM. CLARKE.</header>

## MR. LEIBNITZ'S FIRST PAPER: Being an Extract of a Letter written in November, 1715.

1. *Natural religion itself* seems to decay [*in England*] very much. Many believe human souls to be material; others make *God himself* a corporeal Being.

2. Mr. Locke and his followers are *uncertain*, at least, whether the soul is not material and naturally perishable.

3. Sir *Isaac Newton* says that space is an *organ* which God uses to perceive things by. But if God stands in need of any organ to perceive things by, it will follow that they do not depend altogether upon him, nor were they produced by him.

4. Sir *Isaac Newton* and his followers also have a very odd opinion concerning the work of God. According to their doctrine, God Almighty needs to *wind up* his watch from time to time; otherwise, it would cease to move. He did not, it seems, have sufficient foresight to make it a perpetual motion. Indeed, the machine of God's making is so imperfect, according to these gentlemen, that he is obliged to *clean* it now and then by an extraordinary intervention, and even to *mend* it, as a clockmaker mends his work; who must consequently be considered a less skillful workman the more often he is obliged to mend his work and set it right. In my opinion, the same force and vigor always remains in the world and only passes from one part of matter to another, in agreement with the laws of nature and the beautiful *pre-established order*. And I hold that when God works miracles, he does not do it in order to supply the needs of nature, but those of grace. Whoever thinks otherwise must necessarily have a very poor notion of the wisdom and power of God.

<summary>Leibniz initiates his correspondence with Samuel Clarke by criticizing the Newtonian view of the universe, arguing that the idea of God as a "watchmaker" who must intervene to repair the world diminishes divine perfection. He contrasts this with his own theory of a pre-established order where the universe's energy is conserved without needing constant divine correction.</summary>
<keywords>Leibniz, Samuel Clarke, Isaac Newton, John Locke, Natural religion, materialism, pre-established order, watchmaker analogy, miracles, divine providence</keywords>

<meta>This page begins Leibniz’s second paper in the correspondence, responding to Samuel Clarke’s first reply. Leibniz clarifies his position on materialism and introduces the two fundamental principles of his philosophy: the principle of contradiction and the principle of sufficient reason.</meta>

<page-num>239</page-num>

# MR. LEIBNITZ’S SECOND PAPER: 
## Being an Answer to Dr. Clarke’s 
## First Reply.

1. It is rightly observed in the paper delivered to the *Princess of Wales*, which her *Royal Highness* has been pleased to communicate to me, that, next to the corruption of manners, the *principles of the materialists* contribute very much to sustaining impiety. But I believe the author had no reason to add that the *mathematical principles of philosophy* are *opposite* to those of the materialists. On the contrary, they are the same; with only this difference: that the *materialists*, in imitation of *Democritus*, *Epicurus*, and *Hobbes*, confine themselves entirely to mathematical principles and admit only bodies; whereas the *Christian mathematicians* also admit immaterial substances. Therefore, not mathematical principles (according to the usual sense of that word) but metaphysical principles ought to be opposed to those of the materialists. *Pythagoras*, *Plato*, and *Aristotle*, in some measure, had a knowledge of these principles; but I claim to have established them demonstratively in my *Theodicæa*, though I have done it in a popular manner. The great foundation of mathematics is the *principle of contradiction* or *identity*—that is, that a proposition cannot be true and false at the same time, and that therefore *A* is *A* and cannot be not *A*. This single principle is sufficient to demonstrate every part of arithmetic and geometry, that is, all mathematical principles. But in order to proceed from *mathematics* to *natural philosophy*, another principle is required, as I have observed in my *Theodicæa*: I mean the *principle of a sufficient reason*, *namely*: that *nothing happens without a reason why it should be so, rather than otherwise*. And therefore *Archimedes*, desiring to proceed from mathematics to natural philosophy in his book *De Æquilibrio*, was obliged to make use of a particular case of the great principle of a sufficient reason. He takes it for granted that if there is a balance in which everything is identical on both sides, and if equal weights are hung on the two ends of that balance, the whole will be at rest. It is because no reason can be given why one side should weigh down rather than the other. Now, by that single principle—*namely*: that *there ought to be a sufficient reason why things should be so, and not otherwise*—one may demonstrate the existence of a God and all the other parts of metaphysics or natural theology; and even, in some measure, those principles of natural philosophy,

<summary>Leibniz argues that mathematical principles alone are insufficient to refute materialism and introduces the "principle of sufficient reason" as the necessary foundation for natural philosophy and theology. He explains that while mathematics relies on the principle of contradiction, understanding the physical world requires a reason why things are as they are and not otherwise.</summary>

<keywords>Leibniz-Clarke correspondence, materialism, principle of contradiction, principle of sufficient reason, Archimedes, natural philosophy, metaphysics, Theodicæa</keywords>

that are independent of mathematics: I mean, the *dynamic principles*, or the *principles of force*.

2. The author continues and says—that according to *mathematical principles*, that is, according to *Sir Isaac Newton’s philosophy* (for *mathematical principles* determine nothing in the present case), matter is the *least significant part of the universe*. The reason is because he admits *empty space* besides matter; and because, according to *his notions*, matter fills up only a very small part of *space*. But *Democritus* and *Epicurus* maintained the same thing: they differed from *Sir Isaac Newton* only regarding the quantity of matter; and perhaps they believed there was *more* matter in the world than *Sir Isaac Newton* will allow. In this, I think their opinion ought to be preferred; for the *more* matter there is, the *more* God has occasion to exercise his wisdom and power. This is one reason, among others, why I maintain that there is *no vacuum at all*.

3. I find, in express words, in the *Appendix* to *Sir Isaac Newton’s Optics*, that space is the *sensorium of God*. But the word *sensorium* has always signified the *organ of sensation*. He and his friends may *now*, if they think fit, explain themselves quite differently; I shall not oppose it.

4. The author supposes that the presence of the soul is sufficient to make it perceive what happens in the brain. But this is the very thing which *Father Malebranche* and all the *Cartesians* deny, and they rightly deny it. More is required besides mere presence to enable one thing to perceive what happens in another. Some communication that can be explained—some sort of *influence*—is required for this purpose. *Space*, according to *Sir Isaac Newton*, is intimately present to the body contained within it and commensurate with it. Does it follow from that, that *space perceives* what happens in a body and *remembers* it when that body has moved away? Besides, as the soul is *indivisible*, its immediate *presence* (which may be imagined in the body) would only be in *one point*. How then could it perceive what happens *outside of that point*? I claim to be the first who has shown *how* the soul perceives what happens in the body.

5. The reason why God perceives everything is not his mere presence, but also his *operation*. It is because he preserves things by an action that continually produces whatever is good and

6. The true and principal reason why we praise a machine is based more upon the *effects* of the machine than upon its cause. We do not inquire so much about the *power* of the artist as we do about the *skill* in his workmanship. Therefore, the reason alleged by the author for praising the machine of *God’s* making—based on his having made it *entirely*, without needing any materials to make it from—is not sufficient. It is a mere excuse the author has been forced to resort to; and the reason why God exceeds any other artist is not only because he makes the *whole*, whereas all other artists must have matter to work upon. This excellence in God would be *only* on account of *power*. But God’s excellence arises also from another cause, namely *wisdom*, by which his machine lasts *longer* and moves *more regularly* than those of any other artist whatsoever. Someone who buys a watch does not care whether the workman made every part of it *himself*, or whether he had the various parts made by *others* and only put them together, provided the watch works correctly. And if the workman had received from God even the gift of creating the matter of the wheels, the buyer of the watch would still not be satisfied unless the workman had also received the gift of putting them *well* together. In the same way, whoever is pleased with *God’s* workmanship cannot be so without some reason other than that which the author has alleged here.

7. Thus, the *skill* of God must not be inferior to that of a workman; indeed, it must go infinitely beyond it. The mere production of everything would indeed show the *power* of God, but it would not sufficiently show his *wisdom*. Those who maintain the contrary will fall exactly into the error of the materialists and of *Spinoza*, from whom they claim to differ. In such a case, they would acknowledge power but not sufficient wisdom in the principle or cause of all things.

I do not say the material world is a machine, or watch, that runs *without* God’s interposition; and I have sufficiently insisted that the creation needs to be continually influenced by its Creator. But I maintain it to be a watch that runs *without* needing to be mended by him; otherwise, we must say that God reconsiders his actions

## MR. LEIBNITZ’S THIRD PAPER: Being an Answer to Dr. Clarke’s Second Reply.

1. According to the usual way of speaking, *mathematical principles* concern only mere mathematics, namely: numbers, figures, arithmetic, and geometry. But *metaphysical principles* concern *more general notions*, such as cause and effect.

2. The author grants me this important *principle*: that *nothing happens without a sufficient reason why it should be so, rather than otherwise*. But he grants it only in words, and in reality denies it. This shows that he does not fully perceive the strength of it. And therefore he makes use of an instance, which exactly falls in with one of my demonstrations against *real absolute space*, which is an idol of some modern *Englishmen*. I call it an *idol*, not in a theological sense, but in a philosophical one; as Chancellor *Bacon* says, there are <term>idola tribûs</term> and <term>idola specûs</term>.

3. These gentlemen maintain, therefore, that space is a *real absolute being*. But this involves them in great difficulties; for such a *being* must necessarily be eternal and infinite. Hence some have believed it to be *God himself*, or one of his attributes—his *immensity*. But since space consists of *parts*, it is not a thing that can belong to God.

4. As for my own opinion, I have said more than once that I hold *space* to be something *merely relative*, as *time* is; I hold it to be an *order of coexistences*, just as time is an *order of successions*. For *space* denotes, in terms of *possibility*, an *order of things* which exist at the same time, considered as existing together, without inquiring into their particular manner of existing. And when many things are seen together, one perceives that *order of things among themselves*.

5. I have many demonstrations to refute the notion of those who take space to be a *substance*, or at least an *absolute being*. But I shall only use, at present, one demonstration, which the author here gives me occasion to insist upon. I say then, that if *space* were an *absolute being*, something would happen for which it would be impossible for there to be a *sufficient reason*.

<summary>Leibniz distinguishes between mathematical and metaphysical principles, defining space not as an absolute substance or divine attribute, but as a relative order of coexistences. He argues that the concept of absolute space violates the principle of sufficient reason.</summary>

<keywords>Leibniz, Samuel Clarke, mathematical principles, metaphysical principles, sufficient reason, absolute space, relative space, Francis Bacon, idola tribus, idola specus, coexistences, successions</keywords>
