This is against my axiom. And I prove it in this way: *Space* is something absolutely uniform; and, without the things placed in it, *one point of space does not absolutely differ in any respect whatsoever from another point of space.* Now from this it follows (supposing space to be something in itself, besides the *order of bodies among themselves*) that it is impossible there should be a *reason* why God, preserving the same positions of bodies among themselves, should have placed them in space in *one certain particular way*, and not *otherwise*; why everything was not placed the *exact opposite* way—for instance, by changing *east* into *west*. But if space is nothing else but that *order* or *relation*, and is nothing at all without bodies except the possibility of placing them, then those *two states*—the *one* as it now is, and the *other* supposed to be the exact opposite way—would not differ from one another at all. *Their difference*, therefore, is only to be found in our fanciful supposition of the *reality of space in itself*. But in truth, the *one* would be exactly the same thing as the *other*, since they are absolutely *indiscernible*; and consequently, there is no room to inquire after a reason for preferring one over the other.

6. The case is the same with respect to *time*. Suppose someone should ask why God did not create everything *a year sooner*, and the same person should infer from this that God has done something for which it is not possible there should be a *reason* why he did it so and not *otherwise*. The answer is that his inference would be right if *time* were anything distinct from things existing in time. For it would be impossible for there to be any *reason* why things should be assigned to such particular instants rather than to others, while their succession remained the same. But then the same argument proves that *instants*, considered without things, are *nothing at all*, and that they consist only in the successive order of things. If this order remains the same, one of the two states—namely, that of a supposed earlier start—would not differ at all from, nor could be discerned from, the *other* state which now exists.

7. It appears from what I have said that my axiom has not been well understood, and that the author denies it, though he seems to grant it. *"It is true,"* he says, *"that there is nothing without a sufficient reason why it exists, and why it is like this rather than otherwise"*; but he adds that *"this sufficient reason is often the simple or mere will of God"*; as when it is asked why matter was not placed other-

### MR. LEIBNITZ'S FOURTH PAPER; Being an Answer to Dr. Clarke's Third Reply.

1. In things that are *absolutely indifferent*, there is no foundation for choice; and consequently no election, nor will, since choice must be founded on some reason or principle.
2. A *mere will* without any motive is a fiction, not only contrary to God's perfection, but also chimerical and contradictory; it is inconsistent with the definition of the *will* and sufficiently refuted in my *Theodicy*.
3. It is an *indifferent* thing to place three bodies that are equal and perfectly alike in any order whatsoever; and consequently, they will *never be placed in any order* by Him who does nothing without wisdom. But then, He being the author of things, no such things will be produced by Him at all; and consequently, *there are no such things in nature*.
4. There is no such thing as two individuals *indiscernible* from each other. An ingenious gentleman of my acquaintance, while conversing with me in the presence of Her *Electoral Highness* the Princess Sophia in the garden of *Herrenhausen*, thought he could find two leaves perfectly alike. The princess challenged him to do it, and he ran all over the garden for a long time to look for some; but it was to no purpose. Two drops of water or milk, viewed with a microscope, will appear distinguishable from each other. This is an argument against *atoms*, which are refuted, as well as a *vacuum*, by the principles of true metaphysics.
5. Those great principles of *sufficient reason* and of the *identity of indiscernibles* change the state of metaphysics. That science becomes real and demonstrative by means of these principles, whereas before, it generally consisted of empty words.
6. To suppose *two things are indiscernible* is to suppose the *same thing under two names*. And therefore, to suppose that the universe could have had at first another position of *time* and *place*,

7. The same reason which shows that *extramundane* space is imaginary proves that all empty space is an imaginary thing; for they differ only as greater and less.

8. If space is a *property* or *attribute*, it must be the property of some substance. But *what substance* will that bounded empty space be a quality or property of, which the persons I am arguing with suppose to be between two bodies?

9. If *infinite* space is *immensity*, *finite space* will be the opposite of immensity—that is, it will be *mensurability* or *limited extension*. Now, extension must be the quality of something extended. But if that space is empty, it will be an attribute without a subject, an extension without anything extended. Therefore, by making space a *property*, the author agrees with my opinion, which makes it an order of things and not anything absolute.

10. If space is an *absolute reality*, far from being a property or an accident opposed to substance, it will have a greater reality than substances themselves. God cannot destroy it, nor even change it in any respect. It will be not only immense as a whole, but also immutable and eternal in every part. There will be an infinite number of eternal things *besides God*.

11. To say that infinite space has no *parts* is to say that it does not consist of *finite spaces*, and that infinite space might exist even if all finite space were reduced to nothing. It would be as if one should say, in the *Cartesian* supposition of a material, extended, unlimited world, that such a world might exist even if all the bodies of which it consists were reduced to nothing.

15. It is a similar fiction (that is, an impossible one) to suppose that God might have created the world some millions of years earlier. Those who fall into such kinds of fictions can give no answer to someone who argues for the *eternity* of the world. For since God does nothing without reason, and no reason can be given why he did not create the world sooner, it will follow either that he has created nothing at all, or that he created the world before any specific time—that is, that the world is eternal. But once it has been shown that the beginning, whenever it occurred, is always the *same thing*, the question of why it was not ordered differently becomes unnecessary and insignificant.

16. If *space* and *time* were anything absolute—that is, if they were anything else besides certain *orders* of things—then indeed my assertion would be a *contradiction*. But since it is not so, the hypothesis <note>that space and time are anything absolute</note> is contradictory; that is, it is an impossible fiction.

17. And the case is the same as in *geometry*, where by the very supposition that a figure is larger than it really is, we sometimes prove that it is not larger. This indeed is a contradiction, but it lies in the hypothesis, which appears to be false for that very reason.

18. *Space* being uniform, there can be neither any *external* nor *internal* reason by which to distinguish its parts and to make any choice among them. For any *external* reason to distinguish between them can only be based upon some *internal* one. Otherwise, we would distinguish what is indistinguishable or choose without a distinction. A will without reason would be the "chance" of the *Epicureans*. A God who acted by such a will would be a God in name only. The cause of these errors comes from a lack of care in avoiding what detracts from the divine perfections.

19. When *two things that cannot both exist at once are equally good*, and neither in themselves nor by their combination with other things does one have *any advantage over the other*, God will *produce neither of them*.

20. God is never determined by *external* things, but always by what is *within himself*; that is, by his knowledge of things before anything exists outside of himself.

21. There is *no possible reason that can limit* the quantity of matter; and therefore, such a limitation can have no place.

22. And assuming an arbitrary limitation on the quantity of matter, something could always be added to it without detracting from the perfection of those things that already exist; consequently, something must always be added in order to act according to the principle of the perfection of divine operations.

23. Therefore, it cannot be said that the present quantity of matter is the best fit for the present constitution of things. And even if it were, it would follow that this present constitution of things would not be the most fit absolutely if it prevents God from using more matter. It would therefore be better to choose another constitution of things that is capable of more.

24. I would be glad to see a passage from any philosopher who uses the term *sensorium* in any sense other than the one *Goclenius* <note>Rudolf Goclenius</note> uses.

25. If *Scapula* <note>Johann Scapula</note> says that the *sensorium* is the place where the understanding resides, he means the *organ* of internal sensation. Therefore, he does not differ from *Goclenius*.

26. *Sensorium* has always signified the organ of sensation. The *glandula pinealis* <note>pineal gland</note> would be, according to *Cartesius* <note>René Descartes</note>, the *sensorium* in the sense mentioned above by *Scapula*.

27. There is hardly any expression less appropriate for this subject than one which suggests that God has a *sensorium*. It seems to make God the *soul of the world*. It will be a difficult matter to find a justifiable meaning for this word according to the way Sir *Isaac Newton* uses it.

28. Although the question concerns the meaning Sir *Isaac Newton* gives to that word rather than *Goclenius*, I am not to be blamed for quoting that author's philosophical dictionary, because the purpose of dictionaries is to show how words are used.

29. God perceives things in himself. Space is the place of things, and not the place of *God's ideas*: unless we look upon space as something that creates a union between God and things, in imitation of the imagined union between the soul and the body; which would still make God the *soul of the world*.

30. And indeed the author is much in the wrong when he compares *God's knowledge and operation* with the knowledge and *operation of souls*. The soul knows things because God has put into it a principle representative of things outside. But *God* knows things because he *produces* them continually.

31. The soul does not act upon things, according to my opinion, in any other way than because the body adapts itself to the desires of the soul, by virtue of the *harmony* which God has *pre-established* between them.

32. But those who imagine that the soul can give a *new force* to the body, and that God does the same in the world in order to mend the imperfections of his machine, make God too much like the soul by ascribing too much to the soul and too little to God.

33. For none but God can give a *new force* to nature; and he does it only *supernaturally*. If there were a need for him to do it in the natural course of things, he would have made a very imperfect work. At that rate, he would be with respect to the *world* what the *soul*, in the common notion, is with respect to the body.

34. Those who undertake to defend the common opinion concerning the *soul's influence over the body* by pointing to God's operating on external things make God still too much like a soul of the world. To which I add that the author's tendency to find fault with the words *intelligentia supramundana* <note>supramundane intelligence</note> seems also to incline that way.

35. The images with which the soul is immediately affected are within itself; but they correspond to those of the body. The presence of the soul is imperfect and can only be explained by that correspondence. But the presence of God is perfect and manifested by his operation.

36. The author wrongly supposes against me that the presence of the soul is connected with its *influence* over the body; for he knows I reject that *influence*.

37. The soul's being *diffused* through the brain is no less inexplicable than its being *diffused* through the whole body. The difference is only a matter of degree.

38. Those who imagine that active force diminishes on its own in the world do not well understand the primary laws of nature and the beauty of God's works.

39. How will they be able to prove that this *defect* is a consequence of the dependence of things?

40. The imperfection of our machines, which is the reason why they need to be repaired, proceeds from this very fact: that they do not sufficiently depend upon the craftsman. And therefore the dependence of nature upon God, far from being the cause of such an imperfection, is rather the reason why there is no such imperfection in nature, because it depends so much upon an artist who is too perfect to make a work that needs to be repaired. It is true that every individual machine of nature is, to some extent, liable to be disordered; but not the whole universe, which cannot diminish in perfection.

But if there were no creatures, space and time would exist only in the ideas of God.

42. The author seems to acknowledge here that his notion of a miracle is not the same as that which theologians and philosophers usually have. It is therefore sufficient for my purpose that my adversaries are forced to resort to what is commonly called a miracle.

43. I am afraid the author, by altering the meaning commonly assigned to the word *miracle*, will fall into a problematic opinion. The nature of a miracle does not at all consist in *usefulness* or *uselessness*; for then monsters would be miracles.

44. There are miracles of an *inferior sort* which an angel can perform. He can, for instance, make a man walk upon the water without sinking. But there are miracles which none but God can perform, as they exceed all natural powers. Of this kind are *creating* and *annihilating*.

I lay it down as a principle, that every perfection, which God could impart to things without derogating from their other perfections, has actually been imparted to them. ## Mr. Leibniz’s Fifth Paper: Being an answer to Dr. Clarke’s Fourth Reply.

->Regarding sections 1 and 2 of the previous paper <note>Clarke’s Fourth Reply</note>.<-

1. I shall at this time provide a *longer* answer to clear up the difficulties, and to see whether the author is willing to listen to reason and show that he is a lover of truth, or whether he will only argue pointlessly without clarifying anything.

2. He often endeavors to attribute *necessity* and *fatalism* to me; although perhaps no one has better or more fully explained than I have in my *Theodicy* the true difference between *liberty*, *contingency*, and *spontaneity* on one side, and absolute *necessity*, *chance*, and *compulsion* on the other. I do not know yet whether the author does this because he *insists* on doing it regardless of what I say, or whether he does it (assuming he is sincere in these accusations) because he has *not yet properly considered* my opinions. I shall soon find what I am to think about it, and I shall take my measures accordingly.

3. It is true that *reason* in the mind of a wise being, and *motives* in any mind whatsoever, perform a function that corresponds to the effect produced by *weights* in a balance. The author objects that this notion leads to *necessity* and *fatalism*. But he says so without proving it and without acknowledging the explanations I have previously given to remove the difficulties that might be raised on that subject.

4. He also seems to play with *ambiguous terms*. There are *necessities* that ought to be admitted. For we must distinguish between an *absolute* and a *hypothetical necessity*. We must also dis-

<meta>This page continues Leibniz’s Fifth Paper, specifically his response to Samuel Clarke regarding the definitions of necessity and how God's foreknowledge and the principle of the "best" do not eliminate human or divine liberty.</meta>

...distinguish between a necessity that occurs because the opposite implies a contradiction (which necessity is called *logical, metaphysical, or mathematical*) and a necessity which is *moral*, by which a wise being chooses the best, and every mind follows its strongest inclination.

5. *Hypothetical necessity* is that which the supposition or hypothesis of God’s *foresight* and *pre-ordination* places upon *future contingents*. And this must be admitted, unless we deny—as the *Socinians* do—God’s foreknowledge of *future contingents* and his *providence*, which regulates and governs every specific thing.

6. But neither that *foreknowledge* nor that *pre-ordination* detract from *liberty*. For God—being moved by his supreme reason to choose, among many series of things or worlds possible, the one in which free creatures would make specific resolutions (though not without his <term>concourse</term> <note>Divine cooperation or concurrence in the actions of creatures</note>)—has thereby rendered every event certain and determined once and for all, without detracting from the liberty of those creatures. That simple decree of choice does not change their free natures at all, but only *actualizes* them, as he saw them in his ideas.

7. As for *moral necessity*, this also does not detract from *liberty*. For when a wise being—and especially God, who has supreme wisdom—chooses what is best, he is not any less free on that account. On the contrary, it is the most perfect liberty not to be hindered from acting in the best manner. And when any other being chooses according to the most apparent and most strongly inclining good, he imitates the liberty of a truly wise being in proportion to his own disposition. Without this, the choice would be blind chance.

8. But *good*, whether *true* or *apparent*—in a word, the *motive*—inclines without necessitating; that is, without imposing an absolute necessity. For instance, when God chooses the best, that which he does not choose (and which is inferior in perfection) is nevertheless still possible. But if what he chose were absolutely necessary, any other way would be impossible, which contradicts the hypothesis. For God chooses among possibilities—that is, among many ways, none of which implies a contradiction.

9. But to say that God can only choose what is *best*, and to infer from this that what he does not choose is impossible, is a confusion of terms. It is a blending of *power* and *will*,

<meta>This page continues Leibniz’s response to Samuel Clarke, specifically addressing the distinction between metaphysical and moral necessity and defending his philosophy against accusations of fatalism.</meta>

9. ...*metaphysical necessity* and *moral necessity*, *essences* and *existences*. For what is necessary is so by its essence, since the opposite implies a contradiction; but a contingent thing which exists owes its existence to the principle of *what is best*, which is a *sufficient reason* for the existence of things. And therefore I say that motives incline without necessitating; and that there is a certainty and infallibility, but not an *absolute necessity*, in contingent things. Add to this what will be said hereafter in *Nos.* 73 and 76.

10. And I have sufficiently shown in my *Theodicæa* <note>Theodicy, Leibniz's 1710 work defending God's justice</note> that this moral necessity is a good thing, agreeable to the divine perfection and agreeable to the great principle or ground of existences, which is the requirement of a sufficient reason. Whereas *absolute and metaphysical necessity* depends upon the other great principle of our reasonings, namely that of *essences*, which is the principle of *identity or contradiction*. For what is absolutely necessary is the only possible way, and its contrary implies a contradiction.

11. I have also shown that our *will* does not always exactly *follow the practical understanding*, because it may have or find *reasons* to suspend its resolution until a further examination.

12. To impute to me, after this, the notion of an *absolute necessity*, without having anything to say against the *reasons* which I have just now alleged—and which go to the bottom of things, perhaps beyond what is to be seen elsewhere—this, I say, will be an unreasonable obstinacy.

13. As to the notion of *fatality*, which the author also charges me with, this is another ambiguity. There is a <term>fatum Mahometanum</term> <note>Turkish or Muslim fate</note>, a <term>fatum stoicum</term> <note>Stoic fate</note>, and a <term>fatum Christianum</term> <note>Christian fate</note>. The Turkish fate dictates that an effect will happen even if its cause is avoided, as if there were an absolute necessity. The Stoical fate dictates that a man should be quiet because he must have patience whether he wants to or not, since it is impossible to resist the course of things. But it is agreed that there is a *fatum Christianum*, a certain destiny of everything, regulated by the foreknowledge and providence of God. *Fatum* is derived from *fari* (to speak); that is, to pronounce or to decree; and in its right sense, it signifies the decree of providence. And those who submit to it through a knowledge of the divine perfections—from which the love of God follows—not only have patience, like the heathen philosophers, but are also contented with what is ordained by God, knowing he does everything for the best;

He rejects the label of "absolute necessity" or "Turkish fatalism," which suggests events happen regardless of their causes.</summary>

...and not only for the greatest good in general, but also for the greatest particular good of those who love him.

14. I have been forced to expand on this to remove unfounded accusations once and for all; I hope I shall be able to do so through these explanations, in order to satisfy fair-minded people. I shall now address an objection raised here against my comparison of the weights of a scale with the motives of the *will*. It is objected that a *scale* is merely *passive* and moved by weights, whereas intelligent *agents* endowed with a *will* are *active*. To this I answer that the principle of the lack of a *sufficient reason* is common to both *agents* and *patients* <note>In this context, 'patients' refers to entities that are acted upon</note>: they require a *sufficient reason* for their action as well as for their *passion* <note>'Passion' here refers to the state of being acted upon, the opposite of action</note>. A scale does not act when it is pulled equally on both sides; likewise, the equal weights do not act when they are in an *equilibrium*, so that one of them cannot go down without the other rising by the same amount.

15. It must also be considered that, strictly speaking, motives do not act upon the mind as weights do upon a scale; rather, it is the mind that acts by virtue of the motives, which are its *dispositions* to act. Therefore, to claim—as the author does here—that the mind sometimes prefers weak motives to strong ones, or even that it prefers what is *indifferent* over *motives*, is to separate the *mind* from the *motives*. It treats them as if they were outside the mind, just as a weight is distinct from a scale, and as if the mind had other dispositions to act besides *motives*, by virtue of which it could reject or accept them. In truth, motives *encompass* all the dispositions the mind can have to act *voluntarily*; for they include not only *reasons*, but also the *inclinations* arising from passions or other prior impressions. Therefore, if the mind were to prefer a weak *inclination* to a strong one, it would act against itself and differently than it is disposed to act. This shows that the author's notions, which are contrary to mine, are superficial and have no solidity when they are carefully considered.

16. To also assert that the mind may have *good reasons* to act when it has no motives, and when things are absolutely *indifferent*—as the author explains here—is a *manifest contradiction*. For if the mind has *good reasons* for choosing the side it takes, then the things are not *indifferent* to the mind.

17. And to claim that the mind will act when it has *reasons to act*, even if the *ways* of acting were absolutely *indifferent*—this, I say, is to speak very superficially once again, and in a manner that cannot be defended. For a man never has a sufficient reason *to act* when he does not also have a sufficient reason to act *in a certain particular manner*; since every action is individual and not general, nor abstracted from its circumstances, but always requires some particular way of being carried out. Therefore, when there is a sufficient reason to do any particular thing, there is also a sufficient reason to do it in a certain particular manner; and consequently, several manners of doing it are not *indifferent*. Whenever a man has sufficient reasons for a single action, he also has sufficient reasons for all its requirements. See also what I shall say below, *No.* 66.

18. These arguments are very obvious; and it is very strange to charge me with proposing my principle of the *lack of a sufficient reason* without any proof drawn either from the nature of things or from the divine perfections. For the *nature of things* requires that every event should have its proper conditions, requirements, and dispositions beforehand, the existence of which constitutes the sufficient reason for such an event.

19. And *God’s* perfection requires that all his actions should be consistent with his wisdom, and that it may not be said of him that he has acted without reason, or even that he has preferred a weaker reason over a stronger one.

20. But I shall speak more extensively at the conclusion of this paper concerning the validity and importance of this great principle—the lack of a sufficient reason for every event—the overthrowing of which principle would ruin the best part of all philosophy. It is therefore very strange that the author should say I am guilty here of a <term>petitio principii</term> <note>Begging the question; assuming the very thing one is trying to prove.</note>; and it plainly appears he desires to maintain indefensible opinions, since he is forced to deny that great principle, which is one of the most essential principles of reason.

21. ...that there are not in nature *two* real, absolute beings, *indiscernible* <note>impossible to tell apart; identical</note> from each other; because if there were, God and nature would act without reason, by ordering the one differently than the other; and that therefore God does not produce *two* pieces of matter perfectly equal and alike. The author answers this conclusion without refuting its reasoning; and he answers with a very weak objection. *That argument,* says he, *if it were good, would prove that it would be impossible for God to create any matter at all. For the perfectly solid parts of matter, if we take them with equal shape and dimensions (which is always possible in theory), would be exactly alike.* But it is a manifest *petitio principii* <note>begging the question; a logical fallacy where the conclusion is assumed in the premise</note> to suppose that perfect likeness which, according to me, cannot be admitted. This supposition of two *indiscernibles*, such as two pieces of matter perfectly alike, seems indeed to be possible in abstract terms; but it is not consistent with the order of things, nor with the divine wisdom, by which nothing is admitted without reason. Common people imagine such things because they content themselves with incomplete notions. And this is one of the faults of the *atomists* <note>philosophers who believe the universe is made of identical, indivisible particles</note>.

22. Besides, I do not admit that there are parts in matter that are perfectly solid, or that are the same throughout without any variety or particular motion in their parts, as the supposed atoms are imagined to be. To suppose such bodies is another poorly grounded popular opinion. According to my demonstrations, every part of matter is *actually* subdivided into parts that move differently, and no one of them is perfectly *like* another.

23. The author acknowledges this regarding leaves, and *perhaps* regarding drops of water. But he might have admitted it without any hesitation—without a *perhaps* (as an *Italian* would say, *senzà forse*)—regarding drops of water as well.

26. I admit that if two things perfectly *indiscernible* from each other did exist, they would be *two*; but that supposition is false, and contrary to the *grand principle of reason*. The common philosophers were mistaken when they believed that there are things different *solo numero* <note>only by number; distinct only because they are counted as two, rather than having internal differences</note>, or only because they are *two*; and from this error have arisen their perplexities about what they called the *principle of individuation*. Metaphysics has generally been handled like a science of mere *words*, like a philosophical dictionary, without entering into the discussion of *things*. Superficial philosophy, such as that of the *atomists* and *vacuists*, creates things which *superior reasons* do not admit. I hope my demonstrations will change the face of philosophy, notwithstanding such weak objections as the author raises here against me.

27. The parts of *time* or *place*, considered in themselves, are *ideal things*; and therefore they perfectly resemble one another, like *abstract units*. But it is not so with *two concrete things*, or with *two real times*, or *two filled spaces*, that is, those that are *truly actual*.

...that a straight line cuts another in *two* points; it will be found after all, that those *two* alleged points must coincide and make only *one* point.

29. I have demonstrated that *space* is nothing else but an *order* of the existence of things, observed as existing together; and therefore the fiction of a finite material universe, moving forward in an infinite empty space, cannot be admitted. It is altogether unreasonable and impossible. For, besides the fact that there is no real space outside the material universe, such an action would be without any design; it would be working without doing anything, *agendo nihil agere* <note>Latin: "to do nothing by doing"</note>. No change would occur that could be observed by anyone at all. These are the imaginings of *philosophers who have incomplete notions, who make space an absolute reality.* Mere mathematicians, who are only preoccupied with the whims of imagination, are prone to invent such notions; but they are refuted by superior reasons.

30. Speaking in absolute terms, it appears that God *can* make the material universe *finite* in extension; but the opposite seems more consistent with his wisdom.

31. I do not grant that *every finite thing is movable*. According to the hypothesis of my adversaries themselves, *a part of space*, though *finite*, is not *movable*. What is *movable* must be capable of changing its position relative to *something else*, and being in a new state *discernible* from the first; otherwise, the change is merely a fiction. A *movable finite thing* must therefore be part of *another finite thing* so that any change that occurs can be observed.

32. Cartesius <note>René Descartes</note> maintains that matter is *unlimited*; and I do not think he has been sufficiently refuted. And even if this were granted to him, it still does not follow that matter would be necessary, nor that it would have existed from all eternity; since that unlimited spread of matter would only be an effect of God's choice, judging that to be the better way.

The case is the same with *empty space within the world*, which I also consider to be imaginary for the reasons previously stated.

34. The author objects to my position by citing the *vacuum* discovered by Mr. *Guericke* of *Magdeburg*, which is created by pumping the air out of a *receiver*; and he claims that there is truly a perfect *vacuum*, or a space without matter (at least in part), in that *receiver*. The *Aristotelians* and *Cartesians*, who do not admit a true *vacuum*, have said in answer to that experiment by Mr. *Guericke*, as well as to that of *Torricelli* of *Florence* (who emptied the air out of a glass tube with the help of quicksilver <note>mercury</note>), that there is no *vacuum* at all in the tube or in the receiver. They argue that glass has small pores which the beams of light, the *effluvia* of the lodestone, and other very thin fluids may pass through. I am of their opinion: and I think the receiver may be compared to a box full of holes in the water, having fish or other coarse bodies shut up in it; if these were taken out, their place would nevertheless be filled up with water. There is only this difference: that though water is fluid and more yielding than those coarse bodies, yet it is as heavy and massive as they are, if not more so; whereas the matter which enters the receiver in the place of the air is much more subtle. The new advocates for a *vacuum* allege in answer to this example that it is not the coarseness of matter, but its mere quantity, that creates resistance; and consequently, that there is of necessity more *vacuum* where there is less resistance. They add that the subtlety of matter has nothing to do here; and that the particles of quicksilver are as subtle and *fine* as those of water; and yet that quicksilver resists more than ten times *more*. To this I reply that it is not so much the quantity of matter, as its difficulty in giving way, that creates *resistance*. For instance, *floating timber* contains *less* heavy matter than an equal volume of *water* does; and yet it offers *more resistance* to a boat than the water does.

35. And as for *quicksilver*: it is true that it contains about fourteen times more heavy matter than an equal volume of *water* does; but it does not follow that it contains fourteen times more matter absolutely. On the contrary, *water* contains as much matter, if we include both its own matter, which is heavy, and the external matter devoid of heaviness which passes through its pores. For both *quicksilver* and *water* are masses of heavy matter, full of pores, through which there passes a great deal of matter void of heaviness [and which does not noticeably resist]; such is probably that of the rays of light, and other imperceptible fluids; and especially that

<summary>Leibniz disputes the existence of a vacuum in air-pump experiments, arguing that "empty" space is actually filled with subtle, weightless matter. He further contends that resistance is determined by how easily a substance moves out of the way rather than its total mass.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Leibniz’s rebuttal of the idea that space and time are properties of God, specifically responding to the claim that things exist "in" space and time as if they were subjects within their own attributes.</meta>

we have never heard that a subject is contained within its own property. In the same way, God exists *in all time*. How then can time be *in God*, and how can it be a property of God? These are perpetual *alloglossies* <note>statements that use words in a way that is nonsensical or contradictory to their meaning</note>.

46. It appears that the author confuses immensity, or the *extension* of things, with the *space* according to which that extension is measured. Infinite space is not the immensity of God; finite space is not the extension of bodies, just as time is not their duration. Things retain their extension, but they do not always retain their space. Everything has its own extension and its own duration, but it does not have its own time, nor does it retain its own space.

47. I will show here how people come to form for themselves the notion of *space*. They consider that many things exist at once, and they observe in them a certain order of coexistence, according to which the relation of one thing to another is more or less simple. This order is their *situation* or *distance*. When it happens that one of those coexisting things changes its relation to a multitude of others (which do not change their relation among themselves), and another thing, newly arrived, acquires the same relation to the others as the first one had, we then say it has come into the *place* of the first; and this change we call *motion* in that body in which the immediate cause of the change resides. And even though many, or even all, of the coexisting things should change according to certain known rules of direction and speed, one may always determine the relation of situation which every coexisting thing acquires with respect to every other; and even that relation which any other coexisting thing would have to this one, or which this one would have to any other, if it had not changed, or if it had changed in any other way. And by supposing, or pretending, that among those coexisting things there is a sufficient number of them that have undergone no change, we may then say that those which have the same relation to those fixed existents as others had to them before, now occupy the same *place* that those others occupied. And that which encompasses all those places is called *space*. This shows that in order to have an idea of place, and consequently of space, it is sufficient to consider these relations and the rules of their changes, without needing to imagine any absolute reality outside of the things whose situation we consider. And, to give a kind of definition: *place* is that which we say is the same for *A* and for *B* when the relation of the coexistence of *B* with *C*, *E*, *F*, *G*, etc., agrees perfectly with the

For two different subjects, such as *A* and *B*, cannot have precisely the same individual affection <note>a property or attribute of a substance</note>; it is impossible for the same individual accident <note>a non-essential property that belongs to a specific subject</note> to be in two subjects or to pass from one subject to another. And if to this one were to add the fiction of a *metempsychosis* <note>the transmigration of a soul into a new body</note> and bring back the same human souls, the persons in those lines might change place; he who was a father or a grandfather might become a son or a grandson, *etc.* And yet those genealogical places, lines, and spaces, though they should express real truths, would only be ideal things. Lastly, I observe that the traces left by moving bodies, which they sometimes leave upon the immobile ones they move upon, have given people cause to imagine that some trace still remains even when there is nothing unmoved. But this is a purely ideal thing, and implies only that *if there were any unmoved thing there, the trace might be marked out upon it*. And it is this analogy which makes people imagine *places*, *traces*, and *spaces*, though those things consist only in the truth of relations and not at all in any absolute reality.

<meta>This page continues Leibniz’s arguments against absolute space and time, shifting focus from the nature of duration to the specific arguments for the reality of absolute space based on the motion of the universe and Newton's *Mathematical Principles of Nature*.</meta>

->To § 13.<-

52. In order to prove that space, without bodies, is an absolute reality, the author argued that a finite material universe might *move forward* in space. I answered that it does not appear reasonable that the material universe should be *finite*; and, even if we should suppose it to be finite, it is *unreasonable* that it should have motion in any way other than its parts changing their situation among themselves. This is because such a motion would produce no change that could be *observed* and would be without design. It is another thing when its parts change their situation among themselves; for then there is a motion in space, but it consists in the order of relations which are changed. The author replies now that the reality of motion does not depend upon being *observed*, and that a ship may go forward and yet a man who is in the ship may not perceive it. I answer that motion does not indeed depend upon being *observed*, but it does depend upon being *possible to be observed*. There is no motion when there is no change that can be *observed*. And when there is no change that can be *observed*, there is no change at all. The contrary opinion is grounded upon the supposition of a real absolute space, which I have demonstratively disproven by the principle of the want of a sufficient reason for things.

53. I find nothing in the eighth definition of the *Mathematical Principles of Nature* <note>Newton’s *Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica*</note>, nor in the *scholium* belonging to it, that proves, or can prove, the reality of space in itself. However, I grant there is a difference between an *absolute true motion* of a body and a mere *relative change* of its situation with respect to another body. For when the immediate cause of the change is in the body, that body is truly in motion; and then the situation of other bodies, with respect to it, will be changed consequently, though the cause of that change is not in them. It is true that, *exactly* speaking, there is not any one body that is perfectly and entirely at rest; but we frame an *abstract* notion of rest by considering the thing *mathematically*. Thus have I left nothing unanswered of what has been alleged for the absolute reality of space. And I have demonstrated the falsehood of that reality by a fundamental principle, one of the most certain both in reason and experience, against which no exception or instance can be alleged. Upon the whole, one may judge from what has been said that I ought not to admit a movable universe, nor any place outside the material universe.

<summary>Leibniz argues that motion is only real if it is observable or produces an internal change in relations, rejecting the idea of the entire universe moving through absolute space. He further contends that while "true motion" can be distinguished by its internal cause, space itself remains a relative concept rather than an absolute reality.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Leibniz’s rebuttal to Samuel Clarke (representing Newtonian views), specifically addressing Clarke’s 14th and 15th sections regarding the nature of space and time as quantities and the possibility of the world being created earlier.</meta>

### To § 14.

54. I am not aware of any objection that I think I have not sufficiently answered. As for the objection that *space* and *time* are *quantities*, or rather things endowed with *quantity*, and that *situation* and *order* are not: I answer that *order* also has its quantity; it contains that which precedes and that which follows; there is distance or interval. *Relative* things have their *quantity*, as well as absolute ones. For instance, ratios or proportions in mathematics have their *quantity* and are measured by logarithms; and yet they are relations. Therefore, even though *time* and *space* consist of relations, they still have their *quantity*.

### To § 15.

55. Regarding the question of whether God could have created the world *sooner*, it is necessary here to understand each other correctly. Since I have demonstrated that *time*, without things, is nothing else but a mere *ideal possibility*, it is manifest that if anyone should say that this same world, which has been actually created, might have been created *sooner* without any other change, he would be saying nothing intelligible. For there is no mark or difference by which it would be possible to know that this world was created *sooner*. And therefore (as I have already said), to suppose that God created the same world *sooner* is to suppose a chimerical thing. It is making *time* an absolute thing, independent of God; whereas *time* must coexist with created things and is only conceived by the order and quantity of their changes.

The case is the same with respect to the *destruction* <note>The German edition uses the word for *duration* here.</note> of the universe. 57. Thus it appears how we are to understand that God created things at the *time* he *pleased*; for this depends upon the *things* he resolved to create. But once things are resolved upon, together with their *relations*, there remains no longer any choice about the *time* and the *place*, which in themselves have nothing real about them, nothing that can distinguish them, and nothing that is at all discernible.

58. One cannot, therefore, say, as the author does here, that God's wisdom may have had *good reasons* to create this world at *such a particular time*. That particular time, considered without the things themselves, is an *impossible fiction*; and *good reasons* for a choice cannot be found where everything is indistinguishable.

59. When I speak of this world, I mean the whole *universe* of material and immaterial creatures taken together, from the beginning of things. But if anyone means only the beginning of the *material* world, and supposes *immaterial* creatures existed before it, he would have somewhat more reason for his supposition. For *time* would then be *marked* by things that already existed, it would no longer be indifferent, and there might be room for choice. And yet, this would only be delaying the difficulty. For supposing the whole universe of immaterial and material creatures together to have a beginning, there is no longer any choice about the *time* in which God would place that beginning.

60. And therefore, one must not say, as the author does here, that God created things in whatever particular *space* and at whatever particular *time* he *pleased*. For, since all time and all spaces are in themselves perfectly uniform and indistinguishable from each other, one of them cannot *please* more than another.

<meta>This page continues Leibniz’s arguments against the absolute nature of space and time, specifically addressing the relationship between matter and substance, and the nature of God's choices in creation.</meta>

61. I shall not expand here upon my opinion, explained elsewhere, that there are no created substances entirely lacking matter. For I hold, with the ancients and according to reason, that angels or intelligences, and souls separated from a gross body, always have subtle bodies, even though they themselves are incorporeal. Common philosophy easily admits all sorts of fictions; mine is more strict.

62. I do not say that matter and space are the same thing. I only say, *there is no space where there is no matter*; and that space in itself is not an absolute reality. Space and matter differ as time and motion do. However, these things, though different, are inseparable.

63. But yet it does not follow at all that matter is eternal and necessary, unless we suppose space to be eternal and necessary—a supposition that is ill-grounded in all respects.

### To § 16 and 17.

64. I think I have answered everything; and I have particularly replied to the objection that space and time have quantity, while order has none. *See above, Number 54.*

65. I have clearly shown that the contradiction lies in the hypothesis of the opposing opinion, which looks for a difference where there is none. And it would be clearly unfair to infer from this that I have acknowledged a contradiction in my own opinion.

### To § 18.

66. Here I find again an argument which I have refuted above, in Number 17. The author says God may have good reasons to make two cubes perfectly equal and alike; and then (he says) God must necessarily assign them their places, even though every other respect is perfectly equal. But things ought not to be separated from their circumstances. This argument consists of incomplete notions. God’s resolutions are never abstract and imperfect, as if God decreed first to create the two cubes and then made another decree about where to place them. Men, being the limited creatures they are, may act in this manner. They may decide upon a thing and then find themselves perplexed about the means, ways, places, and circumstances. But God never makes a resolution about the ends without resolving at the same time about the means and all the circumstances. Indeed, I have shown in my *Theodicæa*, that properly

speaking, there is but one decree for the whole universe, by which God resolved to bring it from possibility into existence. And therefore, God will not choose a cube without choosing its place at the same time; and he will never choose among *indiscernibles*.

67. The parts of space are not determined and distinguished except by the things which are in it: and the diversity of things in space determines God to act differently upon different parts of space. But space without things has nothing by which it may be distinguished; and indeed, nothing *actual*.

68. If God is resolved to place a certain cube of matter at all, he is also resolved regarding which particular place to put it in. But this is with respect to other parts of matter, and not with respect to bare space itself, in which there is nothing to distinguish it.

69. But wisdom does not allow God to place *two cubes perfectly equal and alike* at the same time; because there is no way to find any reason for assigning them different places. At this rate, there would be a will without a motive.

70. I compared a will without a motive (such as superficial reasoners suppose to be in God) to *Epicurus's chance*. The author answers that *Epicurus's chance* is a blind necessity, and not a choice of the will. I reply that *Epicurus's chance* is not a necessity, but something indifferent. *Epicurus* introduced it on purpose to avoid necessity. It is true that chance is blind; but a will without a motive would be no less blind, and no less due to mere chance.

### To § 19.

71. The author repeats here what has already been refuted above in *Number 21*: that matter cannot be created without God choosing among *indiscernibles*. He would be right if matter consisted of *atoms*, *similar particles*, or other similar fictions of superficial philosophy. But that great principle, which proves there is no choice among indiscernibles, also destroys these ill-contrived fictions.

### To § 20.

72. The author objected against me in his *third paper* (*Numbers 7 and 8*) that God would not have a principle of acting in himself if he were determined by external things. I answered that the ideas of external things are in him, and that therefore he is determined by internal reasons—that is, by his wisdom. But the author here refuses to understand why I said it.

<meta>This page continues Leibniz's rebuttal to Clarke regarding the nature of God's choices, specifically addressing the differences between God's power and His will in relation to the extension and duration of the universe.</meta>

### To § 21.

73. In his objections against me, he frequently confuses what God *will not* do with what He *cannot* do. See above, *Number 9 [and below Number 76]*. For example, God can do everything that is possible, but He *will* do only what is best. And therefore I do not say, as the author here would have it, that God *cannot* limit the extension of matter; but it is likely He *will not* do it, and that He has thought it better to set no bounds to matter.

74. The conclusion from extension to duration is not valid (*non valet consequentia*). Even if the *extension* of matter were unlimited, it would not follow that its *duration* would also be unlimited; indeed, even *from the beginning* (*à parte ante*), it would not follow that it had no beginning. If it is the nature of things as a whole to grow uniformly in perfection, the universe of creatures must have had a beginning. And therefore, there will be reasons to limit the *duration* of things, even if there were no reasons to limit their extension. Besides, the world’s having a beginning does not detract from the infinity of its duration *into the future* (*à parte post*); but boundaries of the universe would detract from the infinity of its extension. And therefore it is more reasonable to admit a beginning of the world than to admit any boundaries to it, so that the character of its infinite author may be preserved in both respects.

75. However, those who have admitted the *eternity* of the world, or at least (as some famous theologians have done) the possibility of its eternity, did not, for all that, deny its dependence upon God, as the author here charges them without any grounds.

### To § 22, 23.

76. He further objects here, without any reason, that according to my opinion, whatever God *can* do, He *must necessarily* have done. It is as if he were ignorant that I have solidly refuted this notion in my *Theodicæa*, and that I have overthrown the opinion of those who maintain that nothing is possible except what actually happens—as some ancient philosophers did, and among others *Diodorus* in *Cicero*. The author confuses *moral necessity*, which proceeds from the choice of what is *best*, with *absolute necessity*: he confuses the *will* of God with His *power*. God can produce everything that is possible, or whatever does not imply a contradiction; but He *wills* only to produce what is the best among possible things. *See what has been said above, Number 9 [and Number 74].*

85. To say that God perceives what happens in the world because he is present to things, and not by [the dependence that the continuation of their existence has on him and which may be said to involve] a continual production of them, is to say something incomprehensible. A mere presence or proximity of coexistence is not sufficient to make us understand how what happens in one being should correspond to what happens in another.

86. Furthermore, this is exactly falling into that opinion which makes God the soul of the world, since it supposes God to perceive things not by their dependence on him—that is, by a continual production of what is good and perfect in them—but by a kind of perception such as that by which men imagine our soul perceives what happens in the body. This is a significant degrading of God’s knowledge.

87. In truth and reality, this way of perception is completely illusory and has no place even in human souls. They perceive what happens *outside* them by what happens *inside* them, corresponding to the things outside, by virtue of the *harmony* which God has pre-established by the most beautiful and the most admirable of all his productions; whereby *every simple substance is by its nature (if one may so say) a concentration and a living mirror of the whole universe, according to its point of view.* This is likewise one of the most beautiful and most undeniable proofs of the existence of God, since none but God, *namely*, the universal cause, can produce such a harmony of things. But God himself cannot perceive things by the same means by which he makes other beings perceive them. He perceives them because he is able to produce that means. And other beings would not be caused to perceive them if he himself did not produce them in total harmony, and had not

...he has, therefore, in himself a representation of them; not as if that representation came from the things, but because the things proceed from him, and because he is the efficient and exemplary cause of them. 91. The nature of every *simple substance, soul, or true monad* is such that its following state is a consequence of the preceding one; here now is the cause of the *harmony* discovered. ### To § 32.

92. It is true that, according to me, the *soul* does not disturb the laws of the *body*, nor the *body* those of the *soul*; and that the *soul* and *body* *only agree together*; the one acting freely, according to the rules of *final causes*; and the other acting mechanically, according to the laws of *efficient causes*. But this does not detract from the liberty of our souls, as the author here claims. For every agent which acts <insert>with choice—Ger.</insert> according to final causes is free, even though it happens to agree with an agent acting only by efficient causes without knowledge, or mechanically; because God, foreseeing what the *free cause* would do, did from the beginning regulate the *machine* in such a manner that it cannot fail to *agree* with that free cause. Mr. Jaquelot has very well resolved this difficulty in one of his books against Mr. Bayle; and I have cited the passage in my *Theodicæa*, Part I, § 63. 106. It is true, [<insert>I maintain that</insert>] the immensity and eternity of God would subsist even if there were no creatures; but those attributes would not depend on either times or places. If there were no creatures, there would be neither time nor place, and consequently no actual space. The immensity of God is independent of space, as his eternity is independent of time. These attributes signify only [<insert>in respect to these two orders of things</insert>] that God would be present and co-existent with all the things that should exist. And therefore I do not admit what is here alleged: that if God existed alone, there would be time and space as there is now; whereas at that time, in my opinion, they would exist only in the ideas of God as mere possibilities. The immensity and eternity of God are things more transcendent than the duration and extension of creatures—not only with respect to greatness, but also to the *nature* of the things. Those divine attributes do not imply the supposition of things extrinsic to God, such as are actual *places* and *times*. These truths have been sufficiently acknowledged by *theologians and philosophers*.

<meta>This page continues Leibniz’s argument regarding the distinction between natural mechanisms and miracles, critiquing the reintroduction of "occult qualities" like attraction and defending mechanical philosophy.</meta>

112. In good philosophy and sound theology, we ought to distinguish between what can be explained by the natures and powers of *creatures*, and what can be explained only by the powers of the *infinite substance*. We ought to make an infinite difference between the *operation of God*, which goes beyond the extent of *natural powers*, and the *operations* of things that follow the law which God has given them, and which he has enabled them to follow by *their natural powers*, though not without his assistance.

113. This overthrows *attractions*, properly so called, and other operations that cannot be explained by the natural powers of creatures. Those who defend such operations must suppose them to be effected by *miracle*, or else resort to absurdities—that is, to the *occult qualities* of the Scholastic schools, which some men are beginning to revive under the deceptive name of *forces*; but these bring us back again into the kingdom of darkness. This is, *having found corn, to eat acorns* <note>inventa fruge, glandibus vesci</note>.

114. In the time of Mr. Boyle and other excellent men who flourished in England under Charles II, nobody would have ventured to publish such fanciful notions. I hope that happy time will return under such a good government as the present [and that minds a little too much carried away by the misfortune of the times will apply themselves to the better cultivation of sound learning]. Mr. Boyle made it his chief business to teach that everything in *natural philosophy* was done *mechanically*. But it is the misfortune of men to eventually grow dissatisfied with reason itself and to grow weary of light. *Chimeras* are beginning to appear again, and they are pleasing because they contain something wonderful. What has happened in poetry also happens in the *philosophical world*. People have grown weary of rational romances, such as the French *Clelia* or the German *Aramene*, and they have become fond once more of *fairy tales*.

115. As for the *motions of the celestial bodies*, and even the *formation of plants and animals*, there is nothing in them that looks like a *miracle*, except for their beginning. The *organism of animals* is a *mechanism* which presupposes a divine pre-formation. What follows from it is purely natural and entirely mechanical.

It is certain that there is an infinite number of instances where it succeeds <note>or rather, it succeeds</note> in all the known cases in which it has been used. From this one may reasonably judge that it will also succeed in unknown cases, or in those cases that can only become known by its means, according to the method of experimental philosophy, which proceeds *a posteriori*; even if the principle were not perhaps otherwise justified by bare reason, or *a priori*.

130. I have already said enough to justify my own, and I might say more about it, but perhaps it would be too abstruse for this present dispute. And I believe reasonable and impartial men will grant me that having forced an adversary to deny that principle is reducing him *ad absurdum* <note>To an absurdity.</note>.

### EXTRACTS FROM THE NEW ESSAYS ON THE UNDERSTANDING. 1704.

->[From the French.]<-

### PREFACE.

THE *Essay on the Understanding*, by an illustrious Englishman, being one of the most beautiful and esteemed works of the time, I have resolved to make Remarks on it. Because I have for a long time meditated sufficiently on the same subject and upon most of the matters which are touched upon there, I have thought that it would be a good opportunity to put forth something under the title of *New Essays on the Understanding*, and to obtain a favorable reception for my thoughts by putting them in such good company. I have thought also that I should be able to profit by the work of another, not only to lessen my own labor (since in fact it is less difficult to follow the thread of a good author than to work entirely *de novo*), but also to add something to what he has given us, which is always easier than to begin; for I think I have cleared up some difficulties which he had left in their entirety. Thus his reputation is advantageous to me; besides being inclined to do justice, and far from wishing to lessen the esteem in which that work is held, I would increase it, if my approval were of any weight. It is true that I often differ from him, but far from denying the merit of celebrated writers, we bear witness to it by making known in what way and why we separate ourselves from their opinion, when we think it necessary to prevent their authority from prevailing over reason on certain points of importance; besides, by satisfying such excellent men, we make truth more acceptable, and it must be supposed that it is principally for truth that they labor.

In fact, although the author of the *Essay* says a thousand fine things of which I approve, our systems differ very much. His has more relation to Aristotle, and mine to Plato, although we both diverge in many things from the doctrines of these two ancients. He is more popular, and I am forced at times to be a little more <term>acromatic</term> and more abstract, which is not an advantage to me, especially when I write in a living language. I think nevertheless that by

He explains that his goal is to build upon Locke's foundations while correcting points where he believes reason must override authority.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the preface to the "New Essays on the Understanding," where Leibniz explains his choice of the dialogue format to compare his views with those of John Locke.</meta>

...making two people speak, one of whom explains the views taken from the author's *Essay* while the other adds my observations to them; this comparison will be more pleasing to the reader than completely dry remarks, the reading of which would be constantly interrupted by the necessity of referring to his book to understand mine. It will nevertheless be good to compare our writings now and then and not to judge his views except by his own work, although I have usually preserved his own wording. It is true that the constraint of following the thread of another's discourse while making remarks has prevented me from aiming for the stylistic flourishes that a dialogue allows; but I hope that the subject matter will compensate for the lack of style.

The differences between us concern matters of some importance. The question is to know whether the soul in itself is entirely empty, like a tablet on which nothing has yet been written (<term>tabula rasa</term>) according to Aristotle and the author of the *Essay*, and whether everything traced upon it comes solely from the senses and from experience; or whether the soul originally contains the principles of several notions and doctrines which external objects merely awaken on occasion—as I believe, along with Plato and even the schoolmen and all those who interpret the passage from St. Paul (Romans 2:15) in this way, where he notes that the law of God is written in the heart. The Stoics called these principles <term>prolepses</term>, that is to say, fundamental assumptions, or what is taken for granted in advance. Mathematicians call them <term>common notions</term> (κοιναὶ ἔννοιαι). Modern philosophers give them other names, and Julius Scaliger in particular called them <term>semina æternitatis</term>, as well as <term>zopyra</term>—meaning living fires or luminous rays concealed within us, which our sensory encounters cause to appear like sparks struck from steel. And it is not without reason that these glimmers are believed to indicate something divine and eternal, which appears especially in <term>necessary truths</term>. From this arises another question: whether all truths depend on experience—that is, on <term>induction</term> and examples—or whether there are some that have another basis. For if some events can be foreseen before any proof has been made of them, it is clear that we contribute something on our part to them. Although the senses are necessary for all our actual...

knowledge is not sufficient to provide us with everything, since the senses never provide anything except examples—that is to say, particular or individual truths. Now, no matter how many examples confirm a general truth, they are not enough to establish the universal necessity of that same truth; for it does not follow that what has happened before will happen in exactly the same way again. For example, the Greeks, the Romans, and all other peoples of the earth known to the ancients always observed that day changes into night and night into day before twenty-four hours have passed. But we would be mistaken if we believed that the same law holds true everywhere else; for since then, the opposite has been experienced in the region of Nova Zembla. And anyone would still be mistaken who believed that, in our climates at least, this is a necessary and eternal truth that will last forever; for we must consider that the earth and the sun themselves do not exist necessarily, and there will perhaps come a time when that beautiful star, and its entire system, will no longer exist—at least not in its present form.

From this, it would seem that necessary truths—such as those found in pure mathematics, and especially in arithmetic and geometry—must have principles whose proof does not depend on examples nor, consequently, on the testimony of the senses, even though we would never think to consider them without the senses. This ought to be well recognized, and it is what Euclid understood so well that he often demonstrates through reason what is already clearly seen through experience and sensible images. Logic, along with metaphysics and ethics (one of which forms natural theology and the other natural jurisprudence), are also full of such truths; consequently, their proof can only come from internal principles, which are called innate. 

It is true that we must not imagine these eternal laws of reason can be read in the soul as if from an open book, as easily as the edict of the <term>praetor</term> is read upon his *album* without difficulty or investigation; rather, it is enough that they can be discovered within us through focused attention, for which the senses provide the occasion. The success of experiences serves to confirm reason, much like how "proofs" in arithmetic help us avoid errors in calculation when the reasoning is long. This is also how the knowledge of humans differs from that of beasts: beasts are purely empirical and guide themselves only by examples, for—as far as we can judge—they never

It is also for this reason that the faculty which animals have for making logical sequences is somewhat inferior to the reason found in man. The logical sequences of animals are merely like those of simple empiricists, who claim that what has happened sometimes will also happen in a case that appears similar to them, without being able to judge whether the same reasons apply. This is why it is so easy for men to entrap animals and so easy for simple empiricists to make mistakes. This is why people who have become skilled through age or experience are not free from error when they rely too much upon their past experience, as has happened to many in civil and military affairs; because they do not sufficiently consider that the world changes and that men become more skilled by finding a thousand new clever techniques, whereas the deer and hares of the present day do not become more cunning than those of the past. The logical sequences of animals are only a shadow of reasoning; that is to say, they are nothing but connections of the imagination and transitions from one image to another, because in a new situation which appears similar to the previous one, they expect once more what they previously found joined with it, as if things were linked together in fact simply because their images are linked in memory. It is true that reason itself counsels us to normally expect that what happens in the future will conform to a long history of past experience; however, this is not a necessary and infallible truth for that reason, and success may cease when we least expect it if the reasons that sustained it change. This is why the wisest do not rely upon it so much that they fail to try to discover something of the reason (if possible) for this fact, in order to judge when it will be necessary to make exceptions. For reason alone is capable of establishing reliable rules and of supplying what is lacking in those that were not reliable by inserting their exceptions; and finally, of finding certain connections in the force of necessary consequences. This often provides the means of foreseeing an event without needing to experience the sensory connections of images to which animals are restricted; so that whatever justifies the internal principles of necessary truths also distinguishes man from animals.

This being so, can it be denied that there is much that is innate in our mind, since we are innate, so to speak, in ourselves? I have also made use of the comparison of a block of marble which has veins, rather than a block of marble that is entirely uniform, or of blank tablets—that is to say, what is called among philosophers *tabula rasa*. For if the soul resembled these blank tablets, truths would be in us as the figure of Hercules is in marble when the marble is entirely indifferent toward receiving this figure or some other. But if there were veins in the block which marked out the figure of Hercules rather than other figures, the block would be more predisposed to it, and Hercules would be, in a sense, innate within it, even though it would be necessary to labor in order to discover these veins and to clear them by polishing and by cutting away whatever prevents them from appearing. It is in this way that ideas and truths are innate in us—as inclinations, dispositions, habits, or natural capacities, and not as actualities; although these capacities are always accompanied by some actions, often imperceptible, which correspond to them.

It seems that our capable author claims that there is nothing *virtual* in us and nothing of which we are not always actually conscious, but he cannot take this strictly; otherwise, his opinion would be too paradoxical. For acquired habits and the stores of our memory are not always consciously perceived and do not even always come to our aid when needed, although we often easily bring them back to the mind on some slight occasion which makes us remember them, just as we need only the beginning of a song to remember it. Rather, these impressions within the soul and body—lacking the appeal of novelty—are not strong enough to attract our attention and our memory, which are occupied by more engrossing objects. For all attention requires memory, and often, when we are not prompted, so to speak, or advised to attend to some of our own present perceptions, we let them pass without reflection and even without being noticed. But if someone calls our attention to them immediately afterward and makes us notice, for example, some noise that was just heard, we remember it and are conscious of having had some feeling of it at the time. This is how it was with the perceptions of which we were not immediately conscious; consciousness only arises in this case from being alerted after some interval, however small it may be. 

To better judge the <term>minute perceptions</term> which we are unable to distinguish in a crowd, I usually use the example of the roar or noise of the sea which strikes a person when they are on the shore. To understand this noise as it is produced, it would be necessary to hear the parts that compose the whole—that is to say, the noise of each wave—even though each of these small noises only makes itself known within the confused collection of all the others together (that is, in the roar itself) and would not be noticed if the wave that made it were alone. For it must be that we are affected slightly by the motion of this wave, and that we have some perception of each of these noises, however small; otherwise, we would not perceive a hundred thousand waves, since a hundred thousand "nothings" cannot make "something." One never sleeps so deeply that they do not have some faint and confused feeling, and one would never be awakened by the greatest noise in the world if they did not have some perception of its small beginning, just as one would never break a rope with the greatest effort in the world if it were not stretched and lengthened a little by smaller efforts, even though the tiny extension they produce is not visible.

What are these tastes, these images of sensible qualities—clear as a whole but confused in their parts—these impressions that surrounding bodies make upon us (which embrace the infinite), and this connection which every being has with all the rest of the universe? It may even be said that, as a result of these <term>minute perceptions</term>, the present is pregnant with the future and burdened with the past, and that all things "conspire" (σύμπνοια πάντα, as Hippocrates said); and that in the smallest of substances, eyes as piercing as those of God could read the entire course of events in the universe. *What things are, what they have been, and what will soon be brought to pass.* These insensible perceptions also indicate and constitute the identity of the individual, who is characterized by the traces or expressions these perceptions preserve of the individual's preceding states, creating the connection to their present state. These can be known by a superior mind, even if the individual themselves should not be aware of them—that is to say, when the explicit recollection of them is no longer within them. But these perceptions (I say) provide the means of finding this memory again when needed, through the periodic developments that may happen one day. It is for this reason that death can be nothing more than a sleep, and indeed cannot continue indefinitely; perceptions merely cease to be sufficiently distinguished and are, in animals, reduced to a state of confusion which suspends consciousness but which could not last forever—not to speak here of man, who must have great privileges in this respect in order to preserve his personality.

It is also through these insensible perceptions that the admirable <term>pre-established harmony</term> of the soul and the body, and indeed of all <term>monads</term> or <term>simple substances</term>, is to be explained. This harmony takes the place of the unsustainable theory of the direct influence of one substance upon another, and in the judgment of the author of the finest of Dictionaries, it exalts the greatness of divine perfections beyond anything that has ever been conceived. After this, I would add little if I should say that it is these minute perceptions which determine our actions in many a situation without us thinking about it, and which deceive the common people with the appearance of an *indifference of equilibrium*, as if we were entirely indifferent to turning (for example) to the right or to the left. ...just as the small is distinguished from the great, and which nevertheless often constitutes our desire and even our pleasure, by giving it a piquancy which stimulates.
