That is to say, they believe God has given them to the soul according to His good pleasure, without regard for any essential relationship between these perceptions and their objects: an opinion that surprises me and appears to me little worthy of the Author of things, who does nothing without harmony and without reason.

In a word, these insensible perceptions are as useful in <term>pneumatics</term> <note>the branch of philosophy dealing with the soul or spirit</note> as insensible corpuscles are in physics, and it is just as unreasonable to reject the one as the other on the pretext that they are beyond the reach of our senses. Nothing is done all at once, and it is one of my great and most verified maxims that *nature never makes leaps*: this is what I called the *Law of continuity* when I spoke of it in the first *Nouvelles de la Republique des Lettres*, and the use of this law is very significant in physics. It teaches that we always pass from the small to the great, and *vice versa*, through the intermediate stages, in degrees as in parts; and that motion never arises immediately from rest, nor is it reduced to it except by a smaller motion, just as one never completes running any line or length before having completed a shorter line. Although until now those who have laid down the laws of motion have not observed this law, believing that a body can receive in an instant a motion contrary to the preceding. All of this leads us to conclude rightly that noticeable perceptions also come by degrees from those which are too minute to be noticed. To think otherwise is to poorly understand the immense subtlety of things, which always and everywhere encompasses an actual infinite.

I have also noticed that by virtue of insensible variations, no two individual things can be perfectly alike, and that they must always differ more than in *number* (*numero*). This destroys the idea of the soul as a blank tablet, a soul without thought, a substance without action, a vacuum in space, atoms, and even particles in matter that are not actually divided, absolute rest, and entire uniformity in one part of time, space, or

<vocab>Cartesians, insensible perceptions, Law of continuity, physics, pneumatics, nature never makes leaps, Nouvelles de la Republique des Lettres, insensible corpuscles, actual infinite</vocab>

<summary>Leibniz argues that minute, unconscious perceptions are as vital to the study of the mind as atoms are to physics, and he uses the Law of Continuity to explain that all change occurs by degrees. It is in order to distinguish various considerations and to reduce, as far as is possible, the effects to reasons and to foresee some of their consequences, that we proceed thus: for the more attentive we are to neglect no consideration that we are able to regulate, the more practice corresponds to theory. But it belongs only to the Supreme Reason, from which nothing escapes, to distinctly comprehend all the infinite and to see all the reasons and all the consequences. All we can do regarding infinites is to know them confusedly and to know at least distinctly that they exist; otherwise, we judge the beauty and grandeur of the universe very wrongly. So also, we could not have a sound physics that explains the nature of bodies in general, and still less a sound <term>pneumatics</term> <note>the branch of philosophy dealing with the soul or spirit</note> which should comprise the knowledge of God, of souls, and of simple substances in general.

I have *a priori* reasons for this; but this advantage is also found in the doctrine because it resolves all the philosophical difficulties regarding the condition of souls, their perpetual conservation, their immortality, and their action. Since the difference between one of their states and another is never, and has never been, anything but a change from more sensible to less sensible, or from more perfect to less perfect, or vice versa, it makes their past or future state as explicable as their present one. One feels clearly enough, with even a little reflection, that this is rational, and that a leap from one state to another infinitely different state could not be natural. 

I am astonished that by abandoning the natural without reason, the scholastics have been willing to plunge themselves purposely into very great difficulties and to provide material for the apparent triumphs of freethinkers, all of whose arguments fall at a single blow by this explanation of things. Here, there is no more difficulty in conceiving the conservation of souls (or rather, in my view, of the animal) than there is in conceiving the change of a caterpillar into a butterfly, or the conservation of thought in sleep, to which Jesus Christ divinely compared death. I have also already said that a sleep could not last forever, and it will last the shortest time, or almost not at all, for rational souls who are always destined to preserve the personality that has been given to them in the City of God, and consequently their memory; this is so they may be more susceptible to punishments and rewards.

It also seems that we differ further regarding matter, in that the author thinks a vacuum is necessary here for motion because he believes that the minute parts of matter are rigid. And I acknowledge that if matter were composed of such parts, motion in a *plenum* would be impossible, just as if a room were full of a quantity of small pebbles without there being the least vacant space. But this supposition, for which there also appears to be no reason, is not admissible, although this capable author goes so far as to believe that the rigidity or cohesion of minute parts constitutes the essence of a body. It is necessary instead to conceive of space as full of an originally fluid matter, susceptible to all divisions and even actually subject to divisions and subdivisions *ad infinitum*, but nevertheless with this difference: that it is divisible and divided unequally in different places because of the motions which already more or less concur there. This is what causes it to have everywhere a degree of rigidity as well as of fluidity, and what causes no body to be hard or fluid to the highest degree—that is to say, no atom is to be found of an insurmountable hardness, nor any mass entirely indifferent to division. The order of nature, and particularly the law of continuity, destroy both equally.

I have also shown that *cohesion*, which could not itself be the effect of impulse or of motion, would cause a *traction* in the strict sense. For if there were a body that was originally inflexible—for example, an Epicurean atom that had a part projecting in the form of a hook (since we can conceive of atoms of all sorts of shapes)—this hook, when pushed, would carry with it the rest of the atom; that is to say,

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the debate between John Locke and the Bishop of Worcester (Edward Stillingfleet) regarding the nature of substance. It specifically critiques the idea that thought and solidity are merely different modifications of the same underlying substance.</meta>

*and distinct kinds of substances are nothing but different combinations of simple ideas; and that thus the author believed that the idea of thinking and of willing results in a substance different from that which the idea of solidity and impulse results in, and that (§ 17) he observes that these ideas constitute the body as opposed to the mind.*

The Bishop of Worcester might add that from the fact that the general *idea of substance* is in the body and in the mind, it does not follow that their *differences* are modifications of one and the same thing, as our author has just said in the passage which I have cited from his first letter. It is necessary to distinguish carefully between modifications and attributes. The faculties of perception and of action, extension, and solidity are attributes—or perpetual and principal predicates—but thought, impetus, shapes, and movements are modifications of these attributes. Furthermore, we must distinguish between *physical* (or rather *real*) *genus*, and *logical* or *ideal genus*. Things which are of the same physical genus, or which are *homogeneous*, are of the same matter, so to speak, and may often be changed into one another by a change of modification, like circles and squares. But two *heterogeneous* things may have a common logical genus, and then their differences are not simply accidental modifications of the same subject or of the same metaphysical or physical matter. Thus, time and space are very heterogeneous things, and we would be wrong to imagine some unknown real common subject which possessed only quantity in general, and whose modifications would make time or space appear.

Perhaps someone will scoff at these philosophical distinctions between two genera (the one merely logical, the other real) and two types of matter (the one physical, which belongs to bodies, and the other only metaphysical or general)—as if someone said that two parts of space are of the same matter, or that two hours are also of the same matter as each other. Nevertheless, these distinctions are not merely verbal, but of the things themselves; they seem very relevant here, where confusing them has lead to a false conclusion. These two genera have a common notion, and that of the real genus is common to the two types of matter, so that their genealogy will be as follows:

On all this I will remark, before coming to the explanation of my opinion, that it is certain that matter is as little capable of mechanically producing feeling as it is of producing reason, as our author agrees. In truth, I acknowledge that it is not right to deny what we do not understand, but I add that we are right in denying (at least in the natural order) what is absolutely neither intelligible nor explicable. I maintain also that substances (material or immaterial) cannot be conceived in their bare essence without any activity; that activity belongs to the essence of substance in general; and finally, that the conception of creatures is not the measure of the power of God, but that their capacity or power of conceiving is the measure of the power of nature. Everything that conforms to the natural order is capable of being conceived or understood by some creature.

Those who understand my system will think that I could not conform myself in everything to one or the other of these two excellent authors, whose controversy, however, is highly instructive. But to explain myself clearly, it is necessary above all to consider that the modifications that may belong naturally or without a miracle to a subject must come from the limitations or variations of a real genus or of a constant and absolute original nature. For it is in this way that philosophers distinguish the modes of an absolute being from that being itself; just as it is known that size, shape, and movement are clearly limitations and variations of corporeal nature. For it is clear how a limited extension produces shapes, and that the change made to it is nothing but motion. And every time we find some quality in a subject, we must believe that if we understood the nature of this subject and of this quality, we would understand how this quality results from it. Thus, in the order of nature (setting aside miracles), it is not a matter of choice for God to give substances just any qualities arbitrarily, and He will never give them any except those that are natural to them—that is, those that can be derived from their nature as explicable modifications. Thus it may be asserted that matter will not naturally have the previously mentioned attraction, and will not move of itself in a curved line,

<meta>This page continues the philosophical argument regarding the nature of matter and thought, specifically addressing why thought cannot be a natural or mechanical property of material substance.</meta>

<page-num>305</page-num>
<sig>20</sig>

...because it is not possible to conceive how this takes place there—that is, to explain it mechanically. In contrast, that which is natural must be capable of becoming distinctly conceivable if we were admitted into the secrets of things. This distinction between what is natural and explicable and what is inexplicable and miraculous removes all difficulties. By rejecting it, we would support something worse than "occult qualities" <note>hidden properties that cannot be explained by the laws of nature</note>. In doing so, we would renounce philosophy and reason by providing excuses for ignorance and idleness through a dead system. This system suggests not only that there are qualities we do not understand (of which there are all too many) but also that there are some that even the greatest mind—if God gave it every possible insight—could not comprehend. That is, they would be either miraculous or without rhyme or reason. Furthermore, the idea that God would perform miracles as a matter of course is illogical. Thus, this useless hypothesis would equally destroy our philosophy, which seeks reasons, and divine wisdom, which provides them.

Now as to thought, it is certain—and the author recognizes this more than once—that it cannot be an intelligible modification of matter, nor one that could be comprehended and explained. That is to say, a feeling or thinking being is not a mechanical thing like a clock or a mill, where we might conceive of sizes, shapes, and movements whose mechanical combination could produce something thinking or even feeling in a mass where no such thing existed before, and which would likewise cease to exist due to a malfunction in the mechanism. Therefore, it is not natural for matter to feel and think. This can only occur within it in two ways: one is that God joins to it a substance whose nature it is to think; the other is that God places thought in it by a miracle. In this, I am entirely of the same opinion as the Cartesians, except that I extend it even to brutes <note>non-human animals</note>. I believe that they have feeling and immaterial souls (properly speaking) and are as imperishable as the atoms of Democritus or Gassendi. In contrast, the Cartesians—unnecessarily embarrassed by the souls of brutes and not knowing what to do with them if they were preserved (because they had not considered the preservation of the animal reduced to a miniature state)—have been forced, contrary to all appearances and the judgment of the human race, to deny even the capacity for feeling to brutes.

<summary>The author argues that thought is not a mechanical property of matter and must instead arise from an immaterial soul or a miracle. He agrees with the Cartesians that souls are immaterial but departs from them by arguing that animals also possess imperishable, immaterial souls.</summary>

But if someone should say that God at least might add the faculty of thinking to the prepared mechanism, I would reply that if this were done—and if God added this faculty to matter without depositing in it at the same time a substance which was the subject of inhesion <note>the state of existing within a subject</note> for this faculty (as I conceive it), that is to say, without adding to it an immaterial soul—it would be necessary for matter to be miraculously exalted in order to receive a power of which it is not naturally capable. This is similar to how some Scholastics claim that God exalts fire even to the point of giving it the power to directly burn spirits separated from matter, a thing which would be a miracle, pure and simple. And it is enough that it cannot be maintained that matter thinks without adding to it an imperishable soul or a miracle; thus, the immortality of our souls follows from what is natural, since their extinction could be brought about only by a miracle, whether by exalting matter or by annihilating the soul. For we well know that the power of God could render our souls mortal, however immaterial (or immortal by nature alone) they may be, for he can annihilate them.

Now, this truth of the immateriality of the soul is undoubtedly important. For it is infinitely more advantageous to religion and to morals—especially in the times in which we live (when many people hardly respect revelation alone and miracles)—to show that souls are naturally immortal, and that it would be a miracle if they were not, than to maintain that our souls should naturally die, but that they do not die only by virtue of a miraculous grace founded in the promise of God alone. Also, for a long time, it has been known that those who have wished to destroy natural religion and reduce everything to revealed religion, as if reason taught us nothing concerning it, have been viewed with suspicion, and not always without reason. But our author is not among them; he maintains the demonstration of the existence of God, and he attributes to the immateriality of the soul a probability of the highest degree, which could consequently pass for a moral certainty. Thus, I imagine that, having as much sincerity as penetration, he could easily accommodate himself to the doctrine which I have just stated and which is fundamental in every rational philosophy. For otherwise, I do not see how one can prevent himself from falling back into fanatical philosophy, such as the *Philosophia Mosaica* of Fludd, which explains all phenomena by attributing them to

As for the difficulty many people have had in conceiving of an immaterial substance, it will easily vanish (at least for the most part) when they no longer demand substances that are entirely separated from matter; indeed, I do not believe there are ever any such substances naturally among created beings.

### BOOK I.—ON INNATE IDEAS.

#### CHAPTER I. [II IN LOCKE.]

->*Are there Innate Principles in the Human Mind?*<-

I must tell you again that I am no longer a Cartesian, and yet I am farther removed than ever from your Gassendi, whose knowledge and merit I acknowledge elsewhere. I have been impressed by a new system, about which I have read in the philosophical journals of Paris, Leipzig, and Holland, and in the marvelous Dictionary of Mr. Bayle, under the article *Rorarius*; since then, I believe I see a new aspect of the inner nature of things. This system appears to unite Plato with Democritus, Aristotle with Descartes, the Scholastics with the moderns, and theology and ethics with reason. It seems to take the best from every side and then go further than anyone has gone before. In it, I find an understandable explanation of the union of the soul and body, something I had previously despaired of finding. I find the true principles of things in the Unities of Substance which this system introduces, and in their harmony pre-established by the primitive substance. I find in it a surprising simplicity and uniformity, so that it may be said to be everywhere and always the same thing, differing only in degrees of perfection. I see now what Plato meant

§ 1. I have always favored, as I still do, the innate idea of God maintained by Mr. Descartes, and consequently other innate ideas that cannot come to us through the senses. Regarding innate principles, people often hold onto their prejudices and want to avoid the effort of debate; this misuse has fueled the author's passion against this idea. He wanted to fight the laziness and the shallow thinking of those who—under the misleading excuse of innate ideas and truths naturally imprinted on the mind, which we easily accept—do not bother to seek and examine the origins, connections, and certainty of this knowledge. In this, I completely agree with him, and I even go further. I wish our analysis were not restricted, that definitions were provided for all terms capable of being defined, and that all axioms which are not primary should be proven, or the means of proving them be provided. This should be done regardless of people's opinions and without caring whether they agree or not. This would be more useful than people realize. But it seems the author has been pushed too far in the opposite direction by his passion, which is otherwise highly commendable. In my view, he has not sufficiently distinguished the origin of necessary truths, which come from the understanding, from the origin of truths of fact, which are derived from sensory experience and even from the confused perceptions within us. Therefore, sir, you see that I do not accept your claim as a fact that we can gain all our knowledge without needing innate impressions. And what follows will show which of us is correct.

§§ 2. 3. 4. I do not base the certainty of innate principles on *universal consent*, for as I have already told you, I believe we should work to be able to prove all axioms that are not primary. Reminiscence requires some help. And it must be that, within this multiplicity of our knowledge, we are determined by something to renew one thought rather than another, since it is impossible to think distinctly and simultaneously about *all that we know*. In a sense, it must be said that all arithmetic and all geometry are innate and are within us virtually, so that they may be found there if we consider attentively and arrange what is already in the mind, without making use of any truth learned by experience or from the tradition of others. Plato has shown this in a dialogue where he introduces Socrates leading a child to abstract truths through mere questions, without telling him anything. We may, therefore, discover these sciences in our libraries and even with closed eyes, without learning through sight or even touch the truths that we need; although it is true that we would not consider the ideas in question if we had never seen or touched anything.

Since acquired knowledge may be concealed in the soul by memory, as you admit, why could nature not have also hidden some original knowledge there? Must everything that is natural to a substance that knows itself be known there actually in the beginning? Can this substance (such as our soul) not, and must it not, have many properties and modifications, all of which it is impossible to consider at first and all at once? It was the opinion of the Platonists that all our knowledge was reminiscence, and that thus the truths the soul has brought along at the birth of a human being—which are called innate—must be the remains of an explicit earlier knowledge. But this opinion has no foundation. And it is easy to judge that the soul must have already had innate knowledge in the preceding state (if pre-existence were a fact), however distant it might be, just as it does here. It therefore would have to come from another preceding state as well, or it would finally be innate or at least <term>concreate</term>; otherwise, it would be necessary to resort to the infinite and make souls eternal, in which case this knowledge would truly be innate because it would never have a beginning in the soul. And if someone claimed that each previous state had something from another even earlier state which it did not pass on to the succeeding one, the reply will be made that it is manifest that certain evident truths must have been in all these states. Why should it also be necessary that we could possess nothing in the soul that we have never used? And is possessing something without using it the same thing as merely having the faculty of acquiring it? If that were the case, we would never possess anything except the things we are currently using; whereas we know that, in addition to the faculty and the object, there must often be some disposition in the faculty, in the object, or in both, for the faculty to be exercised upon the object.

If the mind had only the simple capacity for receiving knowledge, or a passive power for it—as indeterminate as that which wax has for receiving shapes or a blank tablet for receiving letters—it would not be the source of necessary truths, as I have just shown. For it is undeniable that the senses are not enough to show their necessity, and thus the mind has a disposition (both active and passive) to draw them from its own depths; although the senses are necessary to provide the occasion and the attention for this, and to direct it toward some truths rather than others. You see, therefore, sir, that these people—otherwise very capable—who hold a different opinion, seem not to have sufficiently meditated on the consequences of the difference between necessary or eternal truths and the truths of experience, as I have already remarked and as our entire discussion shows. The original proof of necessary truths comes from the understanding alone, while other truths come from experiences or from the observations of the senses. Our mind is capable of knowing both, but it is the source of the former; and no matter how many particular experiences we may have of a universal truth, we could not be assured of it forever by induction without knowing its necessity through reason.

§ 11. It is the particular relation of the human mind to these truths that makes the exercise of the faculty easy and natural regarding them, and which causes them to be called innate. It is, therefore, not a naked faculty consisting in the mere possibility of understanding them; it is a disposition, an aptitude, a preformation, which determines our soul and brings it about that they may be derived from it. Just as there is a difference between the shapes given to stone or marble arbitrarily, and those which its veins already mark out—or are disposed to mark out—if the craftsman takes advantage of them.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of innate ideas, focusing on the distinction between intellectual ideas derived from reflection and confused sensory ideas, as well as the application of innate principles to specific instances.</meta>

The intellectual ideas, which are the source of necessary truths, do not come from the senses; and you recognize that there are ideas which are due to the reflection of the mind when it reflects upon itself. Furthermore, it is true that the explicit knowledge of truths is posterior (*tempore vel natura* <note>in time or in nature</note>) to the explicit knowledge of ideas; just as the nature of truths depends on the nature of ideas before we explicitly form one or the other, and the truths into which the ideas coming from the senses enter depend on the senses, at least in part. But the ideas which come from the senses are confused, and the truths which depend upon them are confused also, at least in part; whereas the intellectual ideas and the truths which depend on them are distinct, and neither the one class nor the other has its origin in the senses, although it may be true that we would never think of them without the senses.

§ 18. [*If such an assent be a mark of innate, then, that one and two are equal to three, that sweetness is not bitterness, and a thousand the like, must be innate.*] I do not see how this—*what is the same thing is not different*—can be the origin of the principle of contradiction, or why it would be easier; for it seems to me that you give yourself more liberty by advancing that A is not B, than by saying that A is not non-A. And the reason which prevents A from being B is that B includes non-A. Furthermore, the proposition *the sweet is not the bitter* is not innate, according to the meaning which we have given to the term innate truth. For the feelings of sweet and of bitter come from the external senses. Thus it is a mixed conclusion (*hybrida conclusio* <note>a hybrid conclusion</note>), where the axiom is applied to a sensible truth. But as for this proposition—*the square is not a circle*—it may be said to be innate, for in considering it, you make a subsumption or application of the principle of contradiction to what the understanding itself furnishes as soon as you are conscious of innate thoughts.

§ 19. [*Such less general propositions known before these universal maxims.*] We build on these general maxims as we build on major premises which are suppressed when we reason by <term>enthymemes</term> <note>a syllogism in which one of the premises is implied but not stated</note>; for although very often we do not think distinctly of what we do in reasoning, any more than of what we do in walking and jumping, it is always true that the force of the conclusion consists partly in what is suppressed and could not come from elsewhere, as will be found if you should wish to prove it.

§ 20. [*The claim that "one plus one equals two," etc., is neither general nor useful, answered.*] It is true that we begin to perceive particular truths sooner when we start with more complex and coarse ideas; but this does not prevent the order of nature from beginning with the most simple ones, nor does it stop the reasoning behind specific truths from depending on more general ones, of which they are merely examples. And when we wish to consider what exists within us potentially, and before any <term>apperception</term>, we are right to begin with the most simple. For <term>general principles</term> enter into our thoughts, forming their soul and their connection. They are as necessary to thought as the muscles and tendons are for walking, even though we do not think about them. The mind relies on these principles at all times, but it does not easily manage to distinguish them or to represent them to itself clearly and separately, because doing so requires great attention to its own actions, and most people, being little accustomed to <term>meditation</term>, have very little of that attention. Do the Chinese not have articulate sounds just as we do? And yet, being committed to a different way of writing, they have not yet thought of creating an alphabet from these sounds. It is in this way that one possesses many things without being aware of them.

§ 21. [*The fact that these maxims are sometimes unknown until they are proposed proves they are not innate.*] The nature of things and the nature of the mind are in agreement. And since you contrast the consideration of the object with the <term>apperception</term> of what is engraved on the mind, this very objection shows, sir, that those whose side you take understand by <term>innate truths</term> only those which would be naturally approved as if by <term>instinct</term>, and even without knowing it, except in a confused way. There are some of this nature, and we shall have the opportunity to speak of them. But what is called *<term>natural light</term>* assumes a distinct knowledge; and very often, considering the nature of things is nothing other than the <term>knowledge of the mind</term> and of these innate ideas which we do not need to look for externally. Thus, I call "innate" those truths which only require this internal consideration to be verified. I have already replied in § 5 to the objection in § 22, which claimed that when it is said that innate ideas are implicitly in the mind, it must simply mean that the mind has the faculty of knowing them; for I have shown that, in addition to this, the mind has the faculty of finding them within itself and the disposition to approve them when it thinks of them correctly.

# BOOK II.—OF IDEAS.

## CHAPTER I.

### *Of Ideas in general, and whether the soul always thinks.*

§ 1. [*Idea is the object of thinking.*] I admit it, provided that you add that it is an immediate internal object, and that this object is an expression of the nature or the qualities of things. If the idea were the *form* of thought, it would come into existence and cease with the actual thoughts that correspond to it; but by being its object, it might exist prior and subsequent to thoughts. External sensible objects are only *mediate*, because they cannot act immediately upon the soul. God alone is the *immediate external* object. It might be said that the soul itself is its own immediate *internal* object; but it is so only insofar as it contains ideas or what corresponds to things; for the soul is a *microcosm* in which distinct ideas are a representation of God, and confused ideas are a representation of the universe.

§ 2. [*All ideas come from sensation or reflection.*] The *tabula rasa* <note>blank slate</note>, of which so much is said, is, in my opinion, a fiction which nature does not allow, and which has its foundation in the incomplete notions of philosophers—like the vacuum, atoms, and rest (whether absolute or relative) of two parts of a whole, or like the *materia prima* <note>prime matter</note> which is conceived as being without form. Uniform things and those that contain no variety are never anything but abstractions, like time, space, and the other entities of pure mathematics. There

--- Page 332 ---
<meta>This page continues the argument against the soul being a completely blank slate, specifically addressing the nature of substance and the distinction between potential faculties and actual internal tendencies.</meta>

There is no body whose parts are at rest, and there is no substance that has nothing by which to distinguish it from every other. Human souls differ not only from other souls, but also among themselves, although the difference is not of the kind which is called specific. And according to the demonstrations which I think I have, every substantial thing, whether soul or body, has its own relation—which is peculiar to itself—to each of the others; thus, one must always differ from the other by *intrinsic characteristics*. This is not to mention that those who speak so much of this *tabula rasa* <note>blank slate</note>, after having taken away its ideas, are unable to say what is left to it—much like the scholastic philosophers who leave nothing to their *materia prima* <note>prime matter</note>.

It may, perhaps, be answered that this *tabula rasa* of the philosophers means that the soul has naturally and originally only bare faculties. But faculties without some act—in a word, the "pure powers" of the schools—are also but fictions unknown to nature, which are obtained only by abstraction. For where in the world will there ever be found a faculty that confines itself to mere power without exercising any act? There is always a particular disposition toward action, and toward one action rather than toward another. And besides the disposition, there is a tendency toward action, of which there is always an infinity at once in each subject; and these tendencies are never without some effect.

Experience is, I admit, necessary in order for the soul to be determined to such or such thoughts, and in order for it to take notice of the ideas which are in us; but by what means can experience and the senses give ideas? Does the soul have windows? Does it resemble tablets? Is it like wax? It is evident that all who think of the soul in this way make it, at bottom, corporeal. This axiom accepted among the philosophers will be used against me: that there is nothing in the soul which does not come from the senses. But the soul itself and its affections <note>qualities or states</note> must be excepted. *Nihil est in intellectu, quod non fuerit in sensu, excipe: nisi ipse intellectus.* <note>Nothing is in the intellect which was not first in the senses, except the intellect itself.</note> Now the soul comprises being, substance, unity, identity, cause, perception, reason, and many other notions which the senses cannot give.

In order to avoid a discussion upon what has delayed us too long, I declare to you in advance, sir, that when you say that ideas come to us from one or the other of these causes <note>sensation or reflection</note>, I understand it to refer to their actual perception; for I think that I have shown that they are in us before they are perceived, insofar as they have anything distinct about them.

§§ 9 and 10. [*The soul begins to have ideas when it begins to perceive. The soul does not always think.*] Action is no more connected with the soul than with the body; a state without thought in the soul and absolute rest in the body appear to me equally contrary to nature and without example in the world. A substance once in action will always be so, for all impressions remain and are merely mixed with other new ones. By striking a body, we excite—or rather determine—an infinity of vortices, as in a liquid; for at bottom, every solid has a degree of liquidity, and every liquid a degree of solidity, and there is no way to ever entirely stop these internal vortices. Now, we may believe that if the body is never at rest, the soul, which corresponds to it, will never be without perception either.

It is certain that we slumber and sleep, and that God is exempt from this. But it does not follow that while sleeping we are without perception. Rather, the opposite is found to be the case if it is carefully considered.

Real powers are never simple possibilities. There is always tendency and action.

I do not say that it is self-evident that the soul always thinks. A little attention and reasoning are needed to discover it. Most people perceive it as little as they do the pressure of the air or the roundness of the earth.

It is decided in the same way it is proved that there are imperceptible bodies and invisible movements, although certain persons ridicule them. There are, likewise, countless perceptions which are not sufficiently distinguished for them to be noticed or remembered, but they are made known by certain consequences.

I have not read the book which contains this objection <note>that it is an inference from Locke's position that a thing does not exist because we are not conscious of it in our sleep</note>, but it would not have been wrong to object to you that it does not follow that thought ceases simply because it is not perceived. For otherwise, it could be said for the same reason that there is no soul during the time when it is not perceived. And in order to refute this objection, it is necessary to point out specifically regarding thought that it is essential to it that it be perceived <note>consciously noticed</note>.

[...thinks] is, undoubtedly, the heart of the matter and the difficulty that has perplexed capable men. But here is the way to resolve it. We must consider that we think of many things at once, but we pay attention only to those thoughts which are most important. It could not be otherwise, for if we paid attention to everything, it would be necessary to think attentively about an infinite number of things at the same time—all of which we feel and which make an impression upon our senses. I will say even more: something remains of all our past thoughts, and none can ever be entirely erased. Now, when we sleep without dreaming and when we are stunned by some blow, fall, medical symptom, or other accident, an infinite number of minute, confused sensations are formed within us. Even death itself can produce no other effect upon the souls of animals, which undoubtedly must, sooner or later, acquire significant perceptions, for everything in nature proceeds in an orderly manner. I acknowledge, however, that in this state of confusion, the soul would be without pleasure or pain, for these are noticeable perceptions.

§ 12. [*If a sleeping man thinks without knowing it, the sleeping man and the waking man are two different persons.*] In turn, I will offer you another scenario, which seems more natural. Is it not true that we must admit that after some interval or some great change, one may fall into a state of total forgetfulness? It is said that Sleidan <note>Johannes Sleidanus (1506–1556), a historian and diplomat</note>, before his death, forgot everything he knew; and there are many other examples of this sad occurrence. Let us suppose that such a man became young again and learned everything <term>de novo</term>. Would he be a different man because of that? It is not, then, memory that truly makes someone the same man. Nevertheless, the fiction of a soul that animates different bodies in turn—without what happens to it in one of these bodies concerning it in the other—is one of those fictions contrary to the nature of things. These fictions arise from the incomplete notions of philosophers, like space without body or body without motion, and they disappear when one probes a bit deeper. For it must be understood that each soul preserves all its previous impressions and cannot divide itself equally in the way just mentioned. The future in each substance has a perfect connection with the past. It is this which constitutes the identity of the individual. Moreover, memory is not necessary, nor is it even always possible, due to the multitude of present and past impressions which work together to form our present thoughts;

...for I do not believe there are any thoughts in man of which there is not at least some confused effect, or some remnant mixed with subsequent thoughts. Many things can be forgotten, but they could also be remembered long afterward if they were recalled as they should be.

§ 13. [*Impossible to convince those who sleep without dreaming that they think.*]
One is not without some feeble feeling while asleep, even when the sleep is dreamless. Waking itself shows this; the easier it is to awaken someone, the more feeling they have of what is going on outside of them, although this feeling is not always strong enough to cause them to wake.

§ 15. [*Upon this hypothesis, the thoughts of a sleeping man ought to be the most rational.*]
All impressions have their effect, but all the effects are not always noticeable. When I turn to one side rather than to another, it is very often through a series of minute impressions of which I am not conscious, and which make one movement a little more uncomfortable than the other. All our unpremeditated actions are the results of a cooperation of minute perceptions; even our habits and passions, which have such influence on our deliberations, come from them. For these habits grow little by little, and consequently, without these minute perceptions, we would not arrive at these noticeable dispositions. I have already remarked that he who would deny these effects in morals would imitate the poorly instructed people who deny insensible <term>corpuscles</term> <note>microscopic particles or atoms</note> in physics. And yet I see that among those who speak of liberty, there are some who—taking no notice of these insensible impressions capable of tipping the scales—imagine an entire indifference in moral actions, like that of the ass of <term>Buridan</term> <note>A philosophical paradox describing an ass placed between two identical options, unable to choose between them</note> divided equally between two meadows. We shall speak more fully of this in what follows. I acknowledge, however, that these impressions incline without necessitating.

§ 23. [*When does a man begin to have ideas?*]
I am of the same opinion <note>namely, that it is when he has some sensation</note>; but it is by a slightly peculiar principle, for I believe that we are never without thoughts and also never without sensation. I distinguish only between ideas and thoughts; for we always have all pure or distinct ideas independently of the senses, but thoughts always correspond to some sensation.

§ 25. [*In the perception of simple ideas the soul is for the most part passive.*] How can it be that the soul is merely passive regarding the perception of all simple ideas, since, according to your own admission, there are simple ideas whose perception comes from reflection? And since the mind gives itself thoughts through reflection, it is the mind itself which reflects. Whether it can refuse them is another question; undoubtedly, it cannot do so without some reason that turns it away from them when there is an occasion for it.

### CHAPTER IV.
->*Of solidity.*<-

§ 1. [*We receive this idea from touch.*] At its core, solidity—insofar as the notion is distinct—is conceived by pure reason, although the senses provide reason with the evidence to prove that it exists in nature.

### CHAPTER V.
->*Of simple ideas of various senses.*<-

These ideas, which are said to come from more than one sense (such as those of space, shape, motion, and rest), are given to us rather by the common sense <note>The internal faculty that coordinates and interprets the data from the various senses.</note>—that is to say, the mind itself. For these are ideas of pure understanding, yet they relate to external things which the senses make us perceive; they are also capable of being defined and demonstrated.

### CHAPTER VII.
->*Of ideas which come from sensation and from reflection.*<-

§ 1. [*Pleasure and pain, power, existence, etc.*] It seems to me that the senses could not convince us of the existence of perceivable things without the help of reason. Thus, I believe the concept of existence comes from reflection. Those of *power* and of *unity* also come from the same source and are of an entirely different nature than the perceptions of pleasure and of pain.

### CHAPTER IX.

->Of perception.<-

§ 1. <note>Perception is the first simple idea of reflection.</note> It might, perhaps, be added that animals have perception and that it is not necessary for them to have thought—that is to say, for them to have reflection or what its object might be. For if what preceded it made no impression on the soul, this small addition would also make none, and the whole would make no more.

If you weigh my answer, you will find that I have included a condition that can be considered part of the question: that the only issue at stake is one of distinguishing, and that the blind man knows that the two shaped objects he must distinguish are present, and thus each of the appearances he sees is either that of the cube or that of the globe. For I am not speaking of what he might actually do immediately, as he would likely be stunned and confused by the novelty and otherwise unaccustomed to drawing conclusions. 

The basis of my opinion is that on the globe, there are no distinguishable points on the surface itself—everything there is smooth and without angles—whereas the cube has eight points distinct from all the others. If there were no such way to distinguish shapes, a blind man could not learn the basics of geometry by touch. Nevertheless, we see that those born blind are capable of learning geometry and even possess some basics of natural geometry; and geometry is most often learned by sight alone, without using touch, as a paralytic or another person denied the sense of touch might and even must do. It must be that these two geometries—that of the blind man and that of the paralytic—meet and coincide, and even return to the same ideas even though they share no common images. This again shows how necessary it is to distinguish images from exact ideas, which consist of definitions. 

It would certainly be very interesting and even instructive to examine thoroughly the ideas of someone born blind and to hear his descriptions of shapes. For he might achieve this and even understand the doctrine of optics insofar as it depends on distinct and mathematical ideas, although he would not be able to conceive of what is <term>clear-confused</term>—that is to say, the image of light and colors. It would also be very important to examine the ideas that a deaf and mute person might have regarding things that have no shape. Mankind is very negligent in not seeking an exact knowledge of the ways such persons think.

§ 11. Thus, I agree that the movement of the plant called "sensitive" <note>the Mimosa pudica, which folds its leaves when touched</note> comes from mechanism, and I do not approve of resorting to the soul when the details of plant and animal phenomena are to be explained.

§ 13. Very good; and I think almost as much could be said of plants. But as for man, his perceptions are accompanied by the power of reflection, which becomes active when there is an occasion. But when he is reduced to a state resembling a lethargy and is almost without feeling, reflection and consciousness cease, and universal truths are not considered. Nevertheless, the innate and acquired faculties and dispositions—and even the impressions received in this state of confusion—do not cease for that reason and are not erased, even though they are forgotten. They will even have their turn to contribute one day toward some noticeable effect, for nothing in nature is useless. All confusion must eventually unfold itself; even animals, having passed through a state of insensibility, ought to return one day to more elevated perceptions. And since simple substances last forever, it is not appropriate to judge eternity by a few years.

## CHAPTER XI.

### *On the faculty of discerning ideas.*

§ 10. [*Animals do not practice abstraction.*] I am of the same opinion. They apparently recognize whiteness and notice it in chalk as they do in snow; but this is not yet abstraction, for that requires considering what is common as separated from what is particular, and consequently involves the knowledge of universal truths, which is not granted to animals. It is also well observed that those animals that "speak" <note>such as parrots</note> do not use words to express general ideas, and that men deprived of the use of speech and words still manage to invent other general signs.

§ 11. Animals pass from one imagination to another by the connections they have experienced before; for example, when the master takes a stick, the dog fears being struck. And on many occasions, children—and other people as well—have no other method in moving from thought to thought. This might be called *sequence and reasoning* in a very broad sense. But I prefer to follow accepted usage by restricting these words to humans and limiting them to the knowledge of some *reason* for the connection of perceptions, which sensations alone could not provide. The effect of sensations is merely to cause us to naturally expect the same connection to occur another time as was noticed before, even though the underlying reasons are no longer the same—a fact which often deceives those who rely solely on their senses.

### CHAPTER XII.

->*Of complex ideas.*<-

In order to make the comparison more accurate, it would be necessary to imagine that in the dark room, there was a cloth to receive the <term>species</term> <note>sensory images or forms</note> that was not smooth, but varied with folds representing innate knowledge. Furthermore, this cloth or canvas, being stretched, had a sort of elasticity or power of acting—even an action or reaction adapted as much to past folds as to the newly arriving impressions of these sensory images. This action would consist of certain vibrations or oscillations, like those seen in a stretched cord when it is touched, of such a kind that it produces a sort of musical sound. For we do not only receive images or traces in the brain, but we also form them anew when we consider *complex ideas*. Thus the cloth, which represents our brain, must be active and elastic. This comparison would explain fairly well what takes place in the brain; but as for the soul, which is a simple substance or <term>monad</term>, it represents these same varieties of physical matter without itself having physical extension, and it has perception of them.

§ 3. <margin>Complex ideas are either modes, substances, or relations.</margin> This division of the objects of our thoughts into substances, modes, and relations is acceptable to me. I believe that qualities are merely modifications of substances, and that the understanding adds relations to them. This is more important than one might think.

§ 5. [*Simple and mixed modes.*] Perhaps a dozen or twenty are merely relations and are formed by their relationship to the understanding. Units are distinct, and the understanding joins them together, no matter how scattered they may be. Nevertheless, although relations originate from the understanding, they are not without foundation and reality. For the primary Understanding is the origin of things; and even the reality of all things, except simple substances, consists only in the foundation of the perceptions of the phenomena of simple substances. The same is often true regarding mixed modes; that is to say, it would be necessary to refer them back to other relations.

## CHAPTER XIII.

### *Of simple modes, and first of those of space.*

§ 17. [*Whether space is substance or accident is unknown.*] I have reason to fear that I shall be accused of vanity for wishing to determine what you, sir, admit you do not know. But there is reason to believe that you know more about this point than you say or believe you do. Some have believed that God is the place of things. Lessius <note>Leonardus Lessius (1554–1623), a Flemish Jesuit theologian.</note> and Guerike <note>Otto von Guericke (1602–1686), a German scientist and philosopher known for his work on the vacuum.</note>, if I am not mistaken, were of this opinion; but then "place" contains something more than we attribute to space, which we strip of all action. In this way, it is no more a substance than time, and if it has parts, it could not be God. It is a relation, an order, not only among existing things but also among possible things, as if they existed. But its truth and reality are founded in God, like all eternal truths.

It is best, then, to say that space is an order, but that God is its source.

§ 19. [*Substance and accident are of little use in philosophy.*] I admit that I hold a different opinion, and I believe that the consideration of substance is a point of philosophy of the greatest importance and fruitfulness.

### *Of duration and its simple modes.*

§ 24. The void that can be conceived in time indicates, like that in space, that time and space apply to possible things as well as to existing things.

§ 26. Time and space are of the nature of eternal truths which concern the possible and the existing equally.

§ 27. [*Eternity.*] But in order to derive the notion of eternity, it is necessary to conceive more—namely, that the same reason always exists for going further. It is this consideration of reasons that completes the notion of the infinite or of the indefinite in progressions. Thus, the senses alone could not suffice to make us form these notions. And fundamentally, it may be said that the idea of the *Absolute* is prior in the nature of things to that of the *limits* that are added. But we do not notice the former except by beginning with what is limited and what strikes our senses.

# CHAPTER XVII.
## Of infinity.

§ 1. [*Infinity, in its original intention, attributed to space, duration, and number.*] The true infinite, strictly speaking, is only in the *Absolute*, which is prior to all composition and is not formed by the addition of parts.

§ 3. [*Hence we come by the idea of infinity.*] Take a straight line and prolong it in such a way that it is double the first. Now it is clear that the second, being perfectly similar to the first, can be doubled in the same way in order to give a third which is also similar to the preceding; and the same reason always existing, it will never be possible to stop. Thus, the line can be prolonged *ad infinitum*; in such a way that the consideration of the infinite comes from that of similarity or of the same reason, and its origin is the same as that of universal and necessary truths. This shows how that which completes the conception of this idea is found within us and could not come from the experiences of the senses;

<summary>Leibniz argues that space, time, and the infinite are based on eternal truths and the "Absolute" rather than sensory experience alone. He defines the infinite as arising from the endless repetition of the same ratio or reason, which the mind recognizes as a necessary truth.</summary>
<keywords>time, space, eternity, absolute, infinite, continuum, necessary truths, perception, ad infinitum</keywords>

--- Page 343 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of space and time as relations, specifically addressing the concept of the Absolute and the transition into defining various modes of thought like memory and attention.</meta>

just as necessary truths could not be proved by induction or by the senses. The idea of the *Absolute* is in us internally, like that of being. These absolutes are nothing but the attributes of God, and it can be said that they are no less the source of ideas than God himself is the principle of beings. The idea of the absolute in relation to space is nothing other than the immensity of God, and so on for the others. But we deceive ourselves by imagining an absolute space that would be an infinite whole composed of parts. There is no such thing. It is a notion that involves a contradiction, and these infinite wholes and their opposites, the infinitely minute, are only admissible in the calculations of geometers, just like the imaginary roots of algebra.

§ 16. [*We have no positive idea of infinity nor of infinite duration.*] I believe that we have a positive idea of both, and this idea will be true provided it is not conceived as an infinite whole but as an absolute or attribute without limits; this is the case regarding eternity in the necessity of God's existence, without depending on parts and without forming the notion by adding together times. From this it is also seen, as I have already said, that the origin of the notion of the infinite comes from the same source as that of necessary truths.

### CHAPTER XIX.

#### *Of the modes of thinking.*

§ 1. [*Sensation, remembrance, contemplation, etc.*] It is well to clarify these notions, and I shall try to assist in doing so. I will say, then, that it is sensation when we perceive an external object; that remembrance is its repetition without the object returning; but when we know that we have had it before, it is memory. Contemplation is commonly used in a sense different from yours, sir—namely, for a state where we free ourselves from business in order to apply ourselves to some meditation. But since I know of no word that fits your notion, sir, the one you employ may be applied to it. We give attention to the objects that we distinguish and prefer over others. When attention continues in the mind—whether the external object continues or not, and even whether it is present or not—this is consideration; which, when it concerns knowledge without reference to action, will be contemplation. Attention, the aim of which is to learn (that is to say, to

To consider something in order to form a plan is to *meditate*; but reverie appears to be nothing but the pursuit of certain thoughts for the pleasure taken in them without having any other end. This is why reverie may lead to insanity: one forgets oneself, forgets the *dic cur hic* <note>Latin: "say why [you are] here"; a reference to self-awareness or one's purpose in the present moment</note>, approaches dreams and chimeras, and builds castles in Spain. We cannot distinguish dreams from sensations except by the fact that they are not connected with them; they are, as it were, a world apart. *Sleep* is a cessation of sensations, and so a trance is a very profound sleep from which one can be aroused only with difficulty; it arises from a transient internal cause, which distinguishes it from the profound sleep that comes from a narcotic or from some lasting injury to bodily functions, as in lethargy. Trances are sometimes accompanied by visions, but there are some visions without trances; and *vision*, it seems, is nothing but a dream which passes for a sensation, as if it taught us the truth of objects. And when these visions are divine, there is in fact truth, which may be known, for example, when they contain specific prophecies which the event justifies.

§ 4. [*Hence it is probable that thinking is the action, not the essence of the soul.*] Undoubtedly, thought is an action and could not be the essence; but it is an essential action, and all substances have such. I have shown above that we always have an infinity of minute perceptions without our being conscious of them. We are never without perceptions, but it is necessary that we are often without apperceptions—namely, when there are no distinct perceptions. It is for lack of having considered this important point that a philosophy as loose and as lacking in nobility as it is in solidity has prevailed among so many people of good minds, and because we have until now almost ignored what is most beautiful in souls. This has also caused men to find so much plausibility in the error which teaches that souls are of a perishable nature.

### CHAPTER XX.
#### *Of modes of pleasure and pain.*

§ 1. [*Pleasure and pain, simple ideas.*] I believe that there are no perceptions which are entirely indifferent to us, but it is enough that their effect is not noticeable for them to be called so; for pleasure and pain appear to consist in an aid or in a noticeable impediment. I assert that this definition is not merely nominal and that no other can be given.

§ 2. <margin>Good and evil, what.</margin> I am also of this opinion. The good is divided into the praiseworthy, the agreeable, and the useful; but fundamentally, I believe that it must be either itself agreeable or contributing to something else which can give us an agreeable feeling. That is to say, the good is agreeable or useful, and the praiseworthy itself consists in a pleasure of the mind.

§§ 4, 5. <margin>Love. Hatred.</margin> I gave very nearly this same definition of love when I explained the principles of justice in the preface to my <term>Codex Juris Gentium Diplomaticus</term>, namely, that to love is to be led to take pleasure in the perfection, well-being, or happiness of the beloved object. And for this reason, we do not consider nor demand any other pleasure for ourselves than just that which is found in the well-being or pleasure of the one loved. But in this sense, we do not properly love what is incapable of pleasure or of happiness, and we enjoy things of this nature without, for that reason, loving them—unless this is by a *prosopopoeia* <note>A rhetorical device in which an abstract thing or inanimate object is represented as a person</note>, as if we imagine that they themselves enjoy their own perfection. It is not, then, properly love when we say that we love a beautiful picture because of the pleasure we take in thinking of its perfections. 

But it is permissible to extend the meaning of the terms, and usage varies here. Philosophers and theologians even distinguish two kinds of love, namely: the *love* which they call *love of conquest* <note>Also known as concupiscent love or *amor concupiscentiae*</note>, which is nothing else than the desire or feeling we have for what gives us pleasure without our interesting ourselves in whether it receives pleasure; and the *love of benevolence*, which is the feeling we have for someone who, by his pleasure or happiness, gives the same to us. The first causes us to have our own pleasure in view, and the second that of others, but as making—or rather constituting—ours. For if it should not react upon us in some way, we could not interest ourselves in it, since it is impossible, whatever may be said, to be indifferent to one's own good. And this is how *disinterested* or *non-mercenary love* must be understood, in order to properly conceive of its nobility and yet not to fall into the chimerical.

This is why the infinitely wise author of our being has acted for our good by ordaining that we should often be in ignorance and in confused perceptions. This is in order to act more promptly by instinct and not to be troubled by the too distinct sensations of many objects, which do not entirely benefit us, and which nature has not been able to do without in order to achieve its ends. How many insects do we swallow without being conscious of it? how many people do we see who, having too fine a sense of smell, are thereby troubled? and how many disgusting objects would we see if our vision were sufficiently piercing? It is also by this skill that nature has given us the incitements of desire, like the rudiments or elements of pain or, so to speak, <term>semi-pains</term>, or (if you wish to express yourself more forcibly) minute inapperceptible pains, so that we may *enjoy* the *advantage* of *evil* without being troubled by it. For otherwise if this perception were too distinct we would always be miserable while waiting for the good, whereas this continual victory over these <term>semi-pains</term> which are felt in following one's desire and satisfying in some way this appetite or this longing, gives us many <term>semi-pleasures</term>, the continuation and collection of which (as in the continuation of the impulse of a heavy body which descends and acquires force) becomes in the end an entire and real pleasure. And fundamentally, without these <term>semi-pains</term> there would be no pleasure, and there would be no means of perceiving that something, by being an obstacle which prevents us from putting ourselves at our ease, assists us and aids us. In this way, the affinity between pain and pleasure is recognized, which Socrates notices in Plato's *Phaedo* when the feet long to be in action. This consideration of minute aids, or small deliverances and imperceptible releases of a blocked tendency—from which noticeable pleasure finally results—also serves to provide a more distinct understanding of the confused idea we have (and ought to have) of *pleasure* and *pain*. It is just as the feeling of heat or light results from many minute movements that represent those of the objects themselves (as I said above in ch. 9, § 13). They do not differ from those movements except in appearance and because we are not conscious of this analysis. Meanwhile, many people today believe that our ideas of sensible qualities differ *toto genere* from motions and from what happens within objects. They think these ideas are something primitive, inexplicable, and even arbitrary, as if God made the soul feel whatever seems good to him instead of reflecting what actually occurs in the body—an opinion very far removed from the true analysis of our ideas.

But to return to *uneasiness*—that is, the minute, imperceptible solicitations that keep us constantly active—these are confused determinations such that we often do not know what we lack. In contrast, with inclinations and passions, we at least know what we need, although confused perceptions also play a role in how they operate, and these same passions also cause this uneasiness or longing. These impulses are like many small springs trying to uncoil, which cause our machine to act. And I have already remarked that it is because of this that we are never truly indifferent, even when we appear to be most so—for example, when deciding whether to turn right or left at the end of a path. For the direction we choose comes from these insensible determinations, mingled with the influence of external objects and the internal state of the body, which cause us to find ourselves more at ease with one way of moving than the other. The balance wheel of a clock is called in German <term>Unruhe</term>, which means *uneasiness*. It can be said that the same is true of our body, which can never be perfectly at ease. If it were, a new impression from an object or a slight change in the organs, vessels, or viscera would immediately shift the balance and cause them to make a slight effort to regain the best possible state. This produces a continual struggle, which causes, so to speak, the *uneasiness* of our internal clock; therefore, this term is quite satisfactory to me.

§ 7. [*Joy*]. There are no words in languages sufficiently appropriate to distinguish related notions. Perhaps the Latin *gaudium* comes closer to this definition of joy than *laetitia*, which is also translated by the word *joy*; but then it seems to me to signify a state in which pleasure predominates in us. For during the deepest sorrow and amidst the most piercing griefs, one can take some pleasure—as in drinking or in listening to music—but the pain predominates; and likewise, amid the sharpest pains, the mind can be in joy, as happened to the martyrs.

§ 8. [*Sorrow*.] Not only the actual presence but also the fear of a coming evil can make one sad, so that I believe the definitions of joy and of sorrow that I have given come closest to common usage. As for uneasiness, there is in pain (and consequently in sorrow) something more; and uneasiness is present even in joy, for it makes people wide awake, active, and full of hope for going further. *Joy* has been known to cause death by an excess of emotion, and in those cases, there was even more in it than uneasiness.

§§ 9, 10. [*Hope and Fear*.] If uneasiness signifies a pain, I acknowledge that it always accompanies fear; but taking it as this imperceptible incitement which urges us on, it can also be applied to hope. The Stoics considered the passions to be opinions; thus, their hope was the opinion of a future good, and fear was the opinion of a future evil. But I prefer to say that the passions are neither contentments, nor pains, nor opinions, but tendencies—or rather modifications of a tendency—which arise from opinion or from feeling, and which are accompanied by pleasure or displeasure.

§ 11. [*Despair*.] Despair, taken as a passion, will be a sort of strong tendency that finds itself completely blocked, causing a violent struggle and much pain. But when despair is accompanied by rest and inactivity, it will be an opinion rather than a passion.

§ 12. [*Anger*.] Anger seems to be something more simple and more general since animals, to whom no injury has been done, are susceptible to it. There is in anger a violent effort that strives to free itself from evil. The desire for vengeance can remain when one is calm and when one experiences hatred rather than anger.

§ 13. [*Envy*.] According to this <note>Locke's</note> notion, envy would always be a praiseworthy passion and always founded upon justice, at least in my opinion. But I suspect that envy is often felt toward recognized merit which one would not hesitate

# CHAPTER XXI.

## *Of power and of liberty.*

§ 1. [*The idea of power, how it is obtained.*] If *power* corresponds to the Latin *<term>potentia</term>*, it is opposed to *act*, and the passage from power to act is *change*. This is what <term>Aristotle</term> understands by the word *motion* when he says that it is the act or *perhaps* the actuation of *that which is in power*. We can say then that power in general is the possibility of change. Now change, or the act of this possibility—being action in one subject and passion in another—there will also be two powers: one passive, the other active. The active could be called *faculty*, and perhaps the passive could be called *capacity* or *receptivity*. It is true that active power is sometimes taken in a more perfect sense when, in addition to the simple faculty, there is a *tendency*; and it is in this way that I employ it in my *dynamical* considerations. The word *force* might be applied to it in particular; and *force* would be either *entelechy* or *effort*. For *entelechy* (although Aristotle employs it so generally that it also comprises all action and all effort) appears to me more appropriate for *primitive acting forces*, and that of *effort* for *derivative forces*. There is even also a species of passive power that is more particular and more endowed with reality; it is this which exists in matter when there is not only *mobility* (which is the capacity or receptivity for motion), but also *resistance* (which encompasses *impenetrability* and *inertia*). *Entelechies*—that is to say, primitive or substantial tendencies—when they are accompanied by perception, are *souls*.

§ 4. [*The clearest idea of active power is obtained from spirit.*] I am thoroughly in agreement with you that the clearest idea of active power

§ 8. [*Liberty.*] The term *liberty* is very ambiguous. There is liberty of *right* and of *fact*. According to that of *right*, a slave is not free, a subject is not entirely free, but a poor man is as free as a rich man. *Liberty of fact* consists either in the power to *will* as one ought, or in the power to do what one wills. It is of the liberty of *doing* of which you speak, and it has its degrees and varieties. Generally, he who has the most means is most free to do what he wishes; but, in particular, *liberty* is understood as the use of things which are usually in our power, and especially of the free use of our body. Thus, prison or illnesses which prevent us from giving to our body and to our limbs the motion which we wish and which we are normally able to give, lessen our liberty. It is in this way that a prisoner is not free, and that a paralytic does not have the free use of his limbs. *Liberty to will* is also taken in two different senses. One is when it is opposed to the imperfection or to the slavery of the spirit, which is a compulsion or constraint, but internal, like that which comes from the passions. The other sense appears when liberty is opposed to necessity. In the first sense, the Stoics said that only the wise man is free; and in fact, the spirit is not free when it is occupied by a great passion, for one cannot then will as he ought to—that is to say, with the deliberation which is necessary. It is in this way that God alone is perfectly free, and that created spirits are so only in so far as they are superior to the passions. And this liberty concerns our understanding specifically. But the liberty of the spirit opposed to necessity concerns the pure will, insofar as it is distinguished from the understanding. This is what is called *free-will*, and it consists in this: that one wishes that the strongest reasons or impressions which the understanding presents to the will do not prevent the act of the will from being contingent, and do not give an absolute or, so to speak, metaphysical necessity. And it is in this sense that I am accustomed to say that the understanding can determine the will in accordance with the prevalence of perceptions and reasons, in such a way that even when it is certain and infallible, it inclines without necessitating.

§ 13. [*Necessity, what.*] It seems to me that, properly speaking, although volitions are contingent, necessity ought not to be

And if we do not always notice the reason that determines us, or rather by which we determine ourselves, it is because we are as little capable of being conscious of the whole extent of our spirit and its thoughts—which are most often imperceptible and confused—as we are of disentangling all the mechanisms that nature puts into play in the body. Thus, if by necessity is understood the certain determination of man—which a perfect knowledge of all the circumstances of what takes place within and outside the man could enable a perfect mind to foresee—it is certain that since thoughts are just as determined as the motions they represent, every free act would be necessary. 

But the necessary must be distinguished from the contingent, even if the latter is determined; and not only are contingent truths not necessary, but even their connections are not always of an absolute necessity. For it must be acknowledged that there is a difference in the manner of determination between the consequences that exist in necessary matter and those that exist in contingent matter. Geometrical and metaphysical consequences necessitate, but physical and moral ones incline without necessitating; the physical even has something moral and voluntary in relation to God, since the laws of motion have no other necessity than that of the principle of the best. 

Now God chooses freely although he is determined to choose the best; and as bodies themselves do not choose (God having chosen for them), usage has established that they be called *necessary agents*. I am not opposed to this, provided that the necessary and the determined are not confounded, and that it is not imagined that free beings act in an indeterminate manner. This is an error that has prevailed in certain minds and which destroys the most important truths, even this fundamental axiom, *that nothing occurs without reason*, without which neither the existence of God nor other great truths could be well demonstrated. As for constraint, it is useful to distinguish between two species of it. One is *physical*, such as when a man is taken to prison against his will or is thrown over a precipice; the other is *moral*, such as, for example, the constraint of a greater evil, and this action—although in some manner forced—is nevertheless voluntary. § 21. <note>Liberty belongs to the agent, or man.</note> When we reason about the liberty of the will, or about *free will*, we do not ask if the man can do what he wishes, but if there is enough independence in the will itself. We do not ask if he has his limbs free or has enough elbow room, but if he has his spirit free and in what this consists. In this respect, one intelligence could be freer than another, and the supreme intelligence will enjoy perfect liberty of which creatures are not capable.

§§ 41, 42. <note>All desire happiness. What happiness is.</note> I do not know whether a "greatest pleasure" is possible. I believe, rather, that it can grow *ad infinitum*; for we do not know how far our knowledge and our organs can be extended throughout all the eternity that awaits us. I believe, then, that *happiness* is a lasting pleasure, which could not be the case without there being a continual progress toward new pleasures. Therefore, of two persons—one of whom will proceed incomparably faster and through greater pleasures than the other—each will be happy in himself and separately, although their happiness will be very unequal. Happiness is then, so to speak, a road through pleasures; and pleasure is merely a step and an advancement toward happiness, the shortest that can be made according to present impressions, but not always the best. The right road may be missed in the desire to follow the shortest, just as a stone that goes straight may encounter obstacles too soon, which prevent it from advancing all the way to the center of the earth. This shows that it is reason and the will that transport us toward happiness, but that feeling and desire merely lead us to pleasure. Now, although pleasure cannot receive a nominal definition, any more than light or color, it can, however, receive a causal definition like them; and I believe that, at its core, pleasure is a feeling of perfection and pain is a feeling of imperfection, provided it is noticeable enough to make us conscious of it.

§ 47. <note>The power to suspend the pursuit of any desire makes way for consideration, and in this freedom of will consists.</note> The execution of our desire is suspended or stopped when this desire is not strong enough to move us and to overcome the trouble and inconvenience of satisfying it. But when the desire is strong
