...is sufficient in itself to move us; if nothing prevents it, it can be stopped by contrary inclinations, whether they consist of a simple leaning (which is like the element or the beginning of desire) or extend to desire itself. However, since these inclinations, leanings, and contrary desires must already be found in the soul, the soul does not have them in its power. Consequently, it cannot resist in a free and voluntary way where reason can take part, if it did not also have another means: that of turning the mind elsewhere. But how can we think to do this when there is a need? For this is the crux of the matter, especially if we are possessed by a strong passion. Therefore, the mind must be prepared beforehand and find itself already ready to move from thought to thought so as not to linger too long in a slippery and dangerous place.

To achieve this, it is helpful to accustom oneself generally to think of certain things only in passing, in order to better preserve the freedom of the mind. But the best way is to train oneself to proceed methodically and to attach oneself to a train of thoughts whose connection is established by reason rather than by chance (that is, by imperceptible and casual impressions). In order to do this, it is good to accustom oneself to compose oneself from time to time and to rise above the current tumult of impressions—to step outside the moment, as it were, and say to oneself, "*dic cur hic? respice finem*" <note>"Tell me, why are you here? Consider the end."</note>, or "where are we?" or "are we getting to the point?" People would often have need of someone, appointed to an official role (as Philip, the father of Alexander the Great, had), to interrupt them and recall them to their duty. However, in the absence of such an officer, it is good for us to be accustomed to performing this duty for ourselves. Now, once we are in a position to stop the effects of our desires and passions—that is, to suspend action—we can find the means to combat them, whether through contrary desires and inclinations or through diversion (that is, by occupations of a different nature). It is through these methods and these strategies that we become, in a sense, masters of ourselves, and that we can make ourselves think and do in due time what we wish and what reason commands. Nevertheless, this always happens through determined paths and never without cause, nor by the imaginary principle of a perfect indifference or equilibrium—concepts in which some believe the essence of liberty consists, as if one could determine one's own course without reason, or even against all reason, and go directly against the *prevalence* of impressions and inclinations.

<vocab>Philip, Alexander the Great, reason, passion, freedom of the mind, liberty, indifference, equilibrium, prevalence</vocab>

<summary>This page explains how the mind can resist passions not by sheer will, but by redirecting thoughts and preparing oneself beforehand to follow reason. It rejects the idea of liberty as a state of perfect indifference, arguing instead that self-mastery comes from methodical thinking and the ability to suspend action.</summary>

§ 51. [*The necessity of pursuing true happiness is the foundation of liberty.*] True happiness should always be the object of our desires, but there is reason to doubt whether it actually is. For we often hardly think of it, and I have noted here more than once that the less desire is guided by reason, the more it tends toward immediate pleasure rather than happiness—that is to say, toward lasting pleasure, even though desire tries to make the current pleasure last. Compare §§ 36, 41.

### CHAPTER XXIII.

## *Of our complex ideas of substances.*

§ 1. [*How ideas of substances are made.*] On the contrary, it is the *concretum*—as something fragrant, warm, or glittering—that comes into our minds, rather than the *abstractions* or qualities (for it is the qualities that are in the substantial object, not the ideas themselves), such as heat, light, and so on, which are much more difficult to understand. One might even doubt whether these "accidents" are real entities, as they are often actually just relations. It is also well known that abstractions cause the most difficulty when one tries to examine them minutely. This is clear to those familiar with the subtleties of the Scholastics, whose most complex speculations would collapse instantly if we were to banish abstract entities and decide to speak normally only in concrete terms, admitting no other terms into scientific demonstrations except those representing substantial subjects. Thus, to take qualities or other abstract terms as being the easiest to understand, while viewing concrete ones as very difficult, is to *nodum quærere in scirpo* <note>A Latin proverb meaning "to look for a knot in a bulrush," or to find a difficulty where there is none.</note>, if I may say so, and to turn things upside down.

§ 2. [*Our idea of substance in general.*] When we distinguish two things within a substance—the attributes or predicates and the common subject of those predicates—it is not surprising that nothing specific can be conceived within that subject. It must necessarily be this way, since we have already stripped away all the attributes through which any detail could be understood. Therefore, to demand something more from this pure subject in general than what is necessary to conceive that it is the same thing (for example, the thing which understands and wills, or imagines and reasons), is to demand the impossible. It goes against one’s own assumption made when abstracting and separately conceiving the subject and its qualities or accidents. The same alleged difficulty could be applied to the notion of being

[Cf. ART. III.]

§ 15. [*Ideas of spiritual substances, as clear as of bodily substances.*] It is well said, and it is very true, that the existence of the mind is more certain than that of sensory objects.

§ 1. [*What relation is.*] Relations and orders are like *entities of reason*, although they have their foundation in things; for it may be said that their reality, like that of eternal truths and possibilities, comes from the supreme reason.

Thus, although time and place (that is, the relation to the external) serve us in distinguishing things which we do not easily distinguish through themselves, things are nonetheless distinguishable in themselves. The characteristic of identity and of diversity does not consist, therefore, in time and in place.

§ 3. <note>*Principium individuationis* (The principle of individuation).</note> The principle of individuation corresponds in individuals to the principle of distinction that I have just mentioned. If two individuals were perfectly similar and equal, and (in a word) *indistinguishable* in themselves, there would be no principle of individuation; and I even venture to say that, under such a condition, there would be no individual distinction or separate individuals.

§ 9. <note>*Personal identity.*</note> I am also of the opinion that consciousness, or the feeling of the *ego*, proves a moral or personal identity. It is in this that I distinguish the *unceasingness* of the soul of a brute from the *immortality* of the soul of man: both retain *physical and real identity*; but as for man, it is in accordance with the rules of divine providence that the soul also preserves the moral identity that belongs to us in order to constitute the same person, who is consequently capable of feeling punishments and rewards. It appears that you, sir, hold that this apparent identity might be preserved even if there were no real identity. I believe that this might perhaps be possible by the absolute power of God; but according to the natural order of things, the identity apparent to the person himself, who feels himself to be the same, presupposes the real identity at each *following* stage, accompanied by reflection or by the feeling of the ego—since an intimate and immediate perception cannot naturally be deceptive. If man could be merely a machine and also possess consciousness, it would be necessary to agree with your opinion, sir; but I hold that this case is not possible, at least not naturally. I do not mean to say, either, that *personal identity* and even the *ego* do not remain within us, or that I am not the same *ego* that was in the cradle, on the pretext that I no longer remember anything I did then. To find moral identity by itself, it is sufficient that there be a common bond of consciousness from one state to another—whether the states are neighboring or somewhat removed—even if some leap or forgotten interval should be mixed with it. Thus, if an illness had caused an interruption of the continuity of the connection of consciousness so that I should

Real and personal identity is proved as certainly as is possible in a matter of fact by present and immediate reflection; it is proved sufficiently for common use by our memory of the interval or by the corroborating testimony of others. But if God extraordinarily changed the real identity, personal identity would remain, provided that the man preserved the appearances of identity—both the internal (that is, of consciousness) and the external, such as the appearances that are evident to others. Thus, consciousness is not the only means of establishing personal identity; the reports of others or even other signs may take its place. However, there is a difficulty if a contradiction is found between these different types of evidence. Consciousness may be silent, as in forgetfulness; but if it spoke very distinctly of things that were contrary to other evidence, we would be troubled in our decision and sometimes suspended between two possibilities: the error of our memory, or some deception in the external evidence.

§ 14. An immaterial being or a spirit *cannot be stripped* of all perception of its past existence. The late Mr. Van Helmont the younger believed, along with certain rabbis, in the passing of the soul of Adam into the Messiah as if into the new Adam. And I do not know whether he did not also believe that he himself had been one of the ancients—as he was a very capable man in other respects. Now, if this passing of souls were true, at least in the possible way which I have explained above (though it does not appear probable)—that is, that souls, retaining subtle bodies, should pass suddenly into other physical bodies—the same individual would always persist in Nestor, in Socrates, and in some modern person. He might even make his identity known to someone who could sufficiently penetrate into his nature, because of the impressions or characters that would remain there of all that Nestor or Socrates had done, and which some sufficiently penetrating genius might read there. However, if the modern man had no internal or external means of knowing what he had been, it would be, as far as ethics is concerned, as if he had not existed at all. But the probability is that nothing is neglected in the world, even in relation to morals, because God is its monarch, and His government is perfect. Thus, if souls passed into a new physical or sensitive body, they would always retain the expression of everything they perceived in the old one; it would even be necessary for the new body to feel it all so that the individual's continuity will always leave its real marks.

This would not be rational because perceptions that are currently insensible may be developed

## CHAPTER XXVIII.
### *Of other relations.*

§ 5. <note>Moral good and evil.</note> I should prefer, for my part, to take the invariable rule of reason—which God has taken it upon himself to maintain—as the measure of moral good and of virtue. We may also be assured that through Him, every moral good becomes a physical good, or, as the ancients said, everything praiseworthy is useful. However, to express the author's idea, it would be necessary to say that moral good or evil is a *good* or *evil* of decree or institution, which the one who holds power tries to bring about or prevent through punishments or rewards. Good is that which, by God's general ordinance, conforms to nature or reason.

### *Of clear and obscure, distinct and confused ideas.*

Having found it, I know the nature and the properties of the proposed polygon very well, insofar as they are those of a chiliagon, and consequently I have the idea of it. However, I could not have the image of a chiliagon, and it would be necessary to have senses and an imagination more delicate and better exercised to distinguish it from a polygon that has one less side. But knowledge of figures does not depend upon the imagination any more than knowledge of numbers does, although imagination is useful for it; and a mathematician may know exactly the nature of an enneagon or of a decagon because he has the means of constructing and examining them, even though he cannot distinguish them by sight. It is true, then, that a workman or an engineer, who might not perhaps know the nature of the figures sufficiently, might have this advantage over a great geometrician: he could distinguish them merely by seeing them without measuring them. Similarly, there are porters who can tell the weight of what they are to carry without being off by a pound, surpassing the most skillful statistician in the world in this regard. This empirical knowledge, acquired by long practice, may offer great advantages for acting promptly, as an engineer very often needs to do because of the danger to which he exposes himself by hesitating. However, this *clear image*, or this feeling which we may have of a regular decagon or of a weight of ninety-nine pounds, consists only of a confused idea, since it is of no use in discovering the nature and the properties of this weight or of the regular decagon, which requires a distinct idea. And this example serves to show better the difference between ideas, or rather the difference between an idea and an image.

§ 15. <note>An instance regarding eternity.</note> This example does not seem to me to fit your purpose any better; but it is very appropriate to mine, which is to correct your misconceptions on this point. For the same confusion between image and idea prevails here. We have a complete and proper idea of eternity, since we have a definition of it, even though we have no image of it; but the idea of infinites is not formed by the composition of parts, and the errors which are committed in reasoning concerning the infinite do not come from a lack of an image.

## CHAPTER I.
### *Of knowledge in general.*

§§ 1 and 2. <note>1. Our knowledge is concerned with our ideas. 2. Knowledge is the perception of the agreement or disagreement of two ideas.</note> Knowledge is used even more broadly, in such a way that it is also found in ideas or terms before we come to propositions or truths. And it may be said that he who has carefully seen more pictures of plants and animals, more diagrams of machines, and more descriptions or representations of houses or fortresses, and who has read more clever romances or heard more curious narratives—he, I say, will have more knowledge than another, even if there were not a word of truth in all that has been portrayed or related to him. This is because the practice he has in mentally representing to himself many clear and actual conceptions or ideas makes him better able to conceive what is proposed to him; and it is certain that he will be better informed and more capable than another who has neither seen, read, nor heard anything, provided that in these stories and representations he does not take for true what is not true, and that these impressions do not otherwise prevent him from distinguishing the real from the imaginary, or the existing from the possible . . . . But taking knowledge in a narrower sense—that is, for the knowledge of truth, as you do here, sir—I say that it is very true that truth is always founded on the agreement or disagreement of ideas, but it is not generally true that our knowledge of truth is a perception of this agreement or disagreement. For when we know truth only empirically, from having experienced it, without knowing the connection of things and the reason behind what we have experienced, we have no perception of this agreement or disagreement, unless it is meant that we feel it confusedly without being conscious of it. But your examples, it seems, show that you always require a knowledge in which one is conscious of connection or of opposition, and this is what cannot be granted to you.

§§ 3–7. <note>3. This agreement is fourfold. 4. First, of identity or diversity. 5. Second, relative. 6. Third, of co-existence.</note>

7. *Fourthly, of real existence.*] I believe it may be said that connection is nothing other than agreement or *relation*, taken generally. And I have observed on this point that every relation is either one of *comparison* or of *concurrence*. *Comparison* yields diversity and identity, either in their entirety or in some aspect—it determines what is the same or different, and what is like or unlike. *Concurrence* includes what you call co-existence, that is, the connection of existence. But when it is said that a thing exists or that it has real existence, this existence itself is the predicate; that is, it is an idea joined with the idea in question, and there is a connection between these two notions. One may also conceive of the existence of the object of an idea as the concurrence of this object with myself. So I believe it may be said that there is only comparison or concurrence; but comparison, which marks identity or diversity, and the concurrence of the thing with me, are relations that deserve to be distinguished from others. More precise and deeper research might perhaps be conducted, but I content myself here with making these remarks.

## CHAPTER II.

### *Of the degrees of our knowledge.*

§ 1. [*Intuitive.*] Primitive truths, which are known by intuition, are of two kinds, just like derivative truths. They are either truths of reason or truths of fact. Truths of reason are necessary, and those of fact are contingent. Primitive truths of reason are those I call by the general name of *identities*, because it seems they do nothing but repeat the same thing without providing us with any information. They are either affirmative or negative . . . .

As for primitive truths of fact, they are the immediate internal experiences of an *immediateness of feeling*. And it is here that the first truth of the Cartesians or of St. Augustine—*I think, therefore I am*, that is, *I am a thinking thing*—holds true. But it should be understood that just as identities are either general or particular, and one class is as clear as the other (since it is just as clear to say that *A is A* as it is to say that a thing *is what it is*), the same applies to the first truths of fact. For not only is it immediately clear to me that *I think*, but it is just as clear to me that *I have different thoughts*; that sometimes *I think of A*, and that sometimes *I think*

§ 14. [Sensitive knowledge of particular existence.] But let us come to this controversy which the skeptics carry on with the dogmatists over the existence of things *outside of ourselves*. We have already touched upon it, but it is necessary to return to it here. I have previously discussed it thoroughly, both verbally and in writing, with the late Abbé Foucher, Canon of Dijon, a learned and subtle man. Now, I made him admit that the truth of sensible things consisted only in the *connection of phenomena*, which must have its reason, and that it is this which distinguishes them from *dreams*; but that the truth of our existence and of the cause of phenomena is of another kind, because it establishes substances. I also argued that the skeptics ruined whatever good points they made by carrying them too far, and by wishing even to extend their doubts to immediate experiences and to geometrical truths (something which Mr. Foucher, however, did not do), and to the other truths of reason, which he did a little too much. But to return to our own discussion, sir; you are right in saying that there is usually a difference between sensations and imaginings; but the skeptics will say that a difference of degree does not change the nature of the thing. Besides, although sensations tend to be more vivid than imaginings, it is nonetheless a fact that there are cases where a person with a vivid imagination is affected by their imaginings as much as, or perhaps even more than, another person is by the actual truth of things. Therefore, I believe that the true criterion regarding the objects of the senses is the connection of phenomena—that is, the connection between what takes place in different places and times, and in the experience of different men, who are themselves, to one another, very important phenomena in this regard. And the connection of phenomena, which guarantees *truths of fact* in respect to sensible things outside of us, is verified by means of *truths of reason*; just as the appearances in optics are explained by geometry. However, it must be confessed that all this certainty is not of the highest degree, as you have well recognized. For it is not impossible, speaking metaphysically, that there could be a dream, continuous and lasting, like the life of a man; but such a thing is as contrary to reason as would be the fiction of a book which was formed by chance

## CHAPTER III.

->*Of the extent of human knowledge.*<-

§ 6. ["*Whether any mere material being thinks or not.*"] In the first place, I declare to you, sir, that when one has only confused ideas of thought and of matter, as one usually has, it is not surprising that one does not see the means of solving such questions. It is as I have remarked before: a person who only has ideas of the angles of a triangle in a general way will never think of finding out that they are *always equal to two right angles.* One must consider that *matter, taken as a complete being* (that is, secondary matter as opposed to *primary* matter, which is something purely passive and consequently incomplete), is only a mass, or that which results from it, and that every *real mass* presupposes *simple substances* or *real unities*. When we further consider what belongs to the nature of these real unities—that is, *perception* and its consequences—we are transported, so to speak, into another world; that is to say, into the *intelligible world of substances*, whereas before we were only among the *phenomena of the senses*. This knowledge of the interior of matter shows clearly enough what it is naturally capable of, and it shows that whenever God provides organs fitted to express reasoning, the immaterial substance that reasons will also be provided, by virtue of that harmony which is itself a natural result of substances. Matter could not exist without immaterial substances—that is, without unities; after understanding this, one should no longer ask whether God is free to give them to it or not. And if these substances did not have within themselves the correspondence or harmony I have just mentioned, God would not be acting according to the natural order. To speak very simply of giving or granting powers is to return to the bare *faculties* of the schoolmen and to imagine tiny existing beings that can enter and leave like pigeons in a dovecote. It is treating these powers as if they were substances themselves.

<summary>Leibniz argues that matter is a collection of phenomena that presupposes "real unities" or simple substances, and that reasoning requires both physical organs and corresponding immaterial substances according to a natural harmony.</summary>

without thinking of it. Primitive powers constitute substances themselves; and derivative powers—or, if you prefer, faculties—are only modes of being that must be derived from substances. They are not derived from matter viewed merely as a machine; that is, insofar as we consider it abstractly only as the incomplete being of primary matter, which is simply passive. Here, I think you will agree with me, sir, that it is <note>not</note> within the power of a mere mechanism to cause perception, sensation, or reason to arise. These must, therefore, spring from some other substantial thing. To think that God acts differently and gives things accidents that are not *modes of being* or modifications derived from substances is to resort to miracles and to what the Scholastics called <term>obediential power</term>—a kind of supernatural elevation. This is like when certain theologians claim that the fire of hell burns souls separated from their bodies; in that case, it might even be doubted whether it was the fire acting, or if God himself produced the effect by acting in place of the fire. . . .

The remaining difficulty only concerns those who wish to imagine what is only intelligible—as if they wanted to see sounds or hear colors.

### CHAPTER IV.

->*Of the reality of human knowledge.*<-

Moreover, the ground of our certainty regarding universal and eternal truths lies in the ideas themselves, independently of the senses; likewise, pure and intelligible ideas do not depend upon the senses—for example, the ideas of being, of unity, of sameness, etc. But the ideas of sensible qualities, such as color, flavor, etc. (which in reality are only appearances), come to us from the senses—that is, from our confused perceptions. And the ground of truth for contingent and particular things is found in the sequence through which the phenomena of the senses are connected, just as intelligible truths require. The distinction you make here between simple and compound ideas, and compound ideas belonging to substances and to accidents, does not seem to me well founded, since all intelligible ideas have their archetypes in the eternal possibility of things.

## CHAPTER V.
### *Of truth in general.*

§§ 1 and 2. <note>1. What truth is. 2. A right joining or separating of signs; that is, ideas or words.</note> But what I find least to my taste in your definition of truth is that truth is sought there in words. Thus, the same meaning, being expressed in Latin, German, English, or French, would not be the same truth, and it would be necessary to say with Hobbes that truth depends on the arbitrary will of men—which is speaking in a very strange way. Truth is even attributed to God, who you will admit (I think) has no need for signs. Finally, I have already been more than once surprised at the inclination of your friends, who take pleasure in making essences and species into *nominal truths*.

We would therefore have, further, *literal truths*, which may be distinguished into truths of paper or of parchment, of ordinary black ink or printer’s ink, if truths must be distinguished by signs. It is better, therefore, to place truth in the relation between the *objects* of ideas, which causes one to be included or not included in the other. This does not depend on languages and is common to us, to God, and to the angels; and when God reveals a truth to us, we acquire the same one that is in his understanding. For although there is an infinite difference between his ideas and ours regarding perfection and extension, it is always true that there is agreement in the same relationship. It is therefore in this relation that truth must be placed, and we may distinguish between truths, which are independent of our will, and expressions, which we invent as we see fit.

§ 11. <note>Moral and metaphysical truth</note>. *Moral truth* is called *veracity* by some, and *metaphysical truth* is commonly taken by metaphysicians for an attribute of being; but it is a very useless attribute and one almost void of meaning. Let us content ourselves with seeking truth in the correspondence of propositions in the mind with the things in question. It is true that I have also attributed truth to ideas in saying that ideas are true or

<summary>The author critiques the idea that truth depends on linguistic signs or human convention, arguing instead that truth is found in the objective relations between ideas. He asserts that truth is independent of language and is shared between human and divine understanding.</summary>

### CHAPTER VII.
#### *Of maxims.*

§ 1. <note>They are self-evident</note>. This investigation is very useful and even important. But you must not imagine, sir, that it has been entirely neglected. You will find in a hundred places that the scholastic philosophers have said that these propositions are evident *ex terminis*, as soon as their terms are understood; so that they were persuaded that the force of conviction was founded on the apprehension of the terms, that is, in the connection of the ideas. But the geometricians have done much more: for they have undertaken very often to demonstrate them. . . . As regards *maxims*, they are sometimes taken for established propositions, whether they are evident or not. This might be well for beginners, who are stopped by scrupulousness; but when the establishing of science is in question, it is another matter. They are also often taken this way in ethics and even by the logicians in their *Topics*, in which there is an abundance of them, but a part of this contains some which are sufficiently vague and obscure. For the rest, I said publicly and privately a long while ago that it would be important to demonstrate all the secondary axioms of which we ordinarily make use, by reducing them to primitive or immediate and undemonstrable axioms, which are those which I called recently and elsewhere, identical ones.

§ 7. It may always be said that this proposition, *I exist*, is most evident, being a proposition which cannot be proved by any other, or an immediate truth. And to say, *I think therefore I am*, is not properly to prove existence by thought, since to think and to be thinking are the same thing; and to say, *I am thinking* is the same as to say, *I am*. Nevertheless you may exclude this proposition from the number of axioms with some justice, for it is a proposition of fact, founded upon an immediate experience, and it is not a necessary proposition, whose necessity is seen in the immediate agreement of ideas. There is no one but God who sees how these two terms *I* and *existence* are connected—that is, why I exist. But if the axiom is taken more generally as an immediate or *non-provable* truth, it may be said that the proposition *I am* is an axiom; in any case, we may be assured that it is a primitive truth or *unum ex primis cognitis inter terminos complexos*, that is, it is one of the first known statements understood in the natural order of our knowledge. For it is possible that a man may never have thought of expressly forming this proposition, which is yet innate in him.

§§ 8, 9. I had further added that in the natural order, saying that a thing is what it is comes before saying that it is not something else; for here it is not a question of the history of our discoveries, which differs between different men, but of the connection and natural order of truths, which is always the same. But your remark—namely, that what the child sees is only a fact—deserves still more reflection; for the experiences of the senses do not give absolutely certain truths (as you yourself observed, sir, not long ago), nor are they free from all danger of illusion. For if it is permitted to create metaphysically possible fictions, sugar might be changed imperceptibly into a rod to punish a child if he has been naughty, just as water is changed into wine among us on Christmas Eve, if one has been well-behaved [*morigené*]. But the pain (you will say) which the rod inflicts will never be the pleasure which the sugar gives. I reply that the child will think of making an express proposition concerning it as little as of noticing the axiom that it cannot be truly said that *what is, at the same time is not*, although he may very well perceive the difference between pleasure and pain, as well as the difference between perceiving and not perceiving.

§ 10. Thus, you must not here oppose the axiom and the example as different truths in this respect, but regard the axiom as incorporated in the example and rendering the example true. It is quite another thing when the evidence is not noticed in the example itself and when the affirmation of the example is a consequence and not merely a <term>subsumption</term> of the universal proposition, as may also happen in respect to axioms.

## CHAPTER IX.
### *Of our knowledge of existence.*

§§ 2 and 3. [*2. A threefold knowledge of existence. 3. Our knowledge of our own existence is intuitive.*] I fully agree with all of this. And I add that the immediate apperception of our existence and of our thoughts provides us with the first *a posteriori* truths, or truths of fact—that is, the *first experiences*—just as identical propositions contain the first *a priori* truths, or truths of reason—that is, the *first lights*. Both are incapable of being proved and may be called *immediate*; the former because there is immediacy between the understanding and its object, and the latter because there is immediacy between the subject and predicate.

## CHAPTER X.
### *Of our knowledge of the existence of a God.*

§ 1. I do not wish to repeat what has been discussed between us concerning innate ideas and truths, among which I include the idea of God and the truth of his existence.

§§ 2-6. [*2. Man knows that he himself exists. 3. He knows also that nothing cannot produce a being, therefore something is eternal. 4. That eternal being must be most powerful. 5. It is primarily in the passage where you conclude (§ 3) that something has existed from all eternity. I find an ambiguity in it. If it means that *there has never been a time when nothing existed*, I agree with this; and it follows truly from the preceding propositions by a completely mathematical sequence. For if there had never been anything, there would always have been nothing, since nothing is not able to produce being; hence, we ourselves would not exist, which is contrary to the first truth of experience. But what follows shows first that in saying that something has existed from all eternity, you mean an eternal thing. Nevertheless, it does not follow, by virtue of what you have put forward up to this time, that if there has always been something, it has always been a certain thing—that is, that there is an eternal being. §§ 9, 10. [*9. Two sorts of beings, cogitative and incogitative.* *10. An incogitative being cannot produce a cogitative one*]. I think the present reasoning is the strongest in the world, and not only exact but also profound and worthy of its author. I entirely agree with his opinion that there is no combination and modification of parts of matter, however small they may be, which can produce perception; all the more because the larger parts could not provide it (as is clearly evident), and everything in the small parts is proportional to what can take place in the large ones. This is another important observation regarding matter which the author makes here: that it must not be taken for a single thing, or (as I am accustomed to say) for a true and perfect monad or unity, since it is only a mass of an infinite number of beings. Here this excellent author needed but one more step to reach my system. For, in fact, I attribute perception to all these infinite beings, each one of which is like an animal, endowed with a soul (or with some analogous active principle, which forms its true unity) together with whatever is necessary for this being to be passive and endowed with an organic body. Now these beings have received their nature, active and passive (that is, what they possess of the immaterial and material), from a general and supreme cause, because otherwise, as the author well remarks, being independent of each other, they could never produce that *order*, that *harmony*, and that *beauty* which we observe in nature. But this argument, which appears to have only moral certainty, is raised to an entirely metaphysical necessity by the *new kind of harmony* which I have introduced, which is the *pre-established harmony*. ## CHAPTER XI.

### *Of our knowledge of the existence of other things.*

§§ 1–10. [*It is to be had only by sensation, etc.*] I have already remarked in our preceding conversations that the truth of sensible things is proved by their connection, which depends on the intellectual truths founded in reason and on the constant observations of sensible things themselves, even when the reasons do not appear. And as these reasons and observations give us the means of judging the future in relation to our interests, and as success matches our rational judgment, we could not ask for nor even have a greater certainty concerning these objects. We can also account for dreams and for their lack of connection with other phenomena. Nevertheless, I believe that the name of knowledge and of certainty might be extended beyond actual sensations, since clarity and manifestness extend beyond them, which I consider a kind of certainty; and it would undoubtedly be foolish to seriously doubt whether there are men in the world when we do not see any. To doubt seriously is to doubt in relation to practice, and certainty might be taken for a knowledge of truth which one cannot doubt in relation to practice without madness; and sometimes it is taken even more generally and applied to cases where we cannot doubt without deserving to be greatly blamed. But manifestness would be a luminous certainty—that is to say, where we do not doubt because of the connection which we see between

ideas. According to this definition of certainty, we are certain that Constantinople exists in the world, and that Constantine, Alexander the Great, and Julius Cæsar lived. It is true that a peasant from the Ardennes might reasonably doubt these for lack of information; but a man of letters and of the world could not do so without a great mental disturbance.

§ 11. [*Past existence known by memory.*] It has already been remarked that our memory sometimes deceives us. We believe it or not according to whether it is more or less vivid and more or less connected with the things which we know. And even when we are assured of the main fact, we may often question the circumstances.

§§ 13, 14. [13. *Particular propositions concerning existence are knowable.* 14. *And general propositions concerning abstract ideas.*] Your division appears similar to mine—that of propositions of fact and propositions of reason. Propositions of fact may also become general in a way, but it is through induction or observation; so it is only a multitude of similar facts, such as when it is observed that all quicksilver is evaporated by the force of fire. This is not a perfect generalization because we do not see its necessity. General propositions of reason are necessary, although reason also provides some which are not absolutely general and are only probable; for example, when we presume that an idea is possible until the contrary is discovered by more exact research. There are, finally, mixed propositions which are drawn from premises, some of which come from facts and observations, and others are necessary propositions. Such are a number of geographical and astronomical conclusions concerning the globe of the earth and the course of the stars, which spring from the combination of the observations of travelers and astronomers with the theorems of geometry and arithmetic. But as, according to the usage of logicians, the *conclusion follows the weakest of the premises* and cannot have more certainty than they do, these mixed propositions have only the certainty and universality which belong to the observations. As regards *eternal truths*, it must be observed that at bottom they are all conditional and say in effect, *if such a thing is posited, such another thing is*. For example, in saying, *every figure which has three sides will also have three angles*, I do nothing but suppose that if there is a figure with three sides, this same figure will have three angles. . .

<summary>The author distinguishes between propositions of fact, which rely on induction and observation, and propositions of reason, which are necessary and eternal. He also explains that historical certainty and mixed scientific propositions are limited by the reliability of their underlying observations and premises.</summary>
<keywords>certainty, historical facts, memory, propositions of fact, propositions of reason, induction, eternal truths, mixed propositions, logic</keywords>

--- Page 374 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on the foundations of knowledge, transitioning from the certainty of historical and general propositions to the metaphysical basis of eternal truths and the proper use of principles in science.</meta>

The scholastics have debated intensely about *de constantia subjecti* <note>the constancy of the subject</note>, as they called it—that is, how a proposition made about a subject can have real truth if that subject does not exist. The answer is that the truth is only conditional; it states that if the subject ever exists, it will be found to be as described. But it will be further asked: on what is this connection founded, since there is a reality in it that does not deceive? The reply will be that it lies in the connection of ideas. But in response, one might ask: where would these ideas be if no mind existed? And then, what would become of the real foundation for the certainty of these eternal truths? This finally leads us to the ultimate ground of truths: namely, to that *Supreme and Universal Mind*, which cannot fail to exist, and whose understanding—to speak truly—is the realm of eternal truths, as St. Augustine recognized and expressed quite vividly. And so it is not thought unnecessary to resort to this, we must consider that these necessary truths contain the determining reason and the governing principle of even physical existences—in a word, the laws of the universe. Thus, since these necessary truths exist prior to the existence of contingent beings, they must be founded in the existence of a necessary substance. This is where I find the origin of the ideas and truths engraved in our souls—not in the form of propositions, but as the sources from which specific applications and occasions will cause actual statements to arise.

## CHAPTER XII.

### *On the improvement of our knowledge.*

§§ 4—6. <note>It is dangerous to build upon precarious principles. Instead, one should compare clear, complete ideas under stable names.</note> I am surprised, sir, that you turn against maxims—that is, against evident principles—the arguments that can and should be used against principles assumed *gratis* <note>without proof</note>. When someone requires *praecognita* <note>prior knowledge</note> in the sciences, or previous knowledge to serve as a foundation for science, they are requiring *known principles* and not arbitrary positions whose truth is unknown. Even Aristotle understands that the lower and subordinate sciences borrow their principles from other higher sciences where they have been demonstrated—except for the first of the sciences, which we call metaphysics. According to him, metaphysics asks nothing from others and provides them with the principles of which

<summary>The author argues that eternal truths are grounded in a Supreme and Universal Mind and discusses the necessity of building scientific knowledge on proven principles rather than arbitrary assumptions.</summary>
<keywords>scholastics, de constantia subjecti, eternal truths, Supreme and Universal Mind, St. Augustine, necessary truths, metaphysics, Aristotle, maxims, praecognita</keywords>

--- Page 375 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on the use of principles in science, moving from the provisional acceptance of ideas by students to the more rigorous application of hypotheses and experimental methods in the pursuit of knowledge.</meta>

they have need; and when he says δεῖ πιστεύειν τὸν μανθάνοντα <note>the learner must believe</note>, meaning that the apprentice must believe his master, his opinion is that he must do it only while waiting, while he is not yet instructed in the higher sciences, so that it is only provisional. Thus, one is very far from accepting principles without proof. To this must be added that even principles whose certainty is not complete may be useful if we build upon them only through demonstration; for although all the conclusions in this case are only conditional and are valid solely on the assumption that this principle is true, nevertheless, this connection itself and these conditional statements would at least be demonstrated. Therefore, it would be greatly desired that we had many books written in this way, where there would be no danger of error, as the reader or student would be warned of the condition. And practice will not be governed by these conclusions except when the assumption is found to be verified by other means. This method also very often serves to verify assumptions or hypotheses themselves, when many conclusions arise from them whose truth is known otherwise, and sometimes this gives a perfect proof sufficient to demonstrate the truth of the hypothesis.

§ 13. [*The true use of hypotheses.*] The art of discovering the causes of phenomena, or true hypotheses, is like the art of deciphering, where an ingenious guess often shortens the road significantly. Lord Bacon began to organize the art of experimentation into rules, and Sir Robert Boyle had a great talent for practicing it. But if the art of utilizing experiments and of drawing consequences from them is not joined to it, we shall never—even with the greatest expense—attain what a man of great insight might discover at once. Descartes, who was certainly such a man, made a similar remark in one of his letters regarding the method of the Chancellor of England <note>Francis Bacon</note>; and Spinoza (whom I do not hesitate to quote when he says something good), in one of his letters to the late Mr. Oldenburg, Secretary of the Royal Society of England—printed among the posthumous works of this subtle Jew—makes a similar reflection concerning a work by Mr. Boyle. To speak the truth, Boyle stops a little too much to draw no other conclusion from a number of fine experiments than this one, which he might take as a principle: namely, that everything in nature happens mechanically; a principle which can be made certain by reason alone and never by experiments, however numerous they may be.

<summary>The author explains that scientific hypotheses should be treated like codes to be deciphered and argues that while experimentation is vital, it must be guided by reason and demonstration to be truly effective. He critiques the methods of Bacon and Boyle, suggesting that the mechanical nature of the universe is a principle of reason rather than a mere result of repeated observation.</summary>

# NOTES.

## 1. LIFE OF LEIBNITZ.

No more interesting person appears in the history of modern philosophy than Leibnitz. Frederick the Great said of him, “He represents in himself a whole academy;” and by almost universal consent, he is admitted to have possessed the most comprehensive mind since Aristotle. He was on familiar terms with almost every prominent figure—political, ecclesiastical, philosophical, scientific, and literary—of his day, and he himself played a prominent role in each of these spheres. From him, as a statesman, we have a scheme for the unification of Germany, prepared for the Imperial Diet at Ratisbon <note>Modern-day Regensburg</note>; and a far-sighted plan for a French conquest of Egypt, by which the conquering armies of Louis XIV were to have been turned aside from Germany, and the Turks from Austria and Hungary; besides numerous schemes for reforming the currency and the laws of the German states and improving the condition of the people. As a theologian, he has given us an essay *Against Atheism*, a *Defense of the Trinity*, numerous discussions on the arguments for the being of God, a great project for the reunion of the Protestant and Latin churches, a conciliatory *Systema Theologicum* (translated by Russell, 1858) written in the interests of this reunion project, and above all his great work *La Théodicée*. As a mathematician, he contests with Sir Isaac Newton the honor of discovering the Calculus. As a historian, he produced an elaborate work on the *Annals of the House of Brunswick*. To the science of Logic, among other contributions, he has given us the important doctrine of the Quality of Terms. As a physicist, he was the first to give the correct formula for moving force, and in his *Protogaea* <note>Originally spelled Protagäa in the text</note> he became a pioneer in geological investigations. His *New Essays on the Human Understanding* place him alongside his great contemporary Locke as a psychologist. And as a speculative philosopher, or metaphysician, he was the first man of his age on the continent of Europe and the founder of modern German philosophy.

The standard biography of Leibnitz is: *Gottfried Wilhelm Freiherr von Leibnitz. Eine Biographie von Dr. G. E. Guhrauer. Zwei Bände, Breslau, 1842.* Guhrauer’s two-volume work was the basis of the *Life of Godfrey William von Leibnitz, by John M. Mackie, 12mo. <note>Duodecimo, a book size</note>, Boston, 1845.* In his preface, Mackie writes: “I have added little, or nothing, to the German work; and have taken away from it nothing that could be appropriately introduced into a popular biography, or that might be considered as possessing any historical interest for readers outside the borders of Germany.” Excellent accounts of the life of Leibnitz are also found in Kuno Fischer’s *Leibniz (Geschichte d. neuern Philosophie. Zweiter Band, dritte neubearbeitete Auflage, 1888), pp. 1-324, Leibnizens Leben u. Schriften*; and in the little work by Merz, *Leibniz*, in *Blackwood’s Philosophical Classics*, 1884. Compare also, E. Fleiderer <note>Likely Edmund Pfleiderer</note>, *Leibniz als Patriot, Staatsmann u. Bildungsträger*, Leipsic <note>Leipzig</note>, 1870; and T. Kirchner’s *Leibniz: sein Leben u. Denken*, Cöthen, 1877.

<summary>This page introduces the life and diverse intellectual achievements of Gottfried Wilhelm Leibnitz, describing him as a polymath whose work spanned politics, theology, mathematics, and philosophy. It also provides a bibliography of essential 19th-century biographical sources for further study.</summary>
<keywords>Gottfried Wilhelm Leibnitz, Frederick the Great, Calculus, polymath, German philosophy, G. E. Guhrauer, John M. Mackie, biography, Protogaea, Théodicée</keywords>

### 2. LEIBNITZ'S WRITINGS.

There is no complete edition of the writings of Leibnitz. For an account of the different issues of his works, consult Kuno Fischer's *Leibniz* (*History of Modern Philosophy, Second Volume*, Munich, 1888), pp. 307-19, and the preface to Merz's *Leibniz*.

The best edition of his philosophical writings is that of C. J. Gerhardt, *The Philosophical Writings of G. W. Leibniz, 7 vols.*, Berlin, 1875-90. This, however, needs to be supplemented by Erdmann's *All the Philosophical Works of Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz that exist in Latin, French, and German*, Berlin, 1840, and by the theological writings and the correspondence with Wolff.

The best edition of his mathematical works is that of C. J. Gerhardt, forming the third series in the edition of Pertz, *Leibniz's Mathematical Writings, edited by C. J. Gerhardt, 7 vols.*, London and Berlin, 1850; Halle, 1855-63.

The best issue of his historical and political writings is that by Onno Klopp, *The Works of Leibniz, etc., first series, 10 vols.*, Hanover, 1864-77. With this should be compared Foucher de Careil's *Works of Leibniz*, Paris, 1859-75, vols. III to VI.

The best edition of his theological works is that of Foucher de Careil, vols. I and II of his *Works of Leibniz*.

To the above should be added Guhrauer's *Leibniz's German Writings, 2 vols.*, Berlin, 1838-40; Foucher de Careil's *Unpublished Letters and Short Works of Leibniz*, Paris, 1854-57; and Gerhardt's *Correspondence between Leibniz and Wolff*, Halle, 1860.

### 3. EXPOSITIONS AND CRITICISMS OF LEIBNITZ'S PHILOSOPHY.

Hartenstein's *On Locke's and Leibniz's Doctrine of Human Understanding, etc. (Several essays in his Historical-Philosophical Treatises)*, Leipzig, 1870.

T. Kirchner's *Leibniz's Psychology*, Cöthen, 1876.

J. H. v. Kirchmann's *Explanations of Leibniz's smaller, philosophically important writings*, Leipzig, 1879. Also *Explanations of Leibniz's Theodicy* by Kirchmann, and *Explanations of Leibniz's New Essays*, by Prof. Schaarschmidt. The same.

Kuno Fischer's *Leibniz (History of Modern Philosophy. Second Volume, third newly revised edition)*, Munich, 1888.

*In French:—*Condillac's *Exposition and Refutation (in his Treatise on Systems).*

Maine de Biran's *Exposition of the Philosophy of Leibniz*. An English translation of this will be found in the *American Whig Review, vol. IX*, p. 575 ff.

Nourisson's *The Philosophy of Leibniz*, Paris, 1860.

## ARTICLE I.

### 4. LEIBNIZ AND DESCARTES.

While Leibniz was still a boy at Leipzig, he began studying Descartes' writings, and these, more than the works of any other philosopher, determined his thinking. While in Paris, he had access to the manuscripts left by Descartes and continued studying his writings, especially those on mathematics. His own discovery of the integral calculus on October 29, 1675, and of the differential calculus soon after, carried him far beyond Cartesian mathematics, which Descartes' followers considered their master's most important work. This achievement likely led Leibniz to distance himself increasingly from the influence of Descartes in metaphysics. After his move to Hanover, he took a more openly hostile stance toward Descartes. His writings against Descartes and Cartesianism can be found in Gerhardt's edition, vol. iv, pp. 274–406. The most important of them are translated here in Articles I, VII, IX, XVIII, and XXI; see also Articles III, IV, VI, X, XI, XXIX and throughout the text. His general attitude toward Cartesianism is well indicated by his remark that "Cartesianism is to be regarded as the antechamber of the truth," and by the remarks found in the third of the extracts forming Article I.

### 7. PHILIPP (Page 2).

A native of Saxony, quite likely also from Leipzig, who was a councillor and representative of the Saxon government at Hamburg from 1675–1682. In 1682, he became the librarian of the electoral library at Dresden and died shortly afterward. He was deeply interested in the sciences.

### 8. THE *Epicurus* OF LAERTIUS (Page 8).

This refers to the article on Epicurus by Diogenes Laertius in his *Lives of the Philosophers*, in ten books. It contains some original letters of Epicurus and comprises a fairly satisfactory summary of the Epicurean doctrines.

## ARTICLE II.

### 9. RELATION OF LEIBNIZ TO SPINOZA.

The relationship of Leibniz philosophically to Spinoza has long been a subject of dispute. Was Leibniz ever a Spinozist? How much was he influenced by Spinoza? These and other similar questions have given rise to numerous essays. The weight of evidence seems to show that he was never a true follower of Spinoza, but that he nevertheless at first had strong leanings toward the philosophy of the great Jew (compare page 309). Those who wish to pursue the subject will find, in addition to the earlier discussions of the question by Trendelenburg, Erdmann, Guhrauer, and De Careil, the whole subject discussed anew by Professor Stein in his *Leibniz in seinem Verhältniss zu Spinoza auf Grundlage unedirten Materials entwicklungsgeschichtlich dargestellt* <note>Leibniz in his Relationship to Spinoza, developed and presented on the basis of unpublished materials</note> (in the *Sitzungsberichte der Königl. preuss. Akademie* <note>Reports of the Royal Prussian Academy</note> XXV, 1888, p. 615 and following). Two recently discovered letters of Leibniz concerning Spinoza, which bear upon the question, will be found in the *Archiv für Geschichte der Philosophie* <note>Archive for the History of Philosophy</note>, Volume 3, Issue 1, 1889.

Between the years 1676 and 1680, Leibniz carefully studied the writings of Spinoza. He received a copy of the *Opera posthuma* <note>Posthumous Works</note>, containing the *Ethics*, almost immediately after it appeared in January 1678, and several manuscripts still exist in which he has given an extended judgment on this, the masterpiece of Spinoza. One of these, together with two minor pieces bearing on Spinoza, Gerhardt has published in his first volume. This is translated here and should be read in connection with Article XXVII (on which see note 57).

### 11.—THE CONCEPTION OF CONTINGENT (Page 22, proposition 29).

Cf. <note>Compare</note> Articles XXVI, XXXV (p. 254 and following) and XXXVI (p. 337), for fuller statements of Leibniz’s view of contingency and necessity.

### 12.—NATURA NATURANS AND NATURA NATURATA (Page 23, proposition 31).

> “In the most general meaning of the words, Natura Naturans <note>Nature naturing</note> and Natura Naturata <note>Nature natured</note> may be described as related to each other thus: Natura Naturata is the actual condition of a given object or quality, or of the aggregate of all objects and qualities, the Universe, at any given time; Natura Naturans is the immanent cause of this condition, or aggregate of conditions, and is regarded as producing it by a continuous process. Thus when we say ‘How wonderfully Nature works,’ we are speaking of ‘Natura Naturans’; when we say ‘How beautiful is Nature,’ we are speaking of Natura Naturata. Hence, Natura Naturans is related to Natura Naturata as cause to effect. Or, again, we may say that Natura Naturans is the active or dynamic, Natura Naturata the passive or static aspect of nature.”—Fowler’s *Bacon’s Novum Organum*, II, 1, note 4.

## ARTICLE III.

### 13.—THE QUALITY OF TERMS (Page 26).

Cf. <note>Compare</note> *Discourse on Metaphysics*, § 24; *New Essays*, II, chapter 29 and following; Art. XXII, p. 150. The distinctions here made by Leibniz constitute what is known as the logical doctrine of the *quality of terms* and will be found explained in all the ordinary textbooks on logic. The question is, What constitutes clear, distinct, and perfect knowledge? The views of Leibniz’s predecessors should be noted. See Descartes’ *Discourse on Method*, part 4, and *Principles of Philosophy*, I, 45, 46; Spinoza’s *Ethics*, I, axiom 6 and note to proposition 29, and II, definitions 2, 3, and propositions 33–43, and *On the Improvement of the Understanding* <note>De Emendatione Intellectus</note> (pp. 23 and following in Elwes’ translation); Arnauld’s *Port Royal Logic*, pp. 61, 62, in Baynes’ translation. Consult also Locke’s views (published after this essay) in his *Essay*, book II. chapter 29, §§ 2, 4, and chapter 31, § 1. For the doctrine as presented by modern logicians and its value, see Bowen’s *Logic*, Davis’ *Theory of Thought*, Ueberweg’s *Logic* <note>Logik</note> (latest edition, by J. Bona Mayer).

Leibniz’s other statements of the doctrine should be compared with those in this essay.

A brief statement of the doctrine is as follows:

<summary>This page provides a bibliography of 19th-century English and German scholarship on Spinoza and Leibniz. It further defines the philosophical distinctions between contingent and necessary existence, the two aspects of nature (Natura Naturans and Natura Naturata), and the logical quality of terms.</summary>
<keywords>Spinoza, Leibniz, Natura Naturans, Natura Naturata, contingency, necessity, quality of terms, logic, metaphysics, bibliography</keywords>

--- Page 387 ---
<meta>This page continues the commentary on philosophical definitions, moving from the concepts of nature to a detailed classification of the types and qualities of knowledge, specifically as discussed by Leibniz and Descartes.</meta>

Knowledge is:
*   **Clear.**
    *   **Distinct.**
        *   **Adequate.**
            *   **Intuitive = Perfect.**
            *   **Symbolical.**
        *   **Inadequate.**
    *   **Indistinct (Confused).**
*   **Obscure.**

The whole process consists of grasping more and more attributes. *Clear knowledge* relates only to the whole as it is formed. I have clear knowledge of a thing when I can distinguish it as a whole from other things. The knowledge that common people have of Value, Price, and Final Cause is not clear but obscure. The knowledge a patient has of their ailment, an artist has of a flaw in a painting, or a witness has of a prisoner is usually *clear* but not distinct.

*Distinct knowledge* relates to the constituent parts. My knowledge of a thing is distinct when I not only clearly distinguish it from other things but also distinguish its different attributes or characteristics. When I define an elephant as an animal that drinks through its nostrils, my knowledge is distinct, although quite *inadequate*. Our knowledge of simple ideas is at once both distinct and adequate.

*Adequate knowledge* relates to the essential attributes. Knowledge may be said to be adequate when there is exhaustive knowledge of the attributes. Such knowledge is possible for God alone. Again, it may be said to be adequate when it suffices for the objective in view. In this sense, a housewife's knowledge of fish when she goes to the fish market may be called adequate. This is practical adequacy and is scientifically worthless. Logical adequacy is knowledge of the essential attributes—that is, those which (a) contain the common and persistent basis for a multitude of others, and on which (b) the existence of the object, its worth, and its meaning depend.

*Intuitive knowledge* is possessed when we grasp all the qualities, or the essential qualities, in a single act of consciousness. Such knowledge, which is also simultaneously clear, distinct, and adequate, is PERFECT KNOWLEDGE. Very little of our knowledge is of this kind; most of it may be adequate without being intuitive, and therefore is merely symbolical.

#### 17. **ANTOINE ARNAULD’S “ON THE ART OF THINKING WELL”** (Page 32).

This is the celebrated *Port Royal Logic*, the best specimen of the logic of the Cartesian school, written by Arnauld with the assistance of Nicole. It has been translated into English twice. The most recent translation, a most admirable one, is by Professor Baynes, who added an excellent translation of this essay by Leibniz in an appendix. Arnauld’s masterpiece is his work on *True and False Ideas* (1683), in which he attacks—and in many points anticipates—Reid’s objections to the theory of representative ideas. He became an intimate friend of Leibniz and maintained a long correspondence with him on theological and philosophical topics. For this, see Janet’s and Gerhardt’s editions of Leibniz’s works.

#### 18. **THE QUESTION “WHETHER WE SEE ALL THINGS IN GOD”** (Page 32).

This refers to the famous doctrine of Malebranche. See the next note.

#### 19. **MALEBRANCHE AND “THE SEARCH AFTER TRUTH”** (Page 33).

Malebranche has been called the "French Plato" by Cousin. Next to Descartes, he was the most eminent French metaphysician of the seventeenth century. His greatest work is his *Search After Truth* (*De la Recherche de la Verité*), 1672. There are two English translations of this work, the second being by Taylor (London, 1712). The famous doctrine that *we see all things in God* is expounded in the third book in a brief but clear chapter. There is a convenient four-volume edition of the most important works of Malebranche, edited with an introduction by Jules Simon. Leibniz’s correspondence with Malebranche will be found in Gerhardt, volume 1. On his philosophy, see the first volume of Kuno Fischer’s *History of Modern Philosophy*; Ollé-Laprune’s *The Philosophy of Malebranche*; Locke’s *Examination of the Doctrine of Malebranche*; and Leibniz’s criticisms in Articles 28 and 34, and in his *Examination of the Principles of Malebranche* (*Examen des Principes du Malebranche*), in Erdmann, 85.

### ARTICLE IV.

#### 20. **THE LAW OF CONTINUITY.**

This law of continuity is one of the cardinal points in the system of Leibniz. For other statements of it and remarks on it by him, see Articles 5, 7 (page 61), and 36 (page 295); the *Theodicy*, book 3, § 348; and *New Essays*, book 3, chapter 6, § 12; book 4, chapter 16, § 12.

### ARTICLE V.

#### 21. **STATEMENT OF PERSONAL VIEWS ON METAPHYSICS AND PHYSICS.**

This letter to Arnauld is of especial interest as it gives a summary of Leibniz’s system and mentions the monad doctrine in its essential characteristics. Yet the letter of Foucher (Article 12) shows that Leibniz, as early as 1685, had reached the main features of his later published system; and the *Discourse on Metaphysics* (*Discours de Metaphysique*)—the table of contents of which Leibniz sent to Arnauld in his letter to Prince Ernest of Hesse on February 11, 1686—verifies this. It was published first by Grotefend and now again by Gerhardt, volume 4. Compare sections 8, 9, 12, 13, 15, 18, 19, 24, 27, 33, and 34 of that work.

## ARTICLE VI.

### 22. DOES THE ESSENCE OF THE BODY CONSIST IN EXTENSION? (Page 41).

This is the doctrine of Descartes and Malebranche. Compare Descartes, *Principles of Philosophy*, II, 4, “that the nature of the body consists not in weight, hardness, color, and the like, but in extension alone;” and Leibniz’s note on it, p. 59. After being led by his mathematical and physical studies to reject Descartes’ *Laws of Motion*, Leibniz was led toward a thorough investigation of the nature of the body, and on this point, he separates himself from Descartes. Doubtless his youthful studies on the *Principle of Individuation*, as well as his later studies in dynamics, contributed much to convince him that “some higher or metaphysical notion—namely, that of action, power, and force—is needed.” These pieces in Article VI—two letters to the editor of the *Journal des Savants*, June 1691 and January 1693—are important because they shed light on the process by which Leibniz arrived at the cornerstone of his system: the notion of Substance. Compare also Article X and Article XI, pp. 71-72.

### 23. THE SYSTEM OF OCCASIONAL CAUSES (Page 44).

This is the system proposed by Geulincx and advocated by Malebranche to explain the relationship between the body and soul. See Leibniz’s opinion of the doctrine in Article XIX, p. 125, and compare Kuno Fischer’s *History of Modern Philosophy*, vol. I.

## ARTICLE VII.

### 24. DESCARTES’ *Principles of Philosophy*.

This work was written by Descartes in 1644 for Princess Elisabeth, the sister of Leibniz’s friend, the Grand Duchess Sophia, and the aunt of Queen Sophia Charlotte, for whom Leibniz wrote the *Theodicée*. Professor Veitch has translated the First Part of the *Principles* along with selections from the Second, Third, and Fourth Parts. Parts I and II are entitled respectively *Of the Principles of Human Knowledge* and *Of the Principles of Material Things*, and provide a summary of Descartes’ philosophy. Compare Spinoza’s *Renatus Descartes' Principles of Philosophy, Parts I and II, Demonstrated in the Geometric Manner*; Kirchmann’s *Explanations of Spinoza’s Principles of Descartes*; also Joly’s and Brochard’s editions, with notes, of Descartes’ *The Principles of Philosophy*.

### 25. TRUTHS OF FACT AND TRUTHS OF REASON (Page 48).

Compare Articles XXXIII, §§ 33 and 30-38; XXXVI (p. 348 and p. 355).

### 26. THE SOURCE AND NATURE OF ERROR (Page 52).

Compare Descartes, *Meditations*, IV; *Principles of Philosophy*, I, §§ 29, 30, 33, 35, 42, 43; Bacon, *Novum Organum*, I, 38-68 (and Fowler’s notes; also Kuno Fischer’s *Francis Bacon and his Successors*, last edition, pp. 159-173). For Leibniz’s views, see in this Article VII his notes on articles 5, 6, 13 and especially on 31 and 35, and *New Essays*, IV, chapter 20.

### 27. THE AUTHOR OF THE *Philosophia Mosaica* (Page 62).

Robert Fludd (1574-1637), an English physician and mystical philosopher. His *Mosaic Philosophy* appeared in 1638 at Gouda.

### 28. TWO ESSAYS ON MOTION (Page 64).

These were written while Leibniz was at Mainz and dedicated, one to the Royal Society of London and the other to the Royal Academy at Paris. The subject of this Article, *Indivisibilia*, was one that greatly engaged Leibniz's thought.

## ARTICLE IX.

## ARTICLE X.

### 30. THE NOTION OF SUBSTANCE.

If there is one concept that may be called central in the philosophy of Leibniz, it is the notion of substance. Therefore, if his system is to be correctly understood, great attention must be given to his answer to the question, "What is substance?" Compare Articles XI, §§ 2, 3; XIX; XXV; XXXII; XXXIII; and *New Essays*, II, chapter 13, § 19, and chapter 23, § 2. See also Fischer's *Leibniz*, pp. 325 ff.

### 31. MERSENNE (Page 69).

An intimate friend of Descartes and his former fellow student at La Flèche. He supervised the publication of some of Descartes' writings. The work by Descartes mentioned in this sentence is probably the *Replies to Objections to his Meditations*, especially the reply to the Second Objection.

### 34. SWAMMERDAM, MALPIGHI, LEEUWENHOEK, REGIS, HARTSOEKER (Pages 73-74).

*Swammerdam* (1637–1680), a Dutch anatomist, especially famous for his research in entomology; his *General History of Insects* (Utrecht, 1669) and other similar works helped establish the science.
*Malpighi* (1628–1694), of Bologna, the founder of microscopic anatomy.
*Leeuwenhoek* (1632–1723), an eminent Dutch microscopist and discoverer of the capillary circulation of the blood.
*Regis* or *Regius* (1632–1701), a famous Cartesian philosopher who interpreted Descartes through an empiricist lens.
*Hartsoeker* (1656–1725 <note>The OCR text reads 1632-1925, but the correct dates for Nicolas Hartsoeker are 1656–1725.</note>), a Dutch mathematician and physicist.

After the publication of this *New System*, Leibniz was fond of calling himself the "Author of the System of Pre-established Harmony," and he is popularly known as such. For his other statements on it, see Articles XIII, XIV, XV, XXIV, XXXII, XXXIII, etc.

->ARTICLE XVI.<-

### 39. **LEIBNIZ AND LOCKE.**
Leibniz's attention was first drawn to Locke by the summary of his *Essay* published by LeClerc in the *Bibliotheque Universelle* in 1688. Upon the appearance of the *Essay* itself in 1690, he wrote these observations (Article XVI), which were sent to Locke through Burnett. Locke gives his opinion of them in a letter to Molyneux, dated April 10, 1697:

> "I must confess to you that Mr. Leibniz's great reputation had raised an expectation in me which the sight of his paper did not meet; nor did that discourse of his in the *Acta Eruditorum* which he quotes and which I have since read. I had the same thoughts about it when I read it as I find you have. From this, I only draw the inference that even great talents will not master any subject without deep thinking, and even the largest minds have but narrow capacities."

When Leibniz heard that Locke did not understand him, he wrote two pieces, *Sample of Reflections on the First Book of the Essay on Human Understanding (Echantillon de Reflexions sur le I. Livre de l'Essay de l'Entendement de l'Homme)* and *Sample of Reflections on the Second Book (Echantillon de Reflexions sur le II. Livre)*, which were also sent to Locke through Burnett; however, these failed to elicit any direct acknowledgment from Locke. When Coste's French translation of the *Essay* appeared in 1700, Leibniz wrote a notice of it for the *Monthly Extract (Monatlicher Auszug)* and began an extended critique of it—*The New Essays Concerning Human Understanding*. This was completed in 1704 but, because of Locke's death, was not published.

### 40. LITERATURE ON LOCKE.

Locke's *Essay*, next to Kant's *Critique of Pure Reason*, has been the most influential single work in modern philosophy. It has called forth a literature which would itself make a good-sized library. The following are among the most important works on it:

Henry Lee's *Anti-Skepticism; or Notes upon each Chapter of Locke's Essay concerning Human Understanding*. London, 1702.

Leibniz's *Nouveaux Essais sur l'Entendement Humain* (New Essays on Human Understanding). (Vol. 4, in Gerhardt's ed.)

Cousin's *La Philosophie de Locke*, 1829. English translations by Henry and by Wight.

Webb's *Intellectualism of Locke*. London, 1858.

Hartenstein's *Locke's Lehre v. d. menschl. Erkenntness in Vergleichung mit Leibniz's Kritik derselben* (Locke's Doctrine of Human Knowledge in Comparison with Leibniz's Critique of It). Leipzig, 1865.

Marion's *Locke, sa Vie, son Œuvre* (Locke, his Life, his Work). (Alcan), Paris, 1878.

Thomas Fowler's *Locke*. London, 1880.

Green's *Introduction to the Phil. Works of Hume*. London, 1874.

McCosh's *Locke's Theory of Knowledge, with a notice of Berkeley*. New York, 1884.

Kirchmann's *Erläuterungen zu Locke's Versuch über den menschlichen Verstand* (Explanations of Locke's Essay concerning Human Understanding) (cf., also Schaarschmidt's *Erläuterungen zu Leibniz's Neue Abhandlungen*.)

Fraser's *Locke* (in Blackwood's series). Edinburgh, 1890.

### 41. THE FUNCTION *della Crusca* (Page 98).

*La Crusca*, a celebrated academy of Florence, founded in 1582 for the purpose of maintaining the purity of the Italian language—that is to say, of separating the bran (*crusca*) from the flour: hence the name.

## ARTICLE XVII.

### 42. THE LAW OF SUFFICIENT REASON.

This Article XVII was written by Leibniz on November 23, 1697, and was first published by Erdmann in 1841. It deals with the cosmological argument for the existence of God and the problem of the *Theodicy*. The third sentence gives the keynote to the whole: "The sufficient reason of existence can be found neither in any particular thing nor in the whole aggregate or series." The principle of sufficient reason is fundamental in the philosophy of Leibniz. His system, from one end to the other, is inspired by an unshaken and immovable faith in the authority of this principle. At the very end of his life he writes: "Would to God that one had never supposed less clear principles! This principle is that of the need for a sufficient reason, so that a thing exists, an event happens, or a truth takes place" (*Plût à Dieu qu'on n'eût jamais supposé des principes moins claires! Ce principe est celui du besoin d'une raison suffisante, pour qu'une chose existe, qu'un événement arrive, qu'une vérité ait lieu*) (*5th Letter to Clarke*, § 125). For other statements of the principle, see *Monadology*, §§ 32 f., *Theodicy*, §§ 44, 196. See also Nolan's *La Monadologie de Leibniz*, p. 39 f.; Ueberweg's *Logik*, p. 270.

### ARTICLE XVIII.

#### 43. ON THE CONSEQUENCES OF CERTAIN PASSAGES IN DESCARTES.

The occasion for the piece to which this is a reply was a passage in a letter to Nicaise, in which Leibniz speaks of the evil consequences of Descartes' denial of final cause and of his view that matter successively takes all forms of which it is capable. In this letter, he also remarks: "It can also be said that *Spinoza* has only cultivated certain seeds of Descartes' philosophy, so that I believe it is indeed important for religion and for piety that this philosophy be corrected by the removal of the errors that are mixed with the truth."

---

### ARTICLE XIX.

#### 44. ON NATURE IN ITSELF.

The two questions handled in this essay are stated in section 2: *What is nature in itself?* and *Is there any energy or force residing in things?* He answers the first (sections 2–8) by saying that Nature is the handiwork of an all-wise creator—the expression of the truths and ends of Absolute Reason. He answers the second question (sections 9 and following) with his doctrine that *to be is to act.*

#### 45. ARISTOTLE'S DEFINITION OF MOTION (Page 113).

Found in his *Physics*, book V.

#### 46. IMAGING AND INTELLECTUAL CONCEPTION (Page 116).

The important distinction between imaging and intellectual conception—where imaging is impossible—was emphasized by Descartes (*Principles of Philosophy*, I, 73, and *Meditation* VI), Spinoza (*On the Improvement of the Understanding*), and Leibniz (page 188 and *New Essays*, II, chapter 9, section 8, and chapter 29). The absurdities one may be led into by a failure to keep this distinction in mind can be seen by consulting Spencer's *First Principles*.

#### 47. THE PRINCIPLE OF THE “IDENTITY OF INDISCERNIBLES” (Pages 122–3).

This, as Leibniz remarks here, is among his “new and most important axioms.” He says in writing to Clarke (4, section 5): “These great principles of *Sufficient Reason* and the *Identity of Indiscernibles* change the state of metaphysics, which becomes real and demonstrative by their means; whereas formerly it consisted of almost nothing but empty terms.” Compare also section 4 and following; *Letter V*, sections 21 and following; *New Essays*, II, chapter 27.

#### 48. LEIBNIZ'S PREFACE TO HIS *Codex Diplomaticus Juris Gentium* (Page 127).

This Preface is so important for an understanding of Leibniz's ethical views (compare also his letter to Coste of July 4, 1706) that a translation of it is given here:

->ON THE NOTIONS OF RIGHT AND JUSTICE. 1693.<-
->[From the Latin.]<-

I do not know whether, even after so many eminent writers have discussed them, the notions of *right* and of *justice* have been sufficiently clarified. *Right* is a certain moral power, and *obligation* a moral necessity. Moreover,

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Leibniz's philosophical foundations, moving from his definitions of nature and motion into his ethical framework, specifically focusing on his definitions of justice, charity, wisdom, and the grades of natural right.</meta>

<language>English</language>
