By *moral*, I mean that which among good men is equivalent to natural: for, as a celebrated Roman legal expert says, things that are contrary to good morals must be regarded as things that cannot be done. Furthermore, a good man is one who loves everyone as much as reason allows. *Justice*, therefore—the virtue that governs this affection which the Greeks call φιλανθρωπία—we will most properly define, unless I am mistaken, as the charity of the wise man <note>caritatem sapientis</note>, that is, charity according to the dictates of wisdom. Therefore, what Carneades is reported to have said—namely, that justice is the highest folly because it commands us to care for the interests of others while neglecting our own—comes from an ignorance of the definition. Charity is universal benevolence, and benevolence is the habit of loving. Moreover, to love is to take delight in the happiness of another, or, what amounts to the same thing, it is to consider another's happiness as one's own.

From this, the difficult knot (which is also of great importance in theology) is untied: how there can be a disinterested love that is free from hope, fear, and regard for personal advantage. It is evident that the joy of those whose joy enters into our own delights us, for those things which delight are sought after for their own sake. And just as the contemplation of beautiful objects is itself agreeable—and a painting by Raphael affects one who understands it even if it brings no riches, in such a way that it is kept before the eyes and regarded with delight as a symbol of love—so when the beautiful object is also capable of happiness, the affection passes into true love. 

But *divine love* surpasses other loves because God can be loved with the greatest success; since nothing is at once happier than God, and nothing more beautiful and more worthy of happiness can be known than Him. And since He also possesses the highest power and wisdom, His happiness does not only enter into ours (if we are wise—that is, if we love Him), but it also creates it. Since, moreover, wisdom ought to direct charity, there will be a need to define it also. I think, however, that human notions are best satisfied if we say that wisdom is nothing else than the science of happiness itself. Thus we are brought back again to the notion of happiness, the explanation of which does not belong here.

From this source flows *natural right*, of which there are three grades: *strict right* in commutative justice, *equity* (or charity in the narrow sense of the word) in distributive justice, and finally *piety* (or *probity*) in universal justice. From these spring the rules to injure no one, to concede to each his own, and to live honorably (or rather piously), as well as the most general and commonly recognized precepts of right, just as I formerly outlined in my youthful essay, *De Methodo Juris*.

The law of pure or *strict right* is: *no one is to be injured*, so that within the state no cause for action is given to him, and outside the state no right of war. From this comes the justice which philosophers call *commutative* and the right which Grotius calls *power*. The higher grade I call *equity*, or, if you prefer, charity (namely, in the narrower sense), which I extend beyond the rigor of bare right to those obligations that we may not be forced to perform, such as gratitude and almsgiving, for which we have, according to Grotius, an *aptitude* but not a *power*. And just as it belonged to the lowest

grade is to injure no one, so to the middle grade it belongs, *To do good to all*; but only so far as is fitting for each, or as much as each deserves, so that it is not permissible to favor everyone equally. Thus, this is the sphere of <term>distributive justice</term>, and the law of right here is that which commands giving to each his due <note>suum cuique tribui</note>. The political laws in the commonwealth extend this far; they secure the happiness of the subjects and ensure that those who previously only had an aptitude now acquire power—that is, they are able to demand what is fair for others to perform. And while in the lowest grade of right, differences among men were not considered (except those arising from the matter itself, as all men are held as equals), now, in this higher grade, merits are weighed; this is where privileges, rewards, and punishments have their place. 

<term>Xenophon</term> has excellently sketched this difference in the grades of right with the example of the boy <term>Cyrus</term>. Cyrus, chosen as a judge between two boys, encountered a situation where the stronger boy had forcibly exchanged coats with the other because he found the other’s coat more fitting for his own figure, and his own coat better suited to the figure of the other. Cyrus pronounced in favor of the robber. However, his teacher pointed out that the question here was not which coat fit better, but to whom the coat belonged. This form of judgment could only be used rightly if Cyrus himself were the one distributing the coats. For <term>equity</term> itself commends strict right to us in most affairs—that is, equality among men—except when a weighty reason for a greater good commands us to step back from it. Moreover, what is called "regard of persons" has its place not in exchanging the goods of others, but in distributing our own or public goods.

The highest degree of right I have called by the name of <term>probity</term> or, rather, <term>piety</term>. For what has been said so far can be understood as being confined within the considerations of mortal life. Furthermore, pure or strict right springs from the principle of *preserving peace*; equity or <term>charity</term> extends to something more, so that while each person benefits the other as much as they can, they increase their own happiness through the happiness of the other. In a word, strict right avoids misery, and the highest right tends toward happiness—but only such happiness as belongs to this mortal life. 

But the idea that we ought to prioritize life itself, and whatever makes this life desirable, behind another’s great good, or that the greatest griefs ought to be endured for the sake of others—this is more beautifully taught by philosophers than solidly demonstrated. For honor, glory, and the joyous feeling in the virtue of one’s own soul (to which they appeal under the name of honor) are goods of thought or of the mind. Moreover, these have great superiority, but not for everyone or against every bitterness of evil, since not all people are equally affected by the imagination. This is especially true for those whom neither a liberal education, a high-born way of living, the discipline of life, nor the status of rank has accustomed to discerning the goods of the soul. But for it to be settled by a general demonstration that everything worthy is useful and everything base is injurious, the <term>immortality of the soul</term> and the director of all, <term>GOD</term>, must be assumed. Thus, we know that we all live in the most perfect state under a monarch who, because of his wisdom, cannot be deceived, and because of his power, cannot be escaped; and he is also so lovable that

To serve such a master is happiness. Therefore, he who applies his soul to this, with Christ teaching him, wins it. By His power and providence, it comes to pass that all *right* translates into fact, that no one is injured except by himself, and that nothing done rightly is without its reward, just as no sin is without punishment. Since, as Christ has divinely taught, every hair on our heads is numbered, and even a cup of water is not given in vain to a thirsty person, so nothing is neglected in the Commonwealth of the Universe. It is from this consideration that it is called universal justice and includes all other virtues; for even that which otherwise does not concern the interests of another—namely, that we do not misuse our bodies or our resources—is also forbidden outside of human laws by natural right, that is, by the eternal laws of the divine monarchy, since we are indebted to God for ourselves and for what we possess. For just as it is in the interest of the State, it is much more in the interest of the Universe that no one uses his own things poorly. Here, therefore, the highest law of right receives its force, which commands us to *live honorably* (that is, piously). And in this sense, it is rightly demanded of learned men that natural right and the law of nations be taught according to the doctrine of Christians—that is (following the example of Christ), τὰ ἀνώτερα, the sublime and divine wisdom of the wise. Thus, we seem to have explained most appropriately the three laws of right, or three degrees of justice, and to have identified the sources of natural right.

## ARTICLE XXI.

### 49. THE ONTOLOGICAL ARGUMENT FOR THE BEING OF GOD.

On this celebrated argument, consult Anselm's *Proslogion* and *Liber contra Insipientem*, that is, *Liber Apologeticus* (a translation of the *Proslogion* will be found in the *Bibliotheca Sacra*, vol. VIII., pp. 534–553; see also the French translation, with notes, by Bouchitté, *Le Rationalisme Chrétien*, Paris, 1842); Gaunilo's *Liber pro Insipiente*; Thomas Aquinas's *Summa Theologiae*; Descartes' *Meditations*, V; *Replies to Objections*, especially those to objections 1 and 2; and *Principles of Philosophy*, I, §§ 14 f.

The Anselmic form of the argument may be stated thus: We have, as a fact, the idea of the greatest possible or PERFECT BEING; an actually existing being (*in re esse*) has more perfection than one that exists only ideally (*in intellectu esse*); therefore, God exists. In other words, the most perfect conceivable being must be *actual*: otherwise a property—that of actuality, or objective being—is missing.

Descartes' additions to this argument consist of showing that the idea of God is a necessary idea of reason; that it is an idea of a real infinite and could not have originated in us or from any finite source; and that when we think of God, we must think of Him not merely as existing (which we do with everything while we are thinking of it), but as necessarily existing. Descartes' argument may therefore be stated as follows: We have among the necessary ideas of reason the idea of an Absolute or All-perfect Being; this idea contains necessary existence as one of its elements; therefore, God exists.

<meta>This page continues the editorial commentary on Article XXI regarding the ontological argument, specifically examining the contributions and critiques of Spinoza and Leibniz. It transitions into Article XXII, discussing the "Doctrine of a Universal Spirit," and Article XXIII regarding the nature of knowledge.</meta>

Spinoza (in a letter to DeVries) has stated the basis of the ontological argument as follows:
> “The more reality a being or thing has, the more attributes must be assigned to it; and the more attributes I assign to a thing, the more I am forced to conceive of it as existing.”

For remarks by Leibniz related to the argument, see Articles III, p. 29; VII, p. 50; XXI, XXXVI, p. 356; and the Letters to Jacquelot (Gerhardt, vol. 3, pp. 442f.).

Leibnitz claims: 
(1) That the idea of God is unique in this: that if it is the idea of a being possible in fact, then that being must actually exist. But is the idea of God the idea of a being possible in fact?

(2) That merely because we have the idea of God, it does not therefore follow that He actually exists. We have ideas of things which cannot actually exist. It must therefore be shown that the idea of God is a true idea—that is, the idea of a *possible being*. Descartes failed to do this. <note>That Leibnitz is in error here may be seen by examining Descartes’ *Reply to the Second Objection*, where Descartes allows that it must first of all be proved that the conception of an infinite being is possible and does not contain a contradiction; however, he shows that such a proof need not cause any difficulties.</note>

(3) Everything is to be considered possible until its impossibility is proved. Therefore, there is a presumption in favor of the actual existence of God.

(4) This presumption is more than a presumption: it is a fact that God is possible. This is shown on pages 137–138.

For Locke’s examination of Descartes’ argument, see Lord King’s *Life of Locke*, Vol. II, pp. 134 onward. Regarding the value of the argument itself, compare Kant’s *Critique*, Flint’s *Theism*, Dorner’s *System of Christian Doctrine*, and the essays by Huber, Elvenich, and Jahnke, as well as the works named in note 5. For more detailed studies on the theism of Descartes and the theism of Leibnitz, consult Saisset’s *Modern Pantheism*.

### ARTICLE XXV.

#### 54. PROOF OF THE EXISTENCE OF GOD FROM THE DOCTRINE OF PRE-ESTABLISHED HARMONY (p. 165).

Leibnitz often urges this “new argument for the existence of God.” “The agreement of so many substances, none of which has any influence upon another, could only come from a general cause on which all of them depend, and this Cause must have infinite power and wisdom to pre-establish all these harmonies.”

## ARTICLE XXIX.

### 60. LEIBNITZ ON THE NATURE OF THE SOUL.

This Article is of very great importance for the understanding of the Leibnitzian doctrine. He explains here his conception of the soul and the nature of perception.

### 61. THE DIFFERENT CLASSES OF MONADS (p. 191).

This Article assists us in distinguishing the various classes of monads, or different degrees of monad development, which are recognized by Leibnitz:

I. All monads are alike:
(1) In being simple, ultimate, veritable unities; incapable of being generated and indestructible realities.
(2) In that each is essentially energizing power, force, and an active principle.
(3) In that each possesses the power of perception and reflects (mirrors) in its own way the whole universe. “The representation of the external in the internal, of the composite in the simple, of multiplicity in unity, constitutes in reality perception (§ 3).”

II. According as they are or are not *monades reines* <note>pure monads</note> or *dominantes* <note>dominating</note>, and have or have not organizing power over others, they are divided thus:

Monads { Simple (1).
    { Dominating or ruling { Entelechies or *monades vivantes* <note>living monads</note> (2).
              { Souls { Animal souls (3).
                  { Rational souls (4).

III. According as they possess or do not possess sentiency, they are divided thus:

Monads { Non-sentient { Simple monads (1).
           { Entelechies or *monades vivantes* (2).
    { Sentient { Animal souls (3).
         { Rational souls (4).

IV. According as they do or do not possess self-consciousness, they are divided:

Monads { Merely perceptive { Lacking memory { Simple Monads (1).
                      { Entelechies (2).
             { Possessing memory { Animal souls (3).
    { Self-conscious { Rational souls (4).

V. Results. There are four kinds of monads:
1. Simple monads, lacking self-consciousness, memory and organic capacity.

<sig>25</sig>

<summary>This page introduces Leibnitz's commentary on Locke's critique of Malebranche and provides a detailed hierarchical classification of monads based on perception, sentiency, and self-consciousness. Monads are categorized into simple monads, entelechies, animal souls, and rational souls.</summary>
<keywords>Leibnitz, Locke, Malebranche, Monads, perception, soul, Entelechies, self-consciousness, sentiency, classification of monads</keywords>

--- Page 400 ---
<meta>This page continues the classification of monads, distinguishing between those that lack self-consciousness and those that possess it, and introduces the historical context of Leibnitz’s Theodicy.</meta>

2. Dominating or organizing monads (*monades reines* <note>pure monads</note> or *âmes vivantes* <note>living souls</note>), which lack memory and self-consciousness. These and the simple monads are the *sleeping monads*; they perceive unconsciously and without feeling.
3. Animal souls. These organize and possess memory, but lack self-consciousness. They are *dreaming monads*.
4. Rational souls. These have organizing capacity, memory, and, in addition, self-consciousness and the power of recognizing necessary truth; in a word, they are personalities. They are *awakened monads*.

Does a monad of the lower class ever pass into the higher classes? One of Leibnitz's correspondents, Remond, writes to him on January 9, 1715, and asks, among others, the following questions: “How (physically speaking and without using abstract or metaphorical terms), by what means, and through what degrees can a central and dominant monad that constitutes an animal at one time come in another time to make or rather to be a Mr. de Leibnitz?” To this Leibnitz replies as follows: “Since one can conceive that through the development and change of matter, the machine that makes the body of a spermatic animal can become such a machine as is necessary to form the organic body of a human, it must be that at the same time the soul, from being merely sensitive, has become rational, because of the perfect harmony between the soul and the machine. But as this harmony is pre-established, the future state was already in the present, and a perfect intelligence would have recognized long ago in the present animal the future human, both in its soul separately and in its body separately. Thus, a pure animal will never become a human, and the human spermatic animals that do not reach the great transformation through conception remain pure animals.”

### 62. GENII (Page 192).

By *genii*, Leibnitz means *angels and archangels*.

## ARTICLE XXX.

### 63. LEIBNITZ'S *Theodicy*.

This work, as is well known, was written by Leibnitz in memory of Queen Sophia Charlotte of Prussia, and grew out of conversations and discussions with her on the problems of liberty and of evil, occasioned by the objections she found in Bayle's Dictionary. It is the only large work by Leibnitz published in his lifetime. Although written in a popular and diffuse style, it is unquestionably the most celebrated work on the subject. The work itself consists of (1) a Preface; (2) an Introductory Discourse on the Conformity of Faith with Reason; (3) the body of the work, in three parts: the first on the nature of evil in general, the second on moral evil, the third on physical evil; (4) an Index; (5) the Abridgment, here translated; (6) an Examination of Hobbes' work *Questions concerning Liberty, Necessity and Chance*; (7) Remarks on a work by King on *The Origin of Evil*; (8) a more extended abridgment of the work in Latin.

An excellent abridgment of the body of the work, with critical and explanatory notes, has been issued by Th. Desdouits: *Essais de Théodicée de Leibniz. Extraits reliés entre eux par de courtes analyses, précédés d'une introduction et d'une analyse générale, et accompagnés d'appréciations critiques* <note>Essays on the Theodicy of Leibniz. Extracts linked together by short analyses, preceded by an introduction and a general analysis, and accompanied by critical evaluations</note>, Paris, 1878.

Two excellent articles on Leibnitz's Theodicy will be found in the *Andover Review*, vol. 4.

### 64. LEIBNITZ’S OPTIMISM.

The final word of the Leibnitzian philosophy is that, all things considered, the actual world is the best possible world. The doctrine, as it relates to the problem of human existence, is well set forth in the apologue of the *Theodicy* (§§ 405-417) in the story of Sextus. On this subject in general, besides the *Theodicy*, consult the *Monadology* (§ 53 onwards), *The Principles of Nature and of Grace*, the *Letters to Clarke*, Nolan’s *The Monadology* <note>La Monadologie</note>, eleventh clarification <note>onzieme éclaircissement</note>, Fischer’s *Leibniz*, pp. 576-598, and Erdmann, Nourisson, and Feuerbach.

---

## ARTICLE XXXI.

### 65. LEIBNITZ’S RULES FOR THE CONDUCT OF THE MIND AND THE INCREASE OF KNOWLEDGE.

Compare this article with Erdmann’s edition of Leibnitz’s philosophical works, Articles XXVI, *On the True Method of Philosophy and Theology* <note>De vero methodo philosophicæ et theologiæ</note>; LIII, *Precepts for Advancing the Sciences* <note>Preceptes pour avancer les Sciences</note>; and LIV, *Discourse concerning the Method of Certainty and the Art of Invention, to end Disputes and to make great Progress in a short Time* <note>Discours touchant la Methode de la Certitude et l’Art d’Inventer, pour finir les Disputes et pour faire en peu de Tems de grands Progrès</note>; and the *New Essays*, IV, chapter 12, *Of the Means of Increasing our Knowledge* <note>Des Moyens d’Augmenter nos Connaissances</note>.

Leibnitz’s thoughts on this subject may be compared with Descartes’ (*Discourse on Method* <note>Discours de la Methode</note>; *Rules for the Direction of the Mind* <note>Regles pour la Direction de l’Esprit</note>); Spinoza’s (*On the Improvement of the Understanding* <note>De Emendatione Intellectus</note>); and Locke’s (*Conduct of the Understanding*, and the *Essay*, book 4, chapter 12, *Of the Improvement of Our Knowledge*).

## ARTICLE XXXII.

### 66. THE PRINCIPLES OF NATURE AND OF GRACE.

During Leibnitz’s residence in Vienna (1712-1714), he was asked by Prince Eugene of Savoy to provide his philosophical system in a short summary as an aid to understanding the *Theodicy*. With this goal in view, he composed *The Principles of Nature and of Grace, founded on Reason*. He sent a copy of the essay, which was prepared with the utmost care, to Nicolas Remond in Paris, with a letter (Vienna, August 26, 1714) in which he writes:

> "I hoped that this little paper would contribute to a better understanding of my reflections, by adding to it what I have placed in the Journals of Leipzig, Paris, and Holland. In those of Leipzig, I adapt myself more to the style of the Cartesians, and in this last piece, I try to express myself in a manner that can be understood by those who are not yet too accustomed to the style of either."

---

## ARTICLE XXXIII.

### 67. THE MONADOLOGY.

This summary of Leibnitz’s philosophy was written very shortly after the *Principles of Nature and of Grace*, and until recently, it has been confused with it as the work written for Prince Eugene. It is the most complete statement of Leibnitz’s system and deserves the most careful study. Erdmann

### 68. ANALYSIS OF THE MONADOLOGY.

The following analysis may help in understanding the *Monadology*. However, it should be remembered that the thought is so condensed that no completely satisfactory analysis of it can be provided.

### PART I.

->*Substance (or Monad), §§ 1-30.*<-

1. Existence and Simplicity, 1-3.
2. Indestructibility, 4-6.
3. Inner Principle of their Activity, 7-13.
4. Perceptions of the Monads, 14-18.
    (1) What perception is; distinguished from apperception, 14-16.
    (2) Inexplicable by mechanical means, 17.
    (3) Therefore, monads are actualized perfections or entelechies, 18.
5. Kinds of Monads, 19-30.
    (1) Sleeping monads, 19-24.
    (2) Dreaming monads, 25-27.
    (3) Awakened or rational monads, 28-30.

### PART II.

->*Principles of Reason and their source in Absolute Reason, God, §§ 31-48.*<-

6. Principles of Reason and their source, 31-37.
7. God, the Principle of Principles, on whom all contingent things and even necessary truths depend, 37-48.

### PART III.

->*The Pre-established Harmony and the Best Possible Universe, §§ 49-90.*<-

8. Pre-established Harmony, what it is; it explains the apparent interaction of the monads, 49-52 and 56.
9. Why there is a pre-established harmony; the actual world is the *best possible*, 53-55.
10. It explains variety and unity; each monad mirrors the universe, 56-62.
11. Every particle of matter is full of vital monads; there is life everywhere, 63-70.

## ARTICLE XXXIV.
### 69. REMOND DE MONTMORT.

Nicolas Remond de Montmort was *Chief of the Councils of the Duke of Orleans*. He was a great admirer of the Platonic philosophy and, upon reading Leibniz’s *Theodicy*, became a great admirer of him also, and carried on a correspondence with him on philosophical subjects. For this, see Gerhardt’s third volume. This letter (Art. XXXIV) is of especial importance, as in it Leibniz takes the opportunity to explain the points of contact and of divergence between his own system and those of Malebranche on the one hand and of Descartes on the other.

## ARTICLE XXXV.
### 70. LEIBNIZ’S CORRESPONDENCE WITH CLARKE.

Leibniz describes the occasion of this correspondence in a letter (Dec. 23, 1715) to Wolff, thus: “The Princess of Wales <note>Wilhelmina Charlotte of Ansbach</note>, who had read my *Theodicy* with pleasure, fell into a controversy over it, as she herself informed me, with a prelate who frequented the Court. He afterward handed the Princess a paper written in English in which he defended the Newtonian system and attacked mine. I answered him briefly and sent the answer to the Princess.” The correspondence extends to five letters on each side and was terminated by the death of Leibniz. It was published in 1717 by Clarke, who provided an English translation (reprinted here) side by side with Leibniz’s French. The words in <note>brackets</note> in the *Fifth Letter* (except the words "of sense," § 84; "our notion of," § 87; "without diminution," § 99; "an order and merely," § 104; "*general*," § 107, which were added by Clarke) are additions or changes made by Leibniz himself in a second copy. They are inserted here in Clarke’s translation.

These letters belong to the most important documents on Leibniz’s philosophy, as in Clarke he found an antagonist worthy of him, who pointed out the weak points in his system. For lack of space, the letters of Clarke, which are accessible to the student in Clarke’s own works, are omitted here.

### 72. ANALYSIS OF THE SECOND CHAPTER OF BOOK I OF THE *Nouveaux Essais*.

> “The controversy between Locke and Leibniz in the first book of the *New Essays on Human Understanding* (*Nouveaux Essais sur l’Entendement Humain*) relates to the famous question of the origin of ideas. Locke represents the empirical school, and Leibniz the rationalistic school. The first maintains the hypothesis of the *tabula rasa*, and the second the hypothesis of innate ideas. It can be said that they have each exhausted the question and that they have said all that could be said at their time, at least in the terms in which the question was then stated; since then, it has been presented in different forms. In order to allow the arguments of the two authors their full weight, we shall reproduce them as far as possible in their original form and order. Afterward, we shall provide a summary, condensing the whole discussion:
> *Locke’s 1st Objection.*—If innate principles existed, all men would have to agree on them; however, this universal consent does not exist even for the principles of identity and contradiction, for there is a large part of the human race to whom these principles are unknown. Furthermore, even if this consent did exist, it would prove nothing if another way besides innateness could be shown by which men might have arrived at this uniformity of opinion.
> *Leibniz’s Reply.*—I do not base the certainty of innate principles upon universal consent, which, moreover, might actually arise in another way. This consent is an *indication* and not a demonstration of the innate principle; but the exact and decisive proof of these principles consists in showing that their certainty comes only from what is within us. Even if they were not known, they would not cease to be innate, because they would be recognized as soon as they were understood. Fundamentally, however, everyone knows them, and they are used at every moment without being explicitly recognized; it is very much the same as when one holds in the mind the propositions suppressed in <term>enthymemes</term>.
> *2nd Objection.*—To say that there are truths imprinted on the soul which it does not perceive is a real contradiction.
> *Reply.*—I believe that we have a vast amount of knowledge of which we are not always aware, even when we have a need for it.”

<summary>This page introduces Leibniz's *New Essays*, a point-by-point response to Locke's *Essay Concerning Human Understanding* that defends the existence of innate ideas against the concept of the "blank slate." Leibniz argues that innate principles are valid because they originate within the mind, even if they are not always consciously recognized or universally acknowledged.</summary>
<keywords>Leibniz, Locke, New Essays, Nouveaux Essais, innate ideas, tabula rasa, empiricism, rationalism, universal consent, logic, enthymemes</keywords>

--- Page 405 ---
<meta>This page continues the analysis of Leibniz’s *New Essays on Human Understanding*, specifically the dialogue regarding innate ideas as a rebuttal to Locke’s empiricism. It follows the debate over whether the mind is a blank slate or possesses inherent structures for processing truth.</meta>

3rd Obj.—It could then be said that all reasonable propositions are innate.
Reply.—I acknowledge this regarding pure ideas. In this sense, it can be said that the whole of arithmetic and geometry is innate, although it is true to say that one would not be aware of the ideas under consideration unless one saw or touched something . . . for we could not have abstract thoughts which do not have need of something sensible. This does not prevent the mind from deriving necessary truths only from itself. However, there are degrees of difficulty in perceiving what is within us.

4th Obj.—Latent perceptions presuppose at least memory: undoubtedly there may be things in the soul which are not perceived there; but it must always be the case that these have been learned and were formerly known.
Reply.—Why could there not be still another cause? For, since acquired knowledge can be concealed there by the memory, may nature not also have concealed some original knowledge there? These would be natural habits, active and passive dispositions and aptitudes, rather than a *tabula rasa*.

5th Obj.—But innateness does not differ from the simple capacity for knowing.
Reply.—The mind is not only capable of knowing them but also of *finding them within itself*; and if it had only the simple capacity, or passive power, it would not be the source of necessary truths. The mind has a disposition to draw them itself from its own depths.

1st Instance.—But do the words *to be in the understanding* signify anything other than *to be perceived by the understanding*?
Reply.—They mean something entirely different. It is enough that what is in the understanding can be found there, and that the sources or original proofs of these truths are in the understanding alone.

2nd Instance.—But the consent which the mind gives without effort to these truths depends on the faculty of the human mind.
Reply.—Very true; but it is the particular relation of the human mind to these truths which renders the exercise of the faculty easy and natural regarding them, and which causes them to be called innate.

6th Obj.—Truths are subsequent to ideas; and yet, ideas come from the senses.
Reply.—The intellectual ideas which are the source of necessary truths do not come from the senses.

7th Obj.—Particular propositions are more evident than general propositions; and nevertheless they come from the senses; for example, to say that *to be yellow is not to be sweet* is as evident, if not more so, than to say that *it is impossible for a thing to be and not to be at the same time*. Shall we say then that all our sensations are innate?
Reply.—The one is the principle (namely, the general maxim); and the other is only the application. As for the rest, this proposition, *sweet is not bitter*, is not innate; for the sensations of sweet and bitter come from the external senses; but it is a mixed conclusion (*hybrida conclusio*) where the axiom is applied to a sensible truth. As for the general maxim, it is understood within it, just like the major premise which is suppressed in enthymemes. We do not always think distinctly about what we do.

Instance.—But it seems that general and abstract ideas are more foreign to our minds than particular notions and truths.

<summary>This page presents a series of objections and replies concerning Leibniz's theory of innate ideas, arguing that the mind contains inherent dispositions and necessary truths rather than being a mere blank slate. Leibniz distinguishes between purely sensory data and the internal axioms of the understanding that allow us to process that data.</summary>

<keywords>Leibniz, innate ideas, Locke, rationalism, tabula rasa, necessary truths, understanding, arithmetic, geometry, latent perceptions, hybrida conclusio, enthymemes</keywords>

--- Page 406 ---
<meta>This page continues the analysis of Leibniz’s *New Essays on Human Understanding*, specifically addressing the 8th through 11th objections to the theory of innate ideas. It concludes with Leibniz’s famous metaphor of the block of marble to explain how truths exist as natural dispositions within the mind.</meta>

*Reply.*—It is true that we begin to perceive specific truths earlier; but this does not prevent the order of nature from beginning with the most simple ones, nor does it prevent the logic of specific truths from depending on more general ones.

*8th Obj.*—Doesn't immediate agreement with certain truths come from the very nature of the things themselves, rather than from the propositions being naturally engraved in the mind?

*Reply.*—Both are true. The nature of things and the nature of the mind agree here; and very often, considering the nature of things is nothing other than knowing the nature of our own mind.

*9th Obj.*—It seems that if there are innate truths, it is not necessary to learn them since they are already known. However, it is at least necessary to learn the names and words by which these truths are expressed.

*Reply.*—I agree with this; but I cannot accept the claim that everything learned is not innate. The truth of numbers is within us, and yet we still go through the process of learning them.

*10th Obj.*—But how is it that children have no knowledge of these truths which are supposed to be innate and part of their minds? If this were the case, nature would have gone to the trouble for nothing.

*Reply.*—The perception of what is within us depends on attention and order. Now, it is not only possible but even appropriate that children pay more attention to sensory concepts, because attention is guided by necessity.

Same objection, § 27.—> “If general maxims were innate, they should appear more clearly in the minds of certain people. I am speaking of infants, idiots, and savages; for of all men, their minds are the least altered and corrupted by custom.”

*Reply.*—I believe we must reason differently. Innate maxims only appear through the attention given to them; but these individuals exert no attention, or they focus it on very different objects. They think of almost nothing except the needs of the body, and it is reasonable that pure and detached thoughts should be the reward of more noble efforts. I would not want so much honor to be paid to barbarism and ignorance.

*11th Obj.*—If there are innate truths, must there not also be innate thoughts?

*Reply.*—Not at all, for thoughts are actions, while truths are habits or dispositions; we know many things that we rarely think about. To say that a truth cannot be in the mind without having thought of it is like saying there cannot be veins in marble before they are discovered there.

Leibniz had already used this comparison of the marble in a passage with which we close this analysis of the chapter; for it is the best summary of his entire doctrine (*Preface to the New Essays, p. 291*): > “If the soul resembled these blank tablets (<term>tabula rasa</term>), truths would be in us as the figure of Hercules is in a block of marble when the marble is completely indifferent to receiving this figure or some other. But if there were veins in the stone which indicated the figure of Hercules in preference to other figures, this stone would be more inclined to it, and Hercules would be innate in it in some way, although it would be necessary to work to discover the veins and to clean and polish them by cutting away what prevents them from appearing. It is in this way that ideas and truths are innate in us—as inclinations, dispositions, habits, or natural capacities, and not as actions.”

—Prof. PAUL JANET, *New Essays, Book I*, Paris, 1886.

<summary>This page concludes the defense of innate ideas by arguing that truths exist as internal dispositions rather than constant active thoughts. Leibniz uses the metaphor of a block of veined marble to illustrate how the mind is predisposed to certain truths, even if effort is required to uncover them.</summary>
